# Open work

State carried across context compaction. Ordered queue, the decisions already
taken, the findings that motivated them, and the two designs in flight
(module removal, user-code exemption). Update this file when the queue moves.

## IDLE-TIME ARENA GROOMING: A GROWTH RATCHET

Felten and Ott's argument (collect at idle so the active path never pays) is
applied here as a growth ratchet, NOT as a reclaimer. In the select park loop
(`chanSelect`'s wait loop) the domain hands back the unused tail of its root
arena and active frame arena, one page at a time with the select arms re-checked
between pages (`idleTrimPages`, `arenaTrimTail`, `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)`). The
bump offset is not moved, so the next allocation reuses the released range.

The purpose is to stop the committed set ratcheting upward across idle turns: a
burst leaves the tail mapped, the idle pass hands it back, and the next burst
reuses those pages instead of the arena claiming new ones. It does not reduce
RSS of live data and is not supposed to - pages carrying live objects are never
touched. Measured: a 40 MB slice touched, then a parked select, holds resident
`VmRSS` flat; the 24 MB of the 64 MB chain region past the bump offset was never
resident (`/proc/self/statm` field 1 is VmSize, not RSS - field 2 is resident).
That is the expected result for a ratchet, not a failure.

The worst case for a message arriving during the idle pass is one page of delay,
which is why the arm re-check sits inside the page loop. Arenas over
`arenaPoolMaxBytes` are unmapped at return and the pool holds <=512 KB of 64 KB
arenas, so the tail the ratchet actually hands back is the live root/frame arena
slack.

## ROUND 384: OFFSET-FRAME PROTOTYPE AND COMPILER MEMORY

### Compiler memory (measured, not changed)

Cold build of the http_header_api fixture with mxc-s32: resident steady at
~1.6GB, root arena 1355MB over 19 regions. The 4.3GB peak seen earlier was two
compiler processes plus the browser, not one build. `CompileToIR` already frees
each package's compile arena when its object is emitted (the `ci-free` line and
the mapping count dropping prove it). What remains is the ROOT arena: scopes,
type objects, ASTs and export tables for the whole import closure. So "free a
package's arena when its object is emitted" is already true; reducing the peak
means dropping emitted packages' ASTs/type scopes (safe only where generic
bodies are never instantiated later) or compiling in separate processes. Both
are real projects; no code change was made.

### Offset frames (prototype, reverted; diagnosis refined)

The design: a self-contained in-process frame with magic/total/root header, the
value's bytes, then each string/[]byte field's data, and pointer slots holding
uintptr offsets (64-bit native, 32-bit on wasm, where uintptr is the address
integer). Encode is one walk plus a copy; decode is one memcpy into the
receiver's arena plus a rebase of every pointer field. The bare []byte element
worked end to end (encode n=36, size=24, kind=17). The struct case
(`Msg{N int32; Body []byte}`) did not: the field walk found no bytes fields, so
the frame carried only the scalar and the receive produced a zero-length Body
(index panic) or garbage. The walk needs codec.mx's flexible-array pattern
(`nf := int32(st.numField)` + `unsafe.Add(&st.fields[0], i*sizeof(rtStructFieldDesc))`),
and that alone did not make a field appear.

A later pass found the two real causes of the garbage: a named struct's
descriptor must be resolved through `td.Underlying()` before the cast (reading
`st.size`/`st.numField` off the named descriptor returned garbage), and a field
offset is the uvarint inside the field's data blob (`retFieldOffsetAt`), not the
blob's address. With both fixed the encoder is correct: a probe sending
`Msg{N: 7, Body: []byte("hello")}` logs `n=45 N=7 blen=5` from the send side.

The receive side is where it still fails: the worker's receive never enters
`codecFrameDecode` (a print at its entry never fires) and the arm delivers the
zero value, while the same probe on the structural codec prints `msg 7 5 body
104 111`. Reverted to keep the tree green.

Dispatch data (emit-time print in `emitSelectFrame`, later reverted): the
worker's select receive arm is `type=main.Msg tag=named underlying=struct{N
int32; Body []byte} reloc=yes`, so the arm DOES carry the structural descriptor
and the named/parameter-tag hypothesis is ruled out at that site; the direct
send is emitted by a different function and is not printed. A two-message probe
(chan Msg{:2}, send N=7 "hello" and N=9 "world") receives both as N=0 len=0
with the offset codec, and as N=7 / N=9 with the structural codec, so the
failure is in the frame path, not in the channel's element stride - no
consumption bug is visible. The next instrumentation is `tryPipeRecv`: print
`rok`, `len(data)` and `ringIsClosed` on both paths; the zero arm looks like the
`recvZero` branch taken when the ring reports closed/empty. The durable fixes
from this round stay: resolve a named descriptor with `Underlying()`, read field
offsets through `retFieldOffsetAt`, and assert the descriptor kind loudly
(`offsetStruct`/`offsetBytes`) rather than reading garbage.

Filed separately: `println` from a spawned domain is silently dropped (native),
and on wasm worker output needs a channel to the main page script anyway. That
makes every domain-level diagnostic invisible and is its own bug.

The recv-dispatch test to add when the frame path is fixed: a spawn target with
`chan Msg` that sends two messages and asserts both arrive with their bytes; it
must fail if the recv path bypasses `codecFrameDecode`.

### The 2x2 matrix (round 384, done)

    structural + select recv : works  (N=7, N=9)
    structural + direct recv : works  (N=7, N=9)
    offset     + select recv : zeros
    offset     + direct recv : zeros

So endpoint resolution is innocent for the select arm - the same channel and the
same endpoints work with the structural codec - and the failure follows the
FRAME, not the arm. The plumbing counters that were shipped to main showed the
worker calling tryPipeRecv once with `lastLen=8`, but that is the entry's
`<-closed` arm check, not the payload: tryPipeRecv is the select path, while a
direct receive goes through PipeChanRecv. The counters therefore measured the
wrong receive; the next instrumentation belongs in PipeChanRecv/ringRecv, and
the worker must ship its numbers over a channel because runtime prints are lost
in a spawned domain.

Practical lesson: a 45-byte offset frame fails while a 14-byte structural frame
succeeds on the same ring and depth. The next question is whether ringSend
accepted 45 bytes at all (PipeChanSend counts the send before its budget and
space checks), so print `ringSend`'s return and the ring's `writeIdx`/`readIdx`
on both sides.

Entry counters shipped from the worker changed the picture again: on the
STRUCTURAL direct-recv cell the values arrive correctly while
`recvStruct=0` and `codecFrameDecode` frames-seen `=0`. So the working receive
never touches `PipeChanRecvStructural` or the frame decoder at all - the direct
receive for a `chan Msg` element is emitted through a different entry (the
codec-interface or extent dispatch), and the structural cell only proves that
entry works. The offset cells fail because the offset frame is written by
`PipeChanSendStructural`, which the other receive entry does not read back the
same way. Next: identify the receive function the compiler actually emits for
the direct case (grep the emitted IR for the recv call) and route the offset
frame through the same send/receive pair instead of the structural one.

The endianness point is the reason both formats exist: the offset frame is a
memory copy and therefore host-endian, while the wire codec is one fixed
little-endian format for pipes and sockets. Same walk, different byte order and
a formal parse only on the wire side.

## ROUND 383: STDLIB NAMED TYPES, POP FORMS, IDLE GROWTH RATCHET

- net.IP, net.IPMask, net.HardwareAddr are named slice types with methods
  (String, To4, To16, Equal, Is*, ApplyMask, DefaultMask, AppendText,
  MarshalText, UnmarshalText; Size/String on IPMask) and every call site uses
  the method form.
- image.Palette is a named []color.Color with Len/Index/Convert value receivers;
  Config.ColorModel carries a Palette value, the Element struct wrapper is gone.
- http.Header, url.Values and textproto.MIMEHeader are named map types with
  their Add/Set/Get/Values/Del/Write/WriteSubset/Clone/Has/Encode methods.
  Verified with a probe on both compilers (header values ok) and the chanpool
  uintptr-to-pointer conversion fixed to unsafe.Pointer on the way.
- pop statement forms: pop(s) removes the last element, pop(s, xs...) removes
  len(xs); expression pop returns the element without shrinking. Pinned by
  slice_pop_forms.mx on both compilers.
- Idle arena grooming restored as a growth ratchet: the select park loop hands
  back the unused arena tail a page at a time, re-checking the arms between
  pages, so a resumed burst reuses released pages instead of claiming new ones.

### Open: unsigned constant underflow in DECLARATIONS

The runtime-expression form is now rejected: `x := uint64(0) - 1` fails with
"constant 18446744073709551615 overflows uint64" (ssa_builder's constant-fold
range check). The DECLARATION form still wraps: `const c = uint64(0) - 1` and
`const c uint64 = 0 - 1` compile and print the wrapped maximum. Diagnosis:
declared constants are applied through ConvertConstLocal in the typecheck-only
pass, whose compile errors are dropped by design; reportConstOverflow's table is
read at the START of CompileToIR, before that pass records the message, so the
table never carries it for the package being compiled. The fix is to surface the
declaration-pass const errors at the point they are recorded (or fold constant
conversions in tcEvalConstExpr so the existing binary check sees a typed
operand). No fixture ships until the rejection is real.

## ROUND 382: VALUE RECEIVERS OVER NAMED SLICES/MAPS, COMPACTION AT SELECT

- A value receiver over a named slice/map is a REFERENCE receiver in both
  compilers: stage4 binds the receiver variable to the caller's address and
  takes it at the call site; legacy rewrites the method to a pointer receiver
  with `(*name)` uses, using the first type-check's object info so shadowing is
  exact. Struct value receivers remain a compile error.
- `chanSelect` drains the sovereign compaction queue (one group per select), so
  every event loop compacts when idle; a group whose arena is borrowed or
  registered stable is rotated, never moved under a live frame. `SovDrainCompactions`
  now also refuses a group whose data arena appears in the stable-arena stack.
- `push` semantics are documented as they are implemented: nil/zero-cap first
  push -> max(n,4), overflow doubles, garbage is reclaimed by the arena; the
  only fixed-length panic is external storage (cap reads -1).
- Verified on mxc-s25: targeted units 20/20 (named_*, reject_unexported*,
  arena_deep_nest, sovereign_arena, sovereign_map_store, chan/select/spawn
  fixtures); phase 2 selfhost+fixpoint PASS (180 s); the extended
  named_types_methods fixture (both receiver spellings, interface String,
  growth) passes native on both compilers and in Chromium via
  tests/wasm/validate.sh.
- The full 0a/0b sweep was started and then stopped: 190 units recompiling in
  parallel saturated the 8-core box (load 8.5, swap already at 4 GB from
  earlier builds) alongside the browser. Targeted serial runs are the rule.

## ROUND 381: NAMED TYPES OVER SLICES AND MAPS ARE ALLOWED

The ban is gone. A type name over a slice or map is a normal Moxie type with a
method set, and the methods use pointer receivers like every other Moxie
method. That is the whole of the semantics change: `func (n *Names) Add(s
string) { *n = push(*n, s) }` writes the caller's variable, and
`(*c)[k] = v` writes the caller's map. Go's value-receiver copy - element
writes survive, a receiver rebinding does not - cannot occur because value
receivers remain a compile error for every type. Mutation through a
pointer-receiver method is therefore persistent by construction.

Both compilers had to change, and both had latent bugs that only a named type
over a slice or map could reach:

- legacy: the patched `Identical`/`unify` treated ANY byte slice as identical
  to string, so `K(x)` over a named byte slice was a no-op and the value was
  boxed under the []byte type code; every `i.(K)` then failed. Identity is now
  limited to the UNNAMED []byte. The vendored SSA `moxieNormalize` had the
  same hole through `Underlying()`; a named type is now left alone.
- stage4: `collectMethodsDepth`/`hasMethodNamed` substituted the string method
  set for a named byte slice (the name's own methods vanished); the
  substitution is now only for unnamed text types. `runtimeKindOf` emitted
  KindSlice for a named []byte, but the descriptor for []byte is `basic:bytes`;
  the return codec then read an element descriptor from a two-field bytes
  descriptor and crashed in `RawType.Size`. Named []byte is KindBytes.
- stage4: `isForeignNamed` compared against the package the SSA function is
  EMITTED into; a monomorphized generic body is placed in the caller's package
  while its source belongs to the declaring package, so the fips140/ecdh
  generic constructors were told they were naming a foreign package's
  unexported fields. The builder now carries `srcPkgPath`.
- both: the restriction tests that pinned the ban are removed
  (`legacy/tests/restrict/fail_named_slice.mx`, `fail_named_map.mx`, the
  phase-6 `namedslice` fixture, `tests/data/namedslice`).

Named types restored in the stdlib where the wrapper was only there for the
ban: `crypto/ed25519.PublicKey`/`PrivateKey`, `asn1.ObjectIdentifier`,
`asn1.RawContent`, `net.Buffers`, `bidi.bracketPairs` (and the sort.Interface
type it was hiding). Still worth converting when touched, in value order:
`net.IP`/`IPMask`/`HardwareAddr` and `net/http.Header`, `net/url.Values`,
`net/textproto.MIMEHeader` (all aliases with free functions; converting them
restores methods and removes the free-function layer at ~180 call sites), and
`image.Palette` (its `&image.Palette{Element: ...}` construction sites need an
addressable value first). The rest are internal one-field wrappers
(dnsmessage's resource types, dwarf's valBytes/valStr, ...) and can follow
when their package is next opened.

The wasm-specific gaps are closed. Five fixtures legacy could not compile are

ONE PENDING CODE ITEM

`untyped_unsigned_float` - DECIDED: constant overflow is a compile error. The
fixture's wrap assertion is gone. The detection is implemented
(EvalBinaryChecked, the unsigned mark on every unsigned conversion,
tcResolveNameInline resolving predeclared type names, a persistent error table
that survives the typecheck-only pass), but it never runs: stage4 emits
`uint64(0)-1` as RUNTIME arithmetic. Measured with a debug print on the
unsigned-subtract branch: never reached; the built program prints
18446744073709551615. Rejecting it needs expression-level constant folding in
the checker (a feature, not wiring). Then the restriction test can be added:
`// expected: constant subtraction underflows its unsigned type`.

### 1. Legacy wasm: a named residual set, not a wall

`runtimePanic` no longer sends or closes anything: it prints and aborts, and

- runtime: `spawnBreakerMake` and `SigintChan` make an empty-struct breaker

### 3. The `closed` marker - CLOSED, no rename

The export marker is now `(closed)`, not `closed` (writer `main.mx:4491`,
reader `:5068`), so it is not an identifier at all. The collision was already
unreachable: an unexported `func closed` never enters export data, and a
package-level `closed` cannot coexist with a target whose result is `closed` -
the result shadows it and the compiler rejects the package (`Worker: 'closed'
shadows declaration in enclosing scope`, measured with a scratch fixture and
reverted). No identifier was reserved and nothing was renamed.

### 4. `DispatchSpawned` - CLOSED

The pool's two shared addresses travel as spawn arguments (option b): the shell
passes `uintptr` of the slot ring and of the routing table, the worker installs
them in its own TLS before its first receive. Package globals are still
thread-local and the child reads no parent-written global.

Evidence: `./netsmoke-server 127.0.0.1:39177 spawned`, one request, response
`hello path=/smoke` (the same request panicked `chanpool: slot window out of
range` before).

### 5. `ChanServeTimeout` breakers - CLOSED

`chanPool.breakers` keeps every handle `spawn` returned; `closeBreakers()` runs
on the listen failure and on every `serveNextConn` error return, so a return

### 7. Dispatch arms enumerated by method name only - CLOSED

Root cause: `emitInvoke` emitted one arm for every type in the link set that had
a method of the invoked NAME and a matching signature - `sockaddr.String()`
carried `http2FrameHeader`, `io/fs.PathError` and every other Stringer in the
program - because `findIfaceImpls` selects by method name and nobody asked
whether the candidate implements the STATIC interface. Legacy's lowering had
always filtered (`satisfiesInterfaces`), so stage4 was the divergent side.

Fix: `implCoversIface` (`ir_iface.mx`) keeps a candidate only when every other

The panic gate the queue asked for exposed that wasm spawn had never worked:

for its own children. All five are fixed: `WasmSpawnInit` at the top of

1. **Arrays are banned, and most of the tree still has them.** The first batch

   packages and 2 (stage2 == stage3) were green on that batch; phase 6's only
   red unit was `regexp:table`, whose fixture used `copy(nb[:len(b)], b)` - the
   rule working as intended, fixed in `013facfb` and phase 6 then passed 2/2.
   The rule itself is settled: Go had two forms because one was stack and one
   was heap; Moxie has only arenas, so a slice is the type and `resize`/`push`/
   `pop` manage its length. A write through a subslice is rejected in both
   compilers (`ab7a7e82`), and so is `copy` into one (`7f416af4`) - the same
   insight: subslicing is always a copy, so the fix is always resize/push.
   Measured on this tree: **1175 array
   type occurrences in 285 files**, by top-level package:
   `crypto 420`, `vendor 219`, `syscall 166`, `internal 137`, `math 94`,
   `net 75`, `runtime 53`, `image 31`, `compress`, `encoding`, `debug`, `hash`,
   `strconv`, `fmt`, `bytes` below that.
   Clusters, in the order they are safe to take:
   - value buffers filled through `buf[:]` (fmt's `tmp`, base64's `dbuf`,
     ascii85's `buf`/`out`, zstd's `scratch`, profile/proto's `tmp`,
     moxie/codec's `b`, base58's `cksum`): each converts with its fill idiom
     rewritten to `copy(buf, src)` or a cursor write. Small, independent.
   - crypto's fixed tables and hash states (`[256]uint32`, `[8]uint32`,
     `[32]byte`): a table becomes a slice assigned in the package's one init()
     (package-level vars may not have initializers), and a state becomes a
     slice whose length is part of the contract. Large but mechanical.
   - `syscall`'s ABI structs and `*[2]Timeval` / `*[2]_C_int` cast targets:
     this one needs a decision before code - a []T's data pointer is what the
     kernel wants, so the `//sys` marshalling has to pass that rather than a
     pointer to a fixed-size object. Not a mechanical conversion.
   - `runtime`'s `len(*[128]uint16)` / `len(*[512]pollDesc)` shapes, which the
     compiler's own `len` check must keep accepting while they exist.
   The ban itself (rejecting a fixed-size array type in user code) lands LAST,
   with a restrictions fixture and the fixtures that use arrays
   (`array_elem_addr`, `addr_of_composite_lit`, `generic_type_method`,

receiver, so `Paletted.ColorModel` returns `&p.Palette` and `color.Model` is
satisfied again. All 118 `.Palette` sites in image, draw, gif and png gained
`.Element`; gif's ColorModel assertion is now `*image.Palette` and its two
`image.Config` constructions wrap the table; png's palette truncation and growth
use `resize`, which keeps capacity a subslice copy would have dropped. Verified:
an image probe exercises RGBA Set/At, NewPaletted, Paletted
Set/At/ColorIndexAt/Opaque/SubImage and Convert/Index/Len through the interface.

Two compiler defects fell out of making `image` build, both fixed and bilaterally
verified (`1af32054`, `6a3961ad`):

  * a METHOD EXPRESSION `(*T).M` evaluated to a nil function value, silently.
    flate stores its dispatch that way (`d.step = (*compressor).deflate`), so the
    first time flate ran, `d.step(d)` called through nil and the process died
    with SIGSEGV. Nothing had ever compiled flate, so nothing had reached it.
    `tests/regressions/should_compile/method_expression.mx` calls the value in
    both compilers.
  * `resize(xs, n)` coerced `n` to the slice's ELEMENT type, which on a
    `[]color.Color` boxed the length into an interface and made clang reject
    `sext {i64, ptr} to i64`. Push-only now.

What is still broken, measured with the compiled packages rather than guessed:

  * `png.Encode` produces a stream whose one IDAT chunk is 6 bytes: the two-byte
    zlib header plus the four-byte adler32, with all 50 compressed bytes missing.
    flate's close path reports writing them to its `io.Writer` with no error
    (`hbw write: len 50 n 50`), and the bufio that png flushes then holds only 6,
    so those bytes land in a DIFFERENT OBJECT from the one png flushes. flate and
    zlib used directly are correct - `flate` at default and level 0 matches Go's
    byte for byte on a 10 KB buffer, and `zlib` likewise through a bufio.
    The field counts are the tell: the header and the adler go through zlib's own
    `z.w` (its count ends at 6) while the compressed block goes through flate's
    `dictWriter`, so one of the two holds a copy rather than the same pointer.
    MECHANISM, confirmed by the byte at offset 2: the two objects share one
    buffer array but have separate length counters. png's `e.bw` wrote the
    two-byte header (its count 2) and, at close, the four-byte adler (its count
    6); flate wrote its 50 compressed bytes through a SECOND copy of the same
    bufio.Writer struct (its count 52) into the SAME array, so png's flush of
    buf[0:6] emits the header followed by the adler written OVER the first four
    compressed bytes. The IDAT payload is literally `78 9c` + the adler.
    The copies are the codec's stack rule in action: `bufio.NewWriterSize`
    returns a pointer to a composite literal, `codecIsStableAddr` reports stack
    memory unstable ("frames are reclaimed on return but are not arenas"), so a
    return-value relocation that reaches that pointer terminates in a copy. Each
    boundary - `zlib.NewWriterLevelDict` returning `*Writer`, then
    `flate.NewWriterDict` returning `*Writer` - can add one. The fix is on the
    compiler side: a composite literal whose address is RETURNED must be
    arena-allocated (the escape marking `markAddrEscaping` already implements for
    `&`), so that identity survives the relocation. The check that proves it:
    print the bufio's address and its `n` on both sides of
    `zlib.NewWriterLevelDict` and `flate.NewWriterDict`.
  * `flate` level 1 (BestSpeed, `deflatefast`) crashes with SIGSEGV. Levels
    -1/0/6/9 are fine.
  * `image/gif` is FIXED (`6f6d0532`): its encoder only asked for the palette as
    a `*image.Palette` and wrote the global table. An 8x6 paletted image encodes
    to 51 bytes, decodes back to the same indices, and Go 1.25's decoder sees
    every index; the LZW stream is not byte-identical to Go's, which is legal.
  * A cheaper lead for both: boxing a VALUE whose methods have pointer receivers
    into an interface COMPILES and mutates a copy (`takeIface(*bw)` where bw is a
    *bufio.Writer leaves `bw.Buffered()` at 0). That should be a compile error,
    and it is the shape that produces "wrote into a copy" symptoms.

`sig`, `bbig`, `bcache` and the rest of `src/crypto/internal/boring` are the

### Three crypto defects found by making the boring-free paths run

`790817fe` deletes the boringcrypto integration: `boring.Enabled` was constantly
false, so every branch was dead and the whole of `crypto/internal/boring` (C
headers, build scripts, syso, bbig, bcache, sig, the notboring twin) was a stub
that could never run. The `ecdsa`/`rsa` boring halves were build-tagged and never
compiled at all. What remains is the code that actually runs, and running it
found three defects that no gate had ever reached:

  * `094a2159` - `math/rand/v2`'s global Rand was built lazily inside
    `initGlobalRand` and stored into a package global. That store is not
    relocated into the root arena, so the Rand lived in the function's frame:
    the first `rand.Uint64()` worked and the SECOND aborted with "interface
    dispatch: no impl for Uint64". Through `randutil.MaybeReadByte` this is why
    `crypto/rsa` and `crypto/ecdsa` died before doing any work, and why a second
    `crypto/ecdh` key generation failed. It is the same rule the hash batch
    found for crc64: a package global may only be written in init().
  * `a577f4b3` - `ecdh.P256()` returned a fresh `&nistCurve` per call while
    `PrivateKey.ECDH` compares the Curve interface, so every key was its own
    curve and every exchange failed with "curves do not match". The three
    curves are singletons built in init() now.
  * P-256 ARITHMETIC IS FIXED (`7ebc8281`): `_p256B`, the curve constant b, was
    built by a lazy `initP256B` into a package global - the same frame-lifetime
    bug as crc64 and rand/v2, and it has the signature shape a bad b hides:
    adding the identity stayed correct (every b term is multiplied by Z1, zero
    for the identity) while Add(G,G), Double(G) and ScalarMult(G,2) were all
    wrong. With b built in the package init(), Add, Double and ScalarMult match
    Go's elliptic.P256 for every bit and for k = 1..32.
    ScalarBaseMult's precomputed affine-table walk is still wrong for every
    scalar whose Booth digit is negative: it agrees with Go for k = 1..31 and
    diverges from 32 on, 32 being the first scalar whose last-window digit is 32
    with sign 1. Its inputs were verified rather than assumed - all 43 tables'
    32 points equal n * 2^(6*table) * G entry by entry, and fiat's Add, Sub,
    Mul, Square and Select each satisfy their own vectors - so the fault is in
    the walk itself. ScalarBaseMult now computes scalar*G through the generic
    ScalarMult and matches Go for k = 1..40; the walk is the open item, with the
    failing boundary as the test vector.
  * INTERFACE DISPATCH IS THE NEXT COMPILER ITEM, and it is now blocking crypto
    verification rather than one odd path. Three measured instances, all the
    same shape - an interface whose dynamic type is not among the registered
    implementation arms, so the runtime aborts with "interface dispatch: no impl
    for X (N impl(s), none matches)":
      - `Params`, 6 impls, from `ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), ...)`;
      - `Uint64`, 22 impls, from math/rand/v2's global source (fixed by building
        it in init, but the abort is the same mechanism);
      - `Read`, 34 impls, from `ecdh.P256().GenerateKey(rand.Reader())` in one
        link set, while a neighbouring link set instead answers "invalid scalar
        length" from the same call.
    The arms are emitted per link set (`prepareDispatchIndex`, the cache key
    carries `linkSetKey`), and a *missing* arm is a dispatch-table bug, not a
    type bug: the count shows implementations registered and the lookup still
    failing to match. That is the thing to chase before ECDH, ECDSA or TLS can
    be called verified.
  * STILL OPEN: `rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader(), 1024)` never returns (240s
    timeout, no output) inside `crypto/internal/fips140/rsa`'s prime
    generation, which this tree did not touch. 512-bit keys are rejected by the
    minimum-size policy before that. No gate has ever generated an RSA key.

### The image cluster cannot build at all, and why

`src/image` does not compile in EITHER compiler today:

    image.mx:1170: cannot use p.Palette (variable of type []color.Color) as
    color.Model value in return statement: []color.Color does not implement
    color.Model (missing method Convert)

`Paletted.Palette` used to be a `color.Palette`, a named slice type with a
`Convert` method. The named-slice-type ban removed the type and flattened every
palette in the tree to `[]color.Color`, which cannot implement `color.Model` -
so `ColorModel`, `draw`, `gif`, `png` and `jpeg` are all unbuildable, and have
been since the ban landed. Nothing noticed because no gate's closure imports
`image`.

The fix is a `Palette` that is not a named slice: a struct holding
`[]color.Color` with `Convert`, `Index` and `Len`, plus the 118 `Palette` sites
across `src/image/*` (image, draw, gif, jpeg, png). That is a batch of its own,
and the png conversion of `cr [nFilter][]uint8`, the chunk header/footer fields
and the filter rows waits behind it. A png conversion was started and reverted
when this surfaced; the details worth keeping: `e.header[:4]` works only because
`header` is an array today, so a slice conversion must build the chunk header
and trailer with cursor writes, and `cdatK := cr[K][1:]` must become direct
`cr[K][1+i]` indexing because a subslice is a copy.

### A fmt defect found while verifying chacha8

`fmt.Printf("%d", byte(165))` prints `?` in stage4 and `165` in legacy, and
`%x` of the same byte prints `313635` in stage4 (the hex of the decimal string)
and `a5` in legacy. `%v` and `%s` print `165` in both. So the integer verbs on a
`byte` are wrong in both compilers, differently, and the chacha verification had
to cast to int32 to print. Unfixed; it belongs with the fmt/format work, not
with the array queue.

**A compiler bug the math batch measured.** `return 1` from a function whose
result is float64 returned 0 in stage4 while legacy returned 1: buildReturn
checked assignability and boxed interfaces but never ran the numeric coercion
coerceStored runs for an assignment, so the operand stayed an integer where the
caller read a double. math.Tanh was the visible victim - its two saturated
branches are the only ones returning a bare constant, so tanh(1) was right and
tanh(100) was 0. `d12629d8` converts; the fixture is
`tests/regressions/should_compile/untyped_const_return.mx`, and it covers the
switch-case, named-result, negative-constant and float-literal spellings too.

**The rule the hash batch produced.** A slice-valued package global may only be
written from `init()`. Outside `init()` a global store is rejected in user code,
and in a toolchain package - where the restriction does not apply - the store is
NOT relocated into the root arena: the value stays in the writer's frame, and the
next allocation that reuses that frame position overwrites it. Measured on
crc64's lazy `initSlicing8TablesOnce`: `slicing8Tables.ISO = makeSlicingBy8Table(...)`
read back as 8 rows of 256 words immediately after the store, then as 8 rows of
ZERO words after the calling program allocated a 2100-byte buffer, and the
slicing-by-8 CRC came out `b76fff4b8abddbc0` instead of `b02b5db55d155fb7`. Both
compilers reproduced it, which places it in the shared model, not in one emitter.
Building both table sets in `init()` makes the tables root-arena data by
construction, and both compilers then agree with the reference.

So the migration pattern for a package-level table is `init()`, not a lazy
once-guard. Tables that hang off an instance (crc32's, des's feistel box) are
fine built in the constructor: a receiver's fields are relocated, a global's are
not.

**Census at this point:** 1470 array-type occurrences in 285 files (counting
`[N]T` type spellings, not index expressions), led by `syscall` 165, `vendor` 97,
`internal/chacha8rand` 82, `crypto/internal/fips140/nistec` 61, `math` 59,
`runtime` 53, `image/png` 50, `crypto/secp256k1` 43, `nistec/fiat` 40,
`net/http` 39, `x/net/idna` 36, `edwards25519` 33. Still queued, in the order
they are safe to take: crypto/tls's ticket key, `syscall` (needs the codegen
decision: a `[]T` data pointer is what the kernel wants), the pointer-pun
clusters (`edwards25519`, `keccakf`'s `*[200]byte`, the syscall ABI
`*[2]Timeval`), `runtime`'s `len(*[N]T)` shapes, then `math`, `net`, `image`,
`compress`, `encoding`, `vendor`, and the ban itself last with its fixtures.

2. **The user-code exemption declaration**, motivated by `src/syscall/js`: its
   `Value` methods use value receivers because the API is a chain of
   temporaries, and converting them breaks `js.Global().Get("x").Call(...)`.
   They compile only because `src/` is exempt wholesale. The decision you gave:
   eliminate the value receivers - JavaScript has no pointers, so a pointer
   receiver crossing into JS resolves to a copy, a fixed one-to-one translation
   (strings keep their existing pragma because JS really does distinguish them).
   That is a change in `src/syscall/js` plus the jsruntime bridge, not a
   language change.

Also verified while closing the previous round, so it is not open: a store past
a slice's LENGTH panics in both compilers even when capacity allows (probe:
`ys := xs[:2]` with cap 8, `ys[4] = 1` -> index out of range in stage4 and in
legacy), and x/net/idna's tables parse.

### The js bridge: mutators are package functions, and its state is one object  [CLOSED]

**Decision.** `Set`, `Delete`, `SetIndex` and `Release` are package functions whose
first argument is the handle - `js.Set(v, p, x)`, `js.Delete(v, p)`,
`js.SetIndex(v, i, x)`, `js.Release(f)` - and the four value-receiver methods are
gone. Setting a JavaScript property is a JavaScript-side mutation; `Value` is an
immutable handle, so the receiver is the wrong shape for it. A pointer receiver
was rejected because the dominant spelling is a chain - `js.Global().Get("x")` -
which is not addressable, and converting call sites to temporaries would be the
same rename with more lines. A checked exception was rejected because the package
is inside the toolchain tree, where the restrictions are exempt by design, so an
"exception" there would be unenforceable theatre; package functions satisfy the
rule instead of excusing it. 18 call sites migrated (14 in
`src/net/http/roundtrip_js.mx`, 4 inside `syscall/js`), including the two
non-addressable chain shapes.

**Globals audit** (`syscall/js`):

    init-only, package-level   the predefined handles (valueUndefined..jsGo), the
                               Object and Array constructors. jsInit writes each
                               exactly once, before any use; nothing writes them
                               again. They stay package variables because that is
                               what they are - moving them into a mutable object
                               would claim they change.
    runtime-mutable, in `br`   br.funcs, br.nextFuncID (FuncOf and Release change
                               them), br.ready, br.eventHandlerSet (idempotent
                               init flags, written once on first use). One object,
                               one name, so the package's mutable state has a
                               shape and a place.
    lazy write-once exception  net/http's _uint8Array*, _jsFetchMissing* and
                               _jsFetchDisabled* cache a JavaScript handle or a
                               fact read from the global object, which does not
                               exist at Go init time - the module is instantiated
                               first. Documented at the declarations in
                               `roundtrip_js.mx`, and they never change after the
                               first read.

The remaining value receivers in `syscall/js` (`Equal`, `Type`, `Get`, `Index`,
`Call`, `Invoke`, `New`, the conversion and predicate methods) are read-only
accessors on an uncomparable handle: they do not write the receiver and are not
what this item was about.

**Pin:** `tests/wasmfixtures/jsbridge` is compiled by phase 1c and exercises every
mutator, including `js.Set(js.Global().Get("Object").New(), ...)` and
`js.SetIndex(js.Global().Get("Array").New(), ...)`.

### dnsmessage: `Name.Data` is a slice, and the trap class is measured  [CLOSED]

**The change.** `Name` is `{ Data []byte; Length uint8 }`. `NewName` allocates
exactly its length and copies; `unpack` sizes the storage (`[]byte{:255}`) before
the first write and then writes by index, so the write never goes through a
subslice; `pack` refuses a `Length` larger than the storage with `errCalcLen`
instead of indexing past it, and `String` clamps for the same invalid value so a
malformed name prints empty rather than panicking. The root literal is
`Name{Data: []byte{'.'}, Length: 1}`. The maximum encoded name (254 bytes) and
the 63-byte label limit are unchanged.

**Comparability fallout: none.** A slice makes `Name` non-comparable and with it
`Question`, `Resource` and `Message`; the tree has no `==`/`!=` on any of them and
no map keyed by one. The one name comparison, `net.equalASCIIName`, is already
field-by-field (Length plus a case-folded data walk).

**The trap scan, measured rather than assumed.** The class is "a subslice of a
struct field is a copy, so a write through it is lost":

  * `unpack`'s old `name := n.Data[:0]` plus `push` was the real failure, and it
    was specific to `Data` being an ARRAY field: `n.Data[:0]` on an array copies
    the array, so the appends landed in a copy. With a slice field the same
    spelling would alias again - `unpack` still does not rely on that, it writes
    by index into storage it sized first.
  * The two Go-idiom patch sites - `Builder.Finish`'s
    `b.header.pack(b.msg[b.start:b.start])` and `ResourceHeader.fixLen`'s
    `packUint16(msg[lenOff:lenOff], ...)` - are NOT live instances. Measured:
    a zero-length subslice handed to a push-based callee keeps the parent's
    backing array, and a built message round trips with header ID 0x4321,
    QDCOUNT 1, RDLENGTH 4 and A body 192.0.2.1 both with and without a
    by-index rewrite of those two sites. The rewrites were reverted rather than
    kept: they changed code that is correct, and the fixture now pins the
    behavior instead.
  * Across `src`, the remaining `[:0]` uses (`encoding/csv`, `encoding/asn1`)
    assign the result back to the field they truncated, which is the reset
    idiom, not the trap. `fixLen`'s `^uint16(0)` spelling stays 65535 spelled
    out, per the constant-fold fix recorded earlier.

**Pins:** `tests/regressions/should_compile/dns_name_roundtrip.mx` runs, in one
program: plain (`example.com.`), root (`.`), a 63-byte label, the 254-byte
maximum, a 64-byte label (must fail), a non-canonical name (must fail), a `Name`
whose `Length` runs past its storage (pack must fail, String must be empty), a
compression-pointer message built by packing two identical questions, a truncated
name (must fail), and a full `Builder` round trip that checks the header id,
flags, section counts, RDLENGTH and the typed A body. Host and wasm both compile
it; phase 1b and phase 8 are the stdlib and resolver gates.

**Found by the scan, recorded, NOT fixed in this goal:** the compiler accepts a
method called through a function-typed package member. `binary.BigEndian` is a
function (`func BigEndian() *bigEndian`) in this tree, yet
`binary.BigEndian.Uint16(b)` compiles and returns 0 instead of being rejected;
the correct spelling is `binary.BigEndian().Uint16(b)`. That is a silent wrong
answer on an invalid construct and needs its own restriction fixture and
compiler change.

### The transport is the live path only  [CLOSED 3a]

`Transport.RoundTrip` -> `roundTrip` -> `dialAndExchange` is the whole client:
one function dials, writes, reads, materialises the body and closes, because this
domain has no goroutines for a read loop and a write loop to run on. Everything
that existed to pool connections and dial in the background was unreachable from
that path, and is gone: `getConn`, `dialConn`, `dialConnFor`,
`startDialConnForLocked`, `decConnsPerHost`, `queueForDial`, `queueForIdleConn`,
`cancelWantOnError`, `putOrCloseIdleConn`, `tryPutIdleConn`, `removeIdleConn*`,
`dial`, `customDialTLS`, `addTLS`, `writeConnectRequest`, `dialConnWrapErr`,
`readLoop`, `writeLoop`, `readResponse`, `waitForContinue`,
`readLoopPeekFailLocked`, `is408Message`, `handleResponseFor`,
`mapRoundTripError`, `shouldRetryRequest`, `isReused`, `closeConnIfStillIdle`,
`markReused`, `wroteRequest`, `onTimer`, `stopTimer`, `logf`, `resetProxyConfig`,
`maxIdleConnsPerHost`, and the types that only they used (`persistConn`,
`wantConn`, `wantConnQueue`, `connOrError`, `connLRU`, `responseAndError`,
`requestAndChan`, `writeRequest`, `bodyEOFSignal`, `bodyEOFFunc`,
`bodyEarlyCloser`, `readLoopEarlyClose`, `readLoopBodyEOF`, `gzipReader`,
`readWriteCloserBody`, `persistConnWriter`, `proxyAuthHeader`,
`connContinueWaiter`, `handshakeTimerSink`, `erringRoundTripper`,
`tlsHandshakeTimeoutError`), with the `Transport` fields they filled
(`idleConn`, `idleConnWait`, `idleLRU`, `closeIdle`, `connsPerHost`,
`connsPerHostWait`, `dialsInProgress`).

**Reachability proof.** The live path is the three functions above; a call-graph
walk from them (plus the exported API, which must stay) over comment- and
string-stripped bodies leaves every deleted function unreachable, and each of
`getConn`, `dialConn`, `readLoop`, `writeLoop` has no reference outside
`transport.mx` (`grep` across `src/`; the only hits in other files are comments
and the unrelated `h2_bundle` methods of the same name). Two survivors were kept
because other files use them: `cloneTLSConfig` (`server.mx` `ServeTLS`) and
`timeoutError` (`client.mx`), plus `transportReadFromServerError`, which the live
`roundTrip` type-asserts.

**What the public API does now.** `CloseIdleConnections` has nothing to drain: it
still initialises the HTTP/2 transport and closes that one, which is a separate
stack. `Clone`, `RegisterProtocol`, `CancelRequest` and
`prepareTransportCancel` are unchanged in shape; `reqCanceler` is the only
mutable bookkeeping left in the struct, and `altProto` the only other map.

File size: `transport.mx` went from 3196 lines to 1382. The build compiles the
package for host and (phase 1c) for wasm; `tests/netsmoke/muxmatch` still passes
all twelve registration shapes.

### sovGroup pre-fault: measured, no effect, reverted  [CLOSED 3c]

Implemented at the RECYCLE point, not at init or at take: a group reaches the
bounded list of 32 only when it is about to be reused, and at that moment its
slices still describe exactly what was used, so the walk is bounded by the
group's own retained length and a group that is not going to be reused (the list
is full) returns before walking anything. The fault was one read per 4096 bytes
of each retained slice, kept as a blank assignment so it cannot write a retained
record.

Measured with the exact phase-8 no-accumulation sequence (baseline after the
mode's first requests, then 400 exchanges on one connection):

    before (recorded phase 8)      inline 16488 -> 16504 kB (+16)
                                   spawned 5896 -> 5896 kB (+0)
    with the pre-fault             inline 17560 -> 17576 kB (+16)
                                   spawned 6116 -> 6116 kB (+0)

The deltas are identical: the change moved the fault from the request that takes
the group to the request that recycles it, and nothing else, so it was reverted
rather than kept. The absolute baselines differ by ~1MB and ~220kB, which is the
binary changing shape (the transport deletion landed between the two runs), not
the pre-fault; both runs are three orders of magnitude under the 2048kB
threshold.

nothing.

Measured on the fixed driver (`ae421fe8`, "compiler: a field of an instantiated
generic keeps its type in a non-generic method"):

    MOXIEROOT=$PWD GOROOT=/opt/go1.25.3 ./moxie build ./src/net/http
    rc=1 after 1482s, and the only error is the expected
    ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: main.main          (a library target)

Before the compiler fix, the same command with the same direct form failed at
`SSA build` in 145s:

    ; cannot resolve the type of mp in (*routingNode).matchingMethodsPath -
      the right-hand side is not a value
    mxc: compile error for http

The cause was not the field read, and it was not really about net/http. Two
losses met: a generic's type parameters were attached during the per-declaration
Under pass in file order, so `mapping[K,V]` (declared in `mapping.mx` above
`entry[K,V]`, which its slice field names) recorded its element with TArgs but no
TParams; and the shallow instantiated copy made where the field was named kept
Under nil, because the declaration's body did not exist yet, so the substituted
struct lowered to its generic body (`{i8,i8}`) while the value stored was the
substituted `{string,*node}`. Both are fixed as general rules: declaration order
no longer decides whether a type keeps its parameters, and a Named's body
resolves through its declaration object when the copy carries none. No package,
type or function name is special-cased and no TArgs are fabricated.

4. ~~A builtin structural String for structs and named func types~~ -
   implemented: a declared String() always wins, a user-code struct renders
   `{field:value ...}`, and a named func type renders `func(params) (returns)`.
   fmt/Stringer could not do it (fmt asserts `p.arg.(Stringer)` and has no type
   information, and the runtime descriptor carries struct field names and
   offsets but no func signature text), so both compilers synthesize the method
   as source and parse it: `_mxc_stage4/ir_typecheck.mx injectBuiltinString` and
   `legacy/loader/stringers.go`. A struct body calls `runtime.RenderValue`,
   which walks the descriptor (`src/runtime/type_render.mx`; the numeric text
   moved to the untagged `src/runtime/numfmt.mx` so wasm has it too), and a func
   type body returns its signature text. Pin:
   `tests/regressions/should_compile/builtin_string_render.mx` (struct, %+v,
   direct method call, func type, declared override), which phase 0a and phase 5
   (wasm) both run; both compilers print the same bytes.

   **Scope, measured:** the method is synthesized for USER code only (a package
   outside the toolchain's `src/` and `pkg/` trees). Doing it for every stdlib
   struct was tried first and is unshippable: each type gains a method in its
   mxh and in the Stringer dispatch table, and phase 0a's `http_header_api`
   grew past the compiler's type-check arena (128 regions) before it linked. A
   stdlib type that is printed still needs a declared String() (asn1's
   diagnostic has one) until the builtin method is served from the dispatch
   default instead of a per-type declaration; that is the next step if full
   coverage is wanted.

   **Declared is not the same as used.** An unexported type that its own
   package names exactly once (the declaration) gets no method: unexported
   names are package-local, so such a type can never be placed in a Stringer
   slot. Exported types always get one, because another package can place them
   in a slot this package cannot see. The test is the identifier's mention count
   in the package source (`injectMentioned` in stage4, `mentionCountAtLeast` in
   legacy); a second mention may be a field type or even a comment, which can
   only keep a method, never drop one a slot needs. Measured on a fixture
   declaring `type used` and `type dead` with only `used` constructed: the mxh
   has `method used String ->string 1` and no String line for `dead`.

### Repository boundaries - read this before the queue

Four trees, and relay work goes in exactly one of them:

| tree | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| this checkout | the compiler and its stdlib (`src/`, `_mxc_stage4/`, `legacy/`, `tests/`) |
| `../nostr` | the shared protocol library: events, filters, tags, kind, crypto, `ws`, `lol` |
| `../morly` | **the relay** (`git.smesh.lol/morly`) |
| `../smesh` | **the web app only** (`git.smesh.lol/smesh`) |

The relay was carved out of smesh on 2026-10-01 (`morly b7dba37`, "the relay,
wired to the shared nostr module") and smesh's copy was never deleted. That is
what made item 0's port land on the wrong tree: smesh still had `pkg/`, `main.mx`
and `cmd/`, so on 2026-10-15 the port was done there (`smesh
a86a03e6..0cf58ea3`) and then redone correctly in morly (`morly
169bc7e..642db70`). A session that finds a relay in smesh has found a leftover,
not a second relay.

Fixed, with the evidence that says the removal was safe:

- smesh's relay source is gone (`smesh 3da21297`): `pkg/`, `cmd/`, the three root
  `main*.mx`, `go.mod`, six tracked relay binaries (one of them a file literally
  named `smesh`), `test_old`. The app's own closure is the proof nothing here
  needs them - every entry under `web/` reaches 35 packages, **all** under
  `web/`, plus the moxie stdlib; nothing under `web/` or `test/` imported
  `git.smesh.lol/smesh/pkg`. The vendored `smesh/pkg/nostr` went with it: it was
  a strict subset of `../nostr` (57 files against 73) that only the relay
  packages consumed, so there was nothing to repoint.
- smesh's relay was not ahead of morly. No commit touched `smesh/pkg/` between
  the carve and the port except the port itself, and `morly/pkg` is a superset
  apart from smesh's `lol` (now in `../nostr/pkg/lol`) and the vendored nostr.
- phase 7 no longer builds the relay from the app: it takes
  `MOXIE_RELAY_REPO` (default `../morly`) and stages a **copy** of
  `web/static` in a temp dir before building the bundles, so a green run leaves
  the app checkout untouched (`moxie 8874ca31`). Before that, phase 7 wrote nine
  tracked bundles in place and left smesh dirty on every run.

Done since that audit. The relay's tests now split with the code, and the
coverage doc was rewritten to match: `make test-unit` (26 packages / 370 tests)
and `make test-integration` (31 tests: the ORLY_* env contract, the WebSocket
round-trip, the ingest worker pool, the load driver) run in `../morly/test`,
and `smesh/test` keeps the browser layer - the app flows, the signer, the
worker shims, MLS, the memory profile, the served-app smoke tests, and the
feed round-trip that publishes an event and looks for it in the rendered page.
Three files that were two suites in one (`test_relay_roundtrip`) or named for
the relay they no longer test were renamed accordingly.

The re-measurement is what the item below is about: it cannot be done yet, and
the reason is a compiler defect rather than anything about the doc.

### Compiler: `-cover` attributes every package to the toolchain's prefix  [CLOSED `427bb08d`]

**Fixed.** `coverModPrefix()` returns `bst.rootModPrefix` (the repository the
TARGET lives in) and is used by `coverPkg`, `coverReportFile` and the report's
selection prefix; legacy's `cover.ModulePrefix` derives the same thing from the
layout rules when no module file exists. Verified on an out-of-toolchain tree:
7 sites under `git.smesh.lol/covertest`, and `moxie test -cover` prints
`83.3% 5/6 git.smesh.lol/covertest/lib.mx`. The rest of this section is the
original diagnosis, kept as the record.

`-cover` names a site `<pkg.Path>/<basename>:<line>` via
`coverReportFile(pkgPath, modPath, file)`, and `modPath` is `bst.globalModPrefix`.
`ensureModuleRoot` settles that prefix once per process and **hardcodes the
toolchain's own path**:

```
bst.globalModPrefix = "moxielang.dev"
bst.globalModDir    = root                              // MOXIEROOT
bst.rootModPrefix   = targetImportPath(root, target)     // the TARGET's repo
```

There is no module file to read instead - the no-modules design removed it, and
`loadManifest` sets repository pins, not this prefix. So a `-cover` build of any
tree that is not the toolchain itself misreports:

- **Integration** (`moxie build -cover` of the relay): `coverPkg(path)` accepts
  `main`, `command-line-arguments`, or anything under `globalModPrefix`. The
  relay's packages resolve under `rootModPrefix` (`git.smesh.lol/morly`), which
  is not under the toolchain prefix, so they are **skipped entirely** - not
  instrumented, absent from the site table. `mxcover` then reports
  `no sites under git.smesh.lol/morly`. Measured on morly: 1413 sites, all in
  three toolchain files (`main.mx` 702 - including `main.(*relayCtx)` and
  `main.(*relayDB)`, which are the relay's own root package, accepted because
  its path is literally `main` - plus `mxregexp.mx` and `mxutil.mx`).
- **Unit** (`moxie test -cover ./pkg/store` in morly): the synthetic test
  package's path is one `coverPkg` accepts, so it *does* instrument and the
  numbers are real, but every file is attributed to the toolchain directory:
  `91.8% 661/720 moxielang.dev/engine.mx` is
  `git.smesh.lol/morly/pkg/store/engine.mx`. This also means smesh's pre-carve
  percentages were measured through the same misattribution - the numbers hold,
  the reported paths do not.

Fix: attribute by `rootModPrefix` (the repository the target lives in) instead
of `globalModPrefix` in both `coverPkg` and `coverReportFile`, leaving `main`
and `command-line-arguments` accepted as they are. Both values are already
computed in `ensureModuleRoot`. **Legacy computes the same prefix and must
change in the same commit**; this environment has no Go toolchain, so the
legacy half cannot be built or tested here, which is why this is recorded
rather than half-applied. Repro after the fix: `make cover` in `../morly`
should print a table under `git.smesh.lol/morly`, and
`moxie test -cover ./pkg/store` there should name `pkg/store/engine.mx`.

### Compiler: `^` on a sized unsigned constant loses its type  [CLOSED round 15, `f2e91e56`]

**Fixed.** The two halves are the unary const fold in `_mxc_stage4/ssa_builder.mx`
(an operand's `*Basic` now masks the folded value to its width via
`MaskConstToBasic`) and `MaskConstToBasic` itself in `pkg/types/tc_const.mx` (a
uint64 whose bit pattern is negative is `Unsigned: true`, not just one that was
already marked). `tests/regressions/should_compile/const_xor_width.mx` asserts
all four widths THROUGH a conversion, plus the signed and variable controls.
The legacy compiler needs no mirror and this was checked by reading, not running:
its unary `^` is never folded to a constant (`legacy/compiler/compiler.go`,
`case token.XOR` in the unop path, emits `CreateXor(x, all-ones)` at `x`'s own
LLVM type, so i8 all-ones is already 255), and its constant evaluation is the
vendored Go type checker, which follows Go's rules. The divergence was stage4's
own fold, which turned the operand into a signed `ConstInt` before the width was
applied.

The measurement that motivated it, kept as the record:

Re-measured on this tree (one probe, four widths plus the variable control):

    ^uint8(0)  -> int32 -1      want 255            WRONG
    ^uint16(0) -> int32 -1      want 65535          WRONG
    ^uint32(0) -> uint32 4294967295                 right
    ^uint64(0) -> uint64 18446744073709551615       right
    ^int8(0)   -> int32 -1      want -1             right
    ^z(uint16) -> int32 65535   (z a variable)      right

So the defect is narrower than "the type is lost": the masking of `^` is applied
in the typed-constant path (MaskConstToBasic) but NOT when the same operation is
folded as the ARGUMENT of a conversion, so `int32(^uint8(0))` converts the raw
all-ones (-1) instead of the masked 255. The uint32/uint64 rows above are right
because they were printed without an enclosing conversion; `int32(^uint32(0))`
is the row that would show it for 32 bits and it is untested. Fix belongs where
a conversion folds its argument's constant, in both compilers, and the fixture
must assert all four widths THROUGH a conversion.

### Compiler: `^` on a sized unsigned constant loses its type  [OLD NOTE]

Found by the resolver work below; it is what stopped the Go resolver packing a
single DNS query. `int32(^uint16(0))` evaluates to **-1**, not 65535, while the
same value stored into a `uint16` first is correct:

```
var z uint16
zu := ^z                    // 65535   correct
yc := int32(^uint16(0))     // -1      WRONG, expected 65535
var big uint16 = 65535
yb := int32(big)            // 65535   correct, so the conversion is fine
```

So the constant fold of `^` on a typed constant drops the type and produces the
signed all-ones result; assigning that to a sized variable truncates it back to
the right value, which is why it hides in every spelling except the direct
conversion. Repro is the four lines above; a restriction fixture should assert
`int32(^uint16(0)) == 65535`, and the same shape for uint8/uint32/uint64.

Hit in `src/vendor/golang.org/x/net/dns/dnsmessage`'s `ResourceHeader.fixLen`,
which tested `conLen > int32(^uint16(0))` - i.e. `conLen > -1`, always true, so
every resource was "too long" and `newRequest`'s unconditional EDNS0 OPT record
failed to pack. Worked around there by spelling 65535 out; the compiler defect
is untouched.

### Moxie semantics: a subslice of an array field is a copy  [STDLIB PORT TRAP]

The same DNS work hit this twice, and it is the class the "slices replace
arrays" rule is about. `src/vendor/golang.org/x/net/dns/dnsmessage` still has
`type Name struct { Data [255]byte; Length uint8 }` - an array, which the rule
says should be a slice - and Go code that builds a name with

```
name := n.Data[:0]
name = push(name, ...)
```

writes into the copy that `n.Data[:0]` made, never into the receiver: `Length`
came out right, `Data` came out all zeros, and `checkResponse` rejected every
DNS answer while the query went out and the reply arrived. Measured with a
hand-built response: built name bytes `116 114 117 110 99 46 116 101 115 116 46`
("trunc.test."), parsed name `0 x11`.

Fixed by writing the name into `n.Data` by index, which does reach the receiver.
The array itself is still there and should become a slice; scanning the port for
`Data[:0]`-style accumulation and for `f(x[i:i], ...)` calls that rely on append
writing through the zero-length slice (there is a live one in the same file's
`fixLen`, see the commit that fixed the resolver) is open work.

### The net stack serves, and a registered route is matched  [CLOSED round 15, `0047faea`]

Measured against a running stdlib server (net/http on 127.0.0.1): ListenAndServe
listens, accepts, parses the request, dispatches through the handler chain and
answers a real HTTP response with no crash - the `Accept` dispatch panic and the
four lifetime bugs below it are fixed - but `http.HandleFunc("/", h)` followed
by `GET /smoke` answers `404 page not found`. Registration cannot have failed
silently (`(*ServeMux).register` panics on a bad pattern, and it did not panic),
and the root-arena wrap for registration is in place, so the tree holds the
pattern and the MATCH is what fails. Look at `src/net/http/routing_tree.mx` -
what `parsePattern("/")` produces, the `addSegments`/`set` path, and the subtree
case in `matchOrRedirect` - before touching lifetimes again.

**Round 14: re-run after the leak fix - NOT the same bug, and every shape
misses.** The unchanged repro (register `"/"`, ask the mux for `/smoke`) answers
`pattern=[]`, exactly as before, so the orphaned-group leak was not the mux bug.
A one-build probe of five registration shapes sharpens it a lot:

    exact /smoke           pattern=[]
    exact /smoke, /other   pattern=[]
    subtree /              pattern=[]
    subtree /, /           pattern=[]
    method "GET /"         pattern=[]
    host example.com/      pattern=[]
    pkg HandleFunc /       pattern=[]

An EXACT pattern does not match the same path, and `/` does not match `/`, so
nothing about the "/" subtree, hosts or methods is involved: the lookup is dead
for every shape. Registration's first level survives (`root.emptyChild` exists,
flags=1) and the second level does not, which is a write lost between
`n = n.addChild(p.method)` and the match. The hypothesis this points at: the
first `addChild` allocates the host node INSIDE the receiver's sovereign data
arena (a mutating method's direct allocations go there), the second `addChild`
then mutates a receiver that lives in that arena, and a mutating receiver's field
writes are serialised at return and decoded into the CALLER's arena - so the
write lands on a copy the caller never reads. That is a codegen/receiver
relocation question on the classic path, not a lifetime one; the fix shape is to
stop making tree construction depend on mutating a fresh node's fields (allocate
the child explicitly, assign it in the caller), and it needs its own round.

**Round 15: FIXED, and it was three faults in a row, none of them the tree.**
The receiver-relocation hypothesis was tested first with a standalone fixture (a
mutating method allocates a child in the receiver's own arena and returns a
pointer to it, then the caller mutates through that pointer): it did NOT hold in
isolation - the returned child was the stored child, depth 3, in four shapes
including a package-level tree and a keyed map child. Diagnostics inside
`addPattern` then showed the real tree's first level stored but the returned
child a different node, so the write was lost between the levels. Three faults
in sequence:

  1. `routingNode` is self-mutating, so a composite literal inside its methods
     (`c := &routingNode{}`) lands in the receiver's SOVEREIGN data arena, and
     the codec must not alias sovereign data out of a call (a later compaction
     can move it). The child the caller got back was therefore a COPY of the
     child the tree stored. Fix: `newNode()` allocates tree nodes explicitly in
     the ROOT arena (`runtime.ArenaAlloc(runtime.RootArena(), ...)`); a
     root-arena node is process-lifetime and not sovereign data, so identity is
     kept.
  2. The codec treated the root as a callee's transient top frame whenever the
     root-arena idiom made it current (`SetCurrentArena(RootArena())`), so even
     root pointers were copied. Fix: a pointer into the root is never transient,
     in any encode mode (`codecIsStableArenaAddr`), because the root never dies.
  3. The root-arena idiom only covers values returned DIRECTLY to the frame that
     swapped. Registration was `registerErr` (swaps) -> `registerErrInRoot`
     (works), so the `*pattern` objects were decoded into the intermediate frame
     and died with it; once 1 and 2 stopped hiding it, the first match panicked
     in `pattern.lastSegment` with an empty segment list. Fix: registration is
     ONE function whose body runs under the swap, with explicit restores on every
     return (no defer - deferred calls are unreliable in a loop on this compiler).

Before: all seven registration shapes answered `pattern=[]`. After:

    ok   identity         stored child is the returned child
    ok   exact            GET /smoke -> [/smoke]
    ok   exact-miss       GET /other -> []
    ok   subtree-root     GET /a/b/c -> [/]
    ok   subtree-api      GET /api/v1/x -> [/api/]
    ok   method           HEAD /x -> [GET /x]      (and method-miss POST -> [])
    ok   host             GET /y -> [example.com/y]
    ok   host-method-path POST /z/deep -> [POST example.com/z/deep]
    ok   pkg-default      GET /pkg -> [/pkg]

The fixture is `tests/netsmoke/muxmatch` and it runs as the phase-8 unit
`netsmoke:mux-match`: the smoke server serves through the CHANNEL path, whose
router is a plain table, so this is the only unit that would notice a routing
tree that stores nothing. The `identity` check in it is the regression pin for
fault 2.

`tests/phase8_netsmoke.sh` is the gate that reports this; it is wired into
`tests/unitrun.sh` as phase 8. Its build and listen units pass; the curl and
Moxie-client units assert the handler's body and both fail on the same 404.

**Round 2: it is not the matching logic and not request-time state.** An
instrumented dump of the tree - once at registration, right after
`mux.tree.addPattern(p, h)`, and once on every request - shows the same tree in
both places, and it is empty at the level that matters: the root has its
emptyChild (the host level, `flags=1`), and THAT node has no emptyChild of its
own, so the method level and the pattern under it were never stored. Matching
reads an empty tree, correctly. `rootEmpty=1` at request time also means
nothing was lost later, so the arena hypothesis is dead in this form: the lost
writes are the ones `addPattern` makes through `root.addChild(p.host)` ->
`n.addChild(p.method)` before it returns. A faithful standalone repro (the same
three methods, a `Handler` interface field, a `*pattern` field, the same arena
wrap) keeps the whole chain, so the difference is still unidentified. The next
attempt should bisect INSIDE addPattern (print the levels before it returns)
rather than after, and compare the pointer values it writes with the ones the
caller reads back.

The channel path below does not use this tree at all - its router is a plain
table - which is why phase 8 does not wait on this. One more trigger was
tested and excluded: a faithful repro WITH the generic `mapping[string,
*node]` field (the one structural difference from the package) keeps the chain
intact, so the generic field is not what is lost. What remains is the
difference between the package build and every isolated shape tried; bisecting
inside the real addPattern needs instrumentation, and adding it hit the
compiler's "cannot resolve the type of p in matchingMethodsPath" inference
error, so that instrumentation needs a workaround of its own first. This is
pre-existing classic-path work, not part of the channel rework: the route the
smoke phase serves is the one in `ChanMux`, and it is served.

### The pool transport is a queue-owned ring of preallocated slots  [DONE, round 15]

The pool boundary no longer packs messages into an int32-per-four-bytes stream.
The shell writes the whole request into a preallocated MAP_SHARED slot and sends
the SLOT INDEX; the worker answers in the same slot and sends the index back.

  * `runtime.SharedBuffer(n)` maps MAP_SHARED anonymous memory as a []byte. It
    must be allocated BEFORE the spawn: after fork the child's copy of an
    ordinary arena is private (copy-on-write), so a slot written after the fork
    would be invisible to the worker.
  * one slot per message, one copy at a named site (`chanSlotPutReq` /
    `chanSlotPutResp`); the worker decodes into its request arena, which it
    resets, so the steady state allocates nothing.
  * four slots of 64KB, sized by MEASURED in-flight concurrency and message
    size, not connections times slots: the shell is serial and blocks on the response, so one request
    is in flight (`ring_committed_kb=256` in the fixture's /stats). A frame that
    does not fit panics by name instead of truncating.
  * wasm: SharedBuffer panics by name (no shared mapping to hand out as a slice)
    and the structural channel entries route through the SAB bridge with the same
    cross-domain encode, so the wasm target still links and still carries values
    by value.

Measured, spawned, one connection, 1000 keep-alive requests per round (netsrv29):
rss 15396 -> 17668 -> 17680 -> 17716 kB (rounds 2-3: +12kB, +36kB), vmdata 263344
kB identical, mapped net identical across samples. That closes the +440B/request
slope the int32 stream had, which came from the 32MB-per-direction spawn rings
being touched: an index is four bytes.

The ring is PRE-FAULTED at pool startup (`chanSlotPrefault`: one byte per page)
and it is 4 x 64KB, not 4 x 1MB. Both are measures of the same thing - the ring
is queue-owned, so its resident pages are a startup cost, not a thing the request
stream should pay for - and neither of them was the +2096kB.

**The +2096kB was the pool WORKER's decode arena (fixed in `eeb95850`).** The
worker decoded the slot into the frame arena it inherited from spawn (which lives
for the life of the process) and only put the handler call and the write inside
its request arena, so the inherited arena grew ~615B a request, overflowed its
64kB region at ~200 requests and chained a 64MB overflow region. The official
no-accumulation unit measures the FIRST 400 exchanges of the process, so it saw
exactly that step. A warmed-up loop of the same binary read +0, which is why the
diagnosis took a scope report rather than an RSS pair:

    spawned, server6, one connection      scope 0 live used   request arena   rss_kb
      0 requests                              2608/1408            12576        5896
    200 requests                              2608/1408            12544        6156
    800 requests                              2608/1408            12544        6156
   1600 requests                              2608/1408            12544        6164

The two scope-0 values are sample parity, not growth. The rule the fix applies is
the same one the connection loop already had: one iteration, one arena boundary,
entered before the receive that starts the iteration.

The residual +268kB over 1600 exchanges is the slot ring itself: 4 x 64KB is
256kB, it is MAP_SHARED and pre-faulted by the shell, and the pages the WORKER
writes are charged to the worker's RSS the first time it writes them. That is
bounded by the ring and it is a startup cost paid once, not a rate - the same
reason the ring is pre-faulted rather than discovered by the request stream.

### The channel handler path  [DESIGN, src/net/http/chanpath.mx + chanpool.mx]

Status: the one-call-per-request handler path and its arena envelope are in
(`291a5424`, `b06813b1`, and the round-14 commits below). The retention is
attributed and closed: inline mode is flat over 3x1000 (VmData constant, RSS
+4-12kB a run) and spawned mode has no arena retention - what is left there is
the transport's 32MB-per-direction lazily-faulted spawn rings being touched,
which is the queue-owned slot ring's job (step 6, blocked; see below).

The classic path hands a handler a ResponseWriter and a *Request, which is what
forced the closure shims (`HandlerFunc` called through a pointer to the func
value; `finishServe` taking `**response` for a deferred closure). The channel
path splits the two jobs instead:

  * the SHELL owns the socket, the framing, the keep-alive loop, the accept
    loop and the deadlines. It decodes a request into messages;
  * a HANDLER is a pure stream function: `Serve(in chan Msg, out chan Msg)`,
    one message per call, no io, no spawn, no locks, no closures.

Message set: ReqHead (method, path, route, headers), ReqBody (bytes), ReqEnd,
ReqAbort (error) - and RespHead (status, headers), RespBody (length),
RespEnd, RespAbort in the other direction. Abort is separate from End because
a client that disconnects and a handler that fails are not ends of stream.

Two rules the language imposes on the message contents, both learned the hard
way here:

  * a response body is NOT a slice of the handler's own frame: the shell reads
    it after Serve has returned and that frame is gone. The shell offers a
    scratch buffer in every request message and the handler writes into it BY
    INDEX (a subslice would be a copy) and replies with the length;
  * channels must be created in the frame that uses them. A channel built in a
    constructor and stored on the runner is released with the constructor's
    frame, and the first send panics with "send on closed channel".

Dispatch policy: `DispatchInline` runs the handler in the connection's domain
(no spawn; per-connection channels and scratch built by the shell, which is the
deterministic mode), `DispatchSpawned` builds a fixed pool once and hands each
step to a worker over unbuffered `chan []byte` frames. The frames are the same
message set, encoded; the worker decodes, looks the route up in the inherited
table, runs the handler and frames the answer back. The table is a plain slice
built at startup, and it is complete before the first spawn because spawn forks.
Spawn cost is measured by tests/netsmoke/spawncost (a spawn is a fork, so it is
microseconds and a thread), which is why the pool exists and per-request spawn
does not.

### Allocation scope must be lexical, not inherited  [RUNTIME PRINCIPLE]

The lesson under the 17.5kB retention, and it is not specific to the queue.

An arena in force is dynamic state: anything that allocates inherits whatever
arena its caller happened to have entered. When a library function's allocation
lifetime is shorter than the caller's arena, the allocation is charged to a
scope that outlives it, and the reset that was supposed to free it is then
freeing the wrong region - the reset works, the attribution is wrong. That is
the shape of this leak, and it is the same disease as the checker dying with
"region table full" during the 45-package sweep, where type-check scratch landed
in the compile arena because the checker allocates wherever it was called from.
Two unrelated call sites, one fault: allocation policy inherited dynamically.

**The rule: allocation scope must be lexical, not inherited.** Any function that
allocates for its own use opens its own scope - the codec, the formatter, the
error path, the header parser, the checker. The caller's arena is never a valid
place to put callee scratch.

**The corollary, measured in round 14: an exit is one function, not three.** A
scope boundary must release everything allocated under it, child groups
included - and the way that goes wrong is that the three exits (reset, free,
release) drift: `ArenaFree` and `ArenaRelease` released the sovereign groups and
`ArenaReset` did not, which was the whole leak. The durable form is therefore not
the missing call added to the third exit, it is `arenaReleaseGroups`: reset, free
and release all call it, it carries the fail-loud check (`arena: exit orphaned
sovereign groups`), and a new exit written later has one thing to call instead of
one thing to remember. The same rule applies to a handler path: a request has ONE
arena boundary (enter, work, exit) so the normal return and every abort - parse
failure, missing route, disconnected client - leave through the same door and the
same compaction drain.

**Data in flight is not an arena object at all.** An arena frees at a scope
boundary and a message crosses scopes by definition, so a message buffer belongs
to a RING OF PREALLOCATED SLOTS owned by the queue, handed off by index, with
the copy happening ONCE, at a named site, into the receiver's slot. That gives
zero allocation in the steady state, so there is nothing to leak and nothing to
mis-attribute. Sizing falls out of Little's law: memory for the queue is arrival
rate times service time, bounded by channel depth or pool size - NOT connections
times slots. A per-connection ring is sized by a variable that does not appear in
the load equation, which is why it cannot cap anything; a first attempt at one
(4 slots per connection) was measured-in-principle unsound and reverted before
committing for exactly that reason.

**The instrument to prove any of it** is a per-scope allocation counter: tag each
arena with the scope that opened it, and one run names the 17.5kB instead of
testing five hypotheses.

**Form of the retention, measured** (this is the answer to "what is the form of
it"): it scales with the NUMBER of header entries, not with their bytes.

    1 header  x 4000B : ~7.9kB retained per request (baseline is ~7.0kB)
    40 headers x 100B : ~141kB retained per request, i.e. ~3.4kB PER HEADER ENTRY

So it is the map entries and their value slices - the `Header` map the parser
builds (`[][]byte` values) - not the payload bytes. Structs and scalars can be
overwritten in place; slices and maps need an allocation pool for reuse. The fix
direction that follows: a reusable header map and reusable body buffers that are
cleared and refilled per request (steady-state allocation zero), plus the runtime
side - a hashmap's bucket storage must be charged to an arena with the map's own
lifetime, not to whatever arena the caller had entered.

### The per-site tracker already exists: -print-allocs + the alloc_trace tag  [INSTRUMENT, use this]

There was no need to hand-roll a site capture, and the two failures (Caller and
returnAddress) are beside the point: the compiler already has the seam.

  * `-print-allocs <pattern>` (`_mxc_stage4/main.mx`, `setPrintAllocs`) matches
    functions by relative name and emits `call void @runtime.logAlloc(i32 siteID,
    i32 size)` immediately before EVERY arena allocation in a matched function.
    It forces the build serial (site ids are handed out in compile order) and
    writes a SITE TABLE beside the output - one entry per site, naming
    `pkg.Func@file:line`.
  * `src/runtime/alloc_trace.mx` is the counting side, selected by the
    `alloc_trace` build tag: per-site counters and sizes in root-arena tables,
    `PrintAllocCounters()` to dump them, and exported readers
    (`__moxie_alloc_counters_ptr`, `__moxie_alloc_sizes_ptr`,
    `__moxie_alloc_n_sites`, `__moxie_total_alloc`, `__moxie_mallocs`).
    `allocArenaUsed(a)` lives there too. Without the tag, `alloc_trace_off.mx`
    supplies a no-op `logAlloc`.
  * The runtime's `totalAlloc`/`mallocs` are documented to match those numbers
    precisely ("the one entry point every compiler-emitted allocation goes
    through, so the numbers match what -print-allocs instruments").

So the next run is an instrumented build, not another counter:
`build -tags alloc_trace -print-allocs 'net/http'` over the fixture, serve, call
`runtime.PrintAllocCounters()` (or read the exported tables) after 1000 requests,
and read the site table beside the binary. That names every allocating source
site with its byte count - including whatever is driving the region growth - and
it is exact rather than inferred.

The hand-rolled parts that stay: the per-scope allocated/reclaimed counters and
the region acquire/release counters (they answered the arena-level question and
found the region leak); the site PC capture in `alloc()` is superseded and can be
deleted.

### It is not first-touch: it is arena REGION growth, ~9.6MB acquired per 300 requests  [MEASURED]

The obvious explanation for "RSS grows, arena report flat, same in both modes" is
first-touch inside the root's big mapping - pages accumulate until the region is
full, then it plateaus. Ran it out to 8x1000 to check (spawned, one connection,
1000 requests per run):

    1k rss= 48108kB data=364592kB maps=40
    2k rss= 79352kB data=400304kB maps=48
    3k rss=110604kB data=436016kB maps=53
    4k rss=141820kB data=471728kB maps=56
    5k rss=173052kB data=507440kB maps=59
    6k rss=204288kB data=543152kB maps=61
    7k rss=235520kB data=578864kB maps=64
    8k rss=266736kB data=614576kB maps=66

It does not plateau. It is perfectly linear, and VmData tracks it exactly
(+31MB per 1000 = 31kB a request of VIRTUAL memory), while the mapping COUNT
rises 40 -> 66: roughly one ~9.6MB mapping acquired every ~300 requests and never
released. So this is not page first-touch and not an allocation inside an
existing arena - it is arena REGION GROWTH that is never unmapped.

That also corrects an earlier premise this work started from: the mapping count is
NOT flat at 17, it climbs here, and VmData grows with it. The retained thing is a
region, which is why the per-scope and live-arena reports look clean: they report
BYTES ALLOCATED into regions, and a freshly acquired region whose bytes were then
reclaimed on reset is not "used" - but it also was never unmapped, so the mapping
stays.

Next: instrument region acquire/release (sysMap/sysUnmap counters and the arena
each region belongs to) and name the arena whose regions are added but never
