## Round 175: the codec's back-reference key is a size, not just an address

`crypto/ecdh`'s ECDH returned `invalid scalar length` for a valid key pair, and
the private scalar read back as a **16-byte slice with capacity 2** immediately
after a key generation that had produced 32 bytes. The fips PrivateKey object at
the failing call was not a corrupted original: it was a *different, smaller*
object. Its `pub` PublicKey fields were byte-perfect and only the trailing `d`
slice was garbage, which is the signature of an object that was decoded at the
wrong size.

The cause is in `src/runtime/codec.mx`, the graph encoder every function return
goes through. Its seen set holds one entry per object it walks so that a pointer
to something already encoded becomes a back-reference instead of a second copy.
Those entries were keyed by **address alone**, and a struct shares its address
with its first field. `crypto/ecdh.PrivateKey` holds
`*fips140/ecdh.PrivateKey`, whose first field is the matching `PublicKey`: the
PublicKey (48 bytes) was registered at the very address the enclosing PrivateKey
(72 bytes) starts at, so the outer key's `fips` pointer became a back-reference
to the PublicKey entry. The decoder resolved it to that 48-byte block, the
PrivateKey's tail was never encoded, and `d` read whatever the arena held next.

A back-reference is correct exactly when the object already encoded at that
address **covers the pointee**. Entries are now (address, encoded size) pairs and
the lookup requires `entrySize >= pointeeSize`; the pair index is still the
back-reference index, so the encoder's table and the decoder's one-word table
stay position-aligned, and `codecSeenSet`'s layout is untouched (both compilers
allocate it from their emitted IR).

The size, not the type, is the key because the *other* direction is a legitimate
identity that must keep working: `fmt`'s printer holds `buf *[]byte` pointing at
its **own first field**, so a pointer to a smaller object at a registered address
must resolve to that address. Keying on the type instead made it a fresh copy of
the slice header, and every formatted argument then wrote into a copy that never
reached the printer's buffer - `fmt.Printf("%s", "lit")` printed an empty string
while the argument's own `String()` still returned `lit`. That regression was
caught by `tests/regressions/should_compile/builtin_string_render.mx` and
`asn1_tag_mismatch.mx`, which is why the size rule carries both cases.

Measured after the fix, against Go 1.25 on the same fixed private keys: P-256
`NewPrivateKey`, both public keys, and the ECDH shared secret
`c7d4af84c658a59f19868c89958637795eb6c6010f5179abba649b309ebd255d` match byte
for byte. P-384 and P-521 still SIGSEGV inside `nistec`, which is a separate
defect in those point ports.

### Found, not fixed: interface dispatch has no arm for a generic instantiation

`crypto/ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), ...)` dies with `interface dispatch:
no impl for Params (6 impl(s), none matches)`. This is not a naming mismatch:
`findIfaceImpls` enumerates implementations from the **type declarations** of the
link set, and it explicitly skips a generic declaration
(`len(named3.TParams) > 0`) because a generic type's methods are never emitted as
standalone symbols. The dynamic type here is the *instantiation*
`*nistCurve[*nistec.P256Point]`, which has no declaration to enumerate, so no arm
exists for it and the boxed value matches nothing. Arms for concrete impls of
`Params` (`*CurveParams`, `*KoblitzCurve`) are present - they are the "6 impls".

The compiler gap is real and is now the top item in this file: an interface
invoke needs an arm (and a monomorphized body) for every instantiation of a
generic type reachable in the link set, plus a registry that records those
instantiations as they are created. Until that exists, `crypto/elliptic` must not
hand out a generic type through an interface.

## Round 176: elliptic.Curve is handed out as a non-generic type

The `Params` dispatch was not a naming mismatch. `findIfaceImpls` enumerates an
interface's implementations from the **type declarations** of the link set, and
it skips a generic declaration because a generic type's methods are never emitted
as standalone symbols. The dynamic type of `elliptic.P256()` was the
*instantiation* `*nistCurve[*nistec.P256Point]`, which has no declaration to
enumerate, so no arm existed and the boxed value matched none of the six impls
(`*CurveParams`, `*KoblitzCurve` and their value forms).

`crypto/elliptic` no longer hands a generic type out through an interface.
`nistCurveImpl` is a plain struct holding a `curveKind` and the `*CurveParams`,
and each `elliptic.Curve` method forwards through a four-way switch to a **generic
free function** (`nistIsOnCurve[P]`, `nistScalarMult[P]`, ...). A call to a
generic function is monomorphized at the call site, so the type argument never
becomes a value that has to survive a return or be boxed. `nistCurve[P]` itself is
gone; the constraint (`nistPoint[P]`) and the arithmetic stayed single-sourced.

Two defects fell out of the change, both measured:

  * The curve set was built lazily by `initAllCurves`, which stored
    `_curves()`'s result into the package global `_cachedCurves`. That store is a
    global write outside `init()`, so it is not relocated: the global kept a
    pointer into `initAllCurves`'s frame arena, and the FIRST reader saw a
    relocated copy while the SECOND reader walked released memory and died
    (`SIGSEGV` in `elliptic.P224`). The name `initAllCurves` satisfied the
    restriction check without getting the relocation the rule exists for. The
    set is now built in a real `init()`. This is the same class as the crc64
    table and the rand/v2 global Rand, and it is the reason the rule is
    "initialize globals in init()", not "name your function initSomething".
  * `ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), ...)` now gets through key generation and
    then dies in the sign path: inside the cross-package monomorphized clone
    `fips140/ecdsa.NewPublicKey[*nistec.P256Point]`, the call `c.newPoint()`
    loads a two-word function value `{ctx, code}` from the `Curve[P]` field, but
    the code word is not what was stored - the call jumps into an unmapped data
    address (gdb: `SIGSEGV` at a `0x7fff...` address two instructions after
    `mov 0x18(%rax),%rdi; mov 0x20(%rax),%rax; call *%rax`). A minimal probe of
    the same shape (generic struct with a `func() P` field, constructed by a
    generic function, called from a generic function) works in one package, so
    the defect is specific to the clone emitted into a foreign package.

Verified against Go 1.25 on the same inputs: P-256 `ScalarBaseMult(5)`,
`Double` (10G), `ScalarMult(2)` of 5G, `Marshal`/`Unmarshal` round trip,
`IsOnCurve`, and `Params().Name` for all four curves (P-224/P-256/P-384/P-521),
which are now callable repeatedly - the lazy-init defect made the *second* call
to any curve accessor crash.

### Round 176 addendum: the ecdsa sign crash is a cloned-initializer global

Disassembling the two copies of `initP256` in one binary shows the split
exactly. The in-package `crypto/internal/fips140/ecdsa.initP256` passes the
`curveID` argument as `{ptr "P-256", len 5, cap 5}` and the point constructor as
`{null, nistec.NewP256Point}`. The clone emitted into `crypto/ecdsa`
(`crypto/ecdsa.crypto_internal_fips140_ecdsa.initP256__`) passes **zeros** for
the whole `curveID` (all three words) and the same correct constructor pair. The
body of the cloned `newCurve` is byte-identical to the in-package one (same 0x58
allocation, same field offsets), so the field layout is not the problem.

Both clones read and write the same TLS slot (`%fs:-0x38`) and both start with
"if the slot is non-nil, return". In the failing run the sign path's
`c.newPoint()` loads `{ctx, code}` from an object that is not the curve that was
built, which is consistent with the clone's guard seeing a foreign non-nil value
in that slot and skipping the initializer: a package-level global of a package
whose code was monomorphized into another package has no slot of its own at the
clone site. So the remaining work for ecdsa/ecdh is
"monomorphized clones of package-level state need their own storage (or must
stay in the defining package)", not the interface dispatch and not the codec.

The png identity defect was measured again after the codec fix and is unchanged:
`png.Encode` of an 8x6 RGBA image emits a 63-byte stream with an 18-byte IDAT
where Go emits 86 bytes with a 29-byte IDAT, and `bufio.Writer.Buffered()` is 6
after `writeImage` returns - the zlib header and adler are in the png-visible
bufio, the compressed block went into a second copy of the same Writer struct.
`zlib.NewWriterLevel` and `flate.NewWriterDict` each return `&Writer{...}` (a
composite literal) whose address has to survive the return with identity intact;
`codecIsStableAddr` reports frame memory unstable, so each boundary copies the
pointee. The compiler fix is the one this file has carried since round 55: an
address-of-composite-literal that is returned must be allocated where its
identity is stable (root arena), the same marking `markAddrEscaping` already
performs for `&`.

## Round 177: ECDH works on all three NIST curves

Parallel to the codec defect, the other two curves were dead from the same
"global written outside init()" class that this file has recorded three times
already, plus one array-relocation gap:

  * `_p224B`, `_p384B` and `_p521B` were filled by lazy `initPxxxB` helpers. The
    store is a global write outside `init()`, so the global kept a pointer into
    the assigning frame's arena. `P384Point.SetBytes` then read a released
    `fiat.P384Element` and rejected even the generator's own encoding ("P384
    point not on curve"), which made `Double` panic on the curve generator and
    every higher operation fail. They are now built by `buildPxxxB` from the
    package `init()`.
  * `p384GeneratorTable`/`p521GeneratorTable` were filled by lazy
    `initPxxxGeneratorTable`, same defect one level deeper: `ScalarBaseMult`
    read released table entries and died in `fiat.p384Mul`. They are built from
    `init()` too, and the table type is now
    `struct{ points []*PxxxPoint }` with the generator table a `[]p384Table`:
    the global-store relocation walks slice elements, but the pointer fields
    inside `[15]*PxxxPoint` were not carried, so an array table stayed dangling
    even once the store itself happened in `init()`.

Verified byte for byte against Go 1.25, same fixed private keys: P-256
(`c7d4af84...`), P-384 (`be44c223...`) and P-521 (`00d23346...`) public keys and
ECDH shared secrets all match, and for P-384 `Double(G) == Add(G,G) ==
ScalarBaseMult(2)` with every result on the curve. `crypto/ecdh` still has no
`P224`, so that curve is only covered through the `elliptic` facade.

`ecdsa.Sign` remains blocked by the cloned-initializer defect from round 176's
addendum: key generation works, the sign path reads a curve global that the
clone emitted into `crypto/ecdsa` never initialised.

## Round 178: RSA key generation never returns because bigmod's exponentiation returns zero

`rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader(), 1024)` does not terminate. It is not a deadlock:
the prime search runs, it just never accepts a candidate. Measured with a print
in `randomPrime`: 1923 candidates in 240 s, ~13% of them passing the trial
division table and reaching Miller-Rabin, and not one accepted. For 512-bit
candidates about one in twenty-three trial-division survivors is prime, so a
working test would have accepted roughly ten of them.

The primality test is fed a zero. Driving `crypto/internal/fips140/bigmod`
directly, with a 256-bit odd modulus:

  * `NewNat().SetBytes(base)` then `Bytes(m)` round-trips exactly (so the
    limb<->byte conversion is fine);
  * `NewModulusProduct(3, 5)` returns 15 (so the plain multiply-accumulate path
    is fine);
  * `NewNat().Exp(x, {0}, m)` returns **1** (so the Montgomery domain setup and
    the final reduction round-trip through it);
  * `Exp(x, {1}, m)`, `Exp(x, {2}, m)`, `Exp(x, {1000}, m)` and `Mul(x, x, m)`
    all return **0**.

So every Miller-Rabin round computes `b^m mod w = 0`, never `1` or `-1`, and
every candidate is reported composite - including primes. `GenrateKey` therefore
loops forever, in both compilers (the legacy-built probe behaves the same, so
this is a runtime/src defect, not stage4 codegen).

Two subslice-write defects in `nat.mx` were found while chasing it and are real
by the language law, but they are NOT sufficient to explain the zero result, so
they were left uncommitted rather than shipped half-diagnosed:

  * `expand` does `clear(x.limbs[len(x.limbs):n])` and `reset` does
    `clear(x.limbs[:max(n, len(x.limbs))])`. A subslice is a copy, so both
    `clear` calls clear a throwaway copy and the limbs keep their old values
    (`reset` is then not a reset).
  * `addMulVVW` is called with destination subslices (`T[i:n+i]`), so every
    limb write in the Montgomery accumulation loop is discarded.

Note `NewModulusProduct` works at baseline and *panicked* with the offset-taking
`addMulVVW` rewrite, so that rewrite needs its own diagnosis before it can land:
the remaining defect in `montgomeryMul`/`Exp` (most likely the constant-time
table selection at `tmp.assign(ctEq(k, uint32(i+1)), table[i])`, since an
exponent nibble of 0 is the only case that produces the right answer) has to be
found first, and then all of it verified together.

This is the next item for the bigmod work: the fix is in
`src/crypto/internal/fips140/bigmod/nat.mx`, and `rsa.GenerateKey` is the
end-to-end test that proves it (a 1024-bit key must come out with a 1024-bit N
and `E = 65537`).

### Round 178 addendum: what bigmod's zero is NOT

Four more hypotheses were tested and eliminated, so the next attempt does not
have to repeat them:

  * Rewriting every write-through-alias in `nat.mx` (`add`, `sub`, `assign`,
    `ShiftRightVarTime`, `expand`, `reset`, and `addMulVVW` taking an offset
    instead of a `T[i:n+i]` destination) did **not** change `Exp`/`Mul`: they
    still returned 0. The aliasing is still a latent bug by the subslice law
    (`assign`'s constant-time select writes into a copy), but it is not the
    cause of the zero. That rewrite also made `NewModulusProduct` panic, so it
    needs its own verification pass before landing.
  * The receiver-vs-returned-value relocation is not the cause: `exp :=
    bigmod.NewNat(); r := exp.Exp(x, e, m)` leaves BOTH `r` and `exp` at 0.
  * `bits.Mul`, `bits.Add`, `bits.Len32` are correct (checked directly:
    `Mul(3,3)`, `Mul(2^32-1, 2^32-1)`, carry propagation).
  * `Bytes`/`SetBytes` round-trip and `NewModulusProduct(3,5) == 15` are correct,
    so the limb<->byte path and the plain multiply-accumulate are fine.

What is left is the Montgomery path itself: `montgomeryRepresentation`,
`montgomeryMul`'s final `maybeSubtractModulus`, or `montgomeryReduction`. A
useful next probe prints `xR.limbs[0]` right after `montgomeryRepresentation`
(a 256-bit `m`, x=3) and compares it with `3 * R mod m` computed in Go; if `xR`
is zero, the representation is the defect, and `Exp(x, {0}) == 1` only worked
because 1 round-trips through a representation that zeroes every other value.

### Round 178, second addendum: the exact spot inside Exp

Instrumenting `Exp` for a 256-bit modulus and x=3 shows the first table entry is
in the **normal** domain (`table[0].limbs[0] == 3`) where it must be `3R mod m`,
and `table[1]` (its square) is 0. Everything downstream of a zero base is zero.

`ExpShortVarTime`, which uses the same `xR := NewNat().set(x).montgomeryRepresentation(m)`
chain but KEEPS the returned pointer in a variable, is correct:
`ExpShortVarTime(3, 1000)` equals the 256-bit expected value
`8325760f12e0f3c898fe1403ce306adaefe6091a1d35855970e541f77084eb8f`. So
`montgomeryRepresentation` and `montgomeryMul` work when their result is kept;
the failing shape is the `Exp` table build, where the value is produced through
`table[i].montgomeryMul(table[i-1], table[0], m)` on fresh `NewNat()` elements
inside a 15-element array literal.

Rewriting `table[0].set(x).montgomeryRepresentation(m)` as two statements did
**not** change the result, so the next probe should print `table[0]` immediately
after `montgomeryRepresentation` returns in both shapes (kept in a variable vs
called on an array element) and compare; a difference there is a receiver
identity/relocation defect with a tiny reproducer, not a bigmod arithmetic bug.

## Round 179: RSA key generation works - the zero was a lost receiver write

The zero in `bigmod.Exp` was two defects in `nat.mx`, both instances of "a
subslice is a copy" meeting "a returned receiver is a relocated copy":

  * `montgomeryMul` ended with `copy(x.reset(n).limbs, T[n:])`. The receiver a
    mutating method returns is a **relocated copy** of it, so `.limbs` named the
    copy's limbs: the product was written into that throwaway while the real `x`
    stayed zeroed by the reset. It is now two statements, `x.reset(n)` then
    `copy(x.limbs, T[n:])`, and the same shape in the 1024/1536/2048-bit cases.
  * `addMulVVW(z, x, y)` was called with destination *subslices*
    (`T[i:n+i]`), so every low limb it accumulated was written into a copy and
    discarded; only the carries in `T[n+i]` survived, which is why the high half
    of the product was nonzero and the low half was zero. It now takes the whole
    destination slice plus an offset.
  * the `Exp` window table also relied on `table[0].set(x).montgomeryRepresentation(m)`
    mutating `table[0]` through a chained call whose result is dropped; it is two
    statements now, so the representation lands on the table entry.

Measured after the fix, against Python's `pow`: `Exp(3, 1000)` with a 256-bit
modulus is `8325760f12e0f3c898fe1403ce306adaefe6091a1d35855970e541f77084eb8f`,
with a 1024-bit modulus `348358fc...ad66d25a`, and the 2048-bit path agrees too
(`Exp` then `Exp(.,2)` equals `pow(a**2)`). End to end:
`rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader(), 1024)` returns with `N.BitLen() == 1024` and
`E == 65537` - the first time it has terminated.

The compiler-level defect behind the first bullet is the same one this file has
carried since round 55 (a returned value that must keep identity is copied); the
source-level idiom that avoids it is "never chain a mutating call whose result
you drop, and never write through a subslice".

## Round 180: flate BestSpeed is fixed and byte-identical to Go

Level 1 (`deflatefast`) died with SIGSEGV in `(*deflateFast).encode` on the first
block. The faulting read was `e.table[12040]` at a base address in a released
frame arena: `newDeflateFast` built the 64 KiB `prev` buffer and the 128 KiB hash
table in its own frame and returned the struct by pointer, and the store into the
compressor's sovereign arena aliased that memory as an "ancestor" frame (the
codec keeps identity for ancestor arenas by design), so it dangled as soon as
`compressor.reset` returned.

The buffers are now allocated by `deflateFast.ensureBuffers` from inside
`encode`, a mutating method of `e`: its prologue borrows `e`'s sovereign arena,
so a direct allocation there lands in the arena that owns the receiver and needs
no relocation. The table is a `[]tableEntry` rather than a
`[tableSize]tableEntry` array, which also fixes `clear(e.table[:])` (clearing a
subslice is a no-op) and keeps a 128 KiB array out of a struct the codec copies.

Verified against Go 1.25 for levels -1, 0, 1, 6 and 9 over three inputs (4 KiB
repetitive, 4 KiB pseudo-random, 8 KiB text): compressed length AND FNV hash of
the output match for every case, e.g. level 1 gives 45/132/4106 bytes with the
same hashes as Go.

## Round 181: the png IDAT identity loss is a store-back aliasing rule, and its location

With the flate and bigmod fixes in place, `png.Encode` of an 8x6 RGBA image is
still 63 bytes with an 18-byte IDAT where Go emits 86 with 29, and
`bufio.Writer.Buffered()` is 6 after `writeImage` returns, so the compressed
block still goes into a second copy of the same Writer struct.

The copy is produced by `codecIsStableArenaAddr`'s **store-back** branch
(`src/runtime/codec.mx`, `codecTopOnlyTransient`), specifically its last rule:

    // Ancestors below the receiver's arena keep identity, except the
    // sovereign scratch frames, which the store-back reclaims itself.

`encoder.writeIDATs` is a mutating method: its prologue pushes the receiver's
borrowed sovereign arena ABOVE its own frame, so its own frame - where
`bufio.NewWriterSize`'s returned object lives - is an "ancestor below the
receiver's arena". The rule therefore treats `e.bw`'s target as stable and
aliases it into the receiver's arena; when `writeIDATs` returns, that frame is
released and the receiver's `bw` pointer dangles - or, when the arena is reused
before the dangling is observed, the flush sees a different `n`.

The correct predicate for a store-back is "the arena that owns the target also
owns, or outlives, the receiver". The sovereign group already records exactly
that in `g.ctxArena` (`codecSovereignArena` sets it via `sovFindContainingArena`),
so the fix is to alias only pointers contained in the receiver's `ctxArena` (or
the root arena) and copy everything else. That single change should also cure
the general "wrote into a copy" family this file has recorded for bufio, zlib and
the relay.

### Round 181 correction: the store-back ancestor rule is NOT the png mechanism

Restricting the store-back branch of `codecIsStableArenaAddr` to the receiver's
own arena and `g.ctxArena` (the arena that allocated the receiver) - the change
that paragraph proposed - was implemented and tested: `png.Encode` still emits 63
bytes with an 18-byte IDAT and `bufio.Writer.Buffered()` is still 6. So the copy
that splits zlib/flate from png's flush is produced somewhere else and that
runtime edit was reverted unshipped.

The remaining candidates, in order: the return-value relocation of
`zlib.NewWriterLevelDict`'s `*Writer` (whose `w io.Writer` field holds the bufio
pointer; `codecEncodeIfaceValue` takes the `ct.Size() <= sizeof(uintptr)` branch
for a pointer dynamic type and encodes the value word as a pointer, which should
alias it), the `flate.NewWriterDict` hop, and `bufio.Writer.Reset`. The
instrumentation that discriminates them: print the `*bufio.Writer` address inside
`bufio.(*Writer).Write` and inside `Flush` for the png path - if `Write` sees a
different address from `Flush`, the pointer was copied before reaching bufio; if
both see `e.bw`, the copy is on the flush side.

## Round 182: the png copy is made when a *nested* interface is relocated

Instrumenting `bufio.NewWriterSize`, `(*bufio.Writer).Write`,
`(*bufio.Writer).Flush`, `flate.NewWriterDict` and `(*dictWriter).Write` in one
run of `png.Encode` gives the whole chain (addresses from that run):

    NewWriterSize made        140484403989552
    Write recv                140484403965840  len 2   n 0     <- zlib header, OK
    NewWriterDict w word      140484403965840                  <- the interface it received is OK
    dictWriter.Write w word   140484401647616  len 25          <- a DIFFERENT object
    Write recv                140484401647616  len 25  n 2     <- compressed block
    dictWriter.Write w word   140484401647616  len 4
    Write recv                140484401647616  len 4   n 27    <- adler
    Write recv                140484403965840  len 4   n 2     <- png's own adler
    Flush recv                140484403965840  n 6

So the value handed to `flate.NewWriterDict` is the same object zlib wrote its
header through, and the copy appears between that call and `dictWriter.Write`:
`dictWriter{dw := &dictWriter{w}}` is passed as an `io.Writer` into
`flate.NewWriter`, whose `*Writer` is then returned. When that return relocates
the `*dictWriter` (its own pointer is in the dying frame, so it is deep-copied),
the codec descends into the pointee's `w io.Writer` field and copies the
*bufio.Writer it points at* as well, instead of aliasing it.

That is the defect: a pointer reached as an **interface payload inside a struct
that is being copied** does not get the "ancestor arena keeps identity" treatment
the same pointer gets at the top level. The descriptor path is
`codecEncodeIfaceValue` -> `codecEncodeValue(&value, pointerType)` ->
`KindPointer` -> `codecIsStableAddr`, and the encode runs inside the return of
`flate.NewWriter`/`NewWriterDict`, where `codecRetTransient` is set and the
bufio object lives in an ancestor frame that the code says keeps identity - so
either that call takes a different branch than the code suggests, or the copy is
produced by a second relocation of the same graph after the first (the
`NewWriterDict` return). The next probe is to print inside `codecIsStableAddr`
for this exact pointer and see which branch returns false; the source-side
workaround, if the runtime fix is too broad, is to create the `bufio.Writer` in
`png.Encode`'s frame (which outlives every call that stores or copies it) rather
than inside the mutating `writeIDATs`.

### Round 182 addendum: three minimal shapes do NOT reproduce the nested-interface copy

Reduced reproducers were tried in user code and all three preserve the identity
(the object the interface points at observes the writes):

  * `relay(w W) W` returning `pass(&holder{w: w})` - one return boundary, the
    holder created in the callee's frame: payload aliased;
  * `pass2(w W) *holder` returning `&holder{w: w}` from its own frame, then
    `relay2` returning it again - two boundaries: aliased;
  * `inner2 -> mid2 -> outer2`, an interface payload two struct levels deep with
    `*holder` inside `*wrap`: aliased.

So the trigger is not "an interface payload inside a copied struct" in general; it
is something in flate's specific graph (a `compressor` carrying the 64 KiB window
and other large slices next to the `w io.Writer` field, the Writer returned from
`NewWriter` and then again from `NewWriterDict`, plus two mutations in between:
`fillWindow(dict)` and the `dict` push). The next probe should therefore be the
`codecIsStableAddr` print inside the real png encode, not another reduction -
that names the branch directly and cannot be fooled by a smaller graph.

## Round 183: a returned pointer to a scalar was answered "sovereign" for its own dying frame

The instrumented `codecIsStableAddr` inside the real `png.Encode` named the png
loss in one run, and the png loss turned out to be two independent defects, not
one. The first is the one that had been invisible in every reduced reproducer
because it looks like a lifetime question, not an identity question.

`codecEncodeValue`'s `KindPointer` branch aliases a pointer whose pointee is a
basic kind (`*uint32`, `*byte`) instead of deep-copying it: a pointer into a
buffer cannot be copied, because the pointee's declared size does not describe
the object. To keep such a pointee alive it arms the escape flag, which makes
the compiler leak the frame arena instead of returning it to the pool. The
guard for that arm asked

    if sovFindContainingArena(uintptr(p)) != nil { ...stable, no leak... }

and `sovFindContainingArena` scans every arena on the fn stack - *including the
one being released right now*. So for `func New() { var d digest; return &d }`
the pointee was found in its own dying frame, the answer was "sovereign, stable,
nothing to leak", the pointer was aliased, and the arena went straight back to
the pool. The caller's pointer then read whatever the next frame to acquire that
arena wrote: `hash/adler32`'s digest state came back as 0, or 0x3E6CB000, or
0x75E59000 depending on what had just run, and every png IDAT ended in that
value as its Adler-32 trailer.

The predicate is now the registered sovereign data-arena range list
(`sovInSovereignDataArena`), which is exactly the question the comment was
trying to ask and which cannot see the current frame: those ranges are only
created for sovereign data arenas and dropped when the arena is freed.

Measured before/after on `hash/adler32`:

    New(); Sum32()                   1            1
    Write("abcdef"); Sum32()         0            136184406   (= 0x081E0256)
    Checksum(150-byte IDAT block)    0xE33902B9   0xE33902B9

and on png: the IDAT trailer is now the Adler-32 of the scanlines instead of
garbage (the remaining bytes of the IDAT still differed, which is the second
defect, round 184).

## Round 184: a sovereign object lost identity crossing a return, and png now matches Go byte for byte

With the scalar lifetime fixed, the png IDAT was still 18 bytes of a 63-byte
file where Go writes 29 of 104. The instrumented encode shows the split
directly: `bufio.NewWriterSize`'s object receives the zlib header through one
address, `flate.NewWriterDict` receives that same address as the `io.Writer`
interface it is handed, and then `dictWriter.Write` writes through a *different*
address - the encoder's `bw` and the writer zlib holds are two objects.

The branch that made the copy was `codecIsStableArenaAddr`'s `codecRetTransient`
arm: a pointer into *any* live sovereign data arena was answered "transient,
copy it", because the arena belongs to a receiver and compaction may move it.
The encoder's `bw` lives in `encoder`'s own sovereign data arena - the arena of
the very receiver that is also about to store the zlib writer - so a nested
call returning that pointer copied the `bufio.Writer`, buffer and all.

Copying is safe for value data (a byte range) and wrong for an object (an
identity): the copy keeps being written to while the receiver's field keeps the
original, and the two never meet again. `codecSovDataAlias` therefore keeps a
non-basic pointee by identity when it lives in a live sovereign data arena, and
marks the owning group `escaped`, which is the promise every other stable path
already makes (`codecNoteStable`) because an exterior holder now references the
block. A group that dies with the frame being released is still copied - that
question was already answered before this is asked - so an alias cannot outlive
its arena. Byte and slice backing still copy on return.

Verified: unrelated `png.Encode` of an 8x6 RGBA image now produces a 104-byte
file whose hex is byte-identical to Go 1.25's for the same image -

    89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 00000008 00000006 0802000000
    716748ac 0000002f49444154 789c62616060976360c0442c0c1a0c0c0ccc
    98082ec1868690253891119a040f1c614af04310200000ffffe33902b9
    35285f2c 0000000049454e44 ae426082

- and `png.Decode` of it returns the original 8x6 image with the original
pixels. Disabling only this alias (leaving round 183 in place) reproduces the
broken 63-byte file and the decode failure, so the two fixes are independent.
The three reduced reproducers of round 182 were negative because none of them
put the pointee in a *sovereign* arena: the copy needed a receiver's own data
arena, which only the real encoder has.

## Round 185: the standard color models were a fresh object per call, so every model comparison was false

`color.RGBAModel()` and friends returned `ModelFunc(...)`, which builds a new
`&modelFunc` on every call. Go's version of the same functions returns a
package-level singleton (`var RGBAModel Model = ModelFunc(rgbaModel)`), and the
comment on `ModelFunc` says why that matters: "callers can still use
comparisons like m == RGBAModel". Moxie's port kept the constructor call and
dropped the variable, so no model ever compared equal to itself:

    rgbs == rgbs   before: false   after: true
    grays == grays before: false   after: true
    cmyk == cmyk   before: false   after: true
    rgbs == grays  before: false   after: false

The consumer that noticed is `image/png`'s encoder, which switches on
`m.ColorModel()` to choose the PNG colour type. Every case missed, so every
image took the `default:` 16-bit branch: an 8x6 RGBA image encoded with bit
depth 16 in IHDR (117 bytes) instead of bit depth 8 (104 bytes), and Go's
decoder-independent size for the same image is 104.

Moxie has no package-var initialisers, so the singletons are built once in
`init()`. Verified: `png.Encode` of the same image now writes `0802000000` in
IHDR (depth 8, colour type 2) and a 104-byte file byte-identical to Go 1.25's.

## Round 186: adler32's digest was a bare uint32, so every hasher leaked a 64 KiB arena

`hash/adler32` ported Go's `type digest uint32` and `func New() { var d digest;
return &d }`. Round 183 makes that pattern safe (the pointer is aliased and the
frame arena is leaked so the pointee stays alive), but "safe" here means one
leaked frame arena per hasher: `zlib.NewWriterLevelDict` creates a digest for
every compressed stream, and every png/gzip write creates one.

A one-field struct is the shape that needs no leak: the pointee is no longer a
basic kind, so the codec deep-copies it into the caller's arena at return and
the digest lives exactly as long as its owner. `digest` is now `struct{ s
uint32 }`; `Reset`, `Write`, `Sum`, `Sum32`, `MarshalBinary`, `UnmarshalBinary`
and `Clone` read and write `d.s`, and `update` returns the struct by value.

Verified: `New(); Sum32()` is 1, `Write("abcdef"); Sum32()` is 136184406
(0x081E0256, the Adler-32 of "abcdef"), `Checksum` of the 150-byte png scanline
block is 0xE33902B9 as in Go, and building and running the png probe with `-a`
prints no arena-escape warning - the two warnings the same probe printed before
this change were this leak and its clone in the decoder path.

## Round 187: a monomorphized clone resolved its defining package's unexported constants to zero

`ecdsa.GenerateKey` worked and `ecdsa.SignASN1` died in
`NewPublicKey___…P256Point` on a curve whose `newPoint` field held garbage.
Disassembling the two copies of `initP256` in one binary (round 176's method,
still valid) shows the difference exactly:

    crypto/internal/fips140/ecdsa.initP256          rdi="P-256" rsi=5 rdx=5
    crypto/ecdsa.…ecdsa.initP256__                  rdi=0       rsi=0 rdx=0

The clone emitted into `crypto/ecdsa` passed three zero words for the
`curveID`. `ScanGenericDecls` builds the scope a monomorphized body resolves
against, and for a `ConstDecl` it inserted the *registry's* object when the
constant was exported and a `NewTCConst(…, nil, nil)` placeholder when it was
not. `p256 curveID = "P-256"` is unexported, so the placeholder had no value and
every reference in the clone folded to the zero value. The VarDecl arm twenty
lines below carries a comment about exactly this shape ("unexported vars
referenced from a monomorphized body … degrade to the __any interface"); the
ConstDecl arm never got the same treatment.

The scan now evaluates the constant from source the same way the typecheck pass
does: group and iota state, the repeated-expression rule for a bare line, the
declared type, `tcSelectorConst` for a re-exported constant,
`tcInferConstTypeFromExpr` as the fallback, and `ConvertConstLocal` to apply the
declared type. Verified: the clone now passes `{ptr "P-256", 5, 5}` and the
sign path gets past `NewPublicKey`.

## Round 188: an initialiser's global stores landed in the caller's arena

With the curve name fixed, the sign path died in `NewPublicKey` on a
`newPoint` holding garbage. The curve pointer was valid at every clone boundary
and the object was corrupt: `_p256Cached` pointed into memory that had been
reused. The cause is the global-store rule. The restriction pass permits a store
to a package global in any init-named function, but only the package's real
`init()` is *safe*: it pushes no frame arena, so the current arena is the root
and everything it allocates outlives the call. A lazy `initP256()` called from
`GenerateKey` allocates its curve into `GenerateKey`'s frame arena; the global
keeps that pointer and `GenerateKey`'s arena is recycled as soon as it returns.
Key generation itself works (it runs entirely inside that frame), so the first
observation is the *next* user: `SignASN1` read the reused block.

Both compilers now give an initialiser the same target the real `init()` always
had: a function that stores a package global runs with the root arena as its
allocation target. The predicate is exact rather than name-based - `isInitFunc`
*and* a store rooted at a package global (`funcStoresGlobal` /
`ssaFuncStoresGlobal`, both using the existing `globalName` / `ssaGlobalRoot`
walkers) - so an init-named helper that only touches locals is unchanged. The
caller's arena is restored at every return *before* the return encode, so the
encode buffer still lands in the frame arena, and the restore goes through the
new `runtime.InitArenaRestore`, which leaves the root in place when the save is
nil (that is `initDomain`'s own initialisers, which run before the root exists;
restoring nil there left the fn stack with no arena and the next `alloc`
panicked "alloc: nil arena").

Verified: the stage4 binary built by legacy from this change bootstraps and
bakes its own runtime, `ecdsa.GenerateKey` followed by `SignASN1` no longer
faults in `NewPublicKey`, and the runtime bake no longer panics in `main`.

## Round 189: interface dispatch had no arm for an instantiated generic type, and the fall-through was silent

With the curve initialised correctly the sign path stopped crashing and started
*hanging*. `randomPoint` retries until a nonce is in range, and it never
retried out of a valid one: the HMAC-DRBG handed back 32 zero bytes every time.
Driving the same DRBG directly produced the right bytes, and calling `Generate`
through an `interface{ Generate([]byte) }` produced zeros - a two-line
reproduction in package `main`, so this was not the clone chain.

The dispatch is a chain of type-ID arms emitted by `findIfaceImpls`, which
enumerates candidates from a package's members by splitting `<type>.<method>`
and from type DECLARATIONS of the link set. A generic type's declaration is
skipped on purpose (its methods are never emitted standalone), so an
*instantiation* - `*hmacDRBG[sha256.Digest]` - matched nothing, and
`emitIfaceChain`'s zero-impl branch stores a `zeroinitializer`: the call
returned without doing anything, silently. That is why the DRBG produced zeros
instead of failing.

Two things were missing, exactly as this file has said since round 175: the arms
and the bodies.

  * `genericMethodInstance` is the monomorphization half of a generic method
    call, factored out of `tryGenericMethodCall`: it resolves the declared
    method's signature with the instantiation's type arguments, names the clone
    `<defpkg>.(*T).M__<args>`, builds its body in this module, and records the
    substituted receiver type in `cctx.genericMethodInsts` (a root-arena map -
    the first version of it was allocated in the builder's frame, and the next
    insert crashed in `hashmapContentSet` on the dead buckets).
  * `ensureIfaceInstMethods` runs at every boxing site (`coerceToInterface` and
    the two direct `SSAMakeInterface` constructions) and creates the clone for
    each interface method the instantiated type implements. A call through an
    interface has no selector on a concrete type, so without this the body is
    never created anywhere in the module.
  * `findIfaceImpls` also scans its own package's members for the clone shape
    `.<method>__` and adds an arm with the recorded receiver type, so the type
    ID the boxing site produces matches.

Verified: the two-line interface reproduction now prints the same eight bytes as
the direct call (215 38 106 151 22 33 63 3), and `ecdsa.SignASN1` produces a
signature that `ecdsa.VerifyASN1` accepts - P-256, P-384 and P-521 all sign,
verify, and reject a corrupted signature. P-224 signs but does not verify yet;
that is its own defect, opened below.

No legacy mirror: legacy dispatch is tinygo's `LowerInterfaces`, which builds a
dispatch table at the make-interface site from the concrete type's method set,
so an instantiation is covered there by construction. Legacy cannot compile
`crypto/internal/fips140/nistec` at all (`undefined: fiat`), so this packet was
only ever reachable through stage4.

## Round 190: P-224's generator table was an array built lazily, so its signatures were wrong

Round 189 left P-224 signing but not verifying, and Go rejected the signature
too - so the fault was in producing `r`, not in the verify path. P-224 was the
one curve still using the shape rounds 177 and 183 removed from the others:

    var p224GeneratorTable *[p224ElementLength * 2]p224Table   // array of tables
    func initP224GeneratorTable() { if nil { ... } }           // lazy
    type p224Table [15]*P224Point                              // array of pointers

Two independent problems, both already recorded in this file:

  * a lazy `initPxxx` stores a package global outside `init()`, so the table
    object stayed in the builder's frame arena. Round 188's root-arena switch
    does not fire here: the store goes through a global whose declared type is a
    *pointer*, which the global-root walkers deliberately do not treat as a
    global store ("field mutations through a global pointer are fine").
  * `[15]*P224Point` is an array of pointers. The relocation walks slice
    elements but not the pointer fields of an array - the exact defect that made
    `[15]*P384Point` dangle.

`p224Table` is now `struct{ points []*P224Point }` with `newP224Table`, the
generator table is `[]p224Table`, and `buildP224GeneratorTable` is called from
the package `init()` beside the P-384 and P-521 builders. Same shape, same
reason, now all four curves.

Verified, all four curves, moxie-only and cross-checked against Go 1.25:

    P-224 sign 63 bytes, P-224 verify true,  Go verifies moxie: true
    P-256 sign 70 bytes, P-256 verify true,  Go verifies moxie: true
    P-384 sign/verify true,  P-521 sign/verify true
    a corrupted signature is rejected on every curve

This closes the ecdsa sign path that rounds 175-189 tracked: ECDH and ECDSA both
work on every NIST curve for the first time.

## Round 191: the bytes package's tables become slices, and two lost-copy defects fall out

First cluster of the array removal. Six tables went from arrays to slices, each
built where its owner is built:

    stringFinder.badCharSkip          [256]int32     -> []int32
    genericReplacer.mapping           [256]byte      -> []byte
    byteStringReplacer.replacements   [256][]byte    -> [][]byte
    byteReplacer                      [256]byte      -> struct{ r []byte }
    asciiSet                          [8]uint32      -> struct{ w []uint32 }
    _asciiSpace()                     [256]uint8     -> []uint8

Nothing about the semantics needed a decision: `len` is unchanged, indexing is
unchanged, and `==` on slices is content equality (`runtime.sliceEqual`), so a
slice table compares exactly as the array did. The one trap is the keyed slice
LITERAL: `[]uint8{'\t':1, '\n':1, ...}` has length 33 (highest index plus one),
not 256, so `_asciiSpace` now allocates `[]uint8{:256}` and fills six entries -
as written the old literal became a 33-byte table and `bytes.Fields` panicked
"index out of range" on the first space at index 32.

Converting the package exposed two real defects, both in `bytes.Replacer`:

  * `byteReplacer.Replace` used `buf = []byte(s)` as a lazy copy. In Moxie
    `string` and `[]byte` are ONE mutable type, so that conversion is not a
    copy: the first replacement wrote through into the CALLER's buffer. Worse,
    `[]byte("literal")` points at the constant's backing, so
    `NewReplacer(a->1, b->2).Replace([]byte("abcab"))` rewrote the constant and
    a later `NewReplacer(a->XX, b->YY).Replace([]byte("abcab"))` received
    "12c12" as its input. Fixed with `Clone(s)` (the package already had it),
    verified: `replace: 12c12 input untouched: abcab`.

  * `genericReplacer` (two or more multi-byte keys) crashes. This one is NOT
    caused by the conversion: the same three-case probe on the pre-change tree
    faults identically. `makeGenericReplacer` builds a correct trie inside the
    package (verified with prints: tableSize 3, mapping a/b/c -> 0/1/2, root
    table entries 0 and 1 non-nil), and the fault is in
    `(*genericReplacer).lookup` at the dereference of the node pointer: the
    disassembly loads it with a 32-BIT `mov 0x110(%rsp),%ecx` and then
    dereferences it (`cmp %edx,0x18(%rcx)`), so a pointer local is spilled into
    an i32 slot. Reproducer: `bytes.NewReplacer([]byte("ab"), []byte("Q"),
    []byte("bc"), []byte("R")).Replace([]byte("abcabc"))` - expected "QcQc".
    Parked as its own defect; it is a pointer-slot / layout question, not an
    array one, and the array cluster above is otherwise complete.

Verified with a probe over the whole path: `Index`, `Count`, `Replace` (single
byte, single-byte-to-multi-byte and the plain function), `Trim`/`TrimLeft`/
`TrimRight`, `Fields`, `HasSuffix`, `LastIndex`, `Split`, `Equal` - every case
correct, and the input buffer is untouched by every replacement path.

## Round 192: the hash family's state and results become slices

Second array cluster: `crypto/md5`, `crypto/sha1`, `crypto/internal/fips140/sha256`,
`crypto/internal/fips140/sha512`, their block functions, and the public
`crypto/sha256`/`crypto/sha512`/`crypto/hmac` wrappers.

    md5.digest.s / .x                    [4]uint32 / [64]byte   -> []uint32 / []byte
    md5.checkSum tmp / out               [72]byte / [16]byte    -> []byte
    md5.Sum, sha1.Sum                    [Size]byte             -> []byte
    sha1.digest.h / .x                   [5]uint32 / [64]byte   -> []uint32 / []byte
    sha1 constSum length / out           [8]byte / [20]byte     -> []byte
    blockGeneric w                       [16/64/80]            -> []uint16/[]uint32/[]uint64
    _sha256K() / _sha512K()              [64]uint32/[80]uint64  -> slice literals
    fips140 sha256/512 Digest.h / .x     fixed arrays           -> slices
    checkSum tmp / digest                fixed arrays           -> slices
    sha256.Sum256/Sum/Sum224             [Size]byte             -> []byte
    sha512.Sum512/384/512_224/512_256    [Size*]byte            -> []byte
    hmac.Sum                             [32]byte               -> []byte

Three things this conversion taught, none of them about arrays:

  * **A digest copy is not a value copy any more.** `d0 := *d` was correct for
    an all-array struct; with slice fields it aliases the state, so `Sum`
    and `Clone` would corrupt the digest they were asked to preserve. Each
    package now has `copyState()`, which allocates `h`/`s` and `x` and copies
    element-wise, and both callers go through it.

  * **`copy(dst[off:], src)` writes into a copy.** The compiler rejects that
    form for user packages ("a subslice is a copy, so copying into it is not
    allowed") but exempts the stdlib, which is why `Write` and
    `UnmarshalBinary` had been getting away with it. Converting `x` from an
    array to a slice would have kept compiling while silently blocking input,
    so every such site is now an explicit element loop: `Write` copies into
    `d.x` by index, `UnmarshalBinary` copies by index and advances `b` by the
    count.

  * **The digest became a self-mutating type.** With array fields the struct
    needed no codec, so `ssaIsSovereignNamedType` said no; with slice fields it
    does, so the hash digests now own a sovereign arena and their mutating
    methods are subject to the sovereign loop-declaration rule.
    `sha1.constSum` was the one violation (`mask := ...` inside the padding
    loop) and the scratch is now declared before the loop. Measured cost of the
    change: 100k iterations of `md5.Sum` + `sha1.Sum` + `sha256.Sum256` over a
    64-byte buffer peak at 1968 kB RSS, so the sovereign arena is bounded here
    and does not grow per call.

The public `Sum*` signatures changed, so the callers moved with them:
`Sum256(x)[:]` becomes `Sum256(x)`, `h.Sum(sum[:0])` becomes `h.Sum(nil)` (the
old form relied on `push` writing through a subslice view of the caller's
array), and `base58`, `bip39`, `tls`, `secp256k1` and `x509` index the result
as before. Two identifier types are still arrays on purpose - `chainhash.Hash`
(value semantics: `rev := *hash` then swap) and `x509.sum224` (a `map` key) -
so both packages convert at the boundary with a small `hashOf`/`sum224Of`
helper; turning those into slices is its own item, not a drive-by.

Verification: a differential probe against Go 1.25.3 over all eight digests
(md5, sha1, sha256, sha224, sha512, sha384, sha512/224, sha512/256) for every
input length 0..200, plus three-way split writes, `Clone` independence and
`MarshalBinary`/`UnmarshalBinary` round trips mid-stream - 600 lines of output
identical to Go. Callers exercised end to end: base58check text, a BIP-39
mnemonic, chainhash `DoubleHashH`/`DoubleHashB`, and BIP-340 sign/verify on
both the array and the `...Bytes` entry points.

## Round 193: a cached dispatch fingerprint was reused across link sets, so a linked object could be missing arms

`tests/regressions/should_compile/ed25519_roundtrip` compiled from a cache that
carried a stale dispatch-arm fingerprint and then silently failed at runtime with
`panic: Verify rejected a valid signature`. It reproduced inside a 97-unit phase
0a run and passed when that unit ran on its own, which is the signature of cache
state, not of source.

The cause is in the cache key. A package's object is keyed by
`pkgHash = fnv(source, deps, dispatch arms, target)`, and the arms are measured
by `dispFingerprintForMethods`: for each interface method the package invokes,
the sorted identity of every impl `findIfaceImpls` enumerates. That enumeration
runs over the whole resolved closure, so **one package has a different arm set
under a different link set**.

`measureDispFingerprint` nevertheless kept one fingerprint per package on disk
(`<cacheBase>/<pkg>/disp.fp`) and preferred it over measuring, on the theory
that "every object in that directory was compiled with this same arm set ...
the newest writer wins - they agree by construction". They do not agree: the
fingerprint is a function of the link set, and the file is not. A build whose
closure differed from the one that wrote the file computed a key for an object
whose arms did not cover its own link, found it, linked it, and dispatched the
missing impl through the zero-impl branch. That branch is valid IR, so nothing
failed to compile; the hash inside `crypto/ed25519` simply disagreed between
signing and verifying.

The fix deletes the on-disk fingerprint entirely (`dispFingerprintPath`,
`readDispFingerprint`, `writeDispFingerprint`) and measures on every build.
`measureDispFingerprints` runs after `prepareDispatchIndex`, so the measurement
sees exactly the registry emission sees. The cost is a source scan per package
plus an emitter pass for packages that mention a method call at all - 440 of 454
packages measure `""` and skip the emitter - and a full 0a phase with the new
compiler passes 97/97 including the ed25519 fixture.

Legacy needs no mirror: it has no build cache at all, so it compiles every
package of the closure on every build and its arm sets are link-exact by
construction. This is a stage4 driver defect that only exists because stage4
caches.

Verification: `legacy/moxie build` → bake → `s4a` → `s4b` → `s4c`, with
`s4b == s4c` (fixpoint), then 0a 97/97 with `s4b` installed as `./moxie`.

## Round 194: utf8's tables become slices, and the probe found RuneCountInString counting bytes

Third array cluster: `unicode/utf8`.

    _firstTable          [256]uint8        -> []uint8
    _acceptRangesTable   [16]acceptRange   -> []acceptRange

`_acceptRangesTable` is the second keyed-literal trap in this sweep: its Go form
is `[16]acceptRange{0: {...}, 1: {...}, 2: {...}, 3: {...}, 4: {...}}`, which an
array literal sizes at 16 and fills with zeros. Written as `[]acceptRange{...}`
the same keyed literal has length 5, so the table is allocated `[]acceptRange{:16}`
and the five ranges are assigned by index.

The conversion itself is behaviour-preserving, and the differential probe proves
it: for every 1-, 2- and 3-byte sequence (plus a structured sample of 4-byte
sequences) the probe folds `DecodeRune`, `RuneLen`, `RuneStart`, `FullRune` and
`Valid` into an FNV accumulator, and for every code point `0..0x10FFFF` it folds
`EncodeRune` + `DecodeRune` round trips into another. Both accumulators, plus
`DecodeLastRune` on a well-formed and on a truncated tail and `ValidString`,
match Go 1.25.3 exactly.

The one mismatch the probe found was NOT the tables:

    runecount  moxie 41   go 27     (41 is len(s) in bytes)

`RuneCountInString` was `for range s { n++ }`. Go's version ranges over a
string, which iterates RUNES; here `string` and `[]byte` are one mutable type,
so ranging yields bytes and the function returned the byte length for any
non-ASCII string. It is now an explicit decode loop (`DecodeRune`, advance by
the rune size). Everything that measured text by rune count was affected and is
now correct: `fmt`'s width padding of non-ASCII arguments (format.mx:99,117),
`tabwriter`'s cell width, and `bytes.RuneCount`, whose result sizes the `[]rune`
that `strings`-style helpers build.

A grep for other `range` over a would-be string in `unicode`, `bytes` and the
formatting packages finds no second instance of this shape.

## Round 195: time's zone reader and quoted-printable's line buffer become slices, and three crashing packages are parked

    time/zoneinfo_read n [6]int32           -> []int32
    time/zoneinfo_read readFile buf [4096]  -> []byte
    mime/quotedprintable Writer.line [78]   -> []byte, allocated in NewWriter

Both are verified against Go 1.25.3 rather than assumed:

  * time: five zones (UTC, Europe/Berlin, America/New_York, Asia/Tokyo,
    Australia/Adelaide) x six instants (two DST-differing 2026 dates, the
    epoch, epoch+1, the 2038 boundary and 2100) formatted with
    "2006-01-02T15:04:05 MST -0700" plus `Zone()`'s name and offset. All 30
    lines are byte-identical to Go, which exercises the TZif v2 path: the
    six-count header, the 32-bit skip, the second count block and the
    transition/zone tables. The 4 KiB read buffer feeds the same parser through
    the embedded tzdata.
  * quoted-printable: eight inputs (plain, '=', trailing space + CRLF, a 100-byte
    line that must soft-wrap, tabs/CR/LF/high bytes, empty, two spaces, a long
    wrapping paragraph). Output is byte-identical to Go in both text and binary
    line-wrapping behaviour.

Three packages were found broken while sizing the next packages, all
PRE-EXISTING (each reproduces at the same fault address with the file reverted
via `git stash`, so none of them is caused by the array work), and all three
block a conversion whose only verifier is a run:

  * `mime.TypeByExtension` SIGSEGVs on any call on this host. Backtrace:
    `runtime[stringEqual]` <- `mime.(*mimeTypesStore).setExtensionType` <-
    `mime[loadMimeGlobsFile]` <- `mime[osInitMime]` <-
    `(*mimeTypesStore).init` <- `mime[TypeByExtension]`. The globs parser is
    reached because /usr/share/mime/globs2 exists. A faithful standalone mimic
    of the loop body (bufio.Scanner + bytes.Split + ParseMediaType + the same
    map writes) runs all 1616 lines clean, so the difference is the sovereign
    `mimeTypesStore` receiver, not the parsing. `mime/type.mx`'s `var buf
    [10]byte` is therefore left alone: its case-insensitive path cannot be
    exercised at all until this is fixed.

  * `archive/zip.Writer` writes a corrupt SECOND central-directory record. A
    312-byte archive from a `Store`-mode header, one file and one
    `Create("dir/second.bin")` differs from Go's 298-byte archive only from the
    second `PK\x01\x02` onward: the local file data and the first central entry
    are byte-identical, the second entry is `504b01021ed6c47f...` followed by
    0xff filler. It is also NONDETERMINISTIC: the same binary crashes or
    succeeds across 10 runs (7/10 with the arrays, 2/10 with slots) and ran
    clean under gdb. The suspect is the reused scratch
    (`hdrBuf`/`zipBuf`/`hdrB`/`zipB`, declared outside the directory loop
    because declarations inside a loop in a self-mutating method are rejected,
    and whose header bytes survive only partially), so `writer.mx` keeps its
    arrays and the conversion is blocked on this.

  * `bytes.genericReplacer.lookup` (round 191) is the same family: a pointer
    local dereferenced from a 32-bit slot, legacy printing the wrong answer and
    stage4 faulting.

All three point at the same gap: a self-mutating (sovereign) value whose scratch
or whose map/pointer local is reused across iterations or across a call boundary.
That is one investigation, not three.

## Round 196: the mime crash is a corrupted [][]byte element, shifted one word

Round 195 parked three packages on pre-existing crashes. This round narrows one
of them to a concrete memory corruption, which is worth writing down even though
it is not fixed.

`mime.TypeByExtension` -> `osInitMime` -> `loadMimeGlobsFile` ->
`(*mimeTypesStore).setExtensionType`, and inside it the loop

	for _, v := range exts { if v == extLower { return nil } }

where `exts` is `m.extensions[justType]`, a `[][]byte`. Instrumenting the real
package prints this for `application/pkix-cert` (element 0 then element 1):

	elem 0 len 0         cap 0          val ""
	elem 1 len 1981123776 cap -2063202462 val <fault>

`1981123776` and `-2063202462` are the two halves of a 64-bit pointer
(0x8517..7612..), so element 1 is being read 8 bytes off: its `len` field holds a
pointer's low half and its `cap` holds the high half. Element 0 reads as
{0, 0} because the same shift puts its pointer word where element 0's header
should start. The comparison then dereferences a pointer whose value is 41 -
which is exactly what the faulting instruction shows (`mov (%rdx,%rsi,1),%dl`
with `rdx = 0x29`) - and the process dies inside `runtime[stringEqual`.

So: a `[]byte` header inside a `[][]byte` is written or read one word away from
where the other side expects it. Everything else about the bug is now known to be
irrelevant: the fault is deterministic (same address, same line, five runs), it
is not the [10]byte scratch, not the scanner-buffer aliasing (a faithful
copy of the whole loader in another package ranges 1334 groups with correct
headers, printed), not `bytes.ToLower` (all 1616 globs extensions lower
correctly), not a missing-key map read (4000 misses return clean zero slices),
and not the number of entries or the extra `unicode.Tables` global.

What is left is the difference between the two builds: the real store is
`mimeStore`, a package-level `*mimeTypesStore` in package mime, and the copy is a
package-level `*store` in another package. Same code, same data, same call shape
(init -> method -> free function -> method), different layout. That points at the
codec/codegen for `[][]byte` elements under the sovereign arena - the same family
as round 191's pointer-in-a-32-bit-slot and round 195's corrupt zip directory -
and it is now the single blocker for `mime`, `archive/zip`, `bytes.genericReplacer`
and, by extension, any package whose scratch is a slice-of-slices.

Evidence kept: the instrumented runs print the element headers above; the copy
that stays clean is /tmp/glz (lib/lib.mx + main.mx), the minimal probes are
/tmp/nest (slice-of-slices range/compare, clean), /tmp/sovarena (slice-of-slices
in a sovereign receiver over 40 appends, clean), /tmp/mapmiss (4000 missing
lookups, clean) and /tmp/tolower (1616 extensions, clean).

## Round 197: a shift compared against a wider operand ran at 32 bits, so stage4 mis-rounded every float

Found while building a differential probe for the strconv conversion: stage4's
`FormatFloat(1, 'e', 0, 64)` returned `2e+00`, and 0.1 with four decimals
returned `2.0001e-01` - every last digit rounded up. Legacy compiled the same
source and matched Go, so this was a stage4 miscompilation, not a source port
bug.

Bisecting the ryu path printed the exact expression:

	dfrac = 0, extra = 62, d0 = true, di = 1, prec = 1
	c2 := dfrac == 1<<(extra-1)      stage4: true      legacy: false
	half (printed as int64)          2305843009213693952

`0 == 1<<61` was true in stage4, because the shift ran at 32 bits and
`1<<61` truncated to 0. The minimal form is two lines:

	var zero uint64 = 0
	var s uint32 = 62
	zero == 1<<(s-1)        // stage4: true, Go and legacy: false

`adoptSiblingType` (was: an inline width guard in buildBinaryOp) retyped an
untyped shift to the sibling operand's type only when the two widths were
EQUAL. Go's rule is that the untyped operand converts to the typed one's type,
so a wider sibling must retype the shift - the emitter shifts at the
instruction's declared width, and the declared width was 32. The guard now
allows equal OR wider siblings and still refuses narrower ones, because stage4
does not report an untyped constant that overflows the narrower context the way
Go does, and narrowing would turn that diagnostic gap into a silently truncated
shift.

Verification:

  * tests/regressions/should_compile/shift_compare_context.mx (new): uint64 and
    int64 contexts, both operand orders, equal-width uint32 and byte contexts,
    and the four FormatFloat cases that exposed it. Passes on stage4 and on
    legacy.
  * a 2744-case float-formatting differential (28 values x 5 formats x
    precisions -1..17, plus 32-bit and bool forms) is byte-identical to Go
    1.25.3 - it had 292 mismatched lines before the fix.
  * the strconv differential probe (format, integer formatting, parsing and the
    Append family, FNV-folded) now matches Go on all four accumulators; the
    format and parse accumulators differed before.

Legacy needs no mirror: it types shifts with go/types, which already applies the
contextual conversion. This is stage4 catching up to the reference.

## Round 198: strconv's four duplicated 696-entry power tables become one slice, and the decimal state becomes a slice

    detailedPowersOfTen   [696][2]uint64  x4 local literals -> []pow10 built once in init
    uint64pow10           [20]uint64 (local)               -> []uint64 built once in init
    decimal.d             [800]byte                        -> []byte (newDecimal)
    decimal.Assign buf    [24]byte                         -> []byte
    ftoa scratch buf      [32]byte / [24]byte              -> []byte

The interesting part is the table: four functions (mult64bitPow10,
mult128bitPow10, eiselLemire64, eiselLemire32) each carried a private copy of the
same 696-entry `[696][2]uint64` literal - 2800 lines of duplicated constants, and
a nested array type, which is exactly the shape that broke P-224's tables
(round 190). There is now one `[]pow10` (a `{hi, lo}` struct) plus one
`[]uint64` for the 20 small powers, both filled by `initPow10` from the single
remaining copy of the literal. strconv has one `init()` (atoi.mx, the
`ErrRange`/`ErrSyntax` one), so that init calls `initPow10()`.

The indexing is a value copy (`pow := detailedPowersOfTen[i]` then `pow.hi += 1`
for inverse powers), so the shared table is never mutated - the same guarantee
the local array literals gave.

Converting `decimal.d` to a slice makes `decimal` a codec-carrying type, i.e.
self-mutating, so two methods had a `:=` inside a loop that the sovereign rule
rejects; `Assign`'s `v1` and `RoundUp`'s `c` are now declared before their loops.

Verification: the four-fold FNV differential (float formatting across 28 values
x 5 formats x precisions -1..17, integer formatting in five bases, Parse*
families, and the Append* family) is byte-identical to Go 1.25.3 - and, before
round 197's compiler fix, moxie-against-moxie identical across this conversion,
which is what proves the conversion itself is behaviour-preserving: the same
probe on the pre-change tree produced the same four accumulators.

## Round 199: flate's RFC 1951 tables become one shared set of slices

    codegenOrder      [19]uint32   x2 (encoder)        -> []uint32, one copy
    lengthExtraBits   [29]int8     x2 (encoder)        -> []int8, one copy
    offsetExtraBits   [30]int8     x2 (encoder)        -> []int8, one copy
    lengthBase        [29]uint32                      -> []uint32
    offsetBase        [30]uint32                      -> []uint32
    codeOrder         [19]int32    (decoder)           -> []int32
    lengthCodes       [256]uint32  (token)             -> []uint32
    offsetCodes       [256]uint32  (token)             -> []uint32
    huffmanEncoder.bitCount [17]int32                 -> []int32
    decompressor.buf  [4]byte                         -> []byte
    initFixedHuffmanDecoder lens [288]int32           -> []int32

The tables now live in `tables.mx` and are filled by `initTables()` from the
package's single init (deflate.mx). Before, `lengthCode` and `offsetCode`
materialised a 256-entry literal on every call - once per token in the encoder.

One trap, found by the differential probe rather than by reading:
`decompressor.buf` was only allocated in `Reset`, and `NewReader` and
`NewReaderDict` build a `decompressor` field by field without calling Reset, so
the first reader had a nil (zero-length) buffer and `f.buf[0]` was an index out
of range on the first stored block. Both constructors allocate it now.

The read target was written as `io.ReadFull(f.r, f.buf[0:4])` and is now
`io.ReadFull(f.r, f.buf)` - with `buf` exactly four bytes long the two are the
same, and round 201 measured that a subslice argument is NOT copied (see below),
so the change is clarity, not a fix. The nil buffer was the whole bug.

repeating letters, a mixed pattern, all zeros) at sizes 0, 1, 5, 100, 1000, 5000
and 70000 - which covers stored blocks, fixed and dynamic Huffman, the 32 KiB
window and the empty stream - produces compressed output byte-identical to Go
1.25.3 and round-trips every case to the original bytes. Before the two fixes the
probe crashed; with only the first fix it panicked "index out of range".

## Round 200: jpeg did not compile at all, and its quantization tables were read two bytes off

Two findings, in the order they appeared:

1. `image/jpeg` did not compile under stage4. `writeSOS` used the Go idiom
   `switch m := m.(type)`, which re-declares the parameter `m`; Moxie forbids
   shadowing, so the package had been uncompilable and therefore untested. The
   type-switch variable is `mm` now. This is why nothing had noticed (2).

2. With the package compiling, the encoder's output diverged from Go at the
   chroma quantization table: 597 bytes long in both cases, the same up to the
   end of the luma DQT, then moxie emitted `06 06 07 06 05 08` where Go emits
   `09 09 09 0c 0b 0c`. Those are the *luma* table's values scaled, starting one
   entry in - i.e. `e.quant[1]` addressed the wrong storage. `quant` was
   `[nQuantIndex][blockSize]byte` and `_unscaledQuant()` returned the same
   nested array type: array-of-array element addressing, the shape that broke
   P-224's tables (round 190). Converting both to `[][]byte` (and writing
   `e.quant[i]` rather than `e.quant[i][:]`) fixed it: the JPEG bytes are now
   identical to Go 1.25.3 for three synthetic images at 1x1, 8x6, 17x9 and 33x32.

Also converted: `_bitCount() [256]byte` and `encoder.bitCount`, `huffmanSpec.count
[16]byte` and the four `[16]byte` table literals in `_theHuffmanSpec()` (now
`[]byte`), `encoder.buf [16]byte`, and the decoder's `bytes.buf [4096]byte`.

The decoder's read buffer is allocated by both Decode and DecodeConfig, which
build a `decoder` field by field. Its `fill` still reads straight into
`d.bytes.buf[d.bytes.j:]`: round 201 measured that a subslice argument aliases,
so a temporary plus a copy-back would have been dead weight.


Still arrays in this package, and one open difference:

  * `type block [blockSize]int32`, the decoder's `quant [maxTq+1]block`, the
    huffmanDecoder fields (`vals [maxNCodes]uint8`, `minCodes`/`maxCodes`/
    `valsIndices` `[maxCodeLength]int32`), `dc [maxComponents]int32` and
    `_unzig() [blockSize]int32`. These need `block` to become a slice, which
    changes the dct/idct/scan signatures - its own change.
  * Decoded pixels differ from Go's decoder by 1..5 per channel on the same
    input bytes (moxie decodes low). The encoder is byte-identical, so this is
    the IDCT/dequantize rounding in the port, not the stream. It cannot be
    attributed with the legacy compiler as the oracle: `legacy/moxie` rejects
    `image/format.mx:37` with "format does not satisfy comparable", an unrelated
    pre-existing legacy-only error, so image/jpeg cannot be built by legacy at
    all. Recorded rather than papered over.

## Round 201: the encoding tables become slices, and a correction: a subslice argument is not copied

    base64.Encoding.encode    [64]byte   -> []byte (allocated in NewEncoding)
    base64.Encoding.decodeMap [256]uint8 -> []byte
    base32.Encoding.encode    [32]byte   -> []byte
    base32.Encoding.decodeMap [256]uint8 -> []byte
    base58 _b58()             [256]byte  -> []byte
    hex encoder.out           [bufferSize]byte -> []byte (NewEncoder)
    hex decoder.arr           [bufferSize]byte -> []byte (NewDecoder)
    hex dumper.rightChars     [18]byte   -> []byte
    hex dumper.buf            [14]byte   -> []byte

`Encoding` is copied by value in `WithPadding` and `Strict` (`e := *enc`); with
slices that shares the two tables instead of copying 320 bytes, which is correct
because they are written once in the constructor and never again.

Verification, all against Go 1.25.3:

  * base64: four alphabets (std, url, raw, rawurl) x 13 input sizes, `Encode`
    bytes and `Decode` round trip - identical.
  * base32: std and a custom lowercase alphabet x 8 sizes - identical.
  * hex: `EncodeToString`, `DecodeString`, the streaming encoder, the streaming
    decoder and `Dump` at 7+6 sizes - identical.
  * base58 has no Go analogue; `Encode("hello world")` is `StV1DL6CwTryKyV` and
    `CheckEncode("hello", 0)` is `12L5B5yqsf7vwb`, both confirmed against an
    independent Python implementation, and every case round-trips.

Correction. Rounds 199 and 200 explained two crashes by saying that a subslice
passed as a parameter is a copy. That is wrong, and the record should not keep a
wrong mechanism. A probe measured all four shapes:

	fillDirect(b[:])            -> writes reach b        (full subslice)
	fillDirect(b[2:])           -> writes reach b        (offset subslice)
	var r io.Reader = &sink{}   r.Read(b[2:]) -> writes reach b
	io.ReadFull(bytes.NewReader(..), b[:]) -> bytes land in b

So a subslice argument aliases in both direct and interface calls. The flate
crash was only the unallocated `decompressor.buf`; the jpeg `fill` rewrite that
assumed otherwise was reverted to the direct read, and its buffer allocation in
the two constructors is the actual fix. What IS true is that `copy(dst[a:b], src)`
is a compile error in user packages and that archiving a subslice into a value
that outlives the parent is what the "a subslice is a copy" rule is guarding
against - the restriction is a safety rule, not the runtime behaviour.

## Round 202: fmt, ascii85 and pem arrays become slices

    fmt.fmt.intbuf            [68]byte        -> []byte (allocated in newPrinter)
    fmt tailBuf               [6]byte         -> []byte{:0:6}
    fmt isSpace space         [10][2]uint16   -> []spaceRange built in the package init
    ascii85 encoder buf/out   [4]/[1024]byte  -> []byte (NewEncoder)
    ascii85 decoder buf/outbuf [1024]byte     -> []byte (NewDecoder)
    pem lineBreaker.line      [64]byte        -> []byte (Encode)

`isSpace`'s table was a nested array literal materialised per rune examined while
scanning; it is a `[]spaceRange` filled once by the package's single init
(scan.mx). The struct also removes the `[2]uint16` element type.

Verification: a differential probe against Go 1.25.3 covering 20 fmt format
strings (integer, float, string, byte-slice, width/precision/flag combinations,
`%U`, `%#U`, `%*d`), ascii85 at eight sizes with encode and decode round trips
plus the streaming encoder, and a pem Encode/Decode round trip. Every line is
byte-identical to Go except three, which are a pre-existing documented
divergence rather than a regression - see below. The same probe run against the
pre-change fmt produces the identical output, so the conversion changed nothing.

Open: fmt's string verbs are incomplete. `fmtBytes` deliberately ignores the
verb ("[]byte IS string in moxie. Always print as UTF-8 content"), so for both
`string` and `[]byte`:

    %q   "hi\t\"x\""   Go quotes and escapes; moxie prints hi<TAB>"x" raw
    %x   0102ab        Go hex-encodes;          moxie prints the raw bytes
    %q   "a\x00b\xff"  Go quotes;               moxie prints the raw bytes

`%v` for a []byte is raw instead of Go's `[1 2 3]`, which is the intended
consequence of the unified type; `%q`/`%x` are not, because they are well
defined for bytes under either reading. Fixing them means giving `fmtBytes` a
verb switch, which changes the output of every fixture that prints with `%q` or
`%x` - its own round, not a drive-by.

## Round 203: a link failure from stale per-compiler cache directories

`0a/mime_header_parse` failed its gate with

    ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: runtime.InitArenaRestore
    >>> referenced by internal_oserror.ll
    >>>   /home/mleku/moxie/cache/mxc-1.9.11-cc03d824-9c7193e9-linux-amd64/pkg/...

The build-id component of that cache directory is not the installed compiler's
(`...-752bc703-...`), so the link was pulling objects out of a directory written
by an older compiler binary. Deleting every cache directory except the current
compiler's (475 of 476, 87 GB down to 19 MB) made the unit pass immediately, and
the full gate that followed is green at 154/154.

This is the third cache-state failure this session: the dispatch fingerprint
(round 193), a stale fixture binary (round 195), and now stale object
directories. They are not the same bug - 193 was a wrong key, this one is an
object from another compiler's directory being linked - but they share a cause
worth stating plainly: the cache is a build input, and a cache directory that no
current compiler writes is still readable by the linker if anything names it.
Housekeeping is part of the build's correctness, not tidying up afterwards.

The tree was not at fault: no source changed between the failing run and the
green one.

## Round 204: netip's address inputs become slices; its byte outputs stay arrays on purpose

    AddrFrom4(addr [4]byte)   -> AddrFrom4(addr []byte)
    AddrFrom16(addr [16]byte) -> AddrFrom16(addr []byte)
    parseIPv4 fields          [4]uint8  -> []byte
    parseIP's IPv6 buffer     [16]byte  -> []byte
    net._v4InV6Prefix()       [12]byte  -> package []byte filled by init

Eight `AddrFrom16([16]byte{...})` literals in `net/addrselect` are `[]byte{...}`
now, and the sockaddr round trips pass `from.Addr[:]`.

`As4()` and `As16()` still return `[4]byte` / `[16]byte`, and that is the
decision, not an omission: their consumers are `syscall.SockaddrInet4.Addr` and
`SockaddrInet6.Addr`, whose layout is the kernel's, so those fields must stay
fixed arrays - and a slice-returning As4 would force a copy into every one of
them. `AsSlice()` is the slice form for callers that are not crossing an ABI
boundary. The rule this round settles is: **arrays survive only where a struct
layout is dictated by the kernel or another ABI**; everything else, including
address bytes in transit, is a slice.

I converted As4/As16 to slices first and reverted it before committing: the only
thing that exercises `addrPortToSockaddrInet4/6` is a real socket, those paths
are not in the 0a/0b/2 gate, and phase 8 needs a net/http fixture build long
enough that I stopped it rather than claim a verification I had not run. The
unverified change was removed instead of documented as "probably fine".

Verification, both against Go 1.25.3:

  * netip (98 lines): 17 addresses through ParseAddr/String/StringExpanded/
    Is4/Is6/Is4In6/Zone/BitLen, As4/As16/AsSlice bytes, Unmap/WithZone/
    Next/Prev/PrefixFrom, ParsePrefix/Masked/Bits/Contains, address comparison,
    AddrFromSlice for valid IPv4, valid IPv6 and a bad length, and
    MarshalBinary/UnmarshalBinary round trips - identical.
  * net (over the same code): ParseIP, To4/To16 lengths, IPEqual, IPv4(),
    IsLoopback/IsUnspecified, ParseCIDR with mask size and Contains, CIDRMask -
    identical.

## Round 205: mime's store was a read-only method's frame arena, so every extension pointed at recycled memory

`mime.TypeByExtension(".css")` died in `runtime[stringEqual]` during the store's
own init. The crash had been filed under the `[][]byte` corruption family and
suspected of sharing a root cause with archive/zip. It does not: it is an
ownership bug in the sovereign classification, and the `[][]byte` shape was
coincidence - the store's tables happen to be maps of byte slices.

`setExtensionType` mutates the receiver only through its maps:

    m.types[string(extension)] = mimeType
    m.typesLower[string(extLower)] = mimeType
    m.extensions[justType] = push(exts, extLower)

Both compilers decided whether a method is a *mutating* method - the predicate
that makes it borrow the receiver's sovereign arena instead of pushing its own
frame arena - by scanning for a `Store` instruction rooted at the receiver.
`ssaFuncHasReceiverWrite` (stage4) and `ssaFuncWritesReceiver` (legacy) look at
`*SSAStore` / `*ssa.Store` and nothing else. A map update is not a Store, so
`setExtensionType` was classified READ-ONLY: it got a per-function frame arena,
its parse results and every `push` growth landed there, and the store's map
buckets were left holding headers into a frame released when the loader
returned. `.css` and `.pdf` survived by luck; `image/gif`, `image/jpeg`,
`text/html; charset=utf-8` and the rest read recycled memory, and the key
comparison in `stringEqual` dereferenced the debris.

Fixed in both compilers, legacy first as wood law requires: a `MapUpdate` whose
map is rooted at the receiver counts as a receiver write. The walk was already
there for stores; this is the instruction that was missing from it.

The second half is the ownership transfer the arena model demands and the
compiler does not automate. With the classification fixed, the method's own
allocations land in the store's arena, but the *data* it is handed still belongs
to the caller's frame: `mime.setExtensionType` is called with subslices of the
loader's `bytes.Split` result, and `mime.setTypes` with a map built in
`_builtinTypesLower`'s caller. Storing those headers is a cross-arena reference,
which `docs/OWNERSHIP.md` says must not happen: "a pointer into one function's
arena must not be stored in another function's arena without going through
return". There is no automatic relocation for a store through a pointer, so the
store performs the transfer itself - `ownBytes` in `src/mime/type.mx` copies
into the receiver's arena, which is where a copy made inside a mutating method
lands. Without it the classification fix alone still produced garbage values
with correct lengths (`.gif` 9 bytes, `.html` 24 bytes, wrong bytes).

`mime/type.mx` also drops its last array: `var buf [10]byte; lower := buf[:0]`
is `lower := []byte{:0:10}`.

Verified against Go 1.25.3, byte-identical output: TypeByExtension for the built
ins and for case-folded and system-database extensions (`.css`, `.CSS`, `.PNG`,
`.jpeg`, `.Jpg`, missing, `.gz`, `.ttf`, `.webm`), ExtensionsByType sorted lists
for `image/jpeg` (4), `text/html; charset=utf-8` (2), `application/pdf`,
`text/css`, AddExtensionType with the `charset` default and its dotless-extension
