error, and the round trip through ExtensionsByType. The system database is
`/usr/share/mime/globs2`, 1334 entries.

The regression fixture `tests/regressions/should_compile/sovereign_map_store`
isolates the classification: a sovereign type, a method that writes only through
a map, and a loader whose error return gives it a frame arena. Against a compiler
built without the detector change it dies with SIGSEGV in `stringEqual`; against
the fixed compiler it prints `ok`. The loader's keys and values are literals on
purpose - a frame-local argument would dangle for the ownership reason above,
which is mime's own half of the fix.

Open, and now stated as its own class rather than as a `[][]byte` symptom: a
store through a pointer into state that outlives the frame has no automatic
relocation, so any package that keeps data it was handed must copy it into the
owner's arena. Every such site in the tree is a latent use-after-free, and the
compiler cannot currently tell one from a legitimate borrow.

## Round 206: phase 1b cannot run at all - the compiler's arena region table fills while type-checking the 45-package sweep

`tests/unitrun.sh --phases 1b` aborts before any code is emitted:

    mem    tc-in main rss=491MB ...
    panic: runtime error at 0x...: arena: region table full

`tc-in main` is the last package of the type-check phase of the sweep's single
45-package build, so the compiler dies at the transition into SSA build. 491 MB
resident across the closure's type-check arenas overruns the compiler's region
table.

Not caused by the map-update classification change: a compiler built from the
tree before it (`fe2fd3e7`) aborts identically on the same sweep, at the same
point. It has nothing to do with mime or net/http either - the sweep's targets
are not the compiler's own imports.

This is the phase that exists to catch a stdlib package that does not compile,
and it cannot report anything while it cannot run. Recorded as its own open
item: either the type-check phase must not hold 45 packages' arenas live at
once, or the region table needs a bound stated in bytes rather than in regions
(and a diagnostic that names what filled it).

## Round 207: archive/zip stored the caller's pointers; the writer wrote a corrupt directory from a dead frame

The zip bug had been filed as nondeterministic - seven runs in ten failed with
arrays, two in ten with slices, and it never failed under gdb - and parked as
part of the `[][]byte` corruption family. It is the ownership class, twice:

    Writer.Create -> header := &FileHeader{...}      header in Create's frame
    CreateHeader(fh) -> h := &header{FileHeader: fh}  fh kept by pointer
    Close() -> write the central directory from h

`CreateHeader` stored the caller's `*FileHeader` - for `Create`, a header built
in `Create`'s own frame by `w.Create` - and read it back at `Close`. Every
central-directory record was therefore written from whatever the next callee had
left in a released frame. That is why the symptom moved between runs and why
gdb (different allocation pattern) never reproduced it: the record content was
the debris of the previous call, not the header.

`ownFileHeader` performs the transfer the writer's contract already states
("Writer takes ownership of fh and may mutate its fields"): it copies the header
and every byte slice it carries into the caller's arena through the return path,
which is the one relocation the model provides. `CreateHeader` and `CreateRaw`
both own before they build the `header`.

The duplicate-header check went with it. Go rejects a second `CreateHeader` with
the same pointer (issue 11144) by comparing addresses; after ownership transfer
the stored header is a copy, and a freed frame slot's address is handed to the
next allocation, so the comparison fired on unrelated headers (`invalid
duplicate FileHeader` on a plain five-entry archive) and could never have caught
a real duplicate. It is dropped rather than made unreliable, and the comment in
`prepare` says so.

With the archive bytes finally correct, reading it back failed a second way:
`readDirectoryHeader` parses the name, extra field and comment into its own
frame arena and left subslices of that frame in the `File`. The frame is
released at return and reused by the next call, so all five entries read the
LAST entry's name - `e.txt` five times. Those bytes belong to the reader, and
the loop that keeps them is a mutating method of it, so the copies are made
there and land in its arena.

The package's scratch buffers are slices now (`fileHeaderLen`,
`directoryHeaderLen`, `dataDescriptorLen`, `directoryEndLen`, the zip64 record,
the 9-byte extended-timestamp field and the 28-byte zip64 extra); no array type
remains in `archive/zip`.

Verified against Go 1.25.3, byte-identical output for a five-entry archive that
exercises: a deflated entry, a stored entry with 5000 bytes, an entry with a
comment and a `Modified` timestamp (extended-timestamp extra field), a directory
entry, and a non-ASCII name (UTF-8 flag). Compared: the archive's length and
SHA-256, and for every entry its name, method, both sizes, CRC32, modification
time, comment bytes and the SHA-256 of the extracted body, plus one `OpenRaw`
read. Six consecutive runs of the probe agree, so the two-in-ten reproduction is
gone.

This was also the last item the `[][]byte` family was blocking. That family is
now three separate fires, not one: mime was a misclassified method (round 205),
zip was ownership of stored pointers (this round), and `bytes.genericReplacer`'s
32-bit pointer slot remains.

## Round 208: the replay of a trie built by a mutating method, and an empty replacement that was not one

`bytes.NewReplacer` with two multi-byte keys returned its input unchanged. It
had been parked as a "32-bit pointer slot" - the disassembly showed a node
pointer spilled into a 32-bit stack slot - and it is not that. Instrumenting the
trie shows the truth:

    inside makeGenericReplacer   self lookup found true  keylen 2  val Q
    after the return             lookup found false      the terminal node's
                                 priority reads 0

The trie is built correctly and then loses its deeper nodes on the way out. The
build was a METHOD on each node:

    func (t *trieNode) add(key, val []byte, priority int32, r *genericReplacer)

`add` writes receiver fields, so `trieNode` is a self-mutating type and the call
borrows the receiver's sovereign arena. Every node the insertion allocates
therefore lands in the arena of the node it hangs off - a tree scattered across
one group per node - and the root's group is keyed by the address of a node in
`makeGenericReplacer`'s frame. The replacer is built in that frame and returned,
so the codec copies the graph; the copies get new addresses and therefore new
(empty) groups, while pointers into the originals' groups are kept by identity
and those groups die with the frame that owned their receiver.

Nothing about it is 32-bit: the addresses in question are identical before and
after the boundary, which is why the same address read a priority of 4 in the
self-test and 0 outside - the block was released and reused.

Fixed in the source, not the codec: the insertion is a free function,

    func trieAdd(t *trieNode, key, val []byte, priority int32, r *genericReplacer)

so it has no receiver to borrow and every node it allocates lands in the current
arena - the frame the replacer is being built in. The trie is then one graph in
one frame and the return relocation copies all of it. This is the authoring rule
the sovereign model already implies, stated the other way round: a graph that is
built and then returned must be built in the arena it will be returned from, so
do not put the builder's methods on the nodes.

The second defect is a Moxie-specific one. `byteStringReplacer` used a nil
replacement slice as "this byte has no replacement":

    if r.replacements[b] != nil { ... }

Slice equality in Moxie is content equality, so `[]byte("")` is equal to nil and
an EMPTY replacement (`"a" -> ""`) was indistinguishable from an absent one:
`Replace([]byte("banana"))` returned `banana` where Go returns `bnn`. Presence
is its own table (`present []bool`), and every reader asks it.

That is the second time this session that a slice's nil-ness was used as a
sentinel (zip's duplicate check compared header pointers, and mime and zip both
treated a slice as something a receiver could keep for free). In Moxie nil and
empty are the same value; any code that distinguishes them is wrong by
construction, and the fix is always an explicit flag or an explicit copy.

Verified against Go 1.25.3 for eleven shapes, through both `Replace` and
`WriteString`: two multi-byte overlapping keys (`abcabc` -> `QcQc`,
`abcbabc` -> `QcbQc`), priority with nested keys (`aaaaa` -> `bc`), a deep trie
with single-byte keys at the root (`xyzyzz` -> `123YZZ`), an empty replacement
(`banana` -> `bnn`), an empty replacement mixed with a byte replacement
(`banana` -> `bNN`), the single-byte table (`abcab` -> `12c12`), one multi-byte
pattern (`abcabcx` -> `ZZx`), and that a replacement leaves its input untouched.
All identical, and `tests/regressions/should_compile/bytes_replacer` fails on the
old source at the first generic case.

With this, the `[][]byte` corruption family is closed: three separate defects,
none of them a layout bug - mime's misclassified method (round 205), zip's
stored caller pointers (round 207), and this one.

## Round 209: %q and %x on a string printed the string

`fmtBytes` ignored its verb entirely - "[]byte IS string in moxie, always print
as UTF-8 content" - so `Sprintf("%q", "hi\n")` printed `hi` and a newline
instead of `"hi\n"`, and `Sprintf("%x", "hi")` printed `hi` instead of `6869`.
Every fmt consumer that quoted a name or hex-dumped a buffer got the raw bytes.

The verbs are implemented where a string and a `[]byte` agree in Go, which is
where the unification leaves nothing to choose: `%q`, `%x`, `%X`, and `%v`/`%s`
as content. Other verbs now report a bad verb instead of printing the value -
Go reports one too, with its type name where moxie has none (`%!d(?=hi)` against
`%!d(string=hi)`).

What cannot be matched, and is now the only divergence in this area, is that Go
prints `%v` of a `[]byte` as its decimal elements, `[104 105]`. Rendering that
would render every `%v` of a *string* the same way, and `Sprintf("%v", "hi")` is
`hi`. The content reading wins; a caller that wants the element list asks for it.

Verified against Go 1.25.3 on a string carrying a NUL, a tab, a non-ASCII rune
and `<&>`: `%v`, `%s`, `%q`, `%x`, `%X`, `%#v`, `%10q` and `%.3q` are identical,
as are `%q`/`%x`/`%X` and `%s` on a `[]byte`, plus `Sprint` and `Sprintln`. The
two remaining differences are the documented `%v` element list and the type name
inside a bad-verb marker.

## Round 210: X25519 was a new curve per call, so every ECDH exchange failed

`crypto/ecdh.X25519()` returned a freshly allocated curve object:

    func X25519() (out Curve) { return &x25519Curve{} }

Go returns a package singleton, and the identity is part of the contract:
`PrivateKey.ECDH` and `PublicKey.ECDH` compare the key's curve against the
caller's and answer "private key and public key curves do not match" when they
differ. Two keys built through two `X25519()` calls never matched, so every
X25519 exchange failed - including the RFC 7748 section 6.1 vector, and
including `crypto/tls`'s key exchange, which builds the peer key through its own
`X25519()` call.

This is round 185's shape (the standard colour models were a fresh object per
call, so no model ever compared equal to itself) in a place where the failure is
a hard error rather than a wrong branch. The curve is a package singleton now,
built in the package's existing `init()` beside the NIST curves.

Found while converting `x25519ScalarMult`'s clamping buffer to a slice: the
buffer conversion is behaviour-neutral, and the RFC vector was the thing that
proved it - and then failed, for the unrelated reason above. Both are in this
commit.

The singleton was the second-best fix and is not the load-bearing one. Go's
`Curve` is a stateless namespace of operations, and the exchange compared the
two curve OBJECTS, so the answer depended on how a curve was constructed - a
fresh object per call failed, and an arena copy of a curve would fail the same
way for the same reason round 183's png encoder failed. `Curve` now carries an
unexported `kind()`, and `PrivateKey.ECDH`, `PrivateKey.Equal` and
`PublicKey.Equal` compare kinds. Verified by building the tree with
`X25519()` returning `&x25519Curve{}` again: the fixture still passes, so
identity carries nothing. The singleton stays for the other half - the
comparison Go's API invites at the CALL site, `key.Curve() == ecdh.X25519()` -
and the fixture pins that separately.

Verified:

  * RFC 7748 section 6.1 - Alice's private key with Bob's public key gives
    `4a5d9d5ba4ce2de1728e3bf480350f25e07e21c947d19e3376f09b3c1e161742`.
  * A two-party exchange where each key comes from a separate `X25519()` call
    now succeeds and both sides derive the same secret.
  * `io/fs.FileMode.String`'s 32-byte scratch buffer is a slice too; sixteen
    modes (plain, dir, symlink, pipe, socket, device, char device, setuid,
    setgid, sticky, irregular, an out-of-range bit and a combination) print
    identically to Go 1.25.3.

`tests/regressions/should_compile/x25519_ecdh` pins the exchange; against the
old source it fails at the first `ECDH` with the curve-mismatch error.

## Round 211: the secp256k1 byte APIs take slices, and the btcec port compiles for the first time

The `[32]byte` cluster was blocked on the out-parameter puns, and this round
settles the representation decision by just taking it: a 32-byte buffer is a
`[]byte`. A slice header passed by value writes the caller's backing (measured
in round 201), so nothing needs an address-of, and every `(*[32]byte)(x)` in the
tree disappears with it.

Converted:

    FieldVal.SetBytes(*[32]byte)     -> SetBytes([]byte)      (length checked)
    FieldVal.PutBytes(*[32]byte)     -> PutBytes([]byte)
    FieldVal.Bytes()  *[32]byte      -> []byte
    ModNScalar.SetBytes/PutBytes     -> []byte
    ModNScalar.Bytes() [32]byte      -> []byte
    feToBytes/feToLEBytes [32]byte   -> []byte
    VerifySchnorr/VerifySchnorrBytes (pubkey [32]byte, sig [64]byte) -> []byte
    SignSchnorr/SignSchnorrBytes     (seckey/msg/aux [32]byte, sig [64]byte) -> []byte
    PubKeyFromSecKey / ECDH / ScalarAddModN / CompressedPubKey -> []byte
    CustomNonce(auxData [32]byte)    -> []byte, and signOptions.authNonce
    zeroArray32(*[32]byte)           -> zeroBytes([]byte)

`VerifySchnorr` and `VerifySchnorrBytes` now have the same signature, because
string and `[]byte` are one type and the fixed-32-versus-arbitrary distinction
that separated them in Go does not exist here. Both names are kept so existing
callers keep compiling; one delegates.

**This is a breaking change for application code**: a call that passed
`[32]byte` values now passes the bytes (drop the `[:]`), and a signature comes
back as a slice. The in-tree caller, `crypto/bip32`, is updated.

Two findings while verifying:

  * `crypto/ec` (the btcec port) **had never compiled**. `curve.mx` compared two
    `FieldVal` values with `==`; a `FieldVal` holds its limbs in `[10]uint32`, so
    the comparison reached the emitter as one aggregate compare and clang
    rejected the IR: `icmp eq [10 x i32]` (an aggregate is not an integer
    operand). Nothing in the tree imports that package, so no build ever noticed.
    The comparison is `FieldVal.Equals` now, which the rest of the package
    already uses, and the package builds and runs. The compiler gap is real and
    separate: `==` on a pointer-free struct or array should compare field by
    field, and today it emits invalid IR. Recorded, not papered over.
  * `schnorr.CustomNonce` and `signOptions.authNonce` were the last `[32]byte`
    buffer in that package.

Verified:

  * **BIP-340 official vectors, all four tests green** (`moxie test
    ./src/crypto/secp256k1`): 8 sign vectors compared byte for byte, 19 verify
    vectors including every failure case (wrong parity, negated message,
    non-canonical x, s == n, R not on the curve), the radix-16 carry case, the
    Nostr round trip, and the non-canonical-X rejections.
  * **BIP-32 test vector 1**: `m/0'/1` for seed `000102...0f` gives private key
    `3c6cb8d0f6a264c91ea8b5030fadaa8e538b020f0a387421a12de9319dc93368` and
    chain code `2a7857631386ba23dacac34180dd1983734e444fdbf774041578e9b6adb37c19`,
    exactly the published values. That path exercises both the hardened branch
    (`ScalarAddModN`) and the non-hardened one (`CompressedPubKey`).
  * **btcec, first run ever**: ECDSA sign/verify, a rejected wrong hash, a DER
    serialize/parse round trip, schnorr sign/verify and a rejected wrong hash.
  * **Cross-check**: 24 BIP-340 signatures (8 keys x 3 messages, aux varied) from
    the btcec port are byte-identical to the standalone implementation's, and
    the standalone verifier accepts all of them. Two independent implementations
    of the same spec agreeing is the strongest check available in-tree, since
    Go's standard library has no secp256k1.

## Round 212: `==` on an array emitted one icmp on the aggregate, which is not an integer

`crypto/ec` was the first package ever to compare a value containing a
fixed-size array, and the module clang refused was:

    %sf6 = icmp eq [10 x i32] %sf4, %sf5
    error: icmp requires integer operands

`FieldVal` keeps its limbs in `[10]uint32`, so `point.X == inf.X` reached
ir_binop's array branch, which had this:

    if et == "ptr" || e.intBits(et) > 0 {
        // An array of scalars is one integer of element-width times length;
        // compare it whole.
        ... icmp <aggregate>
    }

The comment's premise is false in LLVM: `icmp` takes scalars and vectors, never
a plain aggregate, whatever its element width. The shortcut was unreachable
until an array comparison was actually compiled, and no array comparison had
ever been compiled - which is why a package that does not build survived
unnoticed.

The branch now always compares element-wise, which is what the spec says (array
values are equal when their corresponding elements are equal) and what
`legacy/compiler`'s `createBinOp` has done in its `*types.Array` case all along.
So this is a stage4-only divergence; the legacy side needed no change.

The cost is one compare per element: a `[32]byte` key comparison is 32 icmps and
an and-chain instead of a memcmp. That is a reason to keep converting fixed-size
byte buffers to slices, where `==` reaches `runtime.sliceEqual`, not a reason to
resurrect a shortcut LLVM never accepted.

Verified with `tests/regressions/should_compile/value_equality`, which compares a
struct whose fields are arrays (32 bytes, four words, ten 32-bit words with the
high bits set) and nested structs, and which fails to build on the previous
compiler with `icmp requires integer operands` and prints `ok` on this one. The
bootstrap reached its fixpoint (s4b == s4c) with the change in.

## Round 213: an array was sized as `(n-1)*align + size`, which is not the stride

The type descriptor carries each struct field's byte offset and the struct's
size, and the codec relocates values by them. stage4 computed those sizes itself:

    case *Array:
        es := typeDescSize(tt.Elem)
        ea := typeDescAlign(tt.Elem)
        return (n-1)*ea + es

That is the size of an array only when an element's size equals its alignment.
It is right for `[32]byte`, `[4]uint64`, `[3]uint8` - every array whose elements
are scalars - which is why it survived. For `[3][]T` it is 32 bytes short: a
slice is 24 bytes with 8-byte alignment, so the elements stride by 24 and the
array is 72 bytes, not 40. The descriptors of zstd's `Reader` were therefore:

    seqTables       200        (both agree)
    seqTableBits    240        LLVM: 272
    seqTableBuffers 248        LLVM: 280
    fseScratch      288        LLVM: 352
    checksum        312        LLVM: 376     struct size 376 vs LLVM's 432

The compiled code used LLVM's offsets and the codec used the descriptor's, so
relocating a `Reader` wrote its `checksum` state 64 bytes away from where the
decoder read it: `reset` then cleared a 32-byte buffer whose header it had read
out of an unrelated field, and zstd's first decoded frame died in memset on a
nil pointer with a length of 4 MB.

The size is `n * stride`, with the stride the element size rounded up to the
element alignment, and the descriptor now says 432 for `Reader` like LLVM does.
Legacy compares cleanly here for a structural reason worth stating: it asks LLVM
for the layout (`targetData.ElementOffset` and `TypeStoreSize`) instead of
recomputing it, so it cannot drift. stage4 emits text and has no target data, so
the arithmetic is unavoidable - which is why it needs a test that compares the
two, and now has one.

Verified: `tests/regressions/should_compile/array_of_slices_layout` holds a
struct with `[3][]uint16`, `[3]uint8`, `[3][]uint16`, a slice and a nested struct
with its own slices, built in a frame and returned so the codec relocates all of
it. Against the previous compiler it fails ("scalars wrong" - the fields after
the arrays land somewhere else); against this one it prints ok. The bootstrap
reached its fixpoint (s4b == s4c).

## Round 214: zstd's checksum state is built once, in the constructor, and its buffers are slices

`xxhash64` held `v [4]uint64` and `buf [32]byte`, and the trailing struct-field
shift above is what actually broke the decoder - but the buffers are slices now
too, and the state's storage is allocated in `newXxhash64`, called from
`NewReader`, rather than lazily inside `reset`.

The reason is the ownership rule in its struct-field form: `reset` mutates the
receiver, so a lazy `xh.buf = []byte{:32}` inside it lands in the receiver's
sovereign arena - and the receiver is `&r.checksum`, an address inside a Reader
that was *relocated* into the caller's arena when `NewReader` returned. The
group would be keyed by the address of the frame copy and die with that frame,
leaving the caller's Reader holding a pointer into a dead arena. Building the
state in the constructor puts it in `NewReader`'s frame, so the return
relocation carries it along with everything else. Same shape as md5/sha1's
`newDigest`, for the same reason.

Verified against frames from `zstd --check`:

  * a 3.6 KB text at `-19` and at `-1`: both decode to SHA-256
    `458dad51...` which is the source file's;
  * a 366 KB file at `-19` and at `-3` (multi-block): both decode to
    `ab9265fb...`;
  * a frame with one byte of its XXH64 trailer flipped is rejected with
    "invalid checksum: got 0x1bedee68 want 0xe4edee68" - the checksum is
    computed and compared, so the slice-backed digest state is exercised, not
    bypassed.

## Round 215: poly1305's buffering scratch is a slice, and a zero MAC has no scratch

`poly1305`'s byte API took pointers to fixed arrays (`Sum(out *[16]byte, ...)`,
`New(key *[32]byte)`, `(*mac).Sum(out *[16]byte)`), and `macGeneric` buffered its
message chunk in `buffer [TagSize]byte`. All of it is `[]byte` now, allocated by
`newMACGeneric`.

That last part is where the trap was. `New` built `&MAC{}` and called
`initialize` on the state directly, never going through `newMACGeneric`, so the
buffer field was a nil slice: every buffered chunk of the message was silently
dropped. The tag came out stable, Seal and Open agreed with each other, and a
flipped tag was still rejected - the only thing that could see it was the
published vector:

    RFC 8439 2.5.2   got df33cbbee5c281caf23e2a6065f8a2f4
                     want a8061dc1305136c6c22b8baf0c0127a9

This is flate's shape (round: `decompressor.buf` allocated only in `Reset`, so
the constructors that build the struct field by field got a nil buffer): a
buffer that stops being inline padding and becomes an allocated slice needs
every constructor to allocate it, and the zero value stops being usable.

`New` goes through `newMACGeneric` now. Verified:

  * RFC 8439 2.5.2 poly1305 tag `a8061dc1305136c6c22b8baf0c0127a9`, Verify
    accepting it and refusing the last byte changed.
  * RFC 8439 2.8.2 AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305: the 114-byte ciphertext and the
    16-byte tag byte-identical to the RFC (so chacha20, poly1305, the AAD
    padding and the length framing are all in play), Open round-tripping, and a
    frame with one tag byte flipped refused.

`tests/regressions/should_compile/poly1305_aead` holds both vectors; with `New`
reverted to the direct-initialize form it fails on the tag, which is exactly the
bug the vectors exist to catch.

## Round 216: an index into an array reached through a pointer stepped by the element, not the array

jpeg's decoder read chroma from the luma quantization table. `decoder.quant` is
`[maxTq + 1]block` with `block [blockSize]int32`, and `reconstructBlock` does

    qt := &d.quant[d.comp[compIndex].tq]

so the address of one `block` inside an array of blocks is formed through a
struct field. Every chroma block was dequantized with `quant[0]`'s numbers read
at a 4-byte step: a 1x1 red image decoded to `c3 19 1a` where Go gives
`fe 00 00`. The encoder was byte-identical to Go all along (round 200), so this
was the decoder, and round 200 recorded the 1..5-per-channel difference as
unattributed IDCT rounding. It was not rounding - the luma plane was exact and
only Cb/Cr were wrong, which a plane-level differential against Go showed in one
run (`Y` identical for all 12 images, `C` wrong for all of them).

The wrong IR, for `&h.q[i]` over a struct field `q [4][8]int32`:

    %t55 = getelementptr inbounds {[4 x [8 x i32]]}, ptr %t1, i32 0, i32 0
    %t56 = getelementptr inbounds [8 x i32], ptr %t55, i32 0, i32 %t54

The second GEP steps `i` elements of `[8 x i32]`, i.e. 4 bytes per step, so
`&h.q[1]` pointed at `h.q[0][1]`. `emitIndexAddr` decides whether the indexed
base is an array by looking at the index operand's own type, plus two special
cases (an alloca, a load from an addressable chain). A base whose type is
`*[N]E` - a struct field, a `*[N]E` parameter, a loaded pointer - matched none
of them and fell through to the branch that treats the base as a pointer to a
single element, whose GEP source type is `[8 x i32]`.

The fix is a branch before that machinery: when the base's type is `*[N]E` and
the index is not a slice or a byte step, GEP the array type itself with
`i32 0, <index>`. That is the address of an element of the array, whatever
route the pointer took to get there, and it turns the four cases above into one
shape. The branch emits no alloca, so it also cannot re-enter the per-iteration
frame growth the load-forwarding case exists to avoid.

legacy never had this: it builds the GEP with `CreateGEP` from the pointee type
LLVM already knows, so there is nothing to mirror. Measured rather than assumed:
`legacy/moxie` builds the fixture below and prints every address correctly.

Verified:

  * `tests/regressions/should_compile/nested_array_field_addr.mx` checks the
    address of a row reached four ways - a struct field, a pointer to the
    struct, a `*[n]row` parameter, a pointer loaded from a variable - plus a
    write-back through the address, a plain local array and a slice of arrays.
    On the previous compiler it fails at the first check (`got 1 want 1000`);
    on this one it prints `ok`.
  * `image/jpeg`: 3 synthetic images x 4 sizes (1x1, 8x6, 17x9, 33x32) encode
    byte-identically to Go 1.25.3 and now decode byte-identically as well, both
    per-plane Y/Cb/Cr and as RGBA pixels. Before the fix all 8 multi-component
    cases differed in Cb and Cr; after it all 24 lines match.
  * The bootstrap reached its fixpoint (s4b == s4c) with the change in.

The decoder still holds `block`, `quant`, `huffLUT` and the huffman tables as
arrays; that conversion is unaffected by this and remains open.

## Round 217: a value that fits in a pointer is packed INTO the interface slot, not boxed behind one

The interface representation is `{typecode, value}` with one word for `value`,
and a concrete value that fits in that word is stored *in* it. The shared
runtime decides the representation from the type's size in two places and in
the same way, so this is not a stage4 convention that could drift:

    codecEncodeIfacePayload   t.Size() > PtrSize -> iface.value is a pointer
    RelocMarkIface            t.Size() > PtrSize -> mark the boxed pointee
    RelocFixupIface           t.Size() > PtrSize -> translate the pointer

legacy's `emitPointerPack` packs by `TypeAllocSize <= PtrSize` as well. stage4
packed only *scalars* inline and boxed every aggregate with `runtime.alloc`,
whatever its size - so a four-byte struct in an interface was a pointer to a
box in the returning frame's arena, and the relocator, reading the slot as the
value itself, neither forwarded the box nor fixed the pointer. The interface
dangled.

The failure mode is worth recording because it is silent for a while: the
freed frame's memory is not reused immediately, so the same program prints the
right answer inside one package and starts printing garbage as soon as the
value crosses a package boundary and a return. Reduced to three packages -
`lib` boxes a `Colour{1,2,3,4}` into `[]Color` and returns it, `main` passes it
on, `other` dispatches `RGBA()` - the receiver arrives as `0xf7fdec20` and the
call faults. The same shape is why a `[]color.Color` built from
`color.RGBA{...}` *values* crashed `gif.Encode` while a palette of
`&color.RGBA{...}` worked: the pointer spelling stores a real pointer, the value
spelling is inline, and only the second one was boxed.

`image/gif` was never exercised before this, which is the same reason round
200's jpeg encoder bug survived: an unbuilt package hides every bug in it. The
encoder and decoder are now byte-identical to Go 1.25.3 for four paletted
images (41, 51, 60 and 107 bytes) and round-trip their indices.

The fix decides the representation from the type's store size in stage4 the way
legacy and the runtime do (`ifaceInlineSize`), and unpacks on every consumer
side: dispatch receivers (`materializeIfaceValue`), boxing of concrete method
arguments, and both type-assertion forms. A small aggregate is packed by
storing it into a zeroed pointer word and reading that word back, which is
exactly what legacy's `emitPointerPack` does through its typed alloca; the
unpack never dereferences the slot, so a failed comma-ok assertion or a nil
interface still yields the zero value.

Verified:

  * `tests/regressions/should_compile/iface_inline_box` (lib + main) boxes a
    four-byte struct in one package, returns it, dispatches from two other
    packages, and asserts both the value and the pointer form. On the previous
    compiler it dies with SIGSEGV; on this one it prints `ok`, and legacy
    builds and runs it identically.
  * Nine interface shapes - value and pointer boxing, single and comma-ok
    assertion of a four-byte struct, a 24-byte struct and a four-byte array,
    wrong-type and nil assertions - print byte-identical output under
    legacy and stage4.
  * The whole image stack stays byte-identical to Go 1.25.3: jpeg encode and
    decode (12 images, per-plane and RGBA), png encode and decode (12 images),
    gif encode and decode (4 paletted images).
  * The bootstrap reached its fixpoint (s4b == s4c) with the change in.

## Round 218: jpeg's coefficient blocks and huffman tables are slices, and two traps that found

The last arrays in `image/jpeg`:

    type block [blockSize]int32            -> type block []int32 (+ newBlock)
    decoder.quant      [maxTq+1]block      -> []block, built by newDecoder
    decoder.progCoeffs [maxComponents][]block -> [][]block
    decoder.comp       [maxComponents]component, decoder.tmp [2*blockSize]byte
    huffman.lut/vals/minCodes/maxCodes/valsIndices -> slices, built by newHuffman
    encoder.huffLUT    [4][]uint32         -> [][]uint32
    applyBlack's       [4]struct{src,stride} -> []channelTranslation

`block` becoming a slice is what turns the fixed tables into constructor work:
the huffman tables and the quantization tables are now allocated by
`newDecoder` (which `Decode` and `DecodeConfig` call), so the return relocation
carries them in one move instead of a mutating method allocating them lazily
into the decoder's sovereign arena.

Two traps, both only reachable once `block` was no longer an array:

1. `qt := &d.quant[d.comp[compIndex].tq]` was a pointer to a *block array* in
   Go, where `qt[zig]` indexes its elements. With `block` a slice it is a
   pointer to a *slice header*, and `qt[zig]` indexes the header.
   **stage4 accepted it** and emitted `mul i32 %value, %slice` - clang rejected
   the module with `'%t35' defined with type '{ ptr, i64, i64 }' but expected
   'i32'`. Go itself rejects `p[i]` for `p *[]T` ("cannot index p"), so this is
   a stage4 typechecker gap as well as a source fix: `qt` is the table value
   now. Recorded as open work below.

2. `progCoeffs[sComp] = []block{:n}` was a single allocation in Go, because an
   array of arrays carries its storage inline. A slice of blocks is n empty
   slice headers, so the progressive path panicked with "index out of range" on
   the first coefficient write (`b[0] = dc[sComp] << al` with `len(b) == 0`).
   `newProgCoeffs` allocates in a free function - one block per set and the
   whole graph returned in one move - and the same shape applies to every
   "array of arrays" that becomes a "slice of slices": the storage has to be
   allocated per element.

Verified against Go 1.25.3 on a corpus that the encoder differential cannot
reach, because Go's encoder writes baseline YCbCr only:

    cmyk.jpg  37x29 four-component with Adobe APP14  -> *image.CMYK, identical
    gray.jpg  23x17 grayscale                        -> *image.Gray, identical
    prog.jpg  37x29 progressive 4:2:0                -> *image.YCbCr, identical
    sub422    31x21 4:2:2                            -> identical
    sub444    31x21 4:4:4                            -> identical

So the progressive refine/reconstruct path and the CMYK four-plane interleave
have a reference for the first time. The 12-image encode+decode differential
and the per-plane Y/Cb/Cr differential are unchanged (0 differing lines), and
`tests/regressions/should_compile/jpeg_progressive_cmyk.mx` embeds the
progressive and CMYK files with Go's expected pixels so the gate keeps both
paths covered.

Open from this round: stage4 accepts an index on a pointer-to-slice
(`p[i]` for `p *[]T`), which Go rejects; it emits an index into the slice
header. It should be rejected in both compilers.

## Round 219: indexing a pointer-to-slice is a compile error, and external data binds as a slice

Two compiler changes, both found by the jpeg conversion in round 218.

**1. `p[i]` where `p` is `*[]T`.** Go rejects the expression ("cannot index p");
both Moxie compilers accepted it and left the meaning to codegen. stage4's
index builder checked `isIndexable(t.Base)` - the pointee - so `*[]T` passed and
the index went into the slice *header*: after `quant` became `[]block`,
image/jpeg's `qt := &d.quant[tq]; qt[zig]` emitted

    %t35 = load {ptr, i64, i64}, ptr %t34     ; a slice, not a scalar
    %t36 = mul i32 %t31, %t35                 ; clang: expected 'i32'

`isIndexable`'s own `*Pointer` case no longer recurses either: only a
pointer-to-array is indexable, which is what `*[2]byte` writes in syscall need.
legacy rewrote the same expression through go/types, so it already rejected the
*source* - but `moxieAssignable`'s restriction pass never saw it, and the
`isIndexableType` mirror in `legacy/compiler/restrict.go` had the same recursion.
Both sides are fixed, and `tests/restrictions/reject_index_pointer_to_slice.mx`
names the rule (`// expected: cannot index`).

**2. `//:linkdata <len> <symbol>`.** A package-level `[]byte` can be bound to
data the link step supplies instead of storage the package defines:

    //:linkdata 48 go:fipsinfo
    var Linkinfo []byte

The compiler builds the slice header itself - data pointer is the symbol, `len`
is the declared length - so an external blob never has to be described by a
struct whose layout must match a foreign writer. The symbol is declared
`extern_weak`, so a build without a producer still links and leaves the pointer
null. `cap` is `-1`: the sentinel for storage that is not ours to grow, which
makes any `push` onto the binding fail loud instead of running past the symbol.

The binding is read-only by construction: a package-level var cannot be assigned
outside `init`, and a store through it is a package-global mutation. Writable
storage belongs to the application - created in `main` or by an initializer
function `main` calls, then copied into from the bound slice. `docs/REFERENCE.md`
has the directive documented in full.

`crypto/internal/fips140/check` is converted: `Linkinfo` was
`struct{Magic [16]byte; Sum [32]byte; Self uintptr; Sects [4]struct{Start, End
unsafe.Pointer}}` behind a `//:linkname`, the last "external array" in the tree.
It is now one 48-byte slice over the blob (magic 0:16, digest 16:48); the tail's
layout depends on the target's pointer width and nothing in Moxie computes a FIPS
digest. legacy sees the directive as `//go:linkdata` because the loader rewrites
`//:` pragmas wholesale, and its mirror emits the same header through
`getLLVMRuntimeType("_string")`.

Verified:

  * the restriction fixture is rejected by stage4 (`invalid operation: cannot
    index *[]byte`) and by legacy (`cannot index p (variable of type *[]byte)`),
    and was accepted by the previous stage4;
  * a probe against `crypto/internal/fips140/check` prints `len 48 cap -1`, and
    the binary carries `go:fipsinfo` as a WEAK UND symbol; `leak` of the data is
    a null dereference by design until something defines the blob (recorded, not
    hidden - a defined producer is future work);
  * a 46-bucket blank-import sweep over all 271 stdlib packages produces an
    *identical* failure set under the previous and the new compiler, so nothing
    in the tree relied on indexing a pointer-to-slice. The sweep also measured
    the pre-existing failures that block phase 1b, one place instead of a
    narrative: `net` (arena: region table full), `text` (src/text/scanner casts
    i32 to a slice), `time` (undefined `time.initRegisterLoadFromEmbeddedTZData`),
    `os`/`runtime` (duplicate symbols), `debug` (':=' inside a loop in a
    self-mutating method), `html` (syntax error), `builtin` (sovereign borrow
    stack overflow), `container`/`log` (no reason given), `syscall` and
    `internal` (import paths that still name `src/...`);
  * the bootstrap reached its fixpoint (s4b == s4c).

## Round 220: ed25519's key bytes are slices, pinned to a Go vector

`PrivateKey` held `seed [32]byte`, `pub [32]byte` and `prefix [32]byte`, and
`PublicKey` held `aBytes [32]byte` - fixed storage inline in a self-mutating
type, which is house style only for values that never leave their frame. They
are slices now, allocated by `newPrivateKeyStorage` / `newPublicKeyStorage` and
carried out by the return relocation. `aes/gcm`'s `CounterKDF.DeriveKey`
follows: its 32-byte output and 16-byte CMAC input are slices, and the context
parameter is a `[]byte` whose length is the caller's obligation (it was a
`[12]byte`).

Verification, because a key's bytes are the one thing a round-trip test cannot
check (both sides of the check come from the same code):

  * `tests/regressions/should_compile/ed25519_vectors.mx` pins seed 0x00..0x1f
    to the public key and signature Go 1.25.3 produces for the same seed and
    message, then re-derives the key from its seed and from its public bytes and
    checks the signature is byte-identical in each case.
  * The same two keys, four signatures and the verify/reject results were
    compared between a moxie probe and a Go program: byte-identical output.
  * The 79-package `crypto` bucket (every `src/crypto/...` package) builds.

`//moxie:embed_le` is stage4-only: the bootstrap loader rewrites `//:` pragmas,
not `//moxie:` ones, so a legacy build of `src/unicode/tables.mx` sees
zero-valued tables. Nothing in the legacy bootstrap's closure reads them, which
is why it has never surfaced; recorded here as a bilateral gap, and
`docs/REFERENCE.md` documents `//:embed` as the portable spelling.

## Round 221: ML-KEM was returning the wrong shared key, and it was two slice bugs

`crypto/internal/fips140/mlkem`'s key structs held their 32-byte seeds as
arrays (`d`, `z`, `rho`, `h`) and its encoders took arrays for the ciphertext
and message scratch (`[CiphertextSize768]byte`, `[messageSize]byte`). They are
slices now, allocated by `newDecapsulationKeyStorage*` /
`newEncapsulationKeyStorage*` and carried out by the return relocation. The
polynomial matrices (`[k]nttElement`, `[k*k]nttElement`) stay arrays: they are
fixed-size value matrices inside the key, not buffers.

Converting it exposed two bugs that made ML-KEM **return a wrong shared key for
every ciphertext** - it never failed, it silently took FIPS 203's implicit
rejection path:

1. **Go's `sliceForAppend` does not survive a function return.** The helper
   handed back the grown buffer and a tail view of the same buffer; the
   encoders wrote through the tail and returned the head. Each returned slice is
   relocated on its own, so the tail was a *copy*: `ringCompressAndEncode*` and
   `polyByteEncode` returned zeros. `growFor` replaces it - one slice, callers
   write through an offset - which is the same fix `crypto/cipher/gcm.mx`
   already documents for the same helper. What made this invisible for so long
   is that `moxie test` in-package kept the aliasing (the helper was inlined
   there), while the same code built as a dependency of an application did not:
   the package's own tests passed and every real user got a wrong key.

2. **A slice stored through a receiver pointer aliases, it is not copied.**
   `dk.rho = rho`, where `rho` is a sub-slice of a local `G`, left the key
   pointing into `kemKeyGen`'s frame. The bytes survived as long as nothing
   reused that frame - a small caller saw the right rho, a caller with a few
   more allocations saw garbage that changed between two reads of the same key.
   The fix is the ownership rule stated as an authoring pattern: the
   constructor allocates the key's storage, and the code `copy`s into it
   (`copy(dk.rho, rho)`, and `EncapsulationKey` builds a key with its own storage
   and copies dk's seeds in). **The compiler should have made this copy; see the
   open item below.**

Verified against Go 1.25.3 (`crypto/mlkem`, seed 0x00,0x03,...,0xbd):

  * `dk.Bytes()` and `ephemeralKey.Bytes()` byte-identical;
  * decapsulating a ciphertext Go produced yields Go's shared key
    `f789c54d4e79dbc0...` (before these fixes: `dfdb0058...`, i.e. J(z||c));
  * `tests/regressions/should_compile/mlkem_vectors.mx` pins the seed, dk, ek,
    ciphertext and shared key, and is an *application* so it takes the code path
    users take. It also round-trips ML-KEM-1024 (no Go reference exists for it)
    and checks that a tampered ciphertext takes implicit rejection: 32 bytes, no
    error, not the real key;
  * the 79-package `crypto` bucket builds.

Open item, high priority: **a store into a slice field through a pointer does
not copy the backing.** The documented rule is that a store must copy (there is
no relocation for a store through a pointer, only for returns), and the codec
violates it: `dk.rho = rho` aliased `kemKeyGen`'s frame. Every "field = local
slice" assignment in the tree is a latent dangle, and the workaround above is
per-call-site. A minimal reproducer is worth building next; the symptom is a
value that reads correctly until the frame's arena is reused.

## Round 222: measuring the gap behind ML-KEM's dangle - 189 free functions write through a pointer parameter

Round 221 fixed ML-KEM by copying into storage the constructor allocated, but
the mechanism deserves its own entry because it is not about slices being
stored: it is about **who is allowed to be written**.

The model says only a method receiver can be written, and that a write through a
pointer *parameter* is a compile-time error. It is not enforced. Both compilers
accept

    func f(p *T) { p.n = 5; p.buf = []byte{1, 2, 3} }

and the write reaches the caller. Scalars are fine, because nothing needs
relocating. A slice is not: the callee's frame arena is released when it
returns, and because the compiler does not treat a written-through parameter as
a relocation root, the stored slice keeps pointing into the dead frame. That is
exactly ML-KEM's `kemKeyGen(dk *DecapsulationKey768, ...)`, whose
`dk.rho = rho` pointed at `G` in the callee's frame: the key read back correctly
until the frame was reused, then changed between two reads of the same key.

Measured, not guessed: a scan for free functions with a pointer parameter that
write through it finds **189 functions in 76 files** - `internal/runtime/maps`,
`internal/trace`, `internal/profile`, `internal/coverage`, `internal/chacha8rand`,
`crypto/internal/fips140/*`, and more. So this is not a handful of sites that
can simply be turned into methods; enforcing the documented rule is a refactor of
its own, and the alternative is to make the rule obsolete.

Two coherent fixes, neither taken yet:

1. **Enforce it.** Reject a store through a pointer parameter in both compilers
   and convert the 189 sites to methods (or to an explicit out-parameter
   protocol). This is the model as documented, and it makes the mistake loud.
2. **Honour it.** Treat every written-through pointer parameter as a relocation
   root on return, exactly as a receiver is treated. Callers already expect the
   write to land; this makes the *contents* land too.

Option 2 is the smaller change to the tree and the larger change to the
compiler: the return relocation currently roots on results and receiver writes,
and would gain one root per written-through parameter. Either way the two
compilers move together (wood law).

Meanwhile the authoring rule for new code is the one ML-KEM now follows: storage
a callee hands to a caller through a pointer must already exist - the
constructor allocates it, the callee `copy`s into it - and never be a slice the
callee allocated in its own frame.

## Round 223: base64/base32 stream buffers and itoa's scratch are slices

    base64.encoder  buf [3]byte, out [1024]byte        -> []byte (NewEncoder)
    base64.decoder  buf [1024]byte, outbuf [768]byte   -> []byte (NewDecoder)
    base32.encoder  buf [5]byte, out [1024]byte        -> []byte (NewEncoder)
    base32.decoder  buf [1024]byte, outbuf [640]byte   -> []byte (NewDecoder)
    itoa.Uitoa/Uitox  buf [20]byte                     -> []byte

The stream structs are built by their constructors, so the buffers are allocated
there and carried out by the return relocation; the locals in itoa are allocated
per call, which is what an array was doing anyway.

Verified with a streaming differential against Go 1.25.3: for 16 input sizes
(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17, 31, 100, 1000, 5000) the encoder is fed
in 1-byte writes and the decoder is drained in 3-byte reads, and every encoded
string, decoded round trip and base32 encoding is byte-identical. The itoa
change is covered by the same build path as `strconv`/`fmt`: `Itoa`,
`FormatUint` and `fmt.Sprint` agree on ten signed and seven unsigned values
including the extremes.

## Round 224: what is left of the arrays, and the gate's slowest unit

The sweep has converted every buffer in the packages that run: jpeg, gif, png's
neighbours, zip, mime, fmt, bytes, poly1305, zstd's checksum, secp256k1,
ed25519, mlkem, base64, base32, itoa. What remains, counted by scanning every
`.mx` file for fixed-size array types (`[N]T` with N > 9, subscripts excluded):

    211  returned tables and value vectors  func _deBruijn64tab() [64]byte,
                                            internal/types/errors' code tables,
                                            x/text unicode/norm and bidi,
                                            zstd's fse tables
     63  runtime / syscall                 syscall's Stat_t fields, the allocator
    111  buffers still to convert          aes/gcm's [gcmBlockSize]byte block
                                            scratches and [256]byte product
                                            tables, sha3's state, coverage's
                                            16-byte hashes, xcoff's headers,
                                            net/http's http2 ping keys, zstd's
                                            huff/fse scratch slices

The last row is the same work as the previous rounds and continues one package
at a time. The first row is a **representation decision**, not a mechanical
sweep: `func t() [N]uint16 { return [N]uint16{...} }` is compiled into the
caller's frame for free, while the same literal as `[]uint16` allocates on every
call. These tables become slices only with somewhere to live that is not a
per-call allocation, and the tree already has the mechanism: a data file plus
`//:embed` (or `//moxie:embed_le` for a little-endian typed table) gives a real
slice with `len` and `cap` generated from the file and no allocation at all -
which is how `src/unicode/tables.mx` has always carried its tables. Doing that
per table means generating the data files, so it is its own round per package
family. `//:embed` is the portable spelling (legacy rewrites it to `//go:embed`);
`//moxie:embed_le` remains stage4-only.

The second row stays: an array that an external contract fixes - the kernel's
Stat_t layout, the runtime's own structures - cannot become a slice without a
shim at the boundary, and the boundary is where the layout is defined.

Gate note, measured: `0a/http_header_api` hit its 1800s unit timeout on a cold
cache (its `.bc` stage re-runs whenever the tree source hash changes, and the
clang object stage is serial because `adaptiveJobs` caps at
`(available/2) / 4GB` workers, which is 1 on a 14GB machine). Re-running the
same unit with the `.bc` cache warm passed in 1261552ms, and `tree-cleanliness`
passed. That is a machine-budget artifact, recorded rather than hidden, and not
a reason to widen the timeout.

## Round 225: a link-data binding refuses push, pop and resize

Round 219 gave `//:linkdata` slices an all-ones capacity so `cap()` reads `-1`
as the "not ours to grow" sentinel, and the documentation claimed `push` would
fail because `len >= cap`. That was wrong twice over: the runtime compares
`len` against the capacity as a `uintptr`, so all-ones is *huge*, and `push`
sailed through and wrote past the imported symbol. `pop` and `resize` had the
same hole from the other side - they only look at the length and the capacity,
and both accepted the sentinel.

All three builtins now test the sentinel explicitly:

    slicePush        refuses before the lazy-init/capacity arithmetic
    sliceCheckPop    takes the capacity as well as the length, refuses first
    sliceCheckResize takes the current length as well as the requested one

and the panic is `slice length is fixed: the storage is not ours`. stage4 passes
the extra capacity/length arguments (the pop check had never seen the capacity
and the resize check had never seen the length); legacy compares the capacity
against all-ones with `createRuntimeAssert` before its existing `pop`/`resize`
asserts.

Verified on both compilers:

  * `push`, `pop` and `resize` against `crypto/internal/fips140/check.Linkinfo`
    each die with that message (`len 48 cap -1` printed first), under
    `moxie`-built and `legacy`-built binaries alike;
  * ordinary slices are unchanged: a probe pushing, resizing, popping, lazily
    initialising and re-pushing after a shrink prints identical results under
    both compilers;
  * `tests/regressions/should_compile/linkdata_fixed_length.mx` pins the header
    (`len 48`, `cap -1`, and a local `//:linkdata 16` binding) and that normal
    slice operations still work - a panic itself cannot be asserted in a fixture
    because Moxie has no `recover`.

`docs/REFERENCE.md` now describes the three refusals instead of the wrong
`push` explanation.

The growth helpers had the same hole from a third side: `mxutil.Ensure`,
`Reserve` and `GrowCap` read `cap()` as an `int32`, so the sentinel is `-1`,
`cap(s)*2` is `-2`, the "at least 16" floor turns that into a 16-element
allocation, and `copy(nb[:len(s)], s)` then copies 48 elements into it - a
silent buffer overflow rather than a failed push. All three now refuse the
sentinel before any arithmetic, with the same message. Verified: `Ensure` on
`check.Linkinfo` dies with it, while `Ensure`/`Reserve`/`GrowCap` on ordinary
slices still grow exactly as before (2 -> 16 -> 20 -> 20).

## Round 226: the GCM block scratch and sha3's permutation state are slices

Two of the buffer clusters left by round 224.

**AES-GCM.** `[gcmBlockSize]byte` locals and `*[gcmBlockSize]byte` parameters in
`crypto/internal/fips140/aes/gcm` (both the generic implementation and the
asm-entry file, whose `gcmAes*` bodies are `panic("gcm: asm not available")`
stubs because no `.S` ships) and in `crypto/cipher`'s fallback: `H`, `counter`,
`tagMask`, `mask`, `S`, `tag`, `tagOut`, `expectedTag`, `partialBlock`. The
GHASH key parameter and `GHASH(key, ...)` are slices now, and
`gcmPlatformData.productTable [256]byte` is allocated by `initGCM`.

`ghash._ghashReductionTable()` was a function returning a `[16]uint16` table,
called once per `ghashMul`, which runs once per 16 bytes of input. As a slice it
would allocate on every call, so it is a package-level slice filled by the
gcm package's existing `init` (`initGhashReductionTable`). This is the pattern
for the returned-table arrays counted in round 224, short of a data file.

Verified: AES-GCM against Go 1.25.3 for 3 key sizes (128/192/256) x 6
plaintext sizes (0, 1, 15, 16, 17, 100) with 32 bytes of additional data - 51
lines of ciphertext, open and tamper-rejection results, all byte-identical.

**SHA3.** `Digest.a [1600/8]byte` is a slice allocated by `newDigest` (all six
SHA3/Keccak constructors and both SHAKE constructors go through it) and
`keccakF1600`/`keccakF1600NEON`/`keccakfStoreBack` take slices. The little-endian
pun is `(*[25]uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&da[0]))`; the big-endian branch reads the
lanes into a local and defers the write-back as before. `_rc()` was a function
returning the 24 round constants, called once per permutation - another
per-call allocation as a slice, so `rcTable` is a package-level slice filled by
the sha3 package's new `init`.

Verified: SHA3-224/256/384/512, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 plus a streaming SHA3-256
and SHA3-512 over 9 input sizes (0, 1, 63, 64, 100, 135, 136, 137, 1000), and
the sum-into-a-destination-then-keep-writing shape - 68 lines, byte-identical to
Go 1.25.3. `mlkem_vectors` passes again.

`Digest.Clone` was `ret := *d; return &ret` - a struct copy, which duplicated the
200-byte array but only *shares* it now that `a` is a slice. `sumGeneric` clones
so the caller can keep writing after `Sum`, so the clone's `read` permuted the
caller's sponge: `Sum(b)` corrupted the digest. ML-KEM caught it - `g.Sum` is
called with a destination everywhere in its key schedule, and `mlkem_vectors`
failed with a wrong encapsulation key while the one-shot SHA3 differential
passed. The sha3 differential gained the shape that catches it: sum into a
destination, keep writing, sum again, and compare against a digest fed both
halves.

Copying the state hit a second, sharper bug. The copy's `[]byte{:200}` was
allocated inside `Clone`, which is a **read-only method** on a sovereign type,
and a read-only method's returned pointers are treated as views into the
receiver's data rather than as a graph to relocate - so the allocation was not
copied out of the method's frame and the clone read a dead arena. It presented
as ML-KEM's encapsulation key changing between two runs of the same binary,
because the garbage was whatever the reused frame held. The allocation moved
into a free function (`cloneDigest`), whose return *is* relocated; the method is
a one-line call. That is the same rule round 221 hit from the other side, and it
is worth stating plainly: a read-only method must not return storage it
allocated, and a free function must.

The `:=` inside the absorb/squeeze loops had to be hoisted: with the state no
longer an array, the subslice in `x := subtle.XORBytes(d.a[d.n:d.rate], ...)` is
an allocation, and the self-mutating-method rule rejects a declaration inside a
loop. Both loops now declare `x` once above.

The 79-package `crypto` bucket builds, and `mlkem_vectors` passes deterministically
(three consecutive runs of the rebuilt fixture).

## Round 227: net/http's response buffers are slices, and what stays an array on purpose

    response.dateBuf   [29]byte -> []byte
    response.clenBuf   [10]byte -> []byte
    response.statusBuf [3]byte  -> []byte
    cookie.String      buf [29]byte -> []byte

The three response buffers are allocated by the `&response{...}` literal in
`readResponse`, because the writer appends into them through a zero-length
sub-slice (`AppendFormat(w.dateBuf[:0], ...)`), so their storage has to exist
before the first write.

Two clusters are now deliberately left alone, and the reasons belong in the
record rather than in a future round's surprise:

  * **On-disk and compiler-emitted layouts.** `internal/coverage`'s
    `MetaHash [16]byte` / `MetaFileHash [16]byte` describe the coverage file
    format, and `internal/rtcov`'s `Hash [16]byte` is a layout the compiler
    emits instrumentation against. Converting those is a format change, not a
    buffer change - it has to move both compilers and the file reader at once.
    `internal/xcoff`'s header fields are the same shape: an external file
    format, parsed field by field.
  * **ABI-fixed structures.** `syscall`'s `Stat_t` and friends, and the
    runtime's own structures, are written by the kernel or by the runtime.

The remaining fixed-size array types are therefore: these two categories, the
returned tables (round 224: they need `//:embed` data or an `init`-filled
global, the pattern sha3's round constants and GCM's reduction table now use),
and the polynomial matrices in mlkem/nistec/edwards25519, which are value
vectors inside the key structures.

## Round 228: append is gone in every spelling, and what the removal exposed

    legacy/build/patch-gotypes.go   _Append entry deleted, not renamed
    legacy/compiler/compiler.go     case "push", "__moxie_append" -> case "push"
    pkg/types/tc_object.mx          BuiltinAppend removed from the id list
    pkg/types/tc_universe.mx        "__moxie_append" removed from builtinNames
    _mxc_stage4/ssa_types.mx        ssaBuiltinID case removed
    _mxc_stage4/ssa_builder.mx      buildBuiltinCall case removed

`append` already read as `undefined: append` in both compilers, because the
patched go/types universe had its `_Append` entry *renamed* to
`__moxie_append` rather than deleted, and stage4's universe registered the
same internal name. The rename left a hole that was wider than the user-facing
ban: a source file could write `__moxie_append(xs, 1)`.

Stage4 compiled that and only failed at the link, because the SSA builder
lowered `BuiltinAppend` to an `SSACall` whose IR emitter has no `append` arm -
the call fell through to a generic call to a symbol that does not exist:

    _ = __moxie_append(xs, 1)
    >>> referenced by runtime.ll
    >>>  ./tmp/mxc-build-849233/runtime.bc.o:(runtime.run)
    mxc: linker failed

Legacy had the matching hole with working codegen: `__moxie_append` was a
mention in the same `case` as `push`, so it compiled and ran with full append
semantics. Two compilers, one name, two different failure modes - the
bilateral invariant applied to a builtin that was supposed to be gone.

Both entries are deleted now, so the name is undefined in both compilers and
there is no append lowering left to reach. `tests/restrictions/` pins it from
both sides: `reject_append_builtin.mx` for the user-facing name,
`reject_internal_append.mx` for the internal one.

Two documentation claims fell over while writing the reference section:

  * **push grows.** `slicePush` doubles capacity on overflow (measured: push
    into `[]byte{:0:2}` twice gives len 2, then a third push gives len 3
    cap 4); it only refuses fixed-length storage (`cap == -1`). The reference
    said overflow was a panic and the lazy-init floor was 32; the runtime
    uses 4. Both corrected in `docs/REFERENCE.md`.
  * **A sub-slice is documented as a copy and implemented as a view.**
    Measured against the current compiler:

        x := []byte{:0:8}; x = push(x, 'A', 'B')
        y := x[:0]              // len 0, cap 8
        y = push(y, 'Z')        // x is now "ZB" - the write landed in x

    `emitSliceOp` even says so ("View: sub-slice aliases the parent"). The
    write-through-subslice restrictions only cover `xs[a:b] = v` and
    `copy(xs[a:b], src)`, so `push` into a sub-slice is the remaining way to
    reach the parent's storage. The fix is the next round: an empty sub-slice
    must be a header that refers to nothing, and prefix trims used as cursors
    have to become reader/writer walks (`src/bytes/buffer.mx` and
    `src/bytes/reader.mx` are the model - an offset field over the whole
    buffer), because `x = x[n:]` in a loop copies the whole remainder per
    step once the copy rule is enforced.

## Round 229: the copy conversion's own damage, and 182 trims still standing

    legacy typecheck, 51 packages + crypto closure   clean
    stage4 build of the same main (/tmp/audit.s4)   links
    0a units re-run after the encoding work         8/8 PASS

The previous round's 245 sub-slice destinations were converted by a mechanical
pass, and a mechanical pass cannot tell a slice from an array or a byte from a
`[]edge`. What it produced compiled in the packages the 45-package sweep names
and broke everywhere else. The receipts came from the legacy compiler, which
type-checks with go/types and reports the exact expression:

    invalid copy: argument must be a slice; have sum384 (variable of type [48]byte)
    cannot use d.block (variable of type [128]byte) as []byte value in argument to mxutil.CopyAt
    cannot use newSorted (variable of type []edge) as []byte value in argument to mxutil.CopyAt
    invalid copy: argument must be a slice; have ev.base.args (variable of array type timedEventArgs)

19 sites in 16 files. Two classes:

  * **Array bases lost their `[:]`.** blake2b's blocks and key, the
    chacha20poly1305 keys, chainhash's `*Hash`, secp256k1's ipad/opad and
    keyBuf, tls's nonce fields, lzw's 8 KiB window, x/text's norm buffers and
    the trace package's `timedEventArgs`. Slicing an ARRAY is a view of fixed
    storage and stays one; only slicing a slice becomes a copy. The commit
    that flipped the rule has to keep that distinction, and this is the
    evidence for why.
  * **Non-byte element types reached for a byte helper.** `mxutil.CopyAt`
    writes bytes. hpack's table shift (`[]HeaderField`), bidi's `[]level`,
    punycode's `[]rune` insert, trace/mud's merge and trace/order's queue grow
    (`[]T`) became index loops.

Reading the audit output also surfaced breaks that had nothing to do with that
commit, in packages no phase compiled:

  * `src/html/entity.mx` held `entity = map[string]rune{` twice. A syntax
    error, so the whole `html` package had not compiled for some time - which
    is why `html/escape.mx` still had an `x` and a `dst1` shadowing the
    enclosing scope, and why its last `copy(b[dst:dst1], b[src:src1])` was
    still a sub-slice destination.
  * `text/scanner` converted a rune with `[]byte(tok)`, which is not a
    conversion that exists, and dropped the `[:]` from an array base.
  * `crypto/internal/fips140/bigmod` declared `d, c1, Y, c2` with `:=` inside
    the four multiplication loops of a self-mutating method.
  * `base32.DecodeString` decoded **in place** over `buf := []byte(s)`.
    `[]byte(s)` is not a copy in Moxie - string and `[]byte` are one type - so
    decoding a string rewrote the caller's bytes and then read its own output:
    a 5-byte string came back holding the decoded bytes.

### The cursor conversions that came with it

The remedy is the same everywhere: carry the offset, name the length, never
slice a buffer to move a cursor. Each file needed a different missing
primitive, so those were added first and are now shared:

    internal/bytealg   IndexFrom(a, b, from), IndexByteFrom(s, from, c)
    unicode/utf8       DecodeRuneInStringAt(s, i), DecodeLastRuneInStringAt(s, end)
    path, filepath     scanChunk/matchChunk/getEsc over (pattern, [cstart, cend))
    ascii85            EncodeFrom(dst, src, off, n), DecodeFrom(dst, src, sn, flush)
    base32, base64     EncodeFrom(dst, doff, src, soff, n), DecodeAt(dst, doff, src)
    bytes              Count/genSplit/explode/Index* over an offset, replacer lookup
    strconv            UnquoteCharAt(s, i, quote) -> bytes consumed
    net, textproto     leading trim counted, one prefix slice

The stream decoders also stopped truncating their own output buffer
(`d.out = d.out[n:]` per Read, which is quadratic in the number of reads) for an
`outOff` cursor, and ascii85's input compaction lost
`copy(d.buf, d.buf[nsrc:d.nbuf])` - a sub-slice source, so a temporary - for an
index loop.

### What is still standing, measured

A scan of every `.mx` file for `x = x[...:]` at brace depth inside a `for`
reports **182 sites in 120 functions**. They are not one problem:

  * **Quadratic, hot, worth converting now**: the parsers. `time.parse` (10),
    `csv.readRecord` (6), `encoding/hex` (1), `encoding/base58` (1),
    `net/netip` (3), `archive/tar` reader+writer (7), `archive/zip` (3),
    `compress/flate`, `compress/lzw`, `mime/multipart`, `mime/quotedprintable`,
    `internal/dag/parse` (6), `internal/profile`, `internal/trace` parser.
  * **Bounded to a few bytes or one pass**: `strconv/atoi`'s prefix trims
    (1-2 bytes, once per call), `net/url.unescape`'s error-path slice (3
    bytes), `xxhash`'s 31-byte tail walk, `encoding/asn1`'s BMPString.
  * **State cursors over an owned buffer**: `flate`'s `f.toRead`, `lzw`'s
    `r.toRead`, `mime/quotedprintable`'s `r.line`, `tar`'s `sr.sp`/`sw.sp`.
    These are one trim per Read call, not per byte.

The scan is the measure for the next rounds: a regex over every `.mx` file for
`x = x[...:]` at brace depth inside a `for`, with the loop stack popped when
the depth returns. It is kept here rather than as a test, so a red suite never
depends on a heuristic.

### The flip needs a window primitive, and that is the real blocker

Converting the trims is necessary but not sufficient. The copy rule also
breaks every place that hands a **tail of a buffer to a reader**:

    src/bufio/bufio.mx:117        b.rd.Read(b.buf[b.w:])
    src/encoding/ascii85          d.r.Read(d.buf[d.nbuf:])
    src/encoding/base32, base64   d.r.Read(d.buf[d.nbuf:nn])

After the flip each of those passes a temporary and the read lands in it.
`resize(buf, cap)` does not help: the free space is at the tail, not at index 0.
That is the "proper cursor mechanism ... it needs to be an api" the cursor
directive asked for: a way to name `buf[off:off+n]` as a *view* explicitly,
distinct from the copying `buf[a:b]`. Until it exists the flip cannot land
without breaking every streaming reader in the tree, so the order is:

  1. the window primitive (slice header over existing content, aliasing, by
     construction only - never as a side effect of `[a:b]`),
  2. the flip in both compilers: `s[a:b]` allocates len `b-a`, copies, cap
     `b-a`; `s[:0]` is a header that refers to nothing; array and
     pointer-to-array slicing stay views,
  3. the fixtures: empty sub-slice has cap 0 and pushing into it does not reach
     the parent; a write through a variable sub-slice does not reach the parent;
     `resize` still reuses a buffer.

## Round 230: the copy rule, measured against the tree that has to survive it

    legacy typecheck     51-package audit, crypto closure, io/image closure: clean
    bootstrap            s4a -> s4b -> s4c, s4b == s4c == 68d9bb99...
    math/big probe       Rat.Float64: 0.333..., 0.666..., 0.5 (as Go)

This round set out to flip the rule - a sub-slice of a slice allocates, copies
and takes cap = len - and built it in both compilers to find out what it costs.
The answer is in the tree now, in the shape of every site the flip broke, and
it is worth recording before the rule goes in, because the list is the work.

### What the flip is, in IR

A slice value in stage4 is `{ptr, i64, i64}` (`sliceType`, ir_types.mx:283).
`x := []byte{:8}` is one `runtime.alloc(8)` and three `insertvalue`s, so the
header is a value - registers or a stack slot - not an object. Today
`x[2:5]` is `extractvalue` x3, a `getelementptr` and three `insertvalue`s: the
header moves, the bytes do not. The flip makes that block:

    %n  = sub i64 5, 2
    %p  = call ptr @runtime.alloc(i64 %n, ptr null, ptr null)
    call ipt @runtime.sliceCopy(ptr %p, ptr %sp, ipt %n, ipt %n, ipt 1, ptr null)
    %y  = { %p, %n, %n }

and `x[:0]` becomes `{null, 0, 0}` (runtime alloc already turns a 0-byte
request into a 1-byte one; returning nil instead makes the empty header refer
to nothing, which is the rule the cursor directive asked for).

Both compilers were changed, bootstrapped, and run. What follows is what it
took to get a *compiler* to start, in the order the failures appeared.

### 1. `x[:0]` and `x[:n]` are the buffer-reuse idiom, everywhere

The runtime's own sovereign-group bookkeeping does

    nb := unsafe.Slice(sovRootAlloc(nc*8), nc)
    g.recs = nb[:len(g.recs)]

`nb[:len]` under the flip is a *fresh* slice with cap == len, so the capacity
just carved out of the root arena is thrown away and the next push grows
again: `slicePush -> alloc -> ArenaAllocTD -> sovAddRec -> push` recursed until
the stack died. Every such site is `resize(nb, len)` - same buffer, new length.
Sites: g.recs, g.slots, g.batchStart, a.sovGroupList, mxutil
Ensure/Reserve/GrowCap, mxregexp's grow, fmt's growBuf, bip39's padding grow.

### 2. A reader has to be given somewhere to write

Every buffered reader passed a tail window:

    bufio.Reader.fill        b.rd.Read(b.buf[b.w:])
    bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom    r.Read(b.buf[i:cap(b.buf)])
    ascii85/base32/base64    d.r.Read(d.buf[d.nbuf:])
    os, io/fs, io.ReadAll    f.Read(data[len(data):cap(data)])
    image/jpeg, png, mime/multipart, x/text/transform, pkg/syntax

Under the flip the read lands in a temporary and the bytes never arrive. The
answer is the one the cursor directive named - a scratch plus a forward walk
into the destination - so io gains

    io.ReadInto(r, dst, off, tmp)   tmp owned by the caller (bufio passes a field)
    io.ReadIntoN(r, dst, off)       scratch allocated in ReadIntoN's frame

and mxutil.CopyRange is the walk, eight bytes at a time through a uint64
register.

### 3. `copy(dst[a:b], src)` is never a fast path

24 sites, none quadratic, all wrong: math/big's tail shifts (natLsh has to walk
*backward* because z may alias x shifted up), flate's back-reference copies,
bufio's partial-write shift, base64's input compaction, h2's chunk advance,
x/text's prefix merge, image draw/gif rows, ed25519, chacha20, RSA. All index
loops or CopyRange now. `slices.mx`, `servemux121.mx`, `move_to_front.mx` and
`gcm.mx` already carried the comment explaining why.

### 4. The blocker: a function that writes through a window it was handed

math/big's recursive division does

    uu := u[j-B:]
    natDivRecursiveStep(qhat, stk, uu[s:B+n], v[s:], depth+1)

and the callee writes its remainder *into uu*. A copy there is not slow, it is
wrong: `Rat.Float64(1/3)` panicked "expected exactly 54 bits of result"
because the quotient came out of a buffer nobody looked at. The same shape is
natNorm's returned tail, and it is the reason the flip needs either

  * every such function to take (parent, offset) instead of a window - the
    offset rewrite this campaign has been doing call by call, and math/big's
    division recursion is the worst of them, or
  * a named aliasing constructor (`sliceview(buf, off, n)`) that both
    compilers lower to the header-only block, documented as same-frame-only.

The measurement is the argument: the flip itself is 15 lines per compiler, and
what it costs is this list, of which exactly one item (4) has no mechanical
answer.

### Reverted, not abandoned

The two compiler changes and the runtime's `alloc(0) -> nil` are out of the
tree again, because a half-applied rule compiles and lies. What stays is
everything above: the resize conversions, io.ReadInto, the copy-destination
loops, the 8-byte CopyRange, and the array views and non-byte loops from round
229. None of it depends on the rule; all of it is what the rule will need.

## Round 233: the register copy, measured - the byte assembly was the slow version

    bootstrap   s4a -> s4b -> s4c, s4b == s4c == d30278e5...
    gate 242    169/169 PASS, rc=0

Round 230 added CopyRange's eight-bytes-at-a-time loop as
LEPutUint64At(LEUint64At(...)), on the reasoning that LLVM folds the byte
assembly into one machine move. It does - when it can see the plain loads and
stores. Measured over 64 MiB through the package boundary it was worse than the
byte loop it replaced:

    byte loop                        64 MiB in 273 ms    245 MB/s
    LEUint64At -> LEPutUint64At      64 MiB in 361 ms    177 MB/s

Two calls the optimizer did not inline, with the eight shifts and ors on each
side still there. A uint64 store through unsafe *is* the machine move, and
unrolling it is what makes it fast:

    uint64,           8 B/iteration  64 MiB in  27 ms    2.4 GB/s
    uint64 x4,       32 B/iteration  64 MiB in   8 ms    8.0 GB/s
    uint64 x8,       64 B/iteration  64 MiB in   7 ms    8.6 GB/s

x4 is kept (x8 buys 2% for twice the block), with a byte loop for the tail under
32 bytes so every length is exact. This is the copy every offset-write in the
tree goes through, so the 34x over the byte loop is the number that matters, and
it is now a measurement rather than a claim about codegen.

Correctness for the new form: every length 0..80 through CopyRange, CopyAt and
CopyFrom with a non-zero destination offset; guard bytes on both sides verified
untouched; truncation when dst is short; a request starting past the end; and
lengths 100..140 that cross the 32-byte block at every remainder. 0 mismatches.

CopyRange is a forward copy, not a memmove. Overlapping ranges are shifted by a
loop that knows its direction - math/big's natLsh walks backward, bufio's and
flate's compactions walk forward - and there is a comment saying so.

(tag 30, UTF-16BE) parses in moxie and comes back as
Organization = ["BMP Org"], with the UTF8String fields next to it unchanged
(CN "bmp test"). That is the only way to be sure the tag-30 branch still reads
big-endian pairs after the change.

### Found while testing, not fixed

`x509.CreateCertificate` is not usable from moxie code today:

    moxie: codec arena escape: pointer into a transient frame arena preserved
    instead of copied (unknown-extent pointee); that frame arena is leaked for
    the pointer's lifetime

The call returns an error instead of a DER blob. Parsing is unaffected (that is
what the tree does - TLS servers verify, they do not mint), so this is recorded
rather than patched: it is a codec/relocation diagnostic, not an x509 one, and
"the compiler refuses a pointer into a dead frame" is the compiler doing its
job. The work is to find what CreateCertificate returns that has an
unknown-extent pointee (most likely a pointer into a `big.Int`-shaped local)
and make it own its data.
