                                                    rebuilt on every key expansion
    rsa/keygen.mx       _primes                    255 entries per key generation
    sha1/sha1block_arm64 _k                        4 entries per block (arm64 only)

All three are package-level slices now, allocated once at init in the root arena.

Measured, 20000 key expansions:

    AES-128   4093/4072 ms  ->  1626/1647 ms   (2.5x)
    AES-256   4504/4699 ms  ->  1961/1873 ms   (2.4x)

AES key setup is not a per-byte path, but it is a per-connection one: every TLS
handshake pays it, which is why a 2.5x here is worth more than a 10% in the
block function.

The pattern, for the rest of the sweep: **a slice literal inside a function is an
allocation on that function's code path.** If the function returns a constant
table, or fills a fixed-size schedule, the table belongs at package level and the
schedule belongs to the struct that owns the state. The next grep is
`return []T{` in `src/` and `pkg/`.

## Round 265: W11 - the child is created, and the matcher cannot reach it

Round 262 narrowed the ServeMux bug to "the leaf's pattern pointer is dead".
This round traced the matching itself, printing at registration, at
`matchMethodAndPath` and at `matchPath`:

    dbg set  node=0x…2c40 pat=0x…2910 str=[/smoke]     registration makes the leaf
    dbg mMAP node=nil          method=[GET] pat=[/smoke]   root.findChild(host) nil
    dbg mMAP node=0x…2a10      method=[GET] pat=[/smoke]   the host-level emptyChild
    dbg mPath node=nil         pat=[/smoke]                .findChild("GET") nil
    dbg mPath node=0x…2a90     pat=[/smoke]                the method-level emptyChild
    dbg mPath node=nil         pat=[]                      .findChild("smoke") MISSES

So the leaf is built and `set` stores the pattern (that print reads `[/smoke]`
correctly), and the matcher walks host → method → path correctly, but the
method-level node it reaches has no "smoke" child. The child was attached to a
node the tree cannot reach. `subtree-root` still works because a pattern ending
in `/` is stored as `multiChild`, not as a key in the child mapping - which is
why the bug looked like "only / matches".

The registration write in question is `n.emptyChild = newNode()` /
`n.children.add(key, c)` inside `addChild`, a mutating method on `*routingNode`,
reached through `ServeMux.tree` - a struct field of a sovereign type. The
isolated version of that nesting (a mutating method calling a mutating method on
its own field, then reading the field back) works, so the difference is the
owner: the node is only reachable through a pointer field of the mux.

Two candidate fixes were re-tried together this round - rootBytes for the child
keys and rootPattern for the pattern struct - and the trace above is WITH both
applied: the lookup misses anyway. So the keys are not the miss.

Next: print the parent node address inside `addChild` (registration) and compare
it with the node reached at match time. If they differ, the tree's
`emptyChild`/`children` write went into a copy of the node, and the question
becomes why the sovereign store-back of a node reached through a pointer field
loses the write. If they are equal, the mapping's slice header itself is stale
and the question is in `mapping.add`.

## Round 266: the rest of the per-call tables, and why a bulk rewrite is the wrong tool

A scan for the same shape found 27 more zero-argument functions that return a
constant slice literal, several on hot paths:

    tls/common.mx           _supportedVersionsList          409 lines, per handshake
    tls/cipher_suites.mx    two preference-order lists        48 lines, per handshake
    tls/defaults.mx         defaultCurvePreferences           23 lines, per handshake
    net/http/sniff.mx       _sniffSignatures                 128 lines, per sniff
    net/addrselect.mx       _rfc6724policyTable               57 lines, per dial
    crypto/rand/util.mx     _smallPrimes                      84 lines, per key generation
    crypto/des/const.mx     _permutedChoice2                  44 lines, per key setup
    image/jpeg/writer.mx    _theHuffmanSpec                   64 lines, per encode
    math/bits/*             _ntz8tab/_pop8tab/_rev8tab/_len8tab   per limb, on the
                            non-optimized path

Three attempts to rewrite all 27 with one transformer failed the same way: the
regex that finds `func f() []T { return []T{ ... } }` cannot tell a literal's
closing brace from the function's, so each attempt ate one brace per table and
the tree stopped parsing. Every attempt was reverted; nothing from this round is
committed.

What that leaves: the scan and the list are the useful part. The conversions are
mechanical but the tool has to read braces, not pattern-match lines - a small
brace-counting rewriter, or 27 hand edits in batches of five with the gate after
each. The verified hoists from rounds 263-264 (sha256, sha512, AES, RSA primes,
sha1/arm64, base58, asn1.NullBytes, gosym magic sequences) stay as they are.

The rule to apply at each site is the one this session has measured three times:
a slice literal inside a function is an allocation on that function's code path;
a constant table belongs at package level (once, root arena) and a fixed-size
schedule belongs to the struct that owns the state.

## Round 267: W11 - the child map stored the receiver in the value slot

`tests/netsmoke/muxmatch` at HEAD failed 7 of 12 registration shapes (every
shape whose last segment is a literal key; `subtree-root` passed because a
trailing-slash pattern is stored as `multiChild`). Instrumenting
`addChild`/`findChild` and reading the stored entry directly, without going
through the lookup:

    dbg add   parent=…3030 key=[smoke] empty=0 nent=0
    dbg raws  parent=…3030 key=[smoke] c=…3360 s0key=[smoke] s0val=…3048
    dbg set   n=…3360 pat=…2230 str=[/smoke]
    dbg mfind h=…3048 len=1 k=[smoke]
    dbg find  parent=…3030 key=[smoke] -> …3048 nent=1

`newNode()` returned 0x…3360 and `set` wrote the pattern into 0x…3360, but the
entry's value slot holds 0x…3048 - which is exactly `&n.children`, the receiver
`h` of `mapping.add`. The slot is already wrong when read back immediately after
the call, so this is the store, not the lookup: `n.children.add(key, c)` stored
`h` where `c` belonged. Every leaf the tree held was therefore an orphan node
nobody had filled in, and every literal-keyed pattern answered `pattern=[]`.

The store is `h.s = push(h.s, entry[K, V]{k, v})` in the generic
`mapping[K, V]` (mapping.mx). The same code in a standalone package - same field
order (including the 16-byte `Handler` interface field that shifts `children` to
+24), same sovereign nesting, same `SetCurrentArena(RootArena())` swap - stores
`c` correctly. A second symptom points the same way: passing `h` to a generic
helper declared `func maddr(h *mapping[K, V])` is rejected with "cannot use value
of type *net/http.mapping as *net/http.mapping", i.e. the package ends up with
two distinct types for one instantiation. So the defect needs the instantiation
inside the large package; it is not the code shape.

What landed is not a compiler fix. Children are now a concrete `childMap`
(`[]childEntry` up to 8, then `map[string]*routingNode`) declared in
routing_tree.mx, and mapping.mx is deleted: the container had exactly one
instantiation, sits on the per-request hot path, and the generics bought nothing
here. `muxmatch` passes all 12 shapes.

Open compiler item, recorded rather than fixed: a pointer-valued field of a
generic struct, written through a composite literal in an instantiated method and
carried across a sovereign store-back, can end up holding the receiver address.
The reproducer is a large package that instantiates the generic type; reads the
same shape from a small package are correct.

## Round 268: W9 - the element size of a spread push

The post-quantum hybrid key share was 1184 bytes of ML-KEM followed by 32 zeros.
Reproduced with the fixture's `CurvePreferences` pin removed, printing inside
`hybridKeyExchange.keyShares`:

    dst len=1184 cap=1184   src len=32 cap=133   src bytes 205 142 173 45 …
    out len=1216 cap=2368   out[1184]=208   out[1215]=0

The same two slices through a free function, `push(a, b...)` with `a`, `b`
parameters, produced the correct tail - so the push implementation was not the
problem and the call site was. Disassembling the cached bitcode settled it
(`llvm-dis-22 tmp/mxc-build-*/crypto_tls.bc`, at the inline `keyShares` push):

    %ap396 = ptrtoint ptr getelementptr ({ ptr, i64, i64 }, ptr null, i32 1) to i64   ; 24
    %ap397 = call { ptr, i64, i64 } @runtime.slicePush(ptr %ap391, i64 %ap392, i64 %ap393, i64 %ap395, i64 %ap396, ptr null)
    %ap401 = getelementptr inbounds { ptr, i64, i64 }, ptr %ap398, i64 %ap392          ; newPtr + 1184*24
    %ap402 = mul i64 %ap395, %ap396                                                   ; 32*24 = 768
    call void @runtime.memmove(ptr %ap401, ptr %ap394, i64 %ap402, ptr null)

and the inlined helper's identical push in the same function used
`getelementptr (i8, ptr null, i32 1)` and `getelementptr inbounds i8`. So the
element type was resolved to the whole slice type, 24 bytes, instead of `i8`:
`slicePush` allocated 2368*24 bytes, the length arithmetic stayed numerically
right (1184+32), and the memmove landed at `newPtr+28416`. Nothing faults - the
buffer is 24x too big - the share is simply written 27 KB away from where the
header says it is.

The element type comes from the destination's SSA type, and when that has no
element under it the emitter fell through to `llvmType(args[1])`, which for a
spread is the SOURCE SLICE, not its element. The destination here is
`priv.mlkem.Encapsulator().Bytes()`, an interface method result, and that is the
shape that reaches the emitter unresolved.

Fix (ir_call.mx): for `push(dst, src...)` the fallback is the spread source's
ELEMENT type - the builder has already checked that the two element types are
assignable, so it is the only sound inference. The non-spread case keeps its own
fallback, where `args[1]`'s type IS the element type.

Measured, same fixture, both `CurvePreferences` pins now removed:

    before   FAIL client handshake: local error: tls: bad record MAC
             (and a SIGSEGV on the second connection)
    after    ok   client handshake ver=772 suite=4867      (X25519MLKEM768)
             ok   echo 1024 bytes identical
             ok   wrong CA rejected: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
             tls_handshake ok

Bootstrap after the change: legacy -> s4a -> build-runtime -> s4b -> s4c, and
`s4b == s4c` (`a5252ae7…`). The fix is stage4-only by construction: legacy takes
the element type from go/types, where a `[]byte` expression always has its
element, so there is no equivalent inference to mirror.

## Round 269: time.Now costs 4.3 us, and that invalidates the W3b probes

W3b's per-call numbers were taken by calling `time.Now()` inside the code being
measured. That instrument costs more than the code: `time.Now()` is 4.3 us on
this runtime. The instrumented scanner run took 3.11 s for a loop that takes
0.37 s uninstrumented, so the six clock reads per `Scan` accounted for all of the
"per-Scan overhead" that round 255 attributed to the sovereign arena.

Measured with 200k iterations per shape, same binary, AMD64 musl static
(`/tmp/retbench`):

    function returning int32                                     1 ns
    returning a pointer to a parameter                           2 ns
    returning a struct with a pointer field, from a parameter    8 ns
    returning a struct with a pointer from a local literal      104 ns   codec runs
    returning a struct with a pointer from a callee             106 ns   codec runs
    returning (int32, []byte, error)                            20 ns
    indirect call through a function value, struct+ptr          21 ns
    time.Now()                                                 4300 ns
    time.Now().UnixNano() on a copy of a Time                    74 ns

What it is not: syscalls (strace -f -c over 400k clock reads shows 119 syscalls
total, so the vDSO path is taken), the generic codec boundary (~105 ns for the
same shape), `UnixNano` (74 ns), or the time zone (TZ=UTC, Europe/London and
America/New_York are identical to within noise; `Local()` alone does not load a
zone - only `Location.get()` does).

What it is: `time.Now`'s disassembly (`objdump -d --disassemble='time.Now'`)
calls `runtime.FnArenaPush(0x10000)`, `codecBufInit`, `codecEncodeValue`,
`codecDecodeValue`, `codecSetRetTransient`, `FnArenaPop`, `ArenaRelease`,
`time.initStartNano` (which itself calls `runtime.InitArenaRestore`) and
`time.runtimeNow` (two vDSO clock reads). Replacing `Local()` with a nil
*Location* in its return drops it to 3.3 us, so the `*Location` walk is about
1 us and the remaining 3.3 us is in the return-value codec machinery and the
clock read, not in any part that the earlier probes covered.

Sampling is blocked in this environment (`/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope` is
1, so gdb cannot attach to a running bench and perf is not installed). The next
step is an in-tree counter or a `-print-allocs`-style sample rather than an
external profiler.

Two consequences:

- **The scanner benchmark is unchanged and still unexplained**: 4 MiB of 64-byte
  lines is 366-397 ms (65536 tokens, ~5.6 us each) and the same token count in
  8-byte lines is 270-288 ms, so the cost scales with neither token size nor
  byte count. The 29 ms figure for the same search-and-copy work without a
  Scanner still stands.
- **Any timing code in this tree is paying this**: a server that stamps a
  request or an event with `time.Now()` pays 4.3 us per stamp, which is more
  than most of the work it is timing. That is docs/PLAN_REMAINING.md W13.

## Round 270: compiling net/http as a library hits the root arena's 8 GB cap

`./moxie build -o /tmp/httplib.bin ./src/net/http` - the "does this library
compile" check the plan uses everywhere - dies in discovery:

    discover golang.org/x/net/http2/hpack [hpack.mx, huffman.mx, static_table.mx, encode.mx, tables.mx]
    panic: runtime error at 0x28e144: arena: region table full

Measured, watching `/proc/<pid>` while it ran:

    library build   peak VSZ 8,666,680 KB   peak RSS 7,244,628 KB   panic
    muxmatch build  peak VSZ 8,031,592 KB   peak RSS (see log)      ok

The cap is arithmetic: `arenaMaxRegions` 128 x `arenaDefaultRegion` 64 MiB is
exactly 8 GB (src/runtime/alloc.mx), and the root arena is the arena that
matters because it is process-lifetime - the compiler keeps every discovered
package's parse and symbol data for the whole run and releases only per function
frame. Compiling the net/http closure as a main package peaks at 7.66 GB, i.e.
96% of the cap, which is why the failure looks sudden: the same closure one way
completes, the other way crosses the line.

Not the cause: the spread-push fix (round 268). Reproduced with
`/tmp/s4old`, a stage4 built from 9914050d - the commit before it - and with the
per-call table hoists of round 271 stashed.

Two things to fix, in this order:

1. **Residency.** The compiler keeps everything for the life of the process. The
   scope mechanism exists (`src/runtime/arena_scope.mx`, `arenaScopeArena` in
   `FnArenaPush`) and per-package IR is emitted then discarded; the discovery
   data (ASTs, symbol tables, type graphs) is what is never released. A per
   package scope that is released after that package's IR is written would take
   the peak down by a large factor, and that is the fix that makes big builds
   safe on a 16 GB machine.
2. **The cap.** Raising `arenaMaxRegions` for the root arena only (the registry
   is carved from the first region, so a large arena can afford the entries -
   the 24 KB cost the comment cites is for 1024 entries and it is small arenas
   that cannot) turns a hard "region table full" panic into an ordinary OOM,
   which is honest but is not a fix on its own.

Until then: `moxie build -o /dev/null ./src/<pkg>` is only a usable check for
closures below the cap. For net/http-sized packages, build a fixture that
imports them, which compiles the same code and links.

## Round 271: the last 14 per-call tables, and the tool that could do it

Round 266 listed the sites and recorded why three bulk rewrites failed: the
regex that finds `func f() []T { return []T{ ... } }` cannot tell the literal's
closing brace from the function's, so each attempt ate one brace per table and
the tree stopped parsing. The tool has to count braces, and it is thirty lines:
find the function, take the literal's opening brace, walk to its match, and emit
`var fTable = <literal>` plus `func f() (r []T) { return fTable }`.

Applied to 14 tables in nine files:

    crypto/tls/common.mx          _supportedVersionsList        409 entries
    crypto/tls/cipher_suites.mx   _cipherSuitesPreferenceOrder   48
                                  _cipherSuitesPreferenceOrderNoAES
    crypto/tls/defaults.mx        defaultCurvePreferences        7
    net/http/sniff.mx             _sniffSignatures             128 lines
    net/addrselect.mx             _rfc6724policyTable           57 lines
    crypto/rand/util.mx           _smallPrimes                  84
    crypto/des/const.mx           _permutedChoice2, _ksRotations
    image/jpeg/writer.mx          _theHuffmanSpec              64 lines
    math/bits/bits_tables.mx      _ntz8tab _pop8tab _rev8tab _len8tab

No call site changed: the function stays as a one-line accessor, so `len(f())`
and `f()[i]` compile as before. The accessor returns a root-arena slice, which
the codec keeps by identity, so the accessor is an address load and the table is
built once.

Not measured this round: these are per-call or per-connection costs that are
small in absolute terms compared with the AES and hash tables of rounds 263-264,
and the fixtures that exercise them do not time the relevant paths. The reason
to do it anyway is that it is the same defect the earlier rounds measured at
2.5x - a slice literal inside a function is an allocation on that function's
code path - and it is now the last of them.

## Round 272: a dependency that is not in the memo was not in the key

`pkgHash` is the stage4 package content key: own sources plus the hashes of the
imports, memoized per package path in `pkgKeyMemo`. The import loop was

    if dh, ok := bst.pkgKeyMemo[imp]; ok {
        acc = acc | []byte("|") | dh
    }

- an import that was not memoized yet contributed **nothing**. That is not a
matter of build order being what we think it is: `pkgHash` has twenty call
sites, and while the serial package loop and the worker's hash loop both walk
resolver order (dependencies first), six of those sites hash a *dependency* to
compare or report it, and the memo is then filled in whatever order those
reached. A key computed while a dependency was unmemoized was byte-identical to
the key of the same package with that import deleted from the source, and a
dependency's layout change does not change it - so the dependent's cached `.bc`
survives an ABI change in exactly the case the key exists to prevent. That is
the shape of the W12 sightings (rounds 260-263: a slice header read at the old
offset after a field was added, correct under `-a`).

The fix: resolve the import through `pkgByPath` and recurse into `pkgHash`,
guarded by `pkgHashBusy` so a cycle cannot loop; only an import that resolves
to no package at all - a baked package, `C`, a builtin-only path that the
resolver intentionally does not push - falls back to `"|?" + path`. The
fallback still enters the key, so the key changes when the import set changes,
and the key is now a function of the package graph rather than of the order the
hashes happened to be computed in.

Wood law, direction reversed: legacy already had this property.
`legacy/builder/build.go` sets `actionID.Imports[imported.Path()] =
importedPackages[i].result` - the dependency's action ID - and the dependency's
key job is a job dependency, so legacy's key has always chained the whole
dependency graph transitively. Nothing to mirror; the stage4 side is what
diverged, and now does not.

Measured, `tests/netsmoke/muxmatch` (147 packages), the compiler built with the
fix and installed:

    build 1  cold   147 packages compiled, 147 .bc written       1316 s
    build 2  warm   147/147 cached, 0 .bc rewritten              1218 s
    build 3  warm, -j 2 workers  147/147 cached, 0 .bc rewritten

Build 2 reported rc=1, and not because of this change: `/tmp/mm2` existed as a
directory from an older session, so ld.lld refused the output path after the
whole build had succeeded. Build 3 is the clean rerun. That the serial build's
147 keys are hit by the parallel build's 147 keys is the point: the worker path
computes hashes from `meta.pkgs` in whatever order that array holds, and it now
resolves a dependency's hash through `pkgByPath` instead of dropping it, so the
two paths agree.

The interesting number is in build 2's wall time. With every package cached it
still took 1218 s, and the phase it spent the time in is `compile objects`:
`clangCompileToObj` execs clang for every `.bc` on every build, so a warm build
re-compiles 147 LLVM modules to objects that already exist on disk next to
them (`<hash>.bc.o`). Found and recorded as W16 rather than fixed here.

## Round 273: the object a build already made

Round 272 measured a warm build of `tests/netsmoke/muxmatch` at 1218 s with 147
of 147 packages cached and no `.bc` written. None of that time was compilation
in any sense the cache understood: it was `compile objects`, where
`clangCompileToObj` execs `clang -c <hash>.bc -o <hash>.bc.o` for every module,
every build, over the `<hash>.bc.o` the previous build left sitting next to the
bitcode. Every build paid for the whole closure's codegen.

An object is now reused when it is there and was made by the same toolchain:

    <hash>.bc.o          unchanged, next to the bitcode
    <hash>.bc.o.stamp    "<clang --version line>|<triple>|-O0 -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections"

Nothing about the source belongs in the stamp. The object lives at its
bitcode's path, and that name carries the package's content hash (`pkgHash`), so
a source change, a `-print-allocs` instrumented build, a different link set or a
different dispatch fingerprint all land on a different `.bc` and therefore a
different `.o`. The toolchain and the flags are the only inputs left that can
change while the path stays the same. If the version cannot be read the stamp is
empty and nothing is reused - a cache that cannot say what it holds must not
answer.

Four things had to be right for that to be worth having:

- **One flag set.** The serial path compiled without `-O0` and the wasm path
  without the section flags, and all three of them wrote to the same
  `<hash>.bc.o`, so the object's contents depended on which caller made it. All
  three call sites (cmdTest's native link, main's wasm link, main's native link)
  are now one `objFiles` and one `objFlags`. `-O0` is clang's default, so
  spelling it changes no object; the section flags are what `--gc-sections`
  needs.
- **Publish by rename.** clang writes `<o>.tmp<pid>`, then the object is renamed
  into place and the stamp written with `cacheWrite`. A build killed mid-clang
  otherwise leaves a truncated object that the next build would stamp as
  complete - the torn-cache-entry failure `cacheWrite` was written for.
  (`objFiles` publishes at the end of the batch, so a killed build leaves only
  `.tmp` files: no published object, nothing to trust wrongly.)
- **Objects follow the bitcode into the cache.** A package this build compiled
  has its bitcode in the scratch directory, which the build deletes; its object
  would be built there and thrown away, so the build *after* a cold build was
  still cold for objects. `cacheCompiledBc` records the cached copy (byte
  identical - mem2reg runs before the copy) and `objFiles` builds from that, so
  the object lands beside it and survives.
- **-a rebuilds objects but still stamps them.** `-a` does not delete the
  package cache, it only stops reading it, so a package's `.bc` keeps its path
  and an object from the previous `.bc` would look reusable. `objReusable`
  refuses under `forceRebuild`; `objPublish` still stamps, so the build after a
  bootstrap starts warm.

Wood law: nothing to mirror. Legacy's cache is cmd/go's, whose action IDs
already include the compiler build ID and every input file; the missing step is
in stage4's own driver, which legacy does not have (legacy emits objects from
LLVM in process).

Measured, `tests/netsmoke/muxmatch`, 148 packages, no source changes between the
two builds:

    build 1  cold   148 compiled, 0 cached, 191 objects+stamps   1532 s
    build 2  warm   147 cached, 1 compiled (the root package)      42 s

and the two binaries are byte-identical (`b8663454...`), which also settles a
worry the stamp raises: two full builds with different scratch directories and
different pids produce the same output, so nothing of the scratch path survives
into the binary. The same pair on the compiler's own closure (44 packages) was
94 s -> 30 s, also byte-identical.

36x on the loop this project actually runs - edit, build, run - and it is the
round-272 finding that made the number visible: with the package cache working,
the only thing left in a warm build was codegen nobody had cached.

The gate shows it without a special test. `tests/quickcheck.sh --fast` on the
cold cache of a compiler that has the object cache ran 275 s; the same command
on the same tree, warm, ran 67 s, with the per-fixture times dropping from
42-180 s to 2-19 s. The two runs differ in one thing only: whether the objects
their closures need were already on disk.

## Round 274: the fingerprint that was built by concatenation

Phase 1b (the 45-package stdlib sweep) was red: the compiler panicked `arena:
region table full` with the peak region count in the ROOT arena while every mem
line before it reported RSS 719 MB and five regions. Two things had to be added
to see it.

`ArenaAllocTD` panicked with no diagnostic at all - the ordinary allocation path,
unlike `arenaAllocRaw`, which prints the region table when it overflows. It now
prints the same line plus the arena's `alloc` total, its scope, `growDouble`,
`sovereign` and whether it is the root. And `memLine` gained `root=<nregions>/
<MB>` (from a new `runtime.ArenaRootUsage()`), because the root arena is the one
that is never reset, so its numbers are the entire residency story. A process
watcher for VmHWM settled the last contradiction: the 719 MB was the reading
*before* the allocations, and the real peak was 8147 MB.

Phase tags in the build path then put the bytes in one place:

    phase          before                 after
    dispindex      5 regions /   471MB     5 /   471MB
    fingerprints 141 regions /  9189MB    23 /  1624MB
    loop-end     144 regions /  9351MB    25 /  1786MB
    objs-pre     157 regions / 10163MB    39 /  2599MB

`measureDispFingerprints` runs for every package before the first `pkgHash`,
because the key it produces is what the build is about to look up. The
measurement deliberately has no arena of its own - an earlier attempt at one
crashed the self-build with "alloc: nil arena", the reason is in the comment -
so everything it allocates is root-lifetime. And
`dispFingerprintForMethods` built the text it hashes by string concatenation:

    acc = acc | "|" | methods[mi] | "="
    for ii := 0; ii < len(ids); ii++ { acc = acc | ids[ii] | "," }

Every `|` allocates a fresh string of the accumulated length. One package with a
few hundred invoked methods and a few thousand impls for them copies tens of
megabytes a few thousand times: 7.6GB for 173 packages, retained to the end of
the process because the root arena is never released. That is where the 8.7GB
came from, from a function whose entire output is an 8-hex-digit hash.

It now hashes as it produces, through `fnvState` (a running form of `fnvHash`).
The byte sequence is exactly the one the concatenation used to build, so the
fingerprint value is unchanged - only the input string is gone.

After: fingerprints 1624 MB, whole build 2599 MB, the sweep links, the binary
runs. The 45-package closure went from "cannot be built" to 2.6GB of root arena.

Tried first and reverted: giving the root arena a bigger region registry
(1024 entries, `arenaRootMaxRegions`). It does let the build finish - root
10163 MB over 157 regions - but the bytes are still retained, so it is the
ceiling round 270 already said is not a fix. Reverted once the real cause was
measured; the diagnostic and `ArenaRootUsage` stayed.

Wood law: nothing to mirror. The fingerprint is stage4's own cache device
(`legacy/builder/build.go` keys a package on its file hashes, its imports' action
IDs and the link set, and folds the whole link set in because it has no
per-package arm measurement), so the loop that had to change does not exist on
the legacy side.

Still residential, and now the rest of W15: the `cached-bc` step adds ~800MB -
`mem2reg` reads every freshly compiled package's bitcode into a frame that
outlives the loop - and the fingerprint phase still keeps ~1.1GB of per-impl
identity strings for the life of the build.

## Round 275: what a method call costs, and why time.Now is 4.2 us

W13 said `time.Now()` costs 4.3 us and blamed the return-value codec plus the
clock read, without separating them. A bench with one loop per shape (200k
iterations, AMD64 musl static, best of three) separates them:

    shape                                                  ns/call
    empty loop                                                  15
    time.Time{} then UnixNano()                                 15
    local pair, pointer-receiver method returning a scalar      15
    local pair, pointer-receiver method, non-mutating            15
    local pair, pointer-receiver MUTATING method                 10
    struct{2 int64; *int64} built locally and returned          15
    time.Time passed through a free function                    95
    time.Unix(1700000000, 0)                                  7280
    time.Local()                                               640
    time.Now()                                                4155
    time.Now().UnixNano()                                     4170
    t.UTC() on a hoisted Time                                16785
    t.Add(0) on a hoisted Time                               10995
    time.FixedZone("x", 0)                                   29985

So the shape of the problem is not "returns cost money". A struct with a
pointer into a package global, built in a local and returned, costs 15 ns, and a
mutating method on a frame-local receiver of a plain type costs 10 ns. Three
different things are expensive:

1. **`time.Local()` is 640 ns to return `&localLoc`.** Its disassembly is the
   whole return-value protocol for one stable pointer:
   FnArenaPush(0x10000), codecBufInit, codecSeenInit, codecSetRetTransient x2,
   codecEncodeValue, codecDecodeSeenInit, codecDecodeValue,
   codecEscapeOccurred, FnArenaPop, ArenaRelease. `codecIsStableArenaAddr` does
   return true for a root-arena pointer, so nothing is copied - the 640 ns is
   the protocol itself, entered for every function whose return value contains
   a pointer whether or not anything needs relocating.

2. **A receiver that is created in the callee's own frame is a new sovereign
   group per call.** `codecSovereignArena` keys groups by receiver address, and
   a frame-local receiver's address changes every call, so each call takes the
   create path: `sovNewArena(8192)` = a fresh mmap, a range registration, a
   root hashmap insert, and a munmap when the frame dies. strace on the shapes
   counts it: `t.Add(0)` does 200,000 mmap + 200,000 munmap for 200,000 calls,
   `t.UTC()` does 400,000 of each, and their time is 11 us and 16.8 us
   respectively. `time.FixedZone` - which builds a Location and mutates it - is
   30 us. A mutating method on a receiver that outlives the call (the bench's
   own local in `main`) is 10 ns: one group, then a hashmap hit.

3. **`time.Now()` is 4.2 us with no mmap and no deep copy.** It calls
   `Local()` (0.64 us), `initStartNano()`, and `runtimeNow()` (the vDSO read),
   and then returns a Time through the protocol of (1) with `loc` pointing at
   `&localLoc`. The protocol for the Time is ~3.5 us, five times what the same
   protocol costs for a bare pointer, and the difference is not the Location
   walk Round 269 measured (1 us) - with `loc` set to nil it is still 3.3 us.
   Not yet explained; the shapes above are what an explanation has to fit.

The scanner bench (W3b/W14) is the same family and is NOT the mmap churn: 393
ms for 65536 tokens with 66 mmaps in the whole run, i.e. pure CPU per token,
in the sovereign borrow/store-back path of `Scan` and the per-call protocol.

Tools built for this round, and worth keeping: the one-loop-per-shape bench
(`/tmp/tb`), and `strace -f -c` restricted to mmap/munmap, which turns "it feels
slow" into a per-call syscall count.

## Round 276: the sovereign arena mmap per call is a pool

Round 275 found that a mutating method whose receiver lives in the callee's own
frame created and destroyed a sovereign data arena per call: 1 mmap + 1 munmap
for `time.Time.Add`, 2 of each for `UTC`, and 11 us / 16.8 us per call. The
model's guarantee is that the group's arena lives as long as the receiver, and a
frame-local receiver dies at its frame's exit either way - so the arena does not
need to go back to the kernel, only back to a freelist.

`sovNewArena` now first-fits a pooled sovereign arena (32 slots, 4 MiB, carved
as a fixed array out of the root arena, and kept separate from the function
frame pool so a frame can never be handed an arena that carries the sovereign
flag and its registered ranges). `sovReleaseArena` replaces the three
`ArenaFree` calls on a group's data/alloc/ref arenas and on a rebuilt alloc
table: it unregisters every region range (region 0 is registered again for
whichever group borrows the arena next), unmaps overflow regions, and pools the
primary region.

Measured with the round-275 bench, before -> after:

    t.Add(0)              10995 -> 5005 ns      (200,000 mmap+munmap -> 9 mmaps total)
    t.UTC()               16785 -> 5470 ns      (400,000 of each -> 0)
    time.Now()             4155 -> 4045 ns      (unchanged: it never mmap'd)
    time.Unix            7280 -> 6890 ns
    time.Local()            640 -> 640 ns       (unchanged)
    struct+ptr local         15 -> 15 ns

The remaining ~5 us of `Add`/`UTC` is pure CPU - the sovereign bookkeeping and
the return protocol - which is W17 items 2 and 3. The pool does not touch the
`time.FixedZone` shape (28830 ns), because that one allocates a Location per
call; its arenas are not a group's data arena.

quickcheck --fast: 15 of 15, including the TLS handshake fixture, which is the
heaviest user of sovereign state in the tree (tls.Conn, the record layer and
crypto/ecdh all mutate through receiver methods).

## Round 277: every /etc file the net package reads was empty

Phase 8 failed at `lookup failed: lookup localhost on 127.0.0.1:53: no such
host`, for a name that is in /etc/hosts. `hostLookupOrder` was not the problem -
instrumenting it printed `files,dns`, the right order - and `readHosts` printed
`/etc/hosts openErr false byName 0 byAddr 0`: the file opened, was read, and
produced nothing.

`io.ReadFullInto` validates its window against `len(dst)`, not `cap(dst)`:

    if off+n > len(dst) || n > cap(tmp) { return 0, ErrShortBuffer }

and `parseFile.readLine` passed `f.data` - whose length is the bytes already
buffered and whose capacity is the buffer - with `off = len(f.data)` and `n =
cap(f.data)-len(f.data)`. `off+n` is exactly `cap(f.data)`, which is greater than
`len(f.data)` on every call, so every read answered ErrShortBuffer with got=0,
`readLine` returned ok=false on its first call, and the caller's loop never ran.
`readLine` now passes `resize(f.data, cap(f.data))`, the idiom `io.ReadAll` next
door already uses.

One caller, and it is the reader behind every fixed-path file in the package:
/etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/services, /proc/net/unix
(sock_linux), the interface list and lookup_unix. What that costs, measured on
this machine before and after:

    net.LookupHost("localhost")   lookup ... 127.0.0.1:53: no such host  -> 127.0.0.1 ::1
    net.LookupHost("smesh")       same failure                          -> 127.0.0.1
    net.LookupPort("tcp","http")  (was unreachable: same reader)         -> 80
    net.LookupPort("udp","domain")                                      -> 53
    net.LookupPort("tcp","ssh")                                          -> 22

The DNS half was never reading /etc/resolv.conf either: it ran on the resolver's
built-in default, which is 127.0.0.1 - the same as this machine's nameserver,
which is why nobody noticed. /etc/nsswitch.conf's source list was empty too, so
`hostLookupOrder` silently took its fallback branch (`files,dns`), which happens
to be right here and would not be everywhere.

Three defects are now visible behind it, and are tracked as W18 in the plan
rather than fixed here: `net.IP.String()` returns the raw 16-byte form instead
of a dotted quad (`ParseIP("8.8.8.8").String()` prints bytes), `net.Dial` on a
hosts name answers "no suitable address found" although the name resolves, and
`net.LookupIP`/`Dial` on a DNS name dies with SIGSEGV.

## Round 278: the resolver's answer outlived the wrong frame

Round 277 made /etc/hosts parse, and the next layer was three failures:
`net.IP.String()` printing bytes, `Dial` on a hosts name answering "no suitable
address found", and `Dial`/`LookupIP` on a DNS name dying with SIGSEGV.

The crash first, because a crash has a core. VmHWM-style memory work does not
need ptrace, but a backtrace does - and ptrace_scope is 1 here, so gdb cannot
attach. gdb can still read a core file, and systemd-coredump had kept them:

    #0  net[lookupIPReturn] ()
    #1  net.(*Resolver).lookupIPAddr ()
    #2  net.(*Resolver).internetAddrList ()
    #3  net.(*Resolver).resolveAddrList ()
    #4  net.(*Dialer).DialContext ()
    #5  net.(*Dialer).Dial ()

`lookupIPReturn` dereferences `unsafe.Pointer` with `*(*[]IPAddr)(val)`, and the
pointer came from `lookupIPCall.Call`:

    addrs, err := l.r.lookupIP(...)
    ...
    return unsafe.Pointer(&addrs), nil

`&addrs` is the address of a local. In Go that escapes to the heap and outlives
the call; in Moxie it points into the call's frame arena, which is released when
the call returns, and singleflight hands it to a collector in a different frame.
So the fix is not in the deref: the publisher has to put the value somewhere both
frames can reach. `Call` now builds the header and a copy of every address in the
root arena (`SetCurrentArena(RootArena())`, the idiom readHosts and time.initLocal
already use) and returns a pointer to that.

After: `Dial("tcp", "example.com:80")` connects, `Dial("tcp", "localhost:1")`
reaches the connect (`connect: cannot assign requested address` on ::1, which is
this machine having no IPv6 loopback - no longer a resolver failure), and
`LookupIP` returns addresses for hosts names and DNS names alike.

`net.IP.String()` is not a bug to fix and is now a documented trap instead: `IP`
is an alias for `[]byte` because the language has no named slice types (the
compiler says so itself: "named slice type 'MyBytes' is not allowed: use []T
directly") and an alias cannot carry methods, so the Go method set is a set of
free functions - `net.IPString`, `IPIsLoopback`, and so on. `ip.String()` on an
`IP` therefore resolves to the *builtin* `[]byte` Stringer and prints the raw
16-byte form. It compiles, it is not the Go method, and nothing warns. Ported
code must call `net.IPString(ip)`.

Cost of the fix, stated plainly: a resolved name's addresses stay in the root
arena forever. Go frees the equivalent when the singleflight call is collected;
with no heap there is nowhere to put it that a different frame can free.

## Round 279: the shared slot ring was written into a private copy

Phase 8's spawned modes answered nothing. Round 278's strace already showed the
shape: the manager forks 4 workers, accepts, reads `GET /smoke`, wakes a worker,
gets a result back - and closes the connection without writing a byte. With a
temporary print in the worker, the worker said both things at once:

    DBG worker: slot decode failed
    DBG worker: no route for -1

`routeID = -1` is `chanSlotGetReq`'s failure sentinel, and it fails when
`chanSlotGetI32(slot, 0)` - the frame length the shell wrote - is out of range.
The shell had written a valid length. The slot the worker read was all zeros.

The queue boundary is a MAP_SHARED ring of preallocated slots, and both sides
named one slot with a bounded sub-slice:

    slot := chanSlotBuf[chanSlotBase(i) : chanSlotBase(i)+chanSlotBytes]

**A bounded sub-slice allocates and copies in this language.** The shell wrote the
request into its private copy, the worker took its own copy of an untouched ring,
and every frame arrived zeroed - which the decoder rejects, and the worker then
wrote an abort frame the shell discards, so the client saw a connection that
closed with no response. The mechanism was correct in Go (a sub-slice is a view
there) and is wrong here by exactly the rule this project keeps repeating.

`chanSlotWindow` builds a real window with `unsafe.Add` over
`unsafe.SliceData(chanSlotBuf)`, and the three sites (shell write, worker read,
shell response read) use it. One slot, four processes, the same bytes.

Phase 8 after the fix - 14 of 18 fixtures pass, both modes:

    PASS  build, mux-match, spawn-bytes, spawn-cost
    PASS  listen-inline, curl-inline, keepalive-inline, repeatable-inline, client-inline
    PASS  listen-spawned, curl-spawned, keepalive-spawned, repeatable-spawned, client-spawned
    FAIL  no-accumulation-inline, client-sync, no-accumulation-spawned

`client-spawned` passing is the one that matters most here: the whole Moxie
client stack - Transport, dial, request, response - completed a real request
against a worker in another domain for the first time.

The four remaining failures are one defect, and it is not the spawn path:
`client-sync` prints `status=200` and then `body=[        ]` - eighteen ZERO
bytes, where the body should be `hello path=/smoke` (eighteen bytes). A body
reader allocated in a frame that is released, then zeroed by the next
allocation in the reused arena, reads back as zeros of the right length. That
is W20.

Also fixed here: `repeatable-spawned` compared three responses to each other, so
three identical EMPTY responses passed it - which is how a spawned mode that
answered nothing was recorded green. It now asserts the body first.

## Round 280: a bounded sub-slice is a copy, including when it is a destination

Round 279 left four phase-8 fixtures failing on one symptom: `client-sync`
printed `status=200` and then eighteen ZERO bytes where `hello path=/smoke` (18
bytes) belongs. Reading straight from `resp.Body` instead of through
`io.ReadAll` gave the same thing - `n=18 err=EOF` with the buffer untouched - so
the reader was returning a length and no data.

`io.LimitedReader.Read` is where a Content-Length body gets its length:

    if int64(len(p)) > l.N {
        p = p[0:l.N]
    }
    n, err = l.R.Read(p)

`p[0:l.N]` is a bounded sub-slice, so in this language it **allocates and
copies**. The underlying reader wrote the eighteen bytes into the copy and the
caller's buffer kept its zeros; `n` came from the copy's length, so the count was
right and the data was gone. The same three lines exist in `SectionReader.Read`
and `SectionReader.ReadAt`, so a section reader's last partial read lost its
bytes too.

`io.readWindow` returns the first n bytes of a buffer as a VIEW
(`unsafe.Slice(unsafe.SliceData(p), n)`) and all three sites use it.

Phase 8 after this and round 279 - **18 of 18 fixtures, both modes**:

    no-accumulation-inline   400 exchanges: rss 25672kB -> 25888kB (+216kB)
    no-accumulation-spawned  400 exchanges: rss 14836kB -> 14836kB (+0kB)
    client-sync              single-domain LookupHost/Dial/Write/ReadResponse
    client-spawned           the client stack against a worker in another domain

The compiler already refuses `copy(x[a:b], src)` ("a subslice is a copy, so
copying into it is not allowed"). It cannot refuse `f(x[a:b])` for a callee that
writes through its parameter, which is the shape that hid here. So: what is a
copy, exactly? Measured rather than assumed:

    var a [8]byte; s := a[:4]; s[0] = 9        a[0] == 9   array slice is a VIEW
    b := []byte{...}; c := b[:2]; c[0] = 8     b[0] == 1   slice slice is a COPY
    fill(a[:2], 5) (callee writes through)     a[0] == 5   array slice views
    fill(b[:2], 4) (callee writes through)     b[0] == 1   slice slice copies

So the rule is `array[a:b]` is a view and `slice[a:b]` is a copy, bounded or not.
With that, the sweep is small: every `X[:]`/`X[a:b]` passed to a read in this
tree is either a full range or an ARRAY slice - including
`crypto/internal/fips140/drbg`'s `sysrand.Read(additionalInput[:16])`, where
`additionalInput` is a `*[SeedSize]byte` - except one:

    archive/tar/reader.mx  tryReadFull:  r.Read(b[n:])   b is a []byte parameter

which read a tar stream into a copy. It uses `io.ReadIntoN` now (the same
allocation rules as the rest of the package, offset write, scratch in a free
function's frame). A grep for `Read(|ReadFull(|ReadAt(|copy(` with a bounded
sub-slice argument now finds only comments.

## Round 281: the array campaign was framed as three exceptions. It has none.

Round 262 rewrote W7 around three groups it called "load-bearing" and therefore
exempt: the kernel ABI mirrors, the fiat/nistec field elements, and the array
view. That framing was wrong and is retracted here. The correction is that an
array's ABI **is** slice-header accounting, and the header says everything
needed:

    base, len, cap   with cap NEGATIVE for a fixed extent

The negative capacity is the mechanism, not a flag on the side. `cap(arr)` is
negative, so `push`, `pop`, `resize` and `append` on it are compile errors rather
than runtime checks; `len(arr)` is the type's length and indexing is
base+i*elemsize bounded by it, which is the same code a slice compiles to; and
the 24-byte header travels wherever a value travels, so there is no second array
ABI to build or to convert.

What that does to the three "exceptions":

- **The ABI.** A mirror does not get an unaccountable size change, it gets the
  accounting written down: the header is the field where Go had `[16]byte`, the
  `//sys` boundary takes base and len, and where the kernel fills bytes in place
  the storage the header points at is what is passed, with its offset recorded -
  which is what a mirror is. 99 sites of bookkeeping.
- **The field element.** A header is not an allocation. `[4]uint64` of storage
  with a negative-cap header is owner-allocated once, exactly as the inline form
  is today; the limbs are loads through the base, and the bounds check is the one
  a slice index already pays. 24 sites of accounting.
- **The view.** `arr[:]` is the cap-sign transition - same base, len = len(arr),
  cap = +len - so it is a genuine slice of the same storage and the 329
  `Read(fd, b[:])` sites keep working because there was never anything to copy.
  `arr[a:b]` remains a sub-slice and copies. The copy rule loses its last
  "carve-out" because there is no carve-out left: a sub-slice copies, and a
  fixed-extent header's whole range is not a sub-slice.

W7 in the plan is rewritten in that order: representation first (both compilers
byte for byte), then indexing, then the refusals, then the whole-range
transition, then the two accounting groups, then the remainder.

## Round 282: an array's capacity is negative, in both compilers

The first piece of the corrected W7, and the one that has to exist before the
representation can change: **`cap(arr)` is `-N`**. The negative value is the
sentinel `mxutil.capFixed` already understands for `//:linkdata` storage, so a
growth guard (`cap(x)-len(x) < n`) answers "no room" without a special case, and
it is the accounting the array header will carry.

Measured, same source, both compilers:

    len(a)  = 8      cap(a)  = -8     a is [8]byte
    len(a[:]) = 8    cap(a[:]) = 8    the cap-sign flip: same storage, growable cap
    len(p)  = 8      cap(p)  = -8     p is *[8]byte

Where the change lives is the interesting part. In stage4 it is the `cap` case in
`ir_call.mx` (the array and pointer-to-array branches now emit `-N`). In legacy
it is **not in the compiler at all**: Go makes `cap(anArrayVar)` a *constant*
expression, so `go/types` folds it and no lowering pass ever sees a `cap` to
rewrite - patching the vendored `go/ssa` builtin folder (the obvious place) had
no effect at all, which is what pointed at the truth. The fold is in
`go/types/builtins.go`, so the legacy side is the `patch-gotypes.go` patcher that
the tree already uses for string=[]byte and the Moxie builtins:

    if t.len >= 0 {
        if id == _Cap { val = constant.MakeInt64(-t.len) } else { val = ... t.len }
    }

`len` keeps the type's length; only `cap` carries the sentinel.

Verified: `s4b == s4c` (bootstrap fixpoint `74799d6e`), quickcheck green, and
phase 8 green in both modes, so nothing in the tree depended on the positive
number. The remaining W7a work is the representation itself - an inline `[N]T`
becoming a header whose cap is this `-N` - which is where the storage and the
struct-field cases get settled.

## Round 283: the return protocol skips itself when there is nothing to relocate

Round 275 measured the return-value protocol at 640 ns for `time.Local` returning
one stable pointer, and several microseconds for a struct that holds one - ten
runtime calls per return, for a value that needs no copying at all. The protocol
exists to copy data out of a frame before it is released; when every pointer in
the value is nil or already stable by identity, encode+decode would write each
one raw and hand the same address back, so the whole sequence can be skipped.

`codecRetStable(value, typeDesc)` answers that question, mirroring
`codecEncodeValue`'s own per-field decisions in return mode: a stable pointer
encodes raw, a slice encodes raw unless its elements can themselves hold
transient data, and anything the codec must walk (map, interface, function,
array) answers false so the real protocol runs. Both compilers branch on it in
the plain return epilogue (stage4 `emitRetWithCodec`, legacy
`compiler.go`'s codec block, guarded by `!sovereignActive`), and the fast block
restores the stable registration, calls `FnArenaPopFree` and returns the value.

    shape                          before     after
    time.Local()                    640ns     200ns
    time.Now()                     4275ns    1315ns
    time.Unix(...)                 7165ns    1950ns
    t.Add(0)                       5200ns    2640ns
    t.UTC()                        5325ns    2990ns
    struct with a stable pointer     15ns      15ns

Two bugs found while landing it, both worth keeping:

1. **The block first landed in `emitSovereignEpilogue`.** The anchor it was
   inserted at (`ipt := e.intptrType(); st := e.sliceType()`) exists in BOTH
   epilogue emitters, and the first match is the sovereign one - where the codec
   also performs the receiver's STORE-BACK. Taking the shortcut there skips every
   write a mutating method made through its receiver, and the bootstrap proved it
   immediately: `s4b`, the compiler built by a compiler that had the shortcut,
   SIGSEGV'd while compiling mxregexp. The sovereign epilogue must never take
   this path; the fast block is only in `emitRetWithCodec` now.
2. **An empty slice with a base in the frame is not stable.** The first version
   answered "stable" for `length == 0 || ptr == nil`, so a returned empty slice
   with a live frame pointer handed the caller a pointer into a released arena.
   It showed up three ways in one quickcheck: an ASN.1 integer whose first byte
   read 00 instead of 02, TLS reporting `index out of range` and a malformed
   certificate, and a DNS name printing binary. A length-zero base still has to
   pass `codecIsStableAddr`.

Gates after the fix: bootstrap fixpoint `93324787`, quickcheck 15/15, phase 8
17/17 in both dispatch modes.

## Round 284: what is left in time.Now, and the scanner re-measured

With the return protocol skipped (round 283), `time.Now()` is 1315-1360 ns.
Taking the marginal cost over `time.Local()` (200 ns) isolates the body: about
1160 ns, and the body is two clock reads.

`now()` (src/runtime/runtime_unix.mx, linknamed as `time.now`) is:

    ts := timespec{}
    clock_gettime(clock_REALTIME, &ts)
    sec, nsec = ...
    mono = nanotime()

and the disassembly of `time.now` shows `runtime.alloc`, `runtime.clock_gettime`
and `runtime.nanotime`. Both reads go through the libc shim
(`libc_clock_gettime`), at about 580 ns each - 30x what a direct vDSO call
costs. So W13's remaining 1.3 us is not codec, not `Local`, and not the arena:
it is two libc calls where Go makes two vDSO calls.

That gives W13 a real plan instead of a mystery:

1. Call the vDSO directly (locate `__vdso_clock_gettime` through
   `AT_SYSINFO_EHDR`, as Go does) - 2 x ~25 ns instead of 2 x ~580 ns.
2. Then `Local()` is the next floor at 200 ns, which is FnArenaPush(64 KiB) +
   the fast-path check for a function that allocates nothing. The fix there is a
   lazy frame arena (acquire on first allocation), not another codec change.

The scanner re-measured with the fast path in place: 4 MiB of 64-byte lines is
349-355 ms against 366-397 before, so the return protocol was about 12% of it and
`Scan`'s cost is still its own work (5.4 us per token), not the codec. W14 keeps
its numbers and its target; the next instrument is a counter inside `Scan`, as
round 269 concluded.

## Round 285: a clock read no longer allocates

`now()` and `getTime()` each built a `local timespec{}` and passed its address to
`clock_gettime`. An address that escapes gets allocated through `runtime.alloc`,
so every `time.Now` made two arena allocations - one for the wall clock, one for
the monotonic - and every `nanotime()` one more. A domain is one thread and spawn
forks, so the scratch can be a package global:

    var clockScratch timespec

    time.Now()   1360 -> 1250 ns

The rest of the round is the attribution W17-3 needed, and it is worth recording
because the obvious answers are wrong:

- The codec is gone from this path (round 283): the fast path is taken, the slow
  one is dead code in the function.
- The two clock reads are CHEAP. Dropping the monotonic read and re-measuring
  moved `time.Now` by 80 ns, so a musl `clock_gettime` - which goes through its
  own vDSO pointer, confirmed in the disassembly - is ~80 ns, not the ~580 the
  first estimate assumed.
- `time.Local()` is 205 ns of it, and `struct with a stable pointer` returned
  from a function is 15 ns, so the return path is not the remainder either.
- The arena push is not it either: `Local()` pays the same one.

So ~850 ns of `time.Now` is still unattributed, inside its own construction path,
and the next instrument has to be an in-runtime counter (call counts and bytes,
not timers) - the same conclusion round 269 reached. What this round does settle
is W13's plan: the vDSO shim was never the problem, so a direct-vDSO rewrite
would buy at most ~160 ns and is off the list.

## Round 286: the walk was paying the protocol it exists to avoid

Round 285 left ~850 ns of `time.Now` unattributed. The ablation that found it was
one line: force `codecRetStable` to answer true and re-measure.

    time.Now()       1245 -> 345 ns      forced true
    time.Local()      200 ->  95 ns      forced true

Three hundred and forty-five is about the floor of the function (arena push, one
clock read, `Local`, the return), so ~900 ns was the *check itself* - and the
reason is that `codecRetStableInner` walked a type descriptor through the
descriptor accessors:

    typ.Kind(), typ.NumField(), typ.StructFieldOffset(i), typ.StructFieldType(i),
    typ.Elem(), typ.Underlying()

Every one of those returns `*RawType` (or `Kind`), and a pointer-returning call
pays the return protocol - ~100 ns each on round 283's fast path, 640 before it.
A three-field struct walk makes about a dozen such calls, so the check cost more
than the protocol it was there to skip. The same defect the round is about, one
level down.

The walk now does its own descriptor arithmetic and never returns a pointer:
`retUnderAddr(tp uintptr) uintptr` follows the named chain, `retFieldOffset`
decodes the field descriptor's varint, and the struct walk reads
`rtStructFieldDesc` directly. Scalars in, scalars out.

    time.Now()       1245 ->  705 ns
    time.Now()+sink  1165 ->  610 ns
    time.Unix(...)   1950 ->  925 ns
    time.Local()      200 ->  215 ns    (unchanged; the check floor)

`time.Local()` is now the floor: its whole body is `return &localLoc`, and the
315 ns it costs is FnArenaPush + `codecIsStableAddr` (an `onStack` call, a scan
of the root arena's regions and a sovereign-range lookup) + FnArenaPopFree. That
is where the next round starts, and it is the same currency: scalar accessors and
a cheaper stability test.

## Round 287: the check is still ~350 ns, and it is not the walk

With the walk rewritten to scalar accessors (round 286), `time.Now` is 705 ns and
`time.Local` 205. Forcing `codecRetStable` to answer true gives 345 for `Now`, so
the check costs ~350 ns for a three-field struct - and this round asked what in
it.

Inlining the accessors changed nothing: the walk now reads the kind out of the
descriptor's meta byte, decodes field offsets without a call, and never returns a
pointer (the slice case uses a scalar `retKindHasPtrs` instead of
`sovTypeHasPtrs`), and the measurement moved by noise (700 -> 715). The arena
root test was made scalar too (215 -> 205; ~10 ns). So the ~350 ns is not the
walk, not the accessors, and not the root fetch: what remains per pointer is
`codecOnStack` (a stack-pointer read), a scan of the root arena's regions, and a
sovereign-range lookup - all of which are cheap in isolation and therefore need a
counter, not another estimate.

What the last three rounds do establish, measured end to end:

    time.Now()   4275 ns    original (round 275)
                 1360 ns    + return fast path and a clock scratch
                  705 ns    + scalar descriptor walk
    time.Local()  640 ns -> 205 ns
    t.Add(0)     5200 ns -> 2640 ns (unchanged since the fast path)

W13's 200 ns accept is not reachable by this route: the floor for a function that
returns a stable pointer is now `time.Local`'s 205 (arena push, check, pop), and
`time.Now` adds one clock pair and a construction on top. Reaching 200 needs the
lazy frame arena (W13b) *and* a cheaper stability test; the plan says so, and the
next round should start with a counter inside `codecIsStableAddr`.

## Round 288: stage4 built every object at -O0, so nothing was ever inlined

Round 287 left one `codecIsStableAddr` at ~125 ns for a pointer to a package
global and asked for a counter. The counter was never needed: the caller's
disassembly answered it first. `time.Local` is `return &localLoc`, and its body
was three calls - `FnArenaPush`, `codecRetStable`, `FnArenaPopFree` - and each
callee began with a stack frame for every local, because that is what -O0
codegen looks like. `codecIsStableAddr` made about a dozen such calls
(`codecOnStack` twice, `rootArenaAddr`, `codecArenaContainsAddr`,
`lookupCheck`, `codecArenaContains`, `sovGroupInDyingArena`,
`sovInSovereignDataArena`), and at ~10 cycles of call overhead each that is
~400 cycles - the whole 125 ns. Nothing was slow except the fact that nothing
was inlined.

The cause was asymmetric by construction. `objFlags` compiled every
`.bc -> .o` with `-O0`, and `mem2regBc` ran `opt -passes=mem2reg` and nothing
else. The legacy compiler, which builds the first binary of every bootstrap,
creates its TargetMachine at `CodeGenLevelDefault` (O2). So the bootstrap
compiler emitted optimized code and the compiler it produced emitted -O0 code
for everything after it: the same source is fast when built by legacy and slow
when built by stage4. That is the wood-law failure this round actually fixes -
not a missing optimization, a missing *agreement about one*.

Change, one function and one variable in `_mxc_stage4/main.mx`:
`mem2regBc` is `optBc` and runs `opt -passes=default<O2>` (the file was already
compiled with `-Xclang -disable-O0-optnone`, so the functions were never
optnone and the pass had something to do); `objFlags` is `-O2` instead of
`-O0`. Both compilers now have the same optimization level. `objFlags` is part
of the object stamp, so the flag change invalidated every cached object once
and the next build rebuilt all of them; the generations after that reused them.

Measured, AMD64 musl static, 200k iterations, same benched sources, O0 -> O2:

    time.Now()                     705 -> 191-197 ns   (W13 accept: under 200)
    time.Local()                   205 ->  55-58 ns    (W17-2 accept: under 100)
    function returning int32         1 ->   0 ns
    call that allocates 16 B        50 ->   9-10 ns
    function returning one stable ptr 15 -> 17-19 ns   (W17-2: under 50)
    t.Add(0)                      2640 -> 436-453 ns
    t.UTC()                       2990 -> 525-583 ns
    scanner, 4 MiB of 64-B lines   349-355 -> 83-84 ms (W14: 1.27 us/token)
    scanner, 65536 8-byte lines     270-288 -> 68-76 ms
    compiler binary              8,769,984 -> 3,900,608 B
    warm compiler build             42 s -> 1.6 s
    full `build -a` of stage4      1532 s -> 120 s
    bootstrap (all generations)     ~36 min -> 5m07s

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == a8634a72…`, and a plain
`build -a ./_mxc_stage4` reproduces the same bytes. quickcheck `--fast`: 14 of
14 fixtures PASS (tree-cleanliness fails only because this commit was not yet
made). Phase 8 follows.

What this does NOT fix, and why the remaining numbers look the way they do: the
unit of optimization is still ONE PACKAGE. `opt` sees a package; clang sees one
package's object; `llvm-link` merges them only at the end. So a runtime helper
called from `bufio` or `time` is still a real call, and the return protocol,
the arena push and the stability check keep their call boundaries across the
package edge. `t.Add(0)`'s remaining 436 ns and the scanner's remaining
1.27 us/token are that edge, not un-inlined local code. The next lever would be
link-time optimization over the merged module, which is a pipeline change with
its own cost; it is not in this round.

## Round 289: -O2 meets a 19 KB aggregate, and the IR that built it

Round 288 turned on `opt -passes=default<O2>` and O2 objects. The bench was
3x faster and the compiler was 2.2x smaller, but building the TLS closure then
needed **10.6 GB of RSS and minutes** on one package
(`x/text/unicode/norm`), which is not a build a 16 GB machine (or this repo's
own phase 8) can run. This round is the two emitter changes that bound it, and
they are worth having on their own: they remove 80% of that package's IR.

**First, what the module was.** `norm` is generated Unicode data. Each
`tables1x.0.0.mx` has eight functions of the shape

    func _decomps() [19105]byte { return [19105]byte{ 0x00, 0x41, ... } }

and a 19 KB array literal written in a *return* position was lowered element by
element: `_decomps` alone was **38,857 SSA instructions** in one basic block,
`_nfkcValues` 10,091, and the package's bitcode was 3.83 MB before any
optimization. The `SSAConstMemCpy` lowering (private constant global + one
memcpy) already existed and was used for `nistec`'s 88 KB table, but only for
`lhs = literal` *assignments* - `tryConstArrayMemcpy` is called from the
assignment path and nowhere else. A returned literal took
`buildArrayLit`'s alloc/store/load path.

Change 1 (`ssa_builder.mx`, `buildArrayLit`): a qualifying all-constant literal
is one memcpy in every position, not only assignment. The package's bitcode is
now **0.73 MB** and `_decomps` is six instructions (alloca, memcpy, load, ret).

**Second, the optimizer still blew up**, now on that six-instruction function:
`-opt-bisect-limit` walked it down to `cgscc(function(sroa,early-cse))` on
`norm._decomps`, where **SROA scalarizes the whole-aggregate load** into one
element per instruction and EarlyCSE then works on a 38,000-instruction block.
No single pass reproduced it in isolation (`sroa<modify-cfg>` alone: 289 MB;
`gvn`/`cgscc(inline)` alone: 4 MB); it is the combination, and `mem2reg` first,
`-O1`, and `-inline-threshold=40` all still hit 9-10 GB, so it is neither the
inliner nor the alloca form.

Change 2 (`ir_emit.mx`): a function whose signature or locals **carry an array
of at least 512 elements by value** is emitted `noinline optnone`. Such a
function is a generated table, cold, and already a memcpy of constant data, so
there is nothing to optimize in it; `noinline` keeps the table from being
duplicated into callers. This is a compile-time bound, and it is the only
reason the -O2 policy is shippable.

Measured, `x/text/unicode/norm` built with `-a`:

    module before opt        3.83 MB  ->  0.73 MB
    largest function         38,857 instr -> 10,091 (a 6208-element table)
    opt on the module        >10 GB, minutes -> 304 MB, 25.8 s
    whole build, peak RSS    10.6 GB -> 867 MB
    return path             unchanged: local 59-69 ns, now 206-227 ns,
                            alloc 9-10 ns, scanner 83 ms / 4 MiB

What is left on the cost side: the inliner duplicates code across this package
(0.73 MB in, 6.36 MB out), so its object compile is tens of seconds. That is a
tuning question (inline threshold, per-object -O level, parallel objects), not
a correctness one, and it is recorded in W22 rather than guessed at now.

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == cc1afd93`, quickcheck `--fast` green.

## Round 290: -O2 has a size, and the backend is llc's job, not clang -c's

Round 289 bounded the *optimizer* on one bad shape (a table-sized aggregate).
Phase 8 then found the bound was in the wrong place: `net/http` is not a bad
shape, it is simply 18 MB of bitcode with a 90,000-instruction function
(`serveContent`), and `opt -passes=default<O2>` on it reaches 10.7 GB of RSS
and runs for many minutes. The netsmoke server build could not finish - the
gate never got past it. Three measurements decided the policy:

- **clang -c -O2 objects: 38 s per module.** 153 objects would have been 97
  minutes (measured: 19 objects in 12 minutes, then killed). clang re-runs the
  MIDDLE-END over bitcode `opt` has just optimized.
- **clang -c -O0 objects: 0.6 s, but 1.5x slower program.** FastISel costs the
  whole win: `time.Local` 59 -> 90 ns, `time.Now` 206 -> 293,
  scanner 83 -> 129 ms.
- **llc -O2: clang -O2's code quality without its optimizer.** 2.2 s for the
  1.8 MB runtime module (clang: 5.4 s), and the bench matches clang -O2:
  `local` 56-59, `alloc` 9-10, `time.Now` 196-217, scanner 78-80 ms.

So the pipeline is now: `opt` owns the middle-end, bounded by module size;
`llc` owns codegen at -O2; clang is only the `.ll` -> `.bc` front end.

- **`optBcBudget` = 6 MB.** Modules under it get `default<O2>`; the runtime
  (~3.5 MB post-opt) and bufio (~3.9 MB) - the two packages every per-call
  number in rounds 288-289 comes from - are inside it. Modules over it
  (`net/http` 18 MB, `crypto/tls` ~9 MB) get `mem2reg`, which is exactly what
  the whole tree got before round 288: bounded cost, no cliff.
- **`objCmd` runs `llc -O2 -filetype=obj -mtriple=<triple>
  -relocation-model=static -function-sections -data-sections`**, beside the
  configured clang (`objTool` swaps the basename). build.sh now checks llc's
  major with the rest of the tools.

Measured on the netsmoke server (153 modules):

    cold build   1545 s (25.7 min), peak RSS 3.67 GB
    warm build   0.6 s, byte-identical binary
    before       killed at 855 s, 19 of 153 objects

`time.Now` is 196-217 ns on this host, so W13's 200 ns target is reached but
not comfortably under it; the scanner is 78-80 ms against W14's 50 ms, and what
is left there is the package boundary (the runtime is a separate object, so its
helpers are still real calls). Both are recorded in the plan as measured, not
claimed.

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == 3476d547`, and the warm rebuild of a
binary is byte-identical to its cold build.

## Round 291: the sovereign group that outlived its arena (W2)

W2 said: `x509.CreateCertificate` leaks ~1 MB per call into the root arena, and
the codec prints "codec arena escape" for it. Round 288's return fast path
removed the warning (the codec no longer runs on that path), so the stated
cause was dead; the leak was not - 100 calls took the root arena from 9.5 MB to
112.9 MB.

**The instrument that answered it** is in `arena_scope.mx` now, and it is the
shape to reach for next time: `fnarena pushed/released/leaked` (a push counter
in `FnArenaPush`, a release counter in `ArenaRelease`, both gated on
`arenaTraceWanted`) and `sovhome root/sov/frame` (where a new group's receiver
was found). One run, 10 certificates:

    fnarena pushed=841789 released=841789 leaked=0
    sovhome root=3 sov=7109 frame=803
    sov created=7915 released=803 live=7112

No arena leaked, so the groups whose arenas were "still alive" had to be bound
to something else - and 7,109 of 7,915 receivers lived *inside another group's
sovereign data arena* (a receiver created while a receiver's method runs). The
frame-homed 803 were released; the nested 7,109 were not, and each kept a
192-byte root struct, its record slice and its data arena.

**The bug**: `sovReleaseArena` pushed the arena back to the pool after clearing
`sovGroupList` and `sovGroups` instead of running `arenaReleaseGroups` - the
fourth copy of the arena-exit teardown, and the only one that did not release
the groups. `ArenaReset`'s own comment records that this exact leak was found
and fixed there; the data-arena exit was missed, and it is the exit that owns
the *nested* receivers, so it is the exit where it matters most.

    after arenaReleaseGroups in sovReleaseArena:  live groups 7112 -> 3

**A second, smaller one** was left visible by the first: growth only fell to
890 KB per call, because `sovGroupFreeMax` was 32 while one certificate builds
~800 concurrent groups - the root-arena free list was smaller than the peak, so
every call carved structs and record slices it had already carved the call
before. Raised to 4096 (a free list has to hold the peak, not a token amount):

    100 certificates, root arena growth   103 MB -> 35.7 MB

What was left after that (357 KB per call) was the largest receiver's
record-slice doubling: `rootsize=131072` and `rootsize=65536` per six calls
were `sovGrowRecs` re-growing a 16,384-record array in the root arena, because
the group that gets recycled keeps whatever array it had and the big one lands
on a group that is not the one needing it next time. A third fix parks that
array: `sovParkedRecs` keeps the largest released record array (one slot, since
only one receiver per call is that large) and `sovGrowRecs` takes it instead of
asking the root arena for another.

    100 certificates, root arena growth   103 MB -> 35.7 MB -> 13.3 MB

133 KB per call still accumulates, spread over the remaining root-lifetime
bookkeeping (16/32-byte slices, a few 192-byte group structs, and record arrays
below the park threshold), and the size histogram no longer accounts for all of
it - the next instrument is the call-site attribution the ledger needs, and
W2's "no growth over 100 calls" is therefore measured, not met.

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == 4a1080da`.

## Round 292: what the compiler does not enforce about parameters, and the
parallel build's failure

Three measurements taken while closing out W5/W22, each of which changes what a
plan item should say.

**A pointer parameter can be written through, in both compilers.** The memory
model in CLAUDE.md says parameters are immutable borrows and that writing
through a parameter pointer is a compile-time error, enforced by the compiler
rather than by page protection, and that this is why parameters never need deep
copying across arena boundaries. It is not enforced:

    type T struct { x int64; y []byte }
    func writeThroughParam(p *T) { p.x = 7; p.y = []byte{:4} }
    func plainParam(n int64) { n = 5 }        // reassigning the parameter itself

Both compile and run (prints 7) with stage4 (`4a1080da`) and with the legacy
compiler, and `legacy/compiler/restrict.go` has no parameter-immutability check
at all. So the two compilers agree - wood law is satisfied - but the property
the model rests on is not a property of the language. It cannot be switched on
now either: W10's note records 570 pointer-parameter field writes in the tree,
so enforcement is a migration, not a bug fix. Recorded as W23; the honest
consequence today is that "a callee cannot write through a parameter" must not
be assumed by any arena argument.

**The parallel package build is broken, not just memory-capped.**
`adaptiveJobs` reports 1 on this machine, so `-j` was never exercised. Forcing
`-j 4` on the netsmoke server fails in 39 s with type-identity errors, not
resource exhaustion:

    nist.mx:56: cannot use value of type crypto/internal/fips140/ecdh.PublicKey
                 as crypto/internal/fips140.PublicKey
    mxc: parallel build failed      (peak RSS 4.0 GB)

Serial builds of the same tree are green (phase 8), so the defect is the
parallel package path's shared type state: two packages that name the same type
get different identities when they are type-checked concurrently. W22 keeps the
parallelism as its target but the blocker is this, not the memory budget.

**W5 closes by measurement, not by conversion.** The TLS record path does copy
the payload once per record (`payload = payload[explicitNonceLen:]`), and the
plan said to convert it only if the record path grows: phase 8's
no-accumulation unit reports rss 21112 kB -> 21344 kB over 400 exchanges
(+232 kB inline, +0 kB spawned), so the copies are frame-transient and the
"convert to an offset" risk (a view returned across a frame) is not worth
taking. `debug/gosym`'s per-symbol slices have exactly one consumer, the
`gosym_pclntab` fixture - the only other mention is a comment in
`encoding/binary` - so the O(n^2) parse has no production path to be slow on.

## Round 293: the runtime may import strconv, so float text is Go's text (W6)

`Float64Text` was a hand-rolled 15-digit formatter: every float printed as
`+1.500000000000000e+000`, no shortest representation, and the value came from
repeated multiplication. The plan called for a Ryu port into the runtime on the
assumption that the runtime cannot depend on the stdlib. It can - nothing in
`strconv`'s own imports (math, mxutil) imports the runtime, there is no cycle,
and the bootstrap self-hosts with the dependency in place:

    func Float64Text(v float64) string { return string(strconv.FormatFloat(v, 'g', -1, 64)) }
    func Float32Text(v float32) string { return string(strconv.FormatFloat(float64(v), 'g', -1, 32)) }

Output, checked against Go for the shapes that used to be wrong:

    1            1              1e-07        1e-07
    1.5          1.5            1e+21        1e+21
    0.1          0.1            1.23456789e+08
    1e6          1e+06          5e-324       5e-324
    1e308        1e+308         -0           -0
    1/3          0.3333333333333333
    float32(0.1) 0.1            +Inf / NaN   +Inf / NaN

`fmt.Sprint(1.5, 0.1, 1e308)` prints `1.5 0.1 1e+308`. The formatted text is now
`strconv`'s, which means one float formatter in the tree instead of two, and the
Ryu port the plan proposed would have duplicated it. Gate: bootstrap fixpoint
`s4b == s4c == 93bb8578`, and the probe output above is the test.

## Round 294: a fixed extent refuses push, pop and resize (W7c, stage4 side)

Measured on the compiler before this round, with an `[8]byte`:

    push(arr, v)      compiled, kept the array type, and SILENTLY DROPPED v
                      (len stayed 8, cap stayed -8)
    pop(arr)          clang: '%t2' defined with type '[8 x i8]' but expected
                      '{ ptr, i64, i64 }'
    resize(arr, 4)    the same clang error

So the refusal W7c asks for was missing exactly where the user's array
correction put the mechanism: the negative capacity already says the extent is
fixed, but stage4 still built the call. `buildBuiltinCall` now refuses all three
at type-check time, naming the fix:

    fixed-extent array: capacity cannot change; slice it with arr[:] to get a
    growable extent

The legacy compiler was already honest here and needed nothing: go/types rejects
the same three programs with "invalid push: argument must be a slice; have arr
(variable of type [8]byte)", "invalid operation: first argument to pop must be a
slice, ...", and the same for resize. A mirror in `legacy/compiler/compiler.go`
was written, measured to be unreachable, and removed - wood law is about the
behaviour, and both compilers now refuse; only the wording differs because the
pipelines differ. `arr[:]` still yields a growable slice (cap +N) and
`push(arr[:], v)` still works: the refusal is about the fixed extent, not about
the bytes.

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == b838bcb8`; the probe above is the
test for all three verbs in both compilers.

## Round 295: the ABI's fixed extents are buffers, not array fields (W7a starts)

The array campaign's design was decided this round: `[N]T` becomes a slice
header in ALL positions, the kernel-mirror layer is converted first (while
arrays still exist, so each family can be verified on its own), and then the
array type is deleted from the language. The reason the mirrors must move first
is physical: the kernel writes bytes at fixed offsets, and a header puts three
words where the kernel writes its first field, so a kernel-filled struct can
never carry one.

The pattern is `struct utsname`, landed whole:

    src/syscall/abi_extent.mx     abiWindow(b, off, n) - a VIEW of n bytes at
                                  off (b[off:off+n] would copy under the copy
                                  rule), abiCString(w) - up to the first NUL,
                                  abiBufferOf(buf) - the base a kernel call gets
    src/syscall/utsname_linux.mx  Utsname { raw []byte } + one accessor per
                                  field + Uname(u) passing abiBufferOf(u.raw)

The generated `Utsname` struct and its `Uname` wrapper are removed from
`ztypes_linux_{amd64,arm64}.mx` and `zsyscall_linux_{amd64,arm64}.mx` with a
comment saying why (they are generated files; the generator emits Go layouts and
cannot emit this, which is part of W7e's cost). The two callers read windows now.
Measured on this host:

    sysname Linux   nodename vivo   release 7.3.0-4-garuda   machine x86_64

against `uname -snrm` = `Linux vivo 7.3.0-4-garuda x86_64`.

The campaign's inventory, counted from the tree rather than estimated: **82
types carry 184 inline array fields** - ~25 kernel mirrors (148 fields, the
`ztypes` layer), ~12 on-disk/format descriptions (coverage defs, xcoff/ar), and
~45 ordinary-code buffers (gzip's [512]byte window, rc4's [256]byte sbox, bzip2,
gif, ...). The order and the per-family plan are in `docs/PLAN_REMAINING.md`
W7a; the next families are sockaddr (phase 8 exercises it end to end), then
