termios/ioctl, then file/stat, then the on-disk formats, then the representation
switch together with the ordinary-code conversions, then A3 (the type becomes a
compile error).

Gates: bootstrap fixpoint `s4b == s4c == c8fd2ccf`.

## Round 296: parameters are mutable - the rule was the lie, not the code

Round 292 measured that neither compiler enforces the documented "parameters are
immutable borrows" rule, and that 570 sites in the tree already write through
parameters. W23 asked for the decision and it is now made: **parameters are
mutable.** The reasoning is the same one that removed the rule's only
justification - there is one thread of execution per domain, so there is no
concurrent mutation for an immutable borrow to prevent. The rule bought nothing
and cost a false premise that arena arguments were being built on.

What the model now says, in CLAUDE.md, docs/REFERENCE.md and the skill's
memory-management page:

- a callee may write through a parameter pointer and may assign to a parameter,
  and the write is visible to the caller after the call;
- what it may NOT do is store a pointer to its OWN frame through a parameter -
  the frame is released at return and only RETURN values and receiver
  store-backs are relocated, so the caller would hold a dangling pointer (the
  W10 class, still open as a class);
- named return values are still REQUIRED, and a named result is assignable like
  any local;
- package-scoped variables are still IMMUTABLE outside `init()`, and the reason
  is domains rather than threads: a forked domain shares the pages, so two
  domains reading a global must see one value, and a value that changes after
  `init()` has no defined meaning across them.

No code changed: the tree already relied on mutable parameters. The comments
that justified a shape by the old rule (big.Float.Int returning instead of
writing an out-parameter, codecEnsure being a free function, the gosym test's
receiver) now say what is actually true - a callee's allocation cannot be
relocated into a caller object through a parameter, only through a return.

## Round 297: the return slot is the callee's, and that is the gap W24 names

The model now says parameters AND results are caller-owned, with a result
assignment being a shallow copy. The parameters half is true. The results half
is true only from the caller's store onwards, and this round measured why:

- `needsSret` in `_mxc_stage4/ir_util.mx` returns `false` unconditionally, and
  `legacy/compiler/` has no sret anywhere. Every result therefore travels in
  registers/an aggregate, the callee builds it in its own frame, and the caller
  stores it into caller memory after the call returns.
- The interior already behaves the way the model wants: a pointer into a caller
  arena (parameter data) is aliased rather than copied, and callee-created
  pointees are relocated into the caller's arena - that is what `codecRetStable`
  (round 283) and the ancestor-arena rule decide.
- The stage4 plumbing for sret exists and is dead: the emitter declares
  `ptr sret(<T>)` and the call sites allocate a slot when `needsSret` says so,
  so the change is to select the right return types and then make it true in
  legacy as well.

Doing it as a footnote would be the wrong shape: it changes the ABI of every
Moxie function that returns pointers, in both compilers, and a half-landed ABI
change breaks the bootstrap rather than a package. W24 carries the four-step
plan, the one trap that matters (the caller's slot must be one alloca per CALL
SITE, not a fresh caller-arena allocation per call, which would grow the
caller's arena linearly in a loop), and the acceptance test. The tree stays
green at `19a2606f` until that campaign starts.

## Round 298: the return slot is already the caller's, and a literal was not one object

W24 asked for sret so a result would be created in the caller's arena. This
round measured the ABI instead of changing it, and the measurement says the
step is already taken - at a lower level, and by every compiler:

- A Moxie slice is `{ ptr, i64, i64 }`. `return_ownership`'s
  `lib.FromParam` (return type `{ {ptr,i64,i64}, i32 }`) compiles to code that
  writes its result through `%rdi` - the caller-provided hidden pointer - with
  the arguments in `%rsi/%rdx/%rcx`. LLVM's backend lowers any aggregate that
  does not fit in registers to exactly the ABI an IR `sret` would spell.
  `llc-22` on an 80-byte `{[80 x i8]}` return does the same (writes through
  `%rdi`), while a 16-byte `{ptr,i32,i32}` comes back in `%rax:%rdx:%rcx`.
- So IR sret would change only the returns that are ALREADY cheaper than
  memory - a bare pointer, a two-word header - and would leave the large ones
  exactly as they are. Every Moxie function that returns pointers would pay a
  memory store instead of a register move. That is a pessimisation with no
  semantic payload, which is why `needsSret` stays `false`: it is the honest
  answer, not a stub.
- The property the rule actually asks for - a parameter's data keeps its
  identity across the return, and only what the callee created itself is
  function-scoped - is the codec's, and it is implemented. The one thing the
  old fixture got wrong is that it lived in `package main`, which
  `funcNeedsCodec` exempts (runtime, unsafe, syscall, os, main, pkg/*): no frame
  arena, no codec, no relocation, so it could not observe the property at all.
  `return_ownership` is now a directory fixture whose callee is a real `lib/`
  package.

Writing that fixture found a defect, in legacy: a string constant was not one
object. `legacy/compiler/compiler.go` `createConst` called `llvm.AddGlobal` on
every call, and it runs once per USE, so one literal occurrence produced
`$string`, `$string.1`, ... - five globals for one `[]byte("caller")`.
Consequence: `b := []byte("caller"); p := b; b[0] = 'X'` printed "copied" under
legacy and "aliased" under stage4, and a parameter assigned into a returned
struct came back detached from the caller's own buffer. Fixed by caching the
object per constant VALUE (legacy) and by `stringConstOperand` (stage4).

The two halves then disagreed about two *occurrences* of the same text: stage4
shared one global by content, legacy kept them distinct. Decided: one object per
occurrence. Content sharing between unrelated sites is action at a distance on a
mutable object - the same hazard that makes package globals immutable outside
`init()` - and it is not observable as inequality, because string equality is by
content (`runtime.stringEqual`). `addStringConst` still folds text for the other
users (panic-message strings); string constants go through
`stringConstOperand`, and `mergeAccumulators` now appends every pending entry so
a provisional `.str.N` index cannot shift onto another literal's bytes.

Measured after the change: `[]byte("abc")` twice, write through the first, both
compilers print `first: Xbc` / `second: abc`; `p := b` aliases in both. The
fixture passes under both compilers.

## Round 298b: what `package main` does not get

While moving the ownership fixture across a package boundary, the exclusion
itself came into view. `funcNeedsArenaCopy` excludes `main` from the per-function
arena and the return codec, in both compilers, with no comment saying why - the
answer is that the compiler is `package main` and manages its arenas by hand.

For a user binary that means a main-package function emits no `FnArenaPush` and
nothing it allocates is reclaimed at return. Measured: 256 iterations of a 4 MiB
allocation inside a main-package helper die with `arena: region mmap failed`
under `ulimit -v 400000` - 1 GiB of unreachable garbage, because the buffers land
in the root arena and stay. Library callees are untouched by this (their own
frame arena is pushed and popped); the loop has to be *written in main* for it to
happen, which is exactly where a small server's request loop lives.

Recorded as W25 with the three shapes a fix can take. It is a decision, not a
patch: (b) - a build flag the compiler passes for its own build, so user main
packages get the full protocol - is the coherent one, because the exclusion
exists for the compiler, not for the language.

## Round 299: the sockaddr family is buffers, and the caller owns them (W7a step 2)

Under the header-everywhere design the sockaddr mirrors had to move first: a
Moxie `[N]T` field will be a slice header, and the kernel writes `sa_family_t` at
offset 0, so an inline array field is exactly where a header cannot go. The
conversion is not a representation change to the mirrors - it deletes them:

- `RawSockaddrInet4/6/Unix/Linklayer/Netlink/Any` and `RawSockaddr` are gone
  from both `ztypes_linux_*` files. Their offsets are in
  `src/syscall/abi_sockaddr.mx` and their sizes stay as `SizeofSockaddr*`.
- The interesting part is not the offsets, it is ownership. The old interface
  was `sockaddr() (unsafe.Pointer, _Socklen, error)` and the storage was an
  inline array inside the `Sockaddr` value, so it lived wherever that value
  lived. A byte-buffer version cannot do that: a buffer allocated inside
  `sockaddr()` lives in that call's frame arena and dies when it returns, and
  the kernel is handed the pointer *after* that. So the method is now
  `sockaddr(buf []byte) (slen, err)` and the caller passes storage it owns -
  `Bind`, `Connect`, `Sendto`, `SendmsgN` and the inet-specific wrappers
  allocate `sockaddrBuf()` in their own frame. That is the user's rule written
  into the interface: both sides of the call belong to the caller.
- Output directions (`Accept4`, `Getsockname`, `Getpeername`, `Recvfrom`,
  `Recvmsg`) allocate the buffer, let the kernel fill it, then read fields back
  through windows (`sockFamily`, `sockPort`, `sockIPv4Addr`, `sockIPv6Addr`,
  `abiGet16/32/8`). The generated wrappers per arch (`accept4`, `getpeername`,
  `getsockname`, `recvfrom`) take `[]byte` and pass `abiBufferOf(...)`; the
  `//sys` lines they are generated from carry the same signature.
- `IPv6MTUInfo` was the only struct embedding a raw mirror (`RawSockaddrInet6`
  plus a 32-bit MTU), so it became a buffer with `addr()`/`mtu()` windows.
- `abi_extent.mx` gained `abiGet/Put8/16/32` and `abiPutBytes`, and its tag
  moved from `linux` to `unix` so the sockaddr code (which is `unix`) and
  `utsname` (which is `linux`) can share it.

Verified end to end, both compilers: a probe binds an IPv4 socket and reads the
bound port and address back through `Getsockname`, does the same for IPv6,
round-trips a path through a Unix-domain socket, sends a UDP datagram with
`Sendto` and reads it with `Recvfrom` including the source address; a net-only
probe does `Listen`/`Dial`/`Accept` and moves a payload. `bind`/`connect`/
`accept`/`getsockname`/`getpeername`/`sendto`/`recvfrom` all cross the new
buffer boundary.

Still array-bearing in this family, and next: `Msghdr` (`Pad_cgo_0/1 [4]byte`),
`IPMreq`, `IPMreqn`, `Inet4Pktinfo`, `Inet6Pktinfo`, `ICMPv6Filter`
(`Data [8]uint32`), `IPv6Mreq`. Those are step 3/4 shapes - `Msghdr` is the one
that matters, because `recvmsgRaw`/`sendmsgRaw` hand it to the kernel.

## Round 300: the object stage was serial, and a keyed table was 26,000 instructions

Two measurements from watching a cold netsmoke build spend forty minutes in one
`llc` after another.

**The object pool inherited the wrong job count.** `objFiles` called
`runPool(todo, bst.buildJobs)`, and the default job count is
`adaptiveJobs()` = `min(nproc-1, (MemAvailable/2) / workerMemBudget)` with
`workerMemBudget = 4 GB`. That budget is sized for a package *compile* worker
holding a whole compile arena; an `llc` process peaks at 594 MB on the largest
module in the tree (x/text/unicode/norm, measured) and 542 MB on net/http's 18 MB
module. So on a 15 GB box with a browser open the object stage ran at **one
parallel**, 153 objects one after another with seven cores idle.

`objectJobs()` is the object stage's own bound: `nproc-1`, capped by
`MemAvailable / llcMemBudget` (768 MB, the measured peak plus headroom), with an
explicit `-j` still an upper bound - it is an instruction, not a default. The
log now says what each stage does: `bitcode: N files, J parallel` for the
clang IR stage and `objects: N files, J parallel` for the llc stage.

Measured on the netsmoke server, cold both times, same sources: **28 min -> 12m28s**
(34m49s of CPU over 7 cores). The remaining critical path is the `net` package
itself: an 11.6 MB module with no oversized function (largest block 1,792
instructions) that llc simply spends ~7 minutes on.

**A keyed constant array literal expanded element by element.** `x/net/idna` and
`x/text/unicode/norm` write their tables as

    func _idnaValues() [8640]uint16 { return [8640]uint16{ 0x00: 0x0080, ... } }

`constArrayLitText` refused keyed elements, so the table became memset + 8,640
stores, and every *read* materialized the returned array: `llc -O2` on idna spent
109 s, of which 76 s was X86 instruction selection and 27 s the machine
scheduler, on five functions each holding ONE basic block of ~25,900
instructions (`-O0` and `-O1` are worse, 141 s and 117 s: same DAG). The block is
`opt`'s aggregate expansion of the 17 KB array copy - 8,648 extractvalue + 8,645
getelementptr, one per element.

`constArrayLitText` now accepts keyed elements (and Go's continuation rule),
fills a zeroed value array, and emits one constant global, so `_idnaValues` is a
memset + one memcpy + a load. The per-element path is still there for
non-constant or non-integer elements, and legacy keeps it for everything: go/ssa
does not present a composite literal as one foldable value, so the reference
compiler emits per-element stores. The IR differs in size, not in meaning, and
that asymmetry is recorded in `docs/PLAN_REMAINING.md` W7a.

What is left on this path is the *array value* itself: `_idnaValues()[i]` copies
the whole table into memory to read one element, at IR level and at run time.
That is W7a step 6's job (the tables become slices, so the index reads rodata
directly), and it is now the only reason these two packages are still slow to
lower.

## Round 301: the Unicode tables are storage, not values (W26 / W7a step 6)

Round 300 removed the *initializer* half of the table problem. This removes the
value half, and the numbers say it was the larger one.

`x/net/idna` and `x/text/unicode/norm` carried their tables as accessor
functions returning arrays, so every read was `_idnaValues()[i]`: the callee
rebuilt the table and the caller copied the whole thing to read one element.
The generated files now declare the storage and build it once:

    var _idnaValuesTbl []uint16
    func init() { _idnaValuesTbl = []uint16{ 0x00: 0x0080, ... } }
    func _idnaValues() []uint16 { return _idnaValuesTbl }

Call sites are untouched (`_idnaValues()[i]` still reads a slice header), and a
Moxie package variable cannot carry an initializer, so the literal lives in the
one `init()` the package is allowed. Two source-level prerequisites landed in
the compiler first, both in `ssa_builder.mx`:

- **A keyed slice literal is indexed by its keys**, and its length is the
  highest key plus one. `buildSliceLit` ignored `KeyValueExpr` entirely and used
  the element position: `[]byte{2: 'a', 5: 'b'}` produced a length-2 slice with
  the bytes at 0 and 1. (An array literal already followed the rule; go/ssa
  already followed it in legacy, so this made stage4 match both.)
- **A large all-constant slice literal takes the memcpy path**, the same
  `SSAConstMemCpy` lowering `buildArrayLit` uses: one private constant global,
  one memcpy into the slice's storage. Without it the conversion would have
  moved the giant block from the readers into `init`.

Measured, before -> after:

    module size   idna 5.3 MB -> 442 KB      norm 9.0 MB -> 569 KB
    llc -O2       idna 109 s  -> 0.87 s      norm 205 s  -> 1.04 s
    llc peak RSS  idna 594 MB -> 99 MB       norm 594 MB -> 94 MB
    largest block idna 25,928 -> 15,289*     norm (decomps) -> 11,761*
    netsmoke server, `-a`, cold: 25.7 min ->  11m26s

\* what remains is `init` itself: the `[]valueRange` tables have struct elements,
so their literals still expand element by element. That is 15,289 instructions
of constant stores once per process instead of 26,000 per lookup, and llc now
spends under a second on it. A constant-global path for struct-element literals
would remove even that, and is the next step if those tables grow again.

Verified: idna's ToASCII round-trip (`bücher.example` -> `xn--bcher-kva.example`)
and a norm probe covering NFC composition, NFD decomposition, NFKC compatibility
(Kelvin sign -> K) and `IsNormal` on normalised and unnormalised input, under the
converted tables and under both compilers' builds of the probe.

## Round 302: the kernel mirrors carry no fixed extents (W7a step 3)

Twenty structs in `ztypes_linux_*` spelled a kernel extent as a Go array field.
An `[N]T` is a slice header in Moxie, so it cannot sit where the kernel writes
its first byte - and fifteen of the twenty had no reader in the tree at all.
Gone with their only users: `Timex`/`Adjtimex`, `Statfs_t`+`Fsid`/`Fstatfs`+
`Statfs`, `Ustat_t`/`Ustat`, `Sysinfo_t`/`Sysinfo`, `FdSet`/`Select`+`pselect`,
`Flock_t`/`FcntlFlock`, `ICMPv6Filter` and its setters, `IPMreq`/`SetsockoptIPMreq`,
`Inet4Pktinfo`, `Inet6Pktinfo`, `TCPInfo`, `InotifyEvent`, `Termios`,
`PtraceRegs` (+`PC`/`SetPC` and the two reg wrappers), and `lsf_linux.mx`
(`SockFilter`, `SockFprog`, and a `[IFNAMSIZ]byte` ioctl extent nothing used).

Kept and converted: `Stat_t`'s trailing 24 bytes are three scalars (the kernel
writes sizeof(struct stat) and they are unused), `Msghdr`/`SockFprog` dropped
their `Pad_cgo_*` (compiler alignment padding, not extent), `IPMreqn`/`IPv6Mreq`
carry `abiAddr4`/`abiAddr16` (one byte per field, layout exact), `Dirent` is
`Dirent*Off` constants over the record `getdents` wrote, `caps` is a 24-byte
buffer read at fixed offsets, and `pipe2`/`socketpair`/`utimes`/`utimensat`/
`futimesat` take a pointer to the first element instead of a pointer to a
two-element array.

Measured against C on this host, field by field: sizeof(struct stat)=144 with
dev@0 ino@8 mtim@88 ctim@104, sizeof(struct msghdr)=56, sizeof(struct sock_fprog)=16,
sizeof(struct ip_mreqn)=12, sizeof(struct ipv6_mreq)=20 - identical before and
after, and identical to the Moxie mirrors. A functional probe covers stat,
lstat, SameFile, readdir, rename, utimensat, utimes, pipe2, socketpair and the
faccessat capability path; phase 8 passed (2/2) and quickcheck 15/15.

## Round 303: the tables that could never be selected, and the ones that were

Every `go1.N` build tag from go1.9 to go1.24 is satisfied, so a `!go1.N` guard
is always false: the five superseded copies each of the idna, norm and bidi
Unicode tables (plus `idna9.0.0.mx`, `pre_go118.mx`, `trie12.0.0.mx` and
`bidirule9.0.0.mx`) were dead weight holding ~65 array types. Deleted.

The tables that DO build became storage: `_bidiValues`/`_bidiIndex`
(x/text/unicode/bidi), `_huffmanCodes`/`_huffmanCodeLen` (hpack),
`_isTokenTable`/`_validHostByte` (httpguts), `_replacementTable` (html), the five
`__Code_index_N` tables (internal/types/errors), and the syscall errno/signal
tables. `runtime/secalloc_chacha`'s and intrinsics' de Bruijn tables are string
constants instead - one byte per index, no array type at all.

The syscall errno and signal tables are the interesting ones: `Errno.Error()`
called `_errors()` and copied 133 strings on EVERY conversion. They are built
once in the package's `init()` now and `Errno.Error`/`Signal.String` read the
variable, so an error string costs a header load.

## Round 304: three stage4 codegen holes, found by RUNNING idna instead of building it

Round 301 verified the converted Unicode tables by building idna and comparing
`bücher.example -> xn--bcher-kva.example` - which is the punycode ENCODER, a path
that never touches the mapping tables. Running the full profile under both
compilers showed stage4 returning `ExAmPle.COM` unchanged and `bToUnicode`
producing interleaved NULs. Three separate bugs, all silent wrong answers:

1. **`string([]rune)` was a header reinterpretation.** `[]rune` and `string`
   share the three-word shape, so `srcType == dstType` returned the value
   untouched: `string([]rune{'a','b','c'})` was a 3-byte string holding
   `"a\x00\x00"`, and `[]rune("aüc")` was four "runes" whose second value was
   0xC3. `emitConvert` now calls `runtime.stringFromRunes` /
   `runtime.stringToRunes`, exactly as legacy does. The runtime's own
   `stringToRunes` was also wrong in BOTH compilers: it walked `for range s`,
   which in Moxie is bytes, not code points; it decodes UTF-8 now.
2. **A keyed composite literal with a NAMED-CONSTANT key dropped the key.**
   `buildCompositeLitInto`'s array path understood only integer-literal keys
   and advanced `posIdx++` instead of `posIdx = key+1`, so
   `[6][2]ruleTransition{ruleInitial: ..., ruleRTL: ...}` in
   x/text/secure/bidirule was written positionally - ruleRTL's row landed at
   index 1 and every ASCII label failed the bidi rule. The key is now resolved
   through the constant folder (named constants and constant expressions), and
   an unkeyed element follows the last KEY, which is Go's rule.
3. **A func-typed field promoted from an embedded struct was invisible.**
   `buildFuncFieldCall` asked `fieldIndex` for the field in the outer type,
   got -1, and reported the field as undefined - so `p.mapping(p, s)` on
   `idna.Profile` (whose `mapping` lives on the embedded `options`) could not be
   built at all. The embedded path is walked now (`fieldTypeAtPath`).

Verified: a probe printing html unescape, errno and signal text, NFC, NFD,
idna ToASCII/ToUnicode and punycode encode gives byte-identical output under
both compilers, and the new fixture
`tests/regressions/should_compile/rune_keyed_promoted/` exercises all three
constructs through a package boundary.

Lesson recorded because it cost four rounds: "it builds and the encoder
round-trips" is not evidence about the encoder's inputs. Compare the OUTPUT of
the same program under both compilers, for the path you actually changed.

## Round 305: more tables are storage (order tables, trace, image, zstd, coverage)

Converted to `var` + the package's one `init()`: the four ECDSA/ECDH curve-order
tables each (`_p224Order` ... `_p521Order`), `_scalarMinusOneBytes`,
`CovMetaMagic`/`CovCounterMagic`, `_rtPkgs`, the trace tables (`_specs`,
`_experiments`, `_eventKindStrings`, `_tracev2*`, `_orderingDispatch`,
`_frameFields`, `EventArgTypes`), zstd's FSE baselines and predefined tables,
`_seqCodeInfo`, `_rfc6979ExtraDataV0`, net's `_defaultNS`/`_flagNames`,
http2's `_http2padZeros`/`_http2frameNames`/`_http2frameParsers`/`_http2stateName`,
`_replacementTable` (already), the gif/png interlacing tables and gif's log2
lookup, and x509's `_publicKeyAlgoName`. Net effect this round: 480 array type
occurrences left in the tree, down from 574 at the start of the session.

`runtime/string.mx` lost its last array too: `encodeUTF8` used to RETURN a
`[4]byte` per code point, which is both an array type in the hottest path in the
runtime and a copy. It writes into the caller's buffer now (`encodeUTF8At`), with
`utf8Len` for the counting pass. Note the writes are at explicit offsets
(`dst[off+1] = ...`), not through `dst[off:]` - a sub-slice is a copy in Moxie, so
the tail would be a throwaway.

Verified: ECDSA sign/verify on P-224/P-256/P-384/P-521, ECDH shared-secret
agreement, and x509 create+parse (which uses the algorithm-name table) all pass
on the bootstrapped compiler; the html/idna/norm/syscall probe, the rune probe,
the mirror (stat/readdir/pipe2/socketpair) probe and the keyed-literal probe all
pass; fixpoint `s4b == s4c == d66002eb`.

## Round 306: OPEN BUG - the second `idna.Lookup().ToUnicode` call corrupts the arena under stage4

Found while probing round 305's tables, and NOT caused by it: it reproduces at
commit 14205680 (round 304) and with `src/runtime/string.mx` reverted to that
commit's version. It is the top open item.

    u := idna.Lookup().ToUnicode("xn--bcher-kva.example")   // OK
    u2 := idna.Lookup().ToUnicode("xn--bcher-kva.example")  // SIGSEGV

What is known, measured:

- One call is fine; the second faults. `Punycode().ToUnicode` twice is fine.
  `Lookup().ToUnicode` on a label WITHOUT the `xn--` prefix, twice, is fine.
  `Lookup().ToASCII` twice is fine. So the trigger is the ace-prefix decode path
  (`decode` -> `labels.set` -> `fromPuny` = `validateFromPunycode` -> NFC +
  `_trie().lookupString`) inside a full profile.
- Under gdb the fault is inside `ArenaReset`: `mov 0x50(%rbx),%eax` (reading
  `a.scope`) and, with tracing, in the region walk - the faulting address is a
  page-aligned mmap base, i.e. the arena that is being reset has already been
  unmapped.
- The function-arena depth is balanced: `0` before the first call and `0` after
  it, so this is not a leaked frame; it is a released arena being reset again.
- Under the LEGACY compiler the same probe prints two `SOVFREE` lines (the
  sovereign-group releases) and succeeds; under stage4 no `SOVFREE` runs at all
  before the crash. The divergence is therefore in stage4's code, and the
  sovereign-group lifetime machinery (`arenaReleaseGroups`,
  `sovInvalidateArena`, `codecSovereignFree`, `sovReleaseArena`) is the shape
  to look at: `labelIter` in idna is a self-mutating type, so `&labels` gets a
  sovereign group keyed by a STACK address, and a group keyed by a stack address
  that is reused by the next call is exactly the aliasing `ArenaReset`'s own
  comment describes.
- It became reachable only after round 304 fixed promoted func-typed fields:
  before that, `p.mapping(p, s)` did not compile correctly, so this path returned
  a wrong answer instead of running. The wrong answer was never the lesser evil;
  the arena bug behind it is now visible.

Nothing in the current gates reaches it (quickcheck and phase 8 pass), which is
why it ships recorded rather than silently. The repro is six lines and is the
first thing to run when picking this up.

### Round 306, further measurement: it is layout-dependent

Running `runtime.ArenaScopeReport()` between the two calls makes the crash go
away, which is the useful part: the corruption is an out-of-bounds WRITE whose
victim is whatever happens to sit past the end of a region, not a deterministic
logic error. The report shows the arena accounting is correct around the call
(`sov created=2 released=1 live=1`, root usage growing by ~9 KB), so the write is
not in the sovereign counters either.

Next steps for whoever picks this up, in order:

1. Find the write. The candidates are the places that bypass bounds checks: the
   runtime's `memcpy`/`memzero`/`unsafe.Slice` users and the `//:nobounds`
   functions (`decodeUTF8`), plus any `unsafe.Add` cursor. `decodeUTF8` is a
   READ; the write is elsewhere. `memzero(addr, unsafe.Sizeof(DomainRoot{}))` in
   `initDomain` is sized by the struct - if stage4's `DomainRoot` layout differs
   from the one the carved offsets assume, the carve writes tables past the
   mapped header and every later reset walks a truncated region. That is worth
   checking FIRST: it is a one-place mismatch, it would corrupt exactly the
   header fields `ArenaReset` reads (`regions`, `nregions`), and a layout
   divergence between the two compilers is the one thing this tree has already
   been bitten by.
2. ~~Compare `unsafe.Sizeof(runtime.DomainRoot{})` and every `rawSlice*` carve
   offset under both compilers.~~ MEASURED and ruled out: a temporary
   `LayoutReport` returns `Arena size 96, DomainRoot size 344,
   domainHeaderSize 352, regions@56, nregions@0, scope@80, alloc@88,
   arenaDataOffset 3072` under BOTH compilers, byte for byte. The carve is
   correct, so the write is somewhere else. Also ruled out: the arena accounting
   (`sov created/released`, root usage) is consistent across the call, and the
   function-arena depth is balanced.

## Round 307: where the compiler's memory goes (the "500 MB very fast" observation)

Measured on a hello-world build with every cache invalidated (`-a`), sampling
/proc and tracing mmap:

    virtual at start    260 MB    (initDomain maps one 256 MB domain region)
    virtual peak        1058 MB
    RSS peak            714 MB    reached inside one package's compile
    RSS after link      208 MB
    large mmaps (>=32MB) 39 calls, 4.6 GB of address space in total

Breakdown:

- **256 MB domain region**, mapped once at startup and never released. Virtual
  only; pages commit on touch. This is the floor for every program.
- **One compile arena per package**: `len(src) * 1000`, floor 64 MB, cap
  512 MB (`ir_typecheck.mx`). The `runtime` package hits the 512 MB cap and
  touches ~400-500 MB during SSA construction and IR emission - that is the
  714 MB peak, and it is what "allocates 500 MB very fast" is. The arena IS
  freed at the end of the package (`ArenaFree`), which is why RSS falls back to
  ~208 MB.
- **`root=1/131 MB`**: the root arena keeps 131 MB of type-universe state for
  the whole run (one region, no growth).
- The eight 256 MB maps during `link` are the `ld.lld` CHILD processes, each
  with its own domain region; they are not the parent's RSS.
- IR text is streamed to the .ll file (`emitter.outFile`), not accumulated, so
  the text is not the spike. The spike is per-package SSA/type state.

Candidate reductions, in order of expected value (not measured yet):

1. Release per-package state earlier: the AST (`src`), SSA graphs and descriptor
   tables are alive together for the whole package. Freeing the AST after type
   check and each function's SSA after its emission would cut the peak without
   changing any output.
2. The 1000x arena sizing factor is a guess. Measure `arena.alloc` at ci-tc per
   package and set the factor from the observed worst case; the cap exists
   precisely so growth can append instead.
3. 256 MB for the domain region is generous when the root only uses 131 MB and
   never grows.

## Round 308: address values are slices (sockaddr, netip, dnsmessage)

A `[4]byte`/`[16]byte` address field is a slice header in Moxie, so every
address VALUE in the tree is a slice now: `SockaddrInet4.Addr`,
`SockaddrInet6.Addr`, `SockaddrLinklayer.Addr` (and the net_fake stubs),
`netip.Addr.As4()`/`As16()`, dnsmessage's `AResource.A`/`AAAAResource.AAAA`,
`net.rawdns`'s nameserver address, and the netip locals behind them.

These structs are converted into the ABI buffer by `sockaddr()` - they are not
handed to the kernel - so their layout was never the kernel's, and the comment
that said otherwise ("As16 returns a fixed 16-byte array ... because their
layout is the kernel's") is deleted with the code it justified.

The trap this class sets, and the reason it was done in one pass: `s[a:]` on a
slice is a COPY, so `copy(sa.Addr[:], ip4)` still compiles and writes into a
throwaway. Every one of those 16 sites became `copy(sa.Addr, ...)`, and every
construction site now allocates the extent (`SockaddrInet4{Port: p, Addr:
[]byte{:4}}`) BEFORE the kernel call fills it. A nil `Addr` would compile too,
and the address would silently stay 0.0.0.0 - so the receive-side buffers in
`net/udpsock_posix.mx` are allocated where the struct is built.

Verified: a probe that binds a TCP listener on 127.0.0.1:0, dials it, accepts,
moves a payload, and reads the accepted peer back (bind/connect build the buffer
from the struct; getsockname/accept fill the struct from the buffer), then does
a UDP send/recv and checks the returned peer's four bytes and port, plus
`netip.As4/As16` lengths and a dnsmessage Message.

## Round 309: two bugs found while probing the address work, both recorded not fixed

- **W29: stage4 accepts `+` for text concatenation in a user package; legacy
  rejects it** ("moxie: '+' is not allowed for text concatenation, use |
  operator"). The restriction exists in `legacy/compiler/restrict.go` and stage4
  only enforces it somewhere the probe did not reach. `src/net/ipsock.mx` uses
  `+` legitimately (stdlib is exempt), so this is about USER packages only.
- **W30: rendering a just-returned IP through `JoinHostPort` gives garbage**,
  under BOTH compilers:
      net.JoinHostPort(net.IPString(ip), "53443")   -> "2.0.0.0:53443"
      net.JoinHostPort("127.0.0.1", "53443")        -> "127.0.0.1:53443"
  and the same call renders a random address on each run (32.76.9.213, 2.0.0.0),
  which is a dangling pointer, not a formatting mistake. The peer's BYTES are
  correct (`IPString(ua.IP)` alone prints "127.0.0.1"), so the sockaddr
  conversion is right and the corruption is in the string path. This is very
  likely the same arena-lifetime class as W27 and is the second symptom to use
  when chasing it: it reproduces with `ufrom.String()` on a received UDP address
  and needs no idna at all.

## Round 310: h2's ping payloads, image/draw's palette entries, and a write that went nowhere

`http2PingFrame.Data`, `sentPingData`, `http2writePing.data`, `WritePing`'s
parameter and the three local ping payload buffers are slices; the in-flight
ping map is keyed by `string(payload)`, which is the same eight bytes compared by
content. `http2incomparable` (`[0]func()`, the Go idiom for "make this struct
non-comparable at zero cost") is deleted: a fixed extent is a slice header here,
so it cost 24 bytes in each of the ten structs that embedded it - and none of
them is ever compared.

`image/draw`'s palette and Floyd-Steinberg error buffers are
`[]paletteEntry{C0..C3 int32}` instead of `[][4]int32`: 16 bytes per entry
instead of a 96-byte slice header, in buffers walked per pixel.

Two bugs fell out of that work, both older than the array campaign:

- **W31: a paletted draw wrote into a copy.** `drawPaletted` did
  `pix = p.Pix[p.PixOffset(...):]` and then `pix[y*stride+x] = index`. A
  sub-slice is a COPY in Moxie, so the index went into a throwaway: every
  `draw.Draw` into an `*image.Paletted` was a silent no-op and the destination
  pixels kept their old values. It is a base slice plus an offset now. Measured
  with a four-colour palette and exact palette colours: before the fix every
  pixel came out 0; after it, red/green/blue/black land on 1/2/3/0 and a
  near-red pixel quantizes to 1, under BOTH compilers.
- **A shadowed package constant made `image/draw` unbuildable by legacy.**
  `const m = 1<<16 - 1` and the `Quantizer.Quantize(p []color.Color, m
  image.Image)` parameter - legacy refuses the file ("'m' shadows declaration in
  enclosing scope"), stage4 accepted it. Renamed to `maxChannel`. This is the
  W29 direction (stage4 enforces fewer restrictions than legacy) with a concrete
  cost: the reference compiler could not build a package the tree ships.

## Round 311 CORRECTED: internal/coverage compiles again; nothing is deleted

An earlier pass in this round deleted `internal/xcoff` and `internal/coverage`
because they were unimported and unbuildable. That was wrong on both counts, and
the reason `internal/coverage` was unbuildable was a bug INTRODUCED BY THIS
CAMPAIGN: round 303 converted `defs.mx`'s two magic tables to `var` + `init()`
and round 305 converted `pkid.mx`'s runtime package list the same way, so the
package ended up with TWO `func init()` - which Moxie rejects outright. The
package was never broken before the conversion; the conversion broke it.

Fixed by consolidating: `pkid.mx`'s single `init()` now builds all three tables
(the two magics and the runtime package list) and `defs.mx` has none. The
package compiles and its accessors return the right bytes again:

    coverage.CovMetaMagic()    -> 4 bytes, {0x00, 'c', 'v', 'm'}
    coverage.CovCounterMagic() -> 4 bytes
    coverage.MetaSymbolHeader  -> usable

`internal/xcoff` is restored as it was (20 array types, still to convert). Its
type-checking succeeds but its IR is rejected by clang for a reason that is a
compiler defect, not a package defect - see W32 below.

The lesson: "unbuildable" has to be traced to a cause before it is used as an
argument. Here the cause was two files each declaring the package's one init
because two separate table conversions were landed in different rounds.

## Round 312: W32 - a stage4 GEP that indexes a slice header with a variable

    %t54 = getelementptr inbounds {ptr, i64, i64}, ptr %t17, i32 0, i32 %t53

`{ptr, i64, i64}` is a slice and `%t53` is a runtime value: an `x[i]` lowered as
a field index into the slice HEADER instead of an index into the data pointer's
element type. clang refuses it, so `internal/xcoff` cannot link. This is a
stage4-only defect of the "wrong IR, silently" class (cf. W29) and it is open.
`internal/xcoff` reaches it through `binary.Read(..., unsafe.TypeOf(hdr),
unsafe.Pointer(hdr))` on its `[8]byte`-bearing header structs; rewriting those
readers as byte blocks + windows (W7a step 5) removes the construct, and the
descriptor path itself still needs the fix.

## Round 313: constructors for structs whose slice fields imply a length

Converting a fixed extent to a slice moves the length OUT of the type, so a bare
composite literal now compiles with a nil or short field - which is how every
IPv4 dial silently became a dial to 0.0.0.0 in round 308. The length has to be
established in one place, so each such struct gets a constructor:

    syscall.NewSockaddrInet4(port int32, addr []byte) SockaddrInet4
    syscall.NewSockaddrInet6(port, zoneId int32/uint32, addr []byte) SockaddrInet6
    syscall.NewSockaddrLinklayer(ifindex int32, halen uint8, addr []byte) SockaddrLinklayer
    dnsmessage.NewAResource(addr []byte) (AResource, error)      // 4 bytes
    dnsmessage.NewAAAAResource(addr []byte) (AAAAResource, error) // 16 bytes

plus unexported `newSockaddrInet4/6`, `newSockaddrLinklayer`, `newAResource`,
`newAAAAResource` and h2's `newPingFrame` for the READ paths, where the point is
"allocate the extent the kernel/file will fill". Call sites use the constructors
and never spell `[]byte{:4}` inline.

Two rules restated with this round, because both were violated on the way here:

- **A slice IS the reference.** No `*[]T` parameter, and no `*[N]T`, is needed
  where a slice will do: passing the slice header gives the callee the same
  backing store, so writers and readers both take `[]byte`, `[]uint16`, ....
  Pointers stay for genuine C ABI arguments (`getrlimit`'s `*uint64`) and for
  receiver-like structs that the callee mutates (`*macState`).
- **The length belongs to the constructor**, not to every call site.

Verified: the net probe (TCP bind/dial/accept/peer, UDP send/recv peer bytes,
netip.As4/As16, dnsmessage round trip) passes under both compilers, the paletted
draw and poly1305 fixtures pass, and `internal/coverage` builds.

## Round 314: keccakf's 25 lanes are a slice view; chacha20's key/nonce conversion is BLOCKED and recorded

`keccakf.mx`: the state was `*[25]uint64`, and on a little-endian host it is
literally a view of the byte buffer (`(*[25]uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&da[0]))`).
It is `[]uint64` now, built with `unsafe.Slice((*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&da[0])),
25)` - the same view, no array type - and the big-endian path decodes into
`[]uint64{:25}` and writes back through `keccakfStoreBack(da []byte, a []uint64)`.
Verified by `tls_handshake` (which exercises the transport crypto end to end)
and by the poly1305 fixture.

`chacha20.Cipher`'s `key [8]uint32` / `nonce [3]uint32` were converted too and
then REVERTED, because the conversion is not safe yet and the failure is subtle:
the standalone RFC 8439 vector PASSES with the slices, but `tls_handshake` fails
with "tls: unexpected message" as soon as the converted Cipher is used. The same
tree with keccakf converted and chacha20 reverted passes, so the cipher
arithmetic is fine - what breaks is the Cipher as a VALUE that crosses a package
boundary inside `cipher.AEAD`. That is the W27/W30 family: a struct with slice
fields loses its contents on the way out. Two consequences worth writing down:

- Converting a struct's fixed extents to slices is only verified by exercising
  the struct ACROSS a package boundary; a same-package vector can pass while the
  boundary path is broken.
- Until that class is fixed, files whose state structs are handed to another
  package in an interface should stay on fixed extents. chacha20 is one; the
  crypto limb conversions planned next (p256, edwards25519, blake2b) must be
  checked the same way, or they will trade one array type for a silent break.

Also still open from the same probe: a `:=` inside a loop of a self-mutating
method is refused once the receiver's struct gains a slice field (chacha20's
`xorKeyStreamBlocksGeneric`), which is why that function's round temporaries were
hoisted above the loop. The hoist is correct and stays; the refusal is Moxie's
rule doing its job.

## Round 315: WHY a slice field does not survive a package boundary (W33, root cause found)

The chacha20 conversion from round 314 is the reproducer, and instrumenting it
named the exact failure. `chacha20poly1305`'s open path derives the Poly1305 key
from the cipher's block 0, verifies the tag, and only then XORs the plaintext:

    s, _ := chacha20.NewUnauthenticatedCipher(c.key[:], nonce)
    s.XORKeyStream(polyKey, polyKey)   // block 0 - CORRECT: polyKey = 7bac2b25...
    s.SetCounter(1)
    ... poly1305 tag work ...
    s.XORKeyStream(plaintext, ciphertext)

Printing the cipher's own state right before the last call:

    OPEN after poly work: counter 1 key0 0 left 0

`key0` is ZERO. `counter` is right, the leftover length is right, and the block-0
keystream derived a moment earlier was right - but by the time the Poly1305 work
has run, the cipher's `key` slice reads zeros. That is not a cipher bug: the
key's BACKING STORE was reclaimed and zeroed under it.

Why the array version was safe and the slice version is not: with
`key [8]uint32` the key bytes are INLINE in the struct, so the struct's value
carries them wherever it goes. With `key []uint32` the struct carries a header,
and the bytes live wherever `NewUnauthenticatedCipher`'s frame arena put them.
`NewUnauthenticatedCipher` returns `*Cipher`; the return protocol decides whether
that pointer needs relocating with `codecRetStable`, and it answers "stable" for
a receiver that the sovereign machinery has registered as stable
(`codecRegStable`/borrowed arena). The callee's frame is then released, its
memory is reused by the Poly1305 work, and the caller holds a pointer whose
slice fields point into recycled memory. The struct's own bytes survived (the
arena block was not overwritten) but its slice's target did not - which is
exactly "counter intact, key zero".

The general rule this gives the array campaign, and the reason three rounds of
crypto conversion were reverted:

  **A self-mutating struct that is handed to another package must keep its
  state INLINE (named scalars) or as a VIEW of memory the caller owns. It must
  not own slices.**

That is why poly1305's limbs became `H0..H2`/`R0/R1`/`S0/S1` (safest form) and
why keccakf's lanes became a view of the caller's byte buffer (also safe), while
chacha20's `key`/`nonce` had to go back to fixed extents. The crypto conversions
still on the list (p256, edwards25519, blake2b) must follow the scalar-field
form, not the slice form.

The real fix, when it is taken up: `codecRetStable` must answer false when the
returned pointer's pointee owns slices whose backing store lives in a transient
(or borrowed) arena, so the full relocation path copies them into the caller's
arena. The evidence above is the test: with the fix, `key0` must stay
0x03020100 after the Poly1305 work, and `tls_handshake` must pass with the
converted `Cipher`.

## Round 316: W33 fixed - a stable ADDRESS is not a stable OBJECT; chacha20's key/nonce are slices

The diagnosis in round 315 was right about the mechanism and wrong about the
place. The return relocation is not skipped: `codecEncodeValue`'s `KindPointer`
branch asks `codecIsStableAddr(p)` about the pointer's TARGET, gets "stable"
because the Cipher lives in an ancestor frame, writes the pointer raw - and
never looks at what the pointee points AT. `NewUnauthenticatedCipher` allocates
the Cipher in its own frame and then calls `newUnauthenticatedCipher(c, ...)`,
which fills `c.key` from ITS OWN frame. Inside that inner return `c` is an
ancestor address (stable, aliased) while `c.key`'s backing store is in the dying
frame. The struct came back intact and its key bytes were recycled.

The fix is `retPointeeDies` in `src/runtime/codec.mx`: before a pointer may be
aliased, walk the pointee's reference fields (struct fields, array elements,
inline structs) and answer "copy" if any of them points into memory that dies
with this return. One level is enough - the answer only chooses between aliasing
the graph and re-encoding it, and the re-encode walks every level. It is asked
in both places that decide: `codecRetStableInner` (the fast path) and the encode
branch itself. A pointer below the existing 1 MiB bad-pointer threshold is never
dereferenced, only aliased as before.

Both compilers get this from the single shared runtime file - wood law holds
without a compiler change.

With that in place the chacha20 conversion went in: `Cipher.key []uint32` and
`Cipher.nonce []uint32`, lengths established by `newUnauthenticatedCipher`, and
the block temporaries hoisted above the `for pos < n` walk (a `:=` inside a loop
is refused in a self-mutating method). Verified: RFC 8439 AEAD vector matches
byte for byte (`ct d31a8d34...`, tag `1ae10b59...`), RFC 7539 2.4.2 keystream
matches, and `tls_handshake` passes end to end.

### The other half: the exporter was stored across a lifetime

Turning the walk on surfaced a real lifetime bug it had been masking. `crypto/tls`
built its keying-material exporter in the handshake state -
`c.ekm = hs.suite.exportKeyingMaterial(...)` - so the Conn held a pointer into
`hs`'s arena. The handshake returns, `hs` dies, and
`(*Conn).connectionStateLocked` later encodes a dangling `EKM` interface value:
SIGSEGV inside the codec walk (measured under gdb at `retPointeeDies`, reached
from `ConnectionState` -> `connectionStateLocked`).

State a Conn owns has to be built by a method on the Conn, where the receiver's
sovereign arena is the current arena, and its byte slices have to be copied
there: `(*Conn).setEKMFromMasterSecret` and `(*Conn).setEKM13` now do exactly
that, and the handshake states call them. `ekmFromMasterSecret` and
`(*cipherSuiteTLS13).exportKeyingMaterial` are gone rather than left as unused
constructors.

Full fixture: handshake, 1 KiB echo in both directions, and the wrong-CA
rejection, all green.

### Still open from this family

- W27 (reset of a freed arena) and W30 (`JoinHostPort(IPString(ip), port)`)
- the walk does not descend into map values: a map allocated inline in a dying
  frame and stored into a stable object is still aliased as a whole
- `codecSetTopOnlyTransient` still has no callers; the receiver store-back path

## Round 317: the array campaign, class by class - state, limbs, buffers

Rounds 316's W33 fix unblocked the conversions that were blocked on structs
crossing a package boundary with slice fields. Since then, one class at a time,
each verified before the next:

- **chacha20** (round 316): `key`/`nonce` are slices with the lengths set by the
  constructor, block temporaries hoisted. RFC 8439 AEAD vector, RFC 7539 2.4.2.
- **nistec field elements** (p224/p256/p384/p521): the four fiat `_fiat64`
  files' limb types are structs of named scalars (`x0..xN`) rather than fixed
  extents, so the Montgomery/non-Montgomery distinction stays in the type and no
  cast is needed; the byte-domain ends of the fiat API take slices whose length
  the caller established. `P256Element` and friends keep value semantics inside
  a point whose coordinates are copied.
- **edwards25519**: the scalar's fiat limbs are one named-scalar struct (the
  domain is documented per function), and the byte buffers are slices. The trap
  worth remembering: after such a change `copy(wideBytes[:], x[:])` still
  COMPILES and copies into a throwaway, because a subslice is a copy - the
  clamped scalar came out zero and every ed25519 public key was the identity's
  encoding. RFC 8032 test 1 catches it.
- **symmetric and hash state**: AES round-key tables, RC4 state, BLAKE2b chain
  state + block + key, Argon2 blocks and scratch, CBC IV + staging block, CTR
  staging buffers, siphash's key words, and the small buffers in entropy, bip39,
  pkcs1v22, jpeg's idct row, cgroup, evloop's frame header, spawn's fd pairs.
  BLAKE2b's IV and message schedule were being rebuilt per block; they are
  package state in the package's single init() now.
- New fixture `tests/regressions/should_compile/crypto_vectors.mx`: AES
  FIPS-197 C.1-C.3 encrypt+decrypt, SP 800-38A CBC, the two standard GCM tag
  cases with an open, RC4's classic vector, BLAKE2b-512/256 one-shot and
  streaming, and an Argon2id repeat/difference check. Those packages had no
  fixture at all before this.

### Holdouts, with the reason each needs more than a mechanical edit

- `runtime/hashmap.mx`: `bucket.tophash [8]uint8` and `_pad [8]uint8` are the
  bucket LAYOUT the compiler's map codegen addresses. Converting them means
  changing the layout contract in both compilers.
- `runtime/ringbuf.mx`: `spawnRingSet [16][2]uintptr` is read by the forked
  child after `fork`, before any allocation is safe to assume.
- `runtime/secalloc_chacha.mx`: the state and block are written through byte
  WINDOWS (`state[48:]`); with slices a window is a copy, so this needs the
  offset-put idiom (`secPutUint32LEAt(b, off, v)`) across ~20 call sites.
- `syscall/exec_linux.mx`: `caps.data [2]capData` is a kernel ABI struct; a
  slice there changes the 8-byte-header layout the kernel reads.
- `internal/xcoff` (20 declarations): not in any build closure (nothing imports
  it), needs `debug/dwarf` to build under the legacy compiler first, and its
  readers are `binary.Read(unsafe.TypeOf(hdr), unsafe.Pointer(hdr))` - the
  structs have to become byte blocks with window accessors before the fields
  can be slices.
- `internal/coverage`: the magic tables are `[4]byte`/`[4]byte` by wire format.
- `image/png` writer/reader: `cr [nFilter][]uint8` (a filter cache) and a
  4096-byte read buffer; mechanical but the encoder allocates its row cache on
  first use.
- `crypto/secp256k1` (`Fe [4]uint64`) and `crypto/ec/secp256k1` (`n [10]uint32`):
  the limb arithmetic indexes the extent in loops (`for i := 0; i < 4; i++`),
  so the scalar-field form means unrolling the field arithmetic, not renaming a
  type.
- `crypto/internal/fips140/nistec/p256_asm.mx` (22): `//:build ignore`, the
  assembly wrapper for a path this tree does not build.

Gate state after the classes above: quickcheck 15/15 (the fixture set, not
counting the new crypto_vectors unit), `tls_handshake` green end to end,
fixpoint `s4b == s4c`.

## Round 318: the read form of the copy rule, and two defects the sweep found

The remaining buffer conversions (bzip2, gif, zlib, chunked, tabwriter, ecdh,
kernel_version, png/gif decoder scratch) turned up a rule that had only been
stated for writes:

  **A read into a window of a slice fills a throwaway.** `io.ReadFull(r, b[:n])`
  consumes the bytes and puts them in a copy, exactly as `b[:n] = x` writes into
  one. Reads therefore take the header *resized* to the bytes being read
  (`resize(b, n)`, then restore), which is what `(*png.decoder).readScratch` and
  `(*gif.decoder).readScratch` do. Both image decoders read their chunk headers,
  color tables and image descriptors that way; png's chunk-skipping loop and
  `net/http/internal`'s two-byte CRLF check were the same shape.

Two real defects came out of compiling packages that no gate had ever compiled:

- **W34, a compiler that refused valid code.** `compress/bzip2` could not be
  built by stage4 at all: `opt -passes=default<O2>` crashes in LLVM's
  slp-vectorizer (`llvm::VectorType::get`) on the IR inlined from
  `slices.insertionSortCmpFunc`, while `opt -passes=verify` accepts the module.
  Nothing in the tree imports bzip2, so no gate saw it. `optBc` now falls back to
  `mem2reg` when the O2 run fails - the same bounded middle-end every module over
  `optBcBudget` already gets - so an optimizer bug costs optimization, not the
  build. Legacy never ran this pipeline; the outcome (the program builds) is
  what both compilers now agree on.
- **W35, an assertion that could never hold.** `image/gif`'s encoder asserted
  `m.ColorModel().([]color.Color)`. Moxie has no named slice types, so a
  `color.Model` can never BE a palette (Go's `color.Palette` is a named slice
  with a `Convert` method). The legacy compiler rejected the impossible
  assertion and stage4 accepted it: one package, two compilers, two answers. The
  branch is deleted rather than fixed - the `*image.Paletted` case above it is
  the only image whose pixels are indices.

Fixtures added (all three are in phase 0a and pass through the harness):

    crypto_vectors          AES FIPS-197 C.1-C.3 (+decrypt), SP 800-38A CBC,
                            both standard GCM tag cases + open, RC4, BLAKE2b
                            512/256 one-shot and streaming, Argon2id repeat
    png_roundtrip           37x23 RGBA encode/decode, pixel exact
    bzip2_gif_roundtrip     a system-bzip2 stream decompressed, a palette GIF
                            encoded and decoded pixel for pixel

Gates after the whole sweep: quickcheck 15/15, the three new units 4/4,
phase 8 netsmoke 2/2 (HTTP/TCP/UDP/spawn plus tree-cleanliness), fixpoint
`s4b == s4c` (b8313a0b).

Array declarations left, each with its reason, are the holdout list in round
317 plus: the png/gif `tmp` scratch (done here), and
`src/internal/trace/internal/tracev1/parser.mx`'s `Args [4]uint64`, which is an
on-disk event record.

## Round 319: W36 - an interface-wrapped writer loses its buffer across a return

`compress/gzip` cannot round trip, and did not before this round's conversion
(the pre-change tree dies with SIGSEGV in the same probe). The evidence, small
enough to state exactly:

    flate alone:  NewWriter(&buf) -> 39 bytes -> NewReader -> identical   OK
    gzip:         NewWriter(&buf) -> 18 bytes -> NewReader -> "flate:
                  corrupt input before offset 5"

18 bytes is the 10-byte gzip header plus the 8-byte footer (`b9 c5 0f 1d` is
crc32 of the payload, `21 00 00 00` is its length): the DEFLATE stream is empty.
Between the two halves the runtime prints

    moxie: codec arena escape: pointer into a transient frame arena preserved
    instead of copied (unknown-extent pointee); that frame arena is leaked for
    the pointer's lifetime

so the compressor it built is writing through a basic-pointee pointer whose
target was in a frame that has been released - the W33 family, on the
`codecEscapeNote` branch instead of the stable-alias branch. `flate.NewWriter(z.w,
z.level)` boxes an `io.Writer` inside the flate writer; the boxed pointer is
"unknown extent" and is preserved rather than copied.

`*gzip.Writer.Write` creates its compressor lazily, so `init` cannot be the
place that fixes this; the fix belongs in the codec's unknown-extent escape path
(or in how a boxed writer is carried), and it needs this probe as its fixture.
Until then `compress/gzip` is broken for both compilers - note that
`net/http/h2_bundle.mx` and `internal/profile` import it, and no gate exercises
a gzip body.

    src/internal/coverage/*                          20   on-disk meta format, padding fields
    src/crypto/secp256k1/{scalar,field}.mx            8   loop-indexed limbs: unroll, not rename

    src/runtime/secalloc_chacha.mx                    5   writes through byte windows

    src/internal/zstd/{huff,fse}.mx, gzip, gif reader  -   done this round
    src/internal/trace/.../parser.mx                  1   on-disk event record

## Round 320: the [:] sweep, and the operator's ruling on it

Asked to stop writing `copy(dst[:], src[:])` (copy already takes the smaller of
the two lengths) and to remove `[:]` where the operand is a slice, the sweep
found 295 full-slice expressions across `src`, `_mxc_stage4`, `pkg` and `tests`.
A first pass tried to enforce it in the compiler; the operator ruled that out:

  **x[:] and x[0:len(x)] are the same expression, and both are copies by the
  slice rule. Banning only the short spelling is asymmetric and bans the very
  thing `slice_copy_rule.mx` exists to document. What is wrong is a subslice in
  a DESTINATION position - and that rule already exists.**

So no new compiler rule: `copy(dst[:], ...)`, `copy(dst[0:len(dst)], ...)` and a
store through either are rejected by the subslice-copy checks that were already
in `checkASTRestrictions` / `checkSubsliceStores`, and `x[:]` stays legal as
explicit copy syntax. Verified after the revert on both compilers: `t := s[:]`
copies (a write through `t` leaves `s` alone) and `copy(dst, s)` returns the
smaller length with no `[:]` on either side.

The cleanup stays, because each of those sites was dead work or a silent
throwaway: `strconv/ftoa`'s `bigFtoa` built a `decimalSlice` over a copy of the
digit buffer, `sha256`/`sha512` passed a copy of the block state to `block`
(so the digest was written nowhere), `ecdh`/`ecdsa` copied an order slice they
only read, `archive/zip` and `internal/zstd` fed their writers copies, and
`x/text/norm`'s trie constructor stored a copy where Go stores a view.

Mechanism, for the next sweep of this kind: the compiler is the classifier. A
temporary `x[:] of a slice` diagnostic in stage4, run by building every package
directory that still contained `[:]`, produced file:line for each real site in
about six rounds; the diagnostic is gone and the sites are clean.

Gates: quickcheck 15/15 (slice_copy_rule restored to `base[:]` and passing),
phase 8 netsmoke 2/2 (1 948 s), fixpoint `s4b == s4c` (d41bd227).

## Round 321: W36 fixed - three defects behind "gzip does not round trip"

A 33-byte payload through `compress/gzip` produced 18 bytes: the 10-byte header
and the 8-byte trailer, with no DEFLATE stream between them, and the reader then
said "flate: corrupt input". It was three separate defects:

1. **gzip's compressor was created lazily inside `Write`.** A pointer allocated
   in the callee's frame and stored through the receiver is the W10 shape, so
   `Close` flushed a released object. It is created in `init()` now - the one
   constructor that `NewWriter` and `Reset` both go through. This is also why
   the codec printed its unknown-extent escape note: the arena was leaked for
   the pointer, and the pointer's state was already gone.
2. **zlib had the same shape one step later**: `writeHeader` created the
   deflater on first use, so its output was `78 9c` and an Adler-32 with nothing
   between them (6 bytes). `NewWriterLevelDict` and `Reset` create it through
   `startCompressor()` now.
3. **Both readers let inflate steal the trailer.** They passed the raw source to
   inflate unless it was already a `flate.Reader`, and Moxie's inflate reads in
   bulk rather than byte-wise: it drained the CRC32+size (gzip) or Adler-32
   (zlib), so the trailer read that follows started from the wrong bytes. A
   `*bytes.Buffer` source therefore decoded the data CORRECTLY and then failed
   with "invalid checksum". Both readers always wrap the source in a
   `bufio.Reader` now.

`net/http/h2_bundle` imports gzip and no gate had ever exercised a gzip body;
the fix leaves crypto/tls, png (zlib) and the netsmoke server green.

New fixture `compress_roundtrip.mx`: gzip read back from a fresh `bytes.Reader`,
from a second buffer, and from the buffer the writer used, plus the same for
zlib, and it asserts a real payload exists (18/6 bytes is the failure
signature). Builds and runs on both compilers.

### W37, found while doing it: legacy rejects string comparison in a condition

    func same(a []byte, b []byte) (ok bool) {
        if string(a) != string(b) { return false }   // legacy: invalid operation
        return true
    }

`a != b` on two `[]byte` compiles on both compilers; `string(a) != string(b)`
is rejected by legacy with "moxie: invalid operation: != ([]byte is not
comparable)" and accepted by stage4. In Moxie `string` and `[]byte` are one
type, so legacy's `moxieComparable` is being consulted with a type it treats as
a plain slice while the bare operand path is patched. The new fixture uses
`bytes.Equal` so it builds on both; the gap itself is open.

Gates: quickcheck 15/15, compress_roundtrip 2/2 through the harness, phase 8
netsmoke 2/2, fixpoint `s4b == s4c` (d41bd227).

## Round 322: W37 fixed - the rewrite layer asked "is it []byte", not "is it text"

The W37 note guessed that `moxieComparable` was being consulted with a slice
where it should see text. The diagnostic said otherwise: in
`string(a) != string(b)` the SSA operands are the two `[]byte` PARAMETERS. The
`string(...)` conversions are identical-type under string=[]byte, so go/ssa
folds them away and the builder receives a bare `a != b` on two slices - the
exact expression that works when written without the conversions.

So the two spellings of one type were being routed differently. A bare `a != b`
is caught by `FindByteComparisons` and lowered to `__moxie_eq`, because the
operand type is `[]byte`. An operand written `string(a)` types as the built-in
`string` while the package is being typed, `isByteSlice` said no to both
operands, the pair looked like a comparison involving no text at all, and it
survived to the SSA builder as an unlowered slice comparison. Legacy then
rejected it (`moxieComparable` on a `*types.Slice`); stage4 accepted it, so the
compilers disagreed about a program that neither could justify.

The predicate is `isTextLike` in both finders now - `FindByteComparisons` and
`FindByteSwitches`, which had the identical blind spot one level down: a
`switch string(x)` lost its tag to the tag-less `__moxie_eq` rewrite only when
the tag happened to be typed `[]byte`, so the `string(x)` form fell through to
case comparisons the SSA builder rejected. The string->[]byte wrapping bridge in
the comparison finder existed to serve the same blind spot (one side `[]byte`,
the other `string`); once both sides are recognised as text there is nothing to
bridge and it is gone.

This is a legacy-only change and no mirror is owed: stage4 parses Moxie source
directly and already treated both spellings as text. The proof that nothing
else moved is the binary - the bootstrap still converges on `d41bd227`, byte for
byte the compiler that has been shipping, because the compiler's own source
contains none of the newly-detected pattern.

Fixture `text_compare_forms.mx` pins equality, ordering, prefix ordering, the
empty value, a named text type, the literal form and switch tags. Every
"different" pair has the SAME LENGTH, so a header comparison cannot pass it.
On the pre-fix compiler it fails to compile with three "[]byte is not
comparable" errors; it passes on both compilers now.

Gates: quickcheck 15/15, text_compare_forms and compress_roundtrip 2/2 through
the harness, phase 8 netsmoke 17/17 + tree-cleanliness, bootstrap fixpoint
`s2 == s3` (d41bd227) with the same hash as the previous round.

## Round 323: W29 fixed - stage4 accepted '+' and '+=' on text in user code

Legacy refuses both in a user's main module: concatenation is `|`, so
`loader`'s `CheckPlusOnText` walks the AST for a text operand on either side of
`+` and for a text left-hand side of `+=`. Stage4 had a `+` check that tested
only the LEFT operand and only through `ssaIsStringType`, which is the string
Basic alone, and it had no `+=` check at all. So these compiled here and were
rejected there:

    a := []byte("x"); b := []byte("y"); s := a + b   // stage4: ok, "xy"
    s := a; s += b                                   // stage4: ok, "xy"

The divergence also ran the wrong way round: the compiler that accepted the
operator had to invent semantics for it, so `+=` on text silently concatenated -
an operator the language reserves, with an error message that named the rule
legacy was enforcing all along.

The predicate is `TextType` (string Basic OR slice of byte), on either operand
for `+` and on the left-hand side for `+=`, and the gate is legacy's
(main-module user code), factored into `(*ssaFuncBuilder).plusIsBanned` so the
two rules share one definition of "user code". The first attempt used
`textSlice` and rejected `n += 3`: that predicate answers "Basic type" for ANY
Basic by design of its other call sites, which is why the numeric forms are now
part of `concat_text_forms` - a check that rejects too much is the same class of
bug as one that rejects too little, and this one proved it on the first try.

Fixtures `reject_plus_text` and `reject_plusassign_text` (phase 0b, each naming
its expected error): the first BUILT and printed "xy" on the old compiler, the
second likewise; both are refused by both compilers now.

Gates: quickcheck 15/15, phase 8 netsmoke 17/17 + tree-cleanliness (2 663 s, rebuild of the whole netsmoke closure plus a loaded host), bootstrap
fixpoint `s2 == s3` (`0c395b6a`, a new hash because stage4 itself changed - the
whole tree, toolchain and stdlib included, still compiles with `+` on text
where it is allowed).

## Round 324: W31 (round 306's idna crash) narrowed to one constructor shape

The reproducer from round 306 still crashes under stage4 and still passes under
legacy, so it was taken apart with measurements instead of reading. What is now
known:

    p := idna.Lookup();  p.ToUnicode("xn--bcher-kva.example")   // stage4: ok
    p.ToUnicode("xn--bcher-kva.example")                        // stage4: SIGSEGV

Under gdb the fault is an indirect call through a garbage pointer inside
`norm.(*formInfo).quickSpan` (`call *0x10(%rax)`, i.e. `f.info(src, i)`), where
`f` came from the form table but points into arena memory that no longer holds a
`formInfo`. The jumped-to address is an arena base or a code address, depending
on the run - a dangling object, not a logic error.

**The constructor shape is the trigger.** With `ToASCII` called twice on each:

    idna.New()                                ok
    idna.New(idna.MapForLookup())             ok
    idna.New(idna.MapForLookup(), BidiRule()) ok
    idna.Display()                            SIGSEGV (inside ArenaReset)
    idna.Lookup()                             SIGSEGV

`New` builds `p := &Profile{}`, mutates it through `apply(&p.options, o)` and
returns `p`. `Lookup`/`Display` return `&Profile{options{...}}` - an addressed
composite literal carrying three func values, an embedded struct and `_trie()`.

Ruled out by experiment, each of which one would otherwise have to re-test:

1. **Arena pooling / reset of a reused arena.** Forcing `ArenaRelease` to always
   `ArenaFree` (never pool, never reset) does not stop the crash; the reported
   address becomes the page-aligned arena base exactly as round 306 described.
2. **Sovereign group release.** Returning early from `codecSovereignFree` so a
   group's arenas are never released does not stop it either, and every arena
   reset at the crash point reports `sov=0 gl=0` - no group is involved.
3. **The lazily built form table** (`initFormTable`, built on first use and
   stored into a package global). Calling it from norm's package `init()`
   instead does not fix the crash - it moves it earlier - and norm's own
   `NFC.Bytes`, `NFC.QuickSpan` and `NFC.String` each work twice on both
   compilers, so the table survives when idna is not in the path.
4. **The literal-return shape in general.** A synthetic package with the same
   shape (embedded options struct, three func fields, a trie with two slices
   passed in, both a literal-return constructor and a mutating one) passes on
   stage4. The trigger needs idna's own init-built tables as well.

Next step, in order: copy `idna` into a probe package, rewrite `Lookup` to the
mutating shape and confirm it passes (that isolates the constructor, not the
package); then diff the IR emitted for `idna.Lookup` between the compilers,
which is where the two disagree and where the fix belongs. The fixture cannot
live in `tests/regressions` until it stops crashing.

Gates unchanged from round 323 (nothing in the tree was modified for this
investigation; every temporary print and probe edit was reverted).

## Round 325: correcting round 324 - the trigger is MapForLookup plus an optionBool, not the constructor

Round 324 concluded that the addressed-literal constructor (`Lookup`, `Display`)
was the trigger because every `New(...)` shape tested was fine. That was an
artefact of which options those tests passed. Told apart one at a time, with
`ToASCII` called twice on each profile:

    idna.New()                                     ok
    idna.New(CheckHyphens(true))                   ok
    idna.New(CheckHyphens(true), StrictDomainName(true))   ok   (two optionBools)
    idna.New(MapForLookup())                       ok
    idna.New(MapForLookup(), BidiRule())           ok   (second option is an EMPTY struct)
    idna.New(MapForLookup(), StrictDomainName(true))       SIGSEGV
    idna.New(MapForLookup(), CheckHyphens(true))           SIGSEGV
    idna.New(MapForLookup(), ValidateLabels(true))         SIGSEGV
    idna.Lookup(), idna.Display()                  SIGSEGV (both are literal constructors)

So the constructor shape is irrelevant: `New(MapForLookup(), <optionBool>)`
crashes exactly like `Lookup`, and `New(...)` with the same options in the same
shape crashes where `Lookup` is not involved at all. What the failing pair has
that the working pairs do not:

- `MapForLookup().applyTo(o)` runs first and writes `o.trie = _trie()` and
  `o.mapping = validateAndMap` - a root-arena pointer and a func value - and
  internally applies two `optionBool` values to the same `o`.
- the second top-level option is an `optionBool`:
  `struct{ set func(*options, bool); v bool }`, boxed into the variadic
  `[]Option`, dispatched as a value-receiver method.
- `BidiRule()` in that position is an empty struct and does not crash, and two
  `optionBool`s with no `MapForLookup` do not crash.

That is the shape to diff next: a variadic `[]Option` of interface values whose
boxted dynamic type is a struct with a func field, applied to a target struct
that already holds a func value and a root-arena pointer. The measured fault is
always an indirect call landing in arena memory or in `runtime.ArenaReset`
(0x26f6xx), i.e. a func value read out of reclaimed memory - the optionBool
`set` function, read through a box or a copy that no longer holds it.

The four experiments in round 324 (pooling, sovereign group release, form-table
init, synthetic literal shape) remain valid: none of them is the cause.

Next step: reproduce in-tree with a `golang.org/x/...`-path probe package (value
receivers are only legal outside user packages, which is why the synthetic
reproducer had to use pointer receivers and could not mirror idna), then diff
the IR for `idna.New`/`apply`/`optionBool.applyTo` between the compilers.

### Round 325, further: the interface box's arena is not the cause either

The prime suspect after the bisect was where stage4 allocates the out-of-line box
for an interface value wider than a pointer: `emitMakeInterface` does
`runtime.alloc(sizeof(T), nil, nil)`, i.e. into the CURRENT arena, which inside a
constructor like `idna.CheckHyphens` is that function's own frame - and the
interface it returns is used in the caller. Made a probe of exactly that: the
out-of-line box allocated from `runtime.RootArena()` instead of the current
arena, compiler rebuilt, same probe re-run.

    idna.Display() with root-allocated interface boxes -> SIGSEGV, as before

So the box's arena is not the cause. Five hypotheses are now eliminated by
measurement (pooling, sovereign-group release, the lazy form table, the
literal-return shape, the box arena), which leaves the write path:

`apply` iterates the variadic `[]Option` and calls `f.applyTo(o)` - an interface
method with a VALUE receiver whose struct holds a func field - and that method
calls `x.set(o, x.v)`, a func value invoked with a parameter and a field of the
receiver copy. A wild store through a wrong `o` would corrupt an arena header
(which is what makes the crash land in `ArenaReset`) and later hand `quickSpan` a
form-table pointer into reclaimed memory. That is the shape to reproduce next,
in a package whose import path exempts it from the value-receiver rule (any path
without a dot, or under `golang.org/x/`), then diff its IR between compilers.

## Round 326: W31 fixed - the pointee of an element literal was a stack alloca

Rounds 324 and 325 chased the crash through five hypotheses and a constructor
bisect without finding it, because the defect is one level below all of them:
not in what flavour of `Profile` was built, but in where the `Profile`'s memory
came from.

The reproducer is ten lines:

    type T struct { n int64 }
    func makeThree(k int64) (s []*T) {
        s = []*T{{n: k}, {n: k + 1}, {n: k + 2}}
        return
    }
    makeThree(9)   // stage4: 9 10 7    legacy: 9 10 11

`[]*T{{...}}` means a slice of `&T{...}` values, so each pointee's address is
stored into the slice's backing array and escapes the frame. stage4's
pointer-to-aggregate branch allocated the pointee with `emitAlloc` (Heap:false,
a stack alloca) and never called `markAddrEscaping`, while the explicit
`&T{...}` path has always called it. A returned slice therefore carried
pointers into a dead frame. The emitted IR also lost the last element's stores
(`store i64 %k+2, ptr %t18` was simply absent), which is why exactly the LAST
element read back garbage and the earlier ones only looked right because their
stack slots had not been reused yet.

The fix is one call in that one place: `fb.markAddrEscaping(alloc)`. Legacy's
`builder.addr(escaping=true)` makes the same decision for `&`, so the two
compilers now agree on the rule rather than one of them being right by accident.

**This was also the idna crash.** With it:

    idna.Display()                                        two ToASCII calls, ok
    idna.Lookup()                                         two ToUnicode calls, ok
    idna.New(MapForLookup(), StrictDomainName(true))      two ToASCII calls, ok

All three segfaulted before. The garbage function value the second call jumped
through was a pointee read out of a recycled frame - the round-306 report was
right about the symptom and about the arena, and the pointee was never in the
arena to begin with.

Fixture `ptr_elem_lit_escape` covers a returned `[]*T`, a returned `[3]*T`, a
`map[K]*T` with elided values, func-typed fields and a slice field, and reads
every element after a 4 KiB churn call. On the pre-fix compiler it panics with
"returned []*T lost an element after the frame died"; it passes on both
compilers now.

The five eliminated hypotheses stand as true negatives, and the method note is
worth keeping: a same-package read of the literal is NOT evidence - the reads
that expose this defect are the ones that happen after the frame dies, which is
why `makeThree(9)` had to return the slice for the bug to show.

Gates: quickcheck 15/15, ptr_elem_lit_escape + text_compare_forms +
compress_roundtrip + crypto_vectors through the harness, phase 8 netsmoke 17/17 (2 544 s),
bootstrap fixpoint `s2 == s3` (cd9258fd).

## Round 327: the two wrong-IR rejections, and phase 1b was red for three reasons

Phase 1b (the stdlib compile sweep) is the gate that catches "some package in
the tree does not compile" - the one thing a green bootstrap does not prove. It
had not been run in a while, and it was red.

### stage4 lowered `string([N]byte)` as an invalid bitcast

    %t20 = bitcast [8 x i8] %t19 to {ptr, i64, i64}

go/types rejects both directions of a text/fixed-extent conversion, and legacy
reports `cannot convert h.Name (variable of type [8]byte) to type string`. stage4
built the SSAConvert anyway and clang refused the module with "invalid cast
opcode" and no source line - the W29 shape: one compiler rejects the source, the
other invents a lowering. `internal/xcoff`'s `println(name, hdr.Name)` is where
it was reached.

`checkTextArrayConv` runs beside the other conversion shape checks and reports
the site in source terms: `cannot convert [8]byte to string (a fixed extent is
not text: work in slices)`. The conversion that exists is `string(buf[:])` - the
array becomes a slice view first. Fixture `reject_string_array` (phase 0b) names
that error. The whole-tree bootstrap compiles with the check in place, so the
tree had no legitimate `string(array)`.

### Three tree breakages behind phase 1b's red

1. `internal/coverage/{encodecounter,encodemeta}`: the on-disk header structs
   carry `Magic [4]byte` (those four bytes are a field of the file format) while
   the exported constants are text. Assigning text to a fixed extent in a struct
   literal is rejected - correctly - so the magic is copied in:
   `copy(hdr.Magic[:], coverage.CovCounterMagic())`. The campaign's real shape
   for these structs (byte blocks with window accessors, because their layout IS
   the wire format) is still the recorded holdout.
2. `internal/trace/tracev2` declared two `init()` functions (events.mx and
   spec.mx) - two table conversions from different rounds, each taking the
   package's one init.
3. `internal/trace` declared three (event.mx, order.mx and tracev1.mx) - the
   same mistake twice in one tree.

Bodies merged into the single init, rule unchanged. Because this class has now
bitten three times (xcoff first), the diagnostic names the declaration:

    b.mx:3: at most one init() per package: merge this body into the package's init()

It was a bare sentence with no line, which meant reading every file in the
directory to find the stray one.

### Gates

### 6: clearzero asserted Go's view semantics

    b := []uint32{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
    clear(b[1:3])
    if b[1] != 0 { panic("clear on a subslice") }   // both compilers panicked

A subslice of a slice is a COPY, so `clear` reaches the copy and the parent
keeps its elements. The fixture had been written with Go's view semantics and
therefore failed on both compilers, which phase 6 reports as two failures. It
now asserts the copy rule, and keeps the one case where a subslice IS a view -
`arr[2:]` of a fixed extent - because that is exactly the distinction the
builtin has to pin.

declared `"unsafe"` with no `unsafe.` reference. Everything on the wasm target
reaches syscall through net, so 59 of the 118 fixtures failed with "wasm build
failed" for that one reason. The imports are gone.
