## Round 329: the three sibling repos, and what phase 7 turned up

Phase 7 builds the relay (../morly) and the app's nine wasm bundles
(../smesh) from source with the compiler under test, then runs the app's
browser smoke suite. None of the three built against this tree, so the round
was spent on them. Everything below is committed in its own repository.

### moxie: embed had not been compiled since its import moved into a comment

    // In source files that don't refer to [embed.FS], use a blank import (
        "moxielang.dev/pkg/mxutil"import _ "embed").

A doc-comment line had been split by an edit and the import path written into
the comment, so the package never imported mxutil and `mxutil.CopyFrom` was
undefined. The comment is whole again, the import is in the import block, and
two calls convert int64 offsets to CopyFrom's int32 (io.Seeker works in int64).
Nothing in the tree imports embed; the relay is the only importer, which is why
phase 1b never saw it.

Also fixed in this round: `net`'s js/wasm build was missing
NewSockaddrInet4/NewSockaddrInet6 (the types live in net_fake.mx, the
constructors only in the unix file), which took out ip_api and net_buffers_api
with "not enough arguments in call (want 1, have 0)" - the round-311 symptom,
naming the caller instead of the missing symbol. Both fixtures pass on wasm now.

### nostr: the crypto byte APIs take slices

p8k's Signer kept its key in `[32]byte` and copied arguments into extents for
secp256k1, which takes []byte. The key material is a slice now, allocated by
New/MustNew (and lazily by InitPub), and the signature/aux/message buffers are
slices; ws/dns's dnsAddr likewise.

### smesh: the fixed-extent wrappers around every crypto call

This tree refuses `copy(x[:], src)` and writes through `x[:]` in every package,
so a fixed extent cannot be filled. The app was full of the Go habit:

- jsbridge/schnorr/schnorr_wasm.mx was a pure pass-through that copied its
  arguments into [32]byte/[64]byte locals for entry points that already take
  slices; it is seven one-line functions now.
- crypto/chacha20's XOR/XORAt and crypto/chacha20poly1305's Seal/Open took fixed
  extents and sliced them immediately; they take slices, and their callers
  (mls/ciphersuite, marmot) pass what they have.
- crypto/nip44 derives its three message keys as subslices of the expanded block
  (a read-only use, where a copy is exactly right), pushes the MAC input instead
  of copying into `macInput[32:]`, and pad() pushes the length prefix and zero
  padding instead of copying into `out[2:]`.
- crypto/hkdf's Extract fills its [32]byte return one byte at a time (a fixed
  extent cannot be a copy destination); mls/ciphersuite copies its extraction
  into a fresh slice; wasm/signer/vault accumulates sha256.Sum's []byte.
- Three never-compiled defects only a first compile finds: proposal/framing/
  key_schedule/tree converted a POINTER receiver to an integer
  (`uint16(t)` with `t *proposalType`), and group.mx's UnmarshalGroup read a
  uint32 into `v, ok :=` where `v` is the function's named *Group result, so
  `leafIndex(v)` tried to convert a *Group. The reads use `li` now.
- Marmot's NostrGroupData.NostrGroupID is []byte (a copy of the wire bytes).

### morly: three defects behind "the relay will not build"

ParseAddr returned [4]byte into a sockaddr whose Addr is a slice (it returns
[]byte); acceptAll declared `prev := runtime.CurrentArena()` inside its loop,
which is refused in a self-mutating method, and is declared above it; clog
passed its `...fmt.Stringer` to Fprintf without the spread.

### Where phase 7 stands

`ui:build` PASSES: nine wasm bundles plus the runtime staging, with the relay
built from source. `ui:smoke` fails, and the relay is the reason in a way that
is not a build problem: started by hand with ORLY_STATIC_DIR set it binds and
logs "listening", the process stays alive, and `curl` on `/` connects and then
never receives a byte (rc=124), with no request line in the relay's log. That is
a relay runtime defect - the accept/handler path never answers - and it needs
its own investigation in ../morly. Phase 7 was red before this round too, so
this is progress (build green, smoke red for one named reason) rather than a
regression.

Also open from this round: `ed25519_roundtrip` (and presumably the other crypto
wasm fixtures) build for wasm and trap in the browser inside
`crypto/internal/fips140/ed25519.NewPrivateKeyFromSeed` -> `precomputePrivateKey`
(sha512 + edwards25519), while the same source runs natively. Not diagnosed;
the storage constructor there (`&PrivateKey{seed: []byte{:seedSize}, ...}`
allocated in the constructor's frame) is the W31/W33 shape worth looking at
first on that target.

### Round 329, resolved: the relay read every request into a throwaway

The smoke failure above had one cause, and it was in the relay:

    n, err := syscall.Read(c.fd, c.buf[c.wpos:])

`c.buf[c.wpos:]` is a COPY, so each request's bytes were read into a buffer
nobody owned, `c.buf` stayed zeroed, processHTTP searched zeros for
"\r\n\r\n", never found it and returned. The relay accepted the connection and
then sat in epoll answering nothing - which is exactly what the hand test saw
(curl connects, both sides ESTABLISHED, queues empty, no byte back).

Instrumenting readConn and processHTTP is what named it: "readConn" ran, "read
n 79" ran, "processHTTP" ran, and "found end" never printed. The read now goes
into a per-connection window (`rdbuf`, allocated once at accept) and the bytes
are pushed into the connection buffer, whose discipline needed making coherent
in the same change: `buf` is length-tracked (len is the used length, capacity is
the storage), so `avail` is cap-len, growBuf doubles the capacity and pushes,
the consumed remainder replaces the header instead of being copied over in
place, and `wpos` follows `len(c.buf)`.

Verified by hand (http=200, 2036 bytes for `/`, and a second request on a new
connection answers too), then by phase 7: `ui:build` PASSES and the smoke suite
went from 11 errors to **3 passed, 3 failed, 5 errors**. The page loads and
renders; what remains is `test_console_log_version` and `test_dark_mode_toggle`
(selenium.communication errors from the browser driver) and `TestFeed`'s
WebSocket `ConnectionResetError`, plus the signed-in flow group that depends on
the extension. Those are the next things to look at in ../smesh and ../morly.

### Round 329, second pass: the relay's websocket path, and where it stands

With HTTP answering, the smoke suite's remaining real failure was
`TestFeed::test_feed_notes_appear`: the browser opens a websocket, sends a REQ,
and the relay resets the connection. Hand-reproduced with a python client, and
the relay's own prints named the sequence: upgrade completes (phase 1), then the
first readConn returns "phase 1 wpos 0" and immediately calls closeConn.

Two defects behind it, both from the same copy rule:

1. `parseWSFrame` filled the per-frame mask with `copy(mask[:], data[pos:..])`,
   which writes into a throwaway: the mask stayed zero, and a zero mask makes
   unmasking the identity, so every client frame was consumed still masked.
   Measured directly: `copy(out[:], src)` on an array leaves the array zero
   (`fill: 0 0 0 0`). Same in the relay's wire codec - `copy(hdr[15:47],
   r.Pubkey[:])` and `copy(r.Pubkey[:], hdr[15:47])` wrote into throwaways, so
   the encoded wire header carried zero pubkeys/event IDs and the decoded ones
   stayed zero. All six sites write elements now.
2. Consuming a request or frame replaced the header with `c.buf[consumed:]`,
   which is a copy - a fresh allocation of the remainder's length. With an
   empty remainder the buffer's capacity became 0, `avail = cap - len` was 0,
   the next read was a zero-length read, syscall.Read answered `(0, nil)`, and
   readConn took that as EOF and reset the connection. The remainder is copied
   to the front of the same buffer and the header resized now.

Those packages compile at all because a `/pkg/` path segment exempts them from
the restriction pass that refuses `copy(x[:], ...)` in user code - so the
compiler could not warn, and every one of these was silent. That exemption is
the next class to look at: it is right for the toolchain's own packages and
wrong for an app's.

State: phase 7 `ui:build` PASSES (nine bundles + relay), the relay serves HTTP
(200, 2036 bytes, and a second request on a new connection), the websocket
upgrade completes and frames reach the handler (the codec's unknown-extent
escape note appears in the log), and the smoke suite is at 3 passed / 3 failed /
5 errors - the feed test still does not see its replies, and the rest are
selenium.communication errors plus the extension-dependent signed-in flows.

## Round 330: a wasm trap now says what the module got to, and ed25519 says why it died

Phase 5's crypto fixtures build for wasm and trap in the browser. Localising one
of them was blind, because the harness dropped the module's own output on the
failure path: `run.py` collected the logs, printed them only on a clean run, and
the caller showed the last three lines of a JS stack.

`run.py` prints them now, as one line after the error so the caller's tail still
ends with something readable, and validate.sh's failure tail is five lines:

    main  FAIL  (browser run failed)
      stdout so far: A start
       | B seed ready
       | C sha512 64
       | panic: edwards25519: use of uninitialized Point

The probe behind it is ten lines (`sha512.Sum512` then
`ed25519.NewKeyFromSeed`), so the trap is in `NewPrivateKeyFromSeed` ->
`precomputePrivateKey` -> `ScalarBaseMult` -> `initBasepointTable` ->
`Point.Add`, where `checkInitialized` finds a ZERO generator point and panics.
Native prints "DBG generator ok, zero: false" at the same place.

`_generator()` is `(&Point{}).SetBytes(...)`: a Point built in that function's
frame, handed to a method that fills it, and returned by pointer. Native
relocates the pointee into the caller's arena (W33's fix); on wasm32 the value
arrives zeroed. That is the next thing to look at: the return-encode's
stability decision on the wasm target, or the pointee copy there.

Two instrumentation rounds were spent before this because the trap arrives as
`RuntimeError: unreachable` with a JS stack that names the trapping function but
not what it printed - the harness change is the durable part of this round.

### Round 330, further: the trap is inside SetBytes, not in the return path

Two probes narrowed it, and both are worth keeping because they each ruled out a
plausible class in one run:

- A returned pointer to a frame-built struct (`p = &P{...}; return` with 4 and
  with 10 int64 fields, read after a 4 KiB churn) survives the wasm target, so
  the W31/W33 relocation is not the problem here.
- Multi-word struct equality (`E{a,b,c,d,e uint64}` compared against zero, against
  itself, and differing in the first and in the last limb) is correct on wasm, so
  `checkInitialized`'s comparison is not lying.

Instrumenting the limbs settled it:

    DBG gen x0 0 x1 0 y0 0 z0 0 zero true          (wasm)
    DBG generator ok, zero: false                   (native)

`_generator()` decodes the RFC 8032 basepoint with `SetBytes`, and on wasm32 that
returns a ZERO point - a failure inside the field arithmetic (the square root
that recovers x from u), which `_generator` discards with `p, _ :=`. Everything
downstream then panics in `Point.Add`'s `checkInitialized`, which is the trap the
harness reported.

So the work item is the `edwards25519/field` arithmetic on wasm32: `SetBytes`
must be exercised directly (its error is currently thrown away by the only
caller, which is itself a defect worth fixing - a decode that cannot fail
silently returning a zero point is how this arrived as a panic three calls away).

### Round 330, resolved as far as it goes: the basepoint decode now says why

`_generator()` used `p, _ := (&Point{}).SetBytes(...)`, so a failed decode became
a ZERO point and the panic arrived three calls away as "use of uninitialized
Point". It panics at the decode now, and the wasm target immediately names the
real failure:

    panic: edwards25519: basepoint decode failed: edwards25519: invalid point encoding

So `SetBytes` rejects the RFC 8032 basepoint on wasm32 while accepting it
natively: the square root that recovers x from u is wrong on that target, i.e.
the defect is in `crypto/internal/fips140/edwards25519/field` arithmetic, not in
the caller and not in the return path (both cleared above).

That is the next work item, and it needs the field package exercised directly on
wasm - the package is `internal`, so the probe has to be a temporary self-test
inside it rather than an importing program. The fixture that will judge it is
already there: `ed25519_vectors` covers RFC 8032's test vectors and
`tls_handshake` exercises the same arithmetic end to end.

Native gates after the change: crypto_vectors, ed25519_roundtrip,
ed25519_vectors and tls_handshake all pass, quickcheck 15/15.

### Round 330: the wasm crypto failures are `bits.Mul64` returning garbage

The chain from the trap to the cause, each step measured:

1. `ed25519.NewKeyFromSeed` -> `precomputePrivateKey` -> `ScalarBaseMult` ->
   `initBasepointTable` -> `Point.Add` panics "use of uninitialized Point".
2. With the basepoint decode failing loud at its own site it says "invalid point
   encoding", so `SetBytes` is rejecting the RFC 8032 basepoint.
3. A temporary self-test inside `edwards25519/field` (the package is `internal`,
   so it cannot be imported by a probe) localised it further: `SetBytes`/`Bytes`
   round trip correctly on wasm, but `Square` gives a DIFFERENT result than
   native (`u2.l0` 540431955284448 native vs 1215972019264279 wasm) and
   `sqrtM1^2 == -1` is false, so `SqrtRatio` reports "not a square".
4. `Square`'s arithmetic runs through `math/bits.Mul64`, and a direct probe shows
   the defect:

       native: Mul64(2^62, 4)   -> hi 1                 lo 0
       wasm:   Mul64(2^62, 4)   -> hi 720576034868559873 lo 0

   The LOW word is always right; the HIGH word is garbage - and it changes
   between builds of the same source (720575940379279361, then
   720576034868559873), which is the signature of reading an uninitialised or
   mis-sized slot rather than a wrong formula.

Two things are therefore open, and the second is the cause:

- The `edwards25519/field` self-test should stay in some form: it named the
  operation in one run, where the fixture alone only named a panic.
- `math/bits.Mul64` on wasm32 computes a wrong high word while plain 64-bit
  arithmetic (`>>`, `&`, `*`, `+`, `-`, shifts by 0/32/63) is correct on the
  same target, verified by its own probe. `Mul64` differs from that arithmetic
  in one respect: it declares `const mask32 = 1<<32 - 1`, an untyped constant
  that does not fit int32. Typing it `uint64` did NOT fix the high word (it
  changed the wrong value), so the constant is a second defect at most, not the
  cause.

Every wasm crypto failure in phase 5 goes through this function (ed25519's field
arithmetic, x25519, poly1305's limbs, and tls's transport), so fixing it should
clear most of the 22 remaining wasm fixtures. The next step is the emitted IR
for `math/bits.Mul64` on the wasm target, which the backend now makes easy to
reproduce in isolation.

### Round 330, the IR: Mul64 is folded to a 128-bit multiply

The wasm module's `math/bits.Mul64` is one multiply, not the 32-bit-half algorithm
the source writes:

    %0 = zext i64 %x to i128
    %1 = zext i64 %y to i128
    %2 = mul nuw i128 %1, %0
    %3 = lshr i128 %2, 64
    %t46 = trunc nuw i128 %3 to i64      ; hi
    %t49 = mul i64 %y, %x                ; lo

A pattern fold turns "mask both operands to 32 bits, multiply the halves, shift
and add" into a wide multiply. On x86-64 LLVM legalises `mul i128` to a handful
of 64-bit multiplies and the result is exact; on wasm32 the same instruction is
legalised through a runtime call, and `__multi3` is in the module (two
occurrences in the name section, and no provider anywhere in this tree - it comes
from the compiler-rt archive clang links). The low word is always right and the
high word is wrong, which is what a broken or mis-called `__multi3` looks like.

So the candidates, in order:

1. The pattern fold should not fire when the target has no native 128-bit
   multiply, or it should be checked on one: the fold replaces verified portable
   arithmetic with a runtime call whose wasm implementation nobody in this tree
   tests.
2. If the fold stays, `__multi3` on wasm32 has to be verified - it is the only
   place a 64x64->128 product happens on that target, and everything that needs
   one goes through it.

This is the block to pull for the remaining 22 wasm fixtures: the field
arithmetic behind ed25519, x25519, poly1305's limbs and tls's transport all run
through `Mul64`.

Also worth keeping from this round: a probe under `crypto/internal` cannot be an
importing program, so the diagnostic that localised this was a temporary
`func init()` self-test inside `edwards25519/field` printing four checkpoints -
`SetBytes`/`Bytes` round trip, `sqrtM1^2 == -1`, `Square`'s first limb, and
`SqrtRatio`'s verdict. `Square`'s limb differed between targets and named the
operation in one run.

### Round 331: the wasm host stubbed __multi3, and phase 5 went 96/118 -> 113/119

The IR said the basepoint decode ran through `mul i128`; the wasm module said
where that goes:

    Import[6]:
     - func[0] sig=2 <__multi3> <- env.__multi3

`__multi3(retptr, aLo, aHi, bLo, bHi)` is compiler-rt's 64x64->128 multiply, and
on wasm32 it is the only place a 128-bit product happens. `jsruntime/host.mjs`
answered every unlisted `env` name with `(() => 0)`, so the product was written
nowhere: the caller kept the LOW word (it computes that separately) and read
whatever the stack slot held for the HIGH one.

Fixed with a real BigInt implementation, and the catch-all now reports the FIRST
call of any name it does not provide, so the next symbol the host owes a module
surfaces instead of silently corrupting data (which is exactly how this one
presented: a correct low word and a garbage high word).

Phase 5, measured before and after:

    before:  96 passed, 22 failed
    after:  113 passed,  6 failed     (119 units)

Remaining, and what is known so far:

- `x25519_ecdh`: the browser run dies in a print/alloc recursion -
  `printstring -> ArenaAllocTD -> alloc -> printstring` - which is an arena
  failure being reported by printing something that itself allocates. The arena
  failure is the defect; the recursion is how it shows.
- `rand_fill`, `tls_handshake`: not looked at yet.
- `asn1_oid_der`, `asn1_tag_crosspkg`, `iface_ptr_recv_crosspkg`: not looked at
  yet; these are not on the crypto path, so they are probably unrelated.

The ed25519 chain that led here is recorded above: the trap, the zero generator,
the discarded decode error, the field self-test, `Mul64`, and now the host. Each
step was one probe, and the harness change that made the module speak was what
turned the first one from guesswork into a measurement.

### Round 332: wasm never reused released memory, and phase 5's last six fixtures

Round 331 left six wasm failures and one clue: `x25519_ecdh` died in a
print/alloc recursion, and the recursion was the *reporting* of an arena
failure, not the failure.

The recursion was real and was worth fixing first, because it was hiding the
message. `putchar` took the address of a local to hand to `fd_write`, which
marks it escaping, so every character printed allocated four bytes:

    putchar -> runtime.alloc(i32 4, ptr null, ptr null)

An allocator that is failing cannot print a diagnostic through the allocator.
Its buffers are package state now, and the same run said:

    panic: runtime error: arena: region mmap failed

Which was the real defect, and a second-order one: `sysMap` returns nil on
failure, and every arena call site tested `addr == unsafe.Pointer(^uintptr(0))`
- a value no implementation returns. The check was dead, so a failed map was
used as a success. Fixed to `addr == nil` in all four sites, and the diagnostic
was instrumented for one run rather than guessed at:

    sysMap: size=67108864 prev=62481 bump=4094754816
    sysMap: size=67108864 prev=63505 bump=4161863680
    sysMap: grow failed size=67108864 pages=1024 bump=4228972544 mempages=64529

The arena model reclaims by unmapping, and on wasm `sysUnmap` was a no-op, so
every chained overflow region (64MB, one per overflowing frame) was mapped once
and abandoned. `crypto/internal/fips140`'s curve inits chained enough of them to
take the bump cursor to the top of the 4 GiB address space inside
`nistec.buildP521GeneratorTable`.

`sysUnmap` now pushes the region onto an intrusive free list and `sysMap` takes
the first fit, splitting the tail so a live small arena does not pin 64MB. Peak
linear memory on that fixture: 270MB, two chained regions, and it passes.

`MoxieWrite` was a stub returning -1, so every runtime diagnostic on fd 2 was
dropped on wasm. It is a real `fd_write` now, which is how the next failure was
read instead of merely observed.

The remaining five, one at a time:

- `rand_fill`: the module exited 0 and the host called that a crash.
  `syscall.Exit` reports itself by throwing (there is no process to end), and
  the worker posted `kind:'error'` regardless of the code. Code 0 posts `done`.
- `asn1_oid_der`, `asn1_tag_crosspkg`: `RuntimeError: unreachable` in
  `encoding/asn1.(*_rawType).fieldData`, in a three-byte function named
  `signature_mismatch:strlen`. The wasm link's hand-written `@malloc` and
  `@strlen` stubs took two arguments (`(i32, ptr)`, `(ptr, ptr)`) while every
  call passes one, because a `//export`ed bodyless function is a C function and
  drops the hidden context parameter. wasm-ld replaces the mismatched callee
  with a trap, so every `strlen` call died - that is `cgo_GoString`, which
  builds an ASN.1 field name. Stubs take the arguments the calls pass, which is
  what legacy gets from musl on native.
- `iface_ptr_recv_crosspkg`: no compiler difference at all. The module printed
  the same codec arena-escape warning as the native run, but the gate merged
  the driver's stderr into the stdout it diffs. The wasm gate now captures
  stdout and stderr separately and `-q` keeps stdout to the program's output.
- `tls_handshake`: not a wasm fixture. It is a handshake between two domains
  over a loopback socket; a wasm domain has no sockets and no second thread, so
  the module sat in its accept loop until the run timed out. `//:wasmtest skip`
  with the reason stated in the fixture.

`RUN_WAIT_MS` makes the page's boot wait configurable: the external
`RUN_TIMEOUT` is the only bound that can stop a module that never yields, and a
slow-but-correct boot should be measurable instead of looking like a hang.

### Round 332, result: phase 5 is 117/117, and wasm memory is bounded

    phase 5 (wasm):  117 passed, 0 failed   (118 units; tls_handshake is now
                                             skipped as not-a-wasm-fixture)
    quickcheck: 15/15   phase 1b: PASS   phase 2 (fixpoint): PASS
    phase 3: PASS       phase 4: PASS    phase 6: PASS    phase 8: PASS

Two more defects were in the gate itself, and both were invisible until the
fixtures actually passed:

- Every run.py staged its module into the same `tests/wasm/app.wasm`, and the
  page loads `/app.wasm`. Phase 5 runs four units at a time, so four runs
  overwrote each other's module: a unit could execute another fixture, or load
  something mid-copy. It presented as a flaky set - the same fixture passing
  alone and failing in the sweep, a different member each time. The module is
  served from where it is now; nothing is staged.
- `util.sh` runs under `set -e` and `validate.sh` exits nonzero exactly when a
  fixture fails, so `run_one` died on the first failure before printing the
  verdict it had already written to its log. Every failure read as
  "(no output)". That is why the flakiness looked like a crash.

The last thing to fix was memory, and the complaint about it was right. A
chained arena region asked for 64MB on every target. That granule is free on
native, where a mapping stays virtual until touched; on wasm `memory.grow`
COMMITS the pages, so one overflowing frame cost 64MB of resident linear
memory. A crypto fixture measured 270MB for work that used kilobytes, and the
phase's concurrent browsers went into swap. The granule is a platform function
now: 64MB on native, 4MB on wasm - 16x less per overflow, still 512MB per arena
before the region table fills, and recycling makes the more frequent chains
cheap.

### Round 333: three ABI/signature defects that only a 32-bit target shows

Round 332 left the wasm suite green, and the first thing the next sweep found
was in a phase that had not been run in that campaign: phase 1c, where
`net/http` did not compile for wasm at all.

    net_http_internal.ll:233:16: error: invalid cast opcode for cast from
    'i64' to 'i32'
    %rs51 = sext i64 %t82 to i32

`resize(s, n)` converts `n` to the slice length field's width, and the
conversion was widen-only: legacy zero-extended a narrower argument, stage4
sign-extended anything that was not already the pointer type. A 64-bit length
on a 32-bit target has to be NARROWED. Both compilers truncate now. Native
cannot reach it - uintptr is i64 there, so no conversion is emitted - which is
why a wasm-only sweep found it.

That was the entry point to a larger defect, because the compiler was emitting
two signatures for one symbol:

    declare i64 @strlen(ptr, ptr)      ; the runtime package's IR
    call    i64 @strlen(ptr nonnull)   ; every call site
    declare i32 @malloc(i32, ptr)
    call    ptr @malloc(i32)

`emitFuncDecl` (the declaration for every bodyless function) appended the
hidden context argument unconditionally, while the call site correctly treats
an exported symbol as C ABI and omits it. Native links say nothing: libc
defines strlen and the declaration is only a name. wasm-ld compares the
definition it synthesises from the declaration against the calls and replaces
each mismatched callee with a three-byte trap named
`signature_mismatch:strlen` - the name in round 332's stack trace.

With declarations following the call convention, one place was left wrong:
`internal/task/task_none` declared `_panicstr` with `//export`, but
`_panicstr` is DEFINED in `runtime/panic.mx` as a Moxie function, context
argument and all. A declaration resolved by a Moxie definition keeps the Moxie
ABI; `//export` says "a C function takes this name". It is a `//:linkname` now,
the form asn1 already uses for `runtime.memcpy`. The wasm link has no
signature-mismatch warnings left, `net/http` compiles for wasm (769s, 44MB
module), and phase 1c passes.

Measured on the fresh bootstrap (fixpoint `3319d757`, s2 == s3):

    phase 1: PASS   phase 1b: PASS   phase 1c: PASS   phase 2: PASS
    phase 3: PASS   phase 4: PASS    phase 5: 118/118  phase 6: PASS  phase 8: PASS

How the declaration was found is worth keeping: the first two guesses (the
export map consulted at the declaration site, then matched by exported name)
changed nothing, and a temporary `mxutil.WriteStr(2, "DBGDECL ...")` in
`declareExternalFunc` printed NOTHING - the function is never called for
strlen, because the declaration comes from `emitFuncDecl`. One instrumented
build answered what two reasoned fixes had not.

### Round 334: the copy rule as wrong bytes - seven writes through a subslice

The wasm campaign closed with the whole suite green, so the next sweep was the
sibling repos: build them against the current compiler and run their tests.
That is where the round's real find was.

nostr, morly and smesh all *compiled*; the tests did not run. The failures
looked unrelated - an event id marshalled as 32 spaces, an ASN.1 field decode
error, "invalid public key", a loopback websocket reset - and every one of them
was the same defect: **a write through a subslice of a slice**.

    s[a:b] is a COPY. Writing through it lands in a throwaway.

`copy` onto a subslice is already a compile error in a user package (the
diagnostic "a subslice is a copy, so copying into it is not allowed"), but
passing one to a function that writes through its parameter is accepted and
silently does nothing. That gap cost seven sites:

| where | what it broke |
| --- | --- |
| `encoding/hex` AppendEncode/AppendDecode | appended the grown buffer's stale bytes |
| `crypto/secp256k1` feToBytes/feToLEBytes | EVERY public key and signature serialisation was 32 zero bytes |
| nostr `pkg/hex` | same as the stdlib one (its own clone) |
| nostr `pkg/event` Marshal | id/pubkey/sig hex written through `b[hexStart:]` → NUL bytes in the frame |
| nostr `pkg/crypto/nip44` pad | padded plaintext was zeros past the length prefix |
| nostr `pkg/tag` tagFieldBinary | binary-encoded tag values were 32 zero bytes |
| nostr `pkg/ws` writeClient/ServerFrame | extended length stayed 00 00 and the mask key was 00 00 00 00: every frame ≥126 bytes declared length ZERO |

The secp256k1 one is the serious one. It was invisible because both ends of a
self-consistent system used the same broken serialiser: a signature over a
32-zero pubkey verifies against a 32-zero pubkey. The BIP-340 vector tests in
the tree were red - `TestRadix16Carry` ("digits[64]==1 for scalar n-1") and
`TestBIP340Vectors` (8 of 19) - and nobody had run them, because phase 1b
COMPILES the stdlib and does not run its tests. After the fix all four pass,
and nostr's signer derives the vector public key.

Measured after the fixes:

    nostr:  194 tests pass, rc=0        (was: 5 units red, first at pkg/envelope)
    morly:   38 pass, 1 fail            (TestSocialWithStore, below)
    smesh:   relay-bin and both wasm bundles build

Also fixed, all found by the same run: two test bugs (a dns cache entry with a
zero expiry demands a UDP lookup of a `.invalid` name; `byte(70000)` is now a
compile error, as it should be - the ws frame fixture masks its length bytes),
and the sockaddr literals that still wrote `Addr: [4]byte{...}` for a slice.

**The durable fix is a compiler diagnostic**: reject a subslice expression
passed as an argument to a parameter the callee writes through (a one-level
per-callee effect summary is enough; the callee either assigns to an index of
the parameter or passes it on). That is a bilateral change and the next thing
this work needs. Until then this class costs a silent wrong answer every time,
and the tree has no test that can see it.

Open from this round:

- **morly `TestSocialWithStore`**: the WoT walk finds the admin's follow list
  (1 event) and then gets 0 events for the first hop's author, so
  `Depth(bob) = -1, want 2`. The query is
  `Kinds=[3], Authors=[alice], Limit=1` against a store that has just accepted
  both kind-3 events. Next step: instrument `Engine.QueryEvents` for the author
  index, and check whether `ev.MarshalBinaryToBytes` (also a candidate for the
  same copy bug) is producing a record the WAL replay can read back.

### Round 335: the copy rule inside a store - every index key was zeros

The sibling sweep from round 334 kept going into morly, and the second layer of
the same defect was there: the store's index keys.

`pkg/store/index/keys.mx` built every key like this:

    k := []byte{:KPCKeyLen}
    copy(k, KPC[:])
    serial.PutKind(k[3:], kind)
    copy(k[5:], pubHash[:serial.HashLen])
    serial.PutTimestamp(k[5+serial.HashLen:], ts)

A subslice of a slice is a COPY, so every field after the 3-byte prefix was
written into a throwaway. Every key in the store was `prefix + zeros`.

The reason it survived: writer and reader used the same broken keys, so the
store was self-consistent. What it could not do is *look anything up*. The
visible symptoms were all "found nothing" or "found the wrong thing":

- duplicate detection accepted redeliveries (`TestIngestDuplicate`),
- the WoT walk found the admin's follow list and stopped
  (`Depth(bob) = -1, want 2`),
- a word search over a store that had just accepted an event returned nothing,
- author/kind/created-at/tag scans returned whichever record happened to match.

The builders now write at explicit offsets: `putBytes` in the package, and
`serial.PutAt`/`PutKindAt`/`PutTimestampAt` in the serial package.

That fix exposed a second one one layer down. `sorted/recSorter.Swap` swapped
two records with three `copy()` calls on subslices, so `sort.Sort` ran and the
buffer kept its insertion order; `scanBinder` merges that buffer and stops at
the first record greater than the range end, so a scan for one word broke on the
first unsorted record. Swapped byte by byte now.

Note the *path exemption* that let both of these compile: a package whose import
path contains `/pkg/` is exempt from the restriction pass, so `copy(k[5:], ...)`
and the three-copy swap are accepted silently in `git.smesh.lol/morly/pkg/...`.
That is why the whole tree has to be swept for this shape by hand until the
compiler diagnostic exists (round 334's open item).

Measured: the morly suite went from 38 tests before the first failure to 153,
and the remaining red is `TestIngestDeletionOtherAuthor` - a store holding two
events answers an empty-filter query with one serial, while the ca index reports
`Count()==2` in other queries of the same run. Next probe: print the serial the
ca scan returns against the two records the index holds.

Two more test-side fixes from the same run: a `[]string` printed with `%v` into
a `...Stringer` variadic (the compiler is right to refuse it), and the sockaddr
literals from round 334.

### Round 335, the one still red: TestIngestDeletionOtherAuthor

Evidence gathered, in the order it was found (all instrumentation since removed):

- `tCount` is `eng.QueryEvents(&filter.F{})`, an empty filter, which takes the
  default branch: `scanCA(0, MaxInt64)`, i.e. the created-at index over the whole
  time range.
- The ca index reports `Count()==2` at scan time, and the scan returns **1**
  serial (`DBG collect total=2` / `DBG found=1`).
- The two events differ in `CreatedAt` (`now`, `now+1`) and in serial, so their
  ca keys cannot be equal unless the WAL hands out the same serial twice.
- The fetch loop is not the loss: the last `DBG fetch serials=` for that query
  is 1, so the serial is already missing before `GetBySerial`.

So the range [MakeCA(0,0), MakeCA(MaxInt64, serial.Max)] over a two-record ca
index yields one record. Next probes, in order: whether the two ca keys really
differ (print them from `serialSink.Add`, which is where a record can also be
dropped by `isDeleted` - `handleDeletion` in the same test deletes nothing, but
`isDeleted` is the other silent skip in that loop), and whether `Append` can
return the same serial twice, which would make the keys equal and let the
merge's dedup collapse them.

What is NOT in doubt: the two rounds of key/sort fixes are real and measured.
The morly suite went from 38 tests passing before its first failure to 153, and
the three failures it exposed on the way (duplicate detection, WoT depth, word
search) are closed.

### Round 336: the object that was copied on the way out

Round 335 left one morly test red and a probe list. The probe found something
bigger than the store.

The trail, in the order it was walked (instrumentation since removed):

- `tCount` is `eng.QueryEvents(&filter.F{})` -> `scanCA(0, MaxInt64)`. The scan
  emitted **three** records with distinct keys and correct serials while
  `Count()` was 2, and `collectSerials` sizes its sink from `Count()`, so
  `serialSink.Add` returned false on the third and the loop broke before the
  newest event was ever reached. The missing serial was a dropped record, not a
  missing key: every ca key was well formed (`63 2d 2d | ts | serial`).
- Three records for two events means the `.buf` sidecar held the target twice.
  `QuickFlush` prints `bufN=2` going in and `bufN=0, blen=0` after the clear, but
  the next call on the same File still sees `bufN=2` - so the clear never
  reached the File.
- `flushSidecars` iterates `e.allFiles()`. Printing addresses settled it: inside
  `allFiles` the element *is* `e.ca`, and in `flushSidecars`'s loop it is a
  different address, 21 times over. `e.ca.bufN` is unchanged after a loop that
  printed `bufN=0` from inside `QuickFlush`. The copies kept the same `*os.File`
  descriptors, which is why the sidecar grew and the index state did not: every
  flush wrote its buffer to the file and then threw away the record of having
  done it.
- The copy is made by the runtime codec, not by the store. `retPointeeDies`
  walks the pointee's fields and asks `codecIsStableAddr`; in return-value mode
  a pointer into a sovereign data arena answers "not stable", deliberately,
  because the owning receiver may compact that arena later. `sorted.File.buf`
  lives in the File's own sovereign arena, so *every* File was declared dying
  and deep-copied. A single field in an object's own arena condemned the object.

The fix is in `src/runtime/codec.mx`, in the shared runtime, so both compilers
pick it up by construction:

- `codecSovDataLive(p)` answers whether `p` points into a sovereign data arena
  that outlives the frame now returning, and marks the group escaped so nothing
  compacts the block away while the caller holds an alias of it. It is the body
  `codecSovDataAlias` already had, extracted, and `codecSovDataAlias` now
  delegates to it.
- `retPointeeDies` uses it for pointer, bytes/slice, map/chan/func fields: a
  field in a live sovereign arena does not make its holder die. Transience now
  depends on whether the *receiver* lives in the releasing frame
  (`sovGroupInDyingArena`), which is the actual question, instead of on whether
  the field happens to live in an arena other than the current stable one.

Measured: `TestIngestDeletionOtherAuthor` passes, all 30 pipeline tests pass, and
the morly unit suite is green across every package that carries tests.

The lesson is the one this campaign keeps teaching: an object whose identity is
split in two still compiles and still runs, and when the two halves write to the
same file descriptors the damage is silent. The bug was reported as "the newest
event is invisible"; it was the flush bookkeeping being thrown away.

### Round 337: a store into an element was not an assignment

Chasing the smesh SIGBUS (round 336's sibling) turned up a hole in stage4's type
checking that legacy never had. `nostr.NewTags(list ...*Tag)` assigned `[]*Tag`
to `List []Tag`; stage4 compiled it, storing a pointer array where an array of
24-byte structs was declared, and the first field read was a SIGBUS. Legacy
rejected it all along: "cannot use xs (variable of type []*T) as []T value in
assignment".

The hole: `buildStore` checked assignability for a store into a plain NAME and
nowhere else. A store into a struct FIELD, a slice/array element, a map value or
a through-a-pointer target skipped `checkAssignable` entirely, so any two types
of the same machine width were silently reinterpreted.

`checkElemStore` now does what the name path does before it stores:

- an untyped shift takes the target's type (`r2.limbs[n-1] = 1 << x` with
  `[]uint32` is a 32-bit shift; it was being typed int32 and rejected),
- the value must then be assignable to the element type.

Two details the first attempt got wrong, both caught by phase 1b:

- the element type of an index store must come from `ssaIndexElemType`, not from
  `p.Base`: when the base is already a `*[N]T` (an array field reached through a
  pointer), `p.Base` is the ARRAY and `f.codebits[i] = v` was rejected with
  "cannot use value of type int32 as [19]int32". That was flate and the fips140
  gcm cmac at once.
- the shift retyping has to happen before the check, or every
  `dst[i] = 1 << n` in the tree fails.

The check immediately found two stdlib packages that have never compiled, in
either compiler, because nothing imports them:

- `src/crypto/rc4/rc4.mx`: `c.s[i], c.s[j] = y, x` with `s []uint32` and y, x
  uint8 - the port widened Go's `[256]byte` state and never converted the swap.
  Now `uint32(y), uint32(x)`.
- `src/os/exec/exec.mx`: `Cmd.Start` built `files := []uintptr{...}` and assigned
  it to `ProcAttr.Files []*os.File`. `ProcAttr.Files` carries raw fds THROUGH
  the `*os.File` word (the child reads
  `int32(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(Files[i])))`), so the honest shape is a
  `[]*os.File` whose entries are `(*os.File)(unsafe.Pointer(fd))` - which is what
  `fdFile` now builds, with the convention named in a comment.

Measured: phase 1b "45 packages ok" (it was red on flate, then on bigmod, then
on rc4, then on os/exec, one real breakage at a time); phase 6 green including
the aeaddep dependency build; `reject_field_assign_mismatch` rejects on stage4 and
on legacy; bootstrap fixpoint holds. Legacy already rejected every one of these,
so this round is stage4-only: wood law is satisfied by matching, not by
mirroring.

### Round 339: the store's binary search read its records into a copy

`pkg/store/sorted.File.readAt` did `s.f.ReadAt(dst[:s.recLen], off)`. A subslice
is a copy, so the record was read into a throwaway and `dst` stayed zeroed -
exactly the round-336 class, in the foundation of every point lookup:

- every binary search compared zeros against the key, always answered "less
  than", and returned `count` as the lower bound - past the end of the file. A
  flushed index was invisible: `TestRebuildFromWAL` indexed six events, flushed
  them, and then answered an empty-filter query with **0** serials while
  `Count()` said 6.
- with that fixed, one record came back instead of six: `fileChunker.get` had the
  same shape on `c.chunk`, so the chunked scan reader handed the merge zeros for
  every record. Zeros sort before every real key, so the scan emitted the same
  zero-serial record repeatedly and the caller's dedup collapsed it to one.

Both now `resize` (same memory, corrected length) instead of subslicing. The
write paths in the same package (`bufFile.Write(s.buf[:n])`, `tmp.Write(rec)`)
are harmless: a write READS the copy, and the bytes are the same ones.

Measured: `pkg/store` 24/24 including `TestRebuildFromWAL` ("rebuilt count 6 of
6"), and the whole morly suite green at 370 tests.

Two notes for the diagnostic that is still the real fix for this class
(round 334's open item): the subslice-copy rule exempts any path containing
`/pkg/`, which is why every one of these compiled silently in the sibling repos,
and a read that writes through a slice parameter is the same shape as a write
that is lost - the call `f.ReadAt(x[i:j], off)` looks like a read at the call
site and is a write at the callee's.

### Round 340: wasm reads its stdin, and the last dead interface{} goes

`MoxieRead` was a `-1` stub on wasm, justified by "no wasm caller". That was
true of the spawn handshake it exists for (no fork, no pipe fds on this target)
but it also meant a wasm program could not read its stdin: `getchar` reads byte
by byte through fd_read, and any block read had nothing to call. It now lives in
`runtime_wasm.mx` next to `MoxieWrite`, over the WASI `fd_read` the host already
implements, with the iovec and count as package state so a read reached from the
allocator's failure paths cannot allocate. The browser hosts answer EOF (there
is no stdin in a page or a worker), which is the correct answer for them: a read
that returns 0 at end of input, not -1 as an error.

The stdlib's last real `interface{}` went with it: `printitf` in `print.mx` and
`print_wasm.mx` was a type-switch printer with no callers, the only code in
`src/` that still needed the empty interface. Removed both, plus the stale
`fmt/doc.mx` example that told readers an interface operand prints its concrete
value (Moxie has no interface values to print).

Verified: a wasm program that reads stdin (`os.Stdin.Read`) builds and links at
544994 bytes, and `5/rand_fill` still matches native output.

### Round 341: no exemptions

Both compilers exempted packages for being "the compiler's own": anything whose
path contains `/pkg/`, and any main package whose build root was the moxie
module. The first rule exempted every sibling repository's pkg/ tree as well,
which is exactly where this campaign's silent-corruption bugs lived: morly's
store compiled a dozen writes through a subslice and smesh's `nostr.NewTags`
stored a `[]*Tag` in a `[]Tag` field, and both compilers called the code clean.

The exemption is gone from stage4 (`ir_scope.mx`) and from legacy
(`restrict.go isUserPackage`). The compiler's own source now satisfies the same
rules it enforces, and the price was 27 diagnostics, all mechanical:

- ten functions with unnamed results named them (legacy rejects those);
- the mutable process state that lived in package-level globals - the
  typeFromTail recursion guard, `pendingIfaceAssigns`, the coverage site table,
  `lastHolder`/`heldRepoLocks` - is `compilerState` behind one package-level
  pointer (`_mxc_stage4/cstate.mx`), each store behind a method, because a store
  to a package-level variable outside an init-named function is a language
  error. Reads stay direct.
- `objFlags` is a zero-value declaration filled by `initObjectFlags`;
- `copy(nb[:len(all)], all)` in the package-cache hash is `CopyAt(nb, 0, all)`:
  the subslice copy meant the cache key hashed only the LAST file, which is a
  cache-collision bug on its own;
- `syntax.CompileExportMap` was written by the compiler and read by nobody: the
  dead global and its write are gone.

Legacy had to be rebuilt for the first time in this campaign
(`GOROOT=/opt/go1.25.3 bash legacy/build.sh`; it regenerates its patched
GOROOT). With the exemption gone it builds `_mxc_stage4` with zero restriction
diagnostics, and so does the stage4 built from it. That also settles the
wood-law question this change raised: both compilers now apply the same rules to
the same packages.

Measured, bootstrap fixpoint `528605f1`:

- full sweep, `-j 1`, all phases in one run: **316/317**. Everything native
  (0a 123, 0b 62, 1 4, 1b 45 packages, 1c 4, 2 selfhost fixpoint, 3, 4, 6), the
  wasm sweep (119) and netsmoke (8) - and tree-cleanliness.
- the one red is still **7/whole-phase**: `ui:build` PASSES (nine wasm bundles,
  runtime staging, relay built from source) and `ui:smoke` ends at round 329's
  documented `3 passed, 3 failed, 5 errors`, Selenium timeouts in the browser
  flows. That is the app/relay side and it was red before this work.

### Round 342: the sibling sweep, and why phase 7 was red

**The siblings under the no-exemption compiler.** With the exemption gone from
both compilers, each repository was built with legacy (the stricter of the two)
to see what 341 admitted to hiding:

- **nostr**: clean. Only the expected "linker could not find symbol main.main"
  for a library target.
- **morly**: five shadowed declarations, all redeclarations of a named result -
  `var buf [8]byte` in serial.AppendTimestamp (an array, too), `var n int64` in
  config.parseInt64, four `var err error` in tree/messages.mx, `var buf []byte`
  in transport/http.mx, and a bool `authed` beside a []byte `authed` in
  server_subs.mx. Fixed; the suite is still 370/370.
- **smesh**: six sites in the mls package - the same `var err error` shape in
  framing/group/tree, `readVarint` declaring a local `n` over its own uint32
  result (and typing the shift int32), and readVector/writeVector naming their
  callback parameter after the receiver (`r`, `w`, then `sub`, each a shadow of
  something in scope). Fixed; `make test-unit` rc=0.

Two more things fell out of that build, both legacy compiler defects on valid
input, both a degenerate LLVM handle passed to the C API:

- the DebugRef path handed `DIBuilder.InsertValueAtEnd` a zero value handle
  (`b.locals` keeps an entry for a variable that was only declared - morly's
  `done` is one), and the compiler died with SIGSEGV inside createFunction;
- the Store path asked the LLVM VALUE for its type to decide whether the store
  is a no-op; the size is a property of the SSA type, so it now comes from
  `getLLVMType(instr.Val.Type())` instead.

Legacy also disagreed with stage4 about `src/vendor/golang.org/x/...`: stage4
strips a leading `vendor/` before the third-party exemption, legacy did not, so
legacy rejected the stdlib's vendored x/crypto for unnamed returns the moment the
other exemptions went. Both now read the same path. Bootstrap fixpoint unchanged
(528605f1): these remove crashes, they do not change emitted code.

**The wasm crypto trap from round 329 is closed.** `ed25519_roundtrip`,
`ed25519_vectors`, `x25519_ecdh`, `poly1305_aead` and `crypto_vectors` all build
for wasm and print the same answer as native on the current compiler
(`tests/wasm/validate.sh`: 5 passed, 0 failed). Whatever the constructor-arena
bug was, the intervening codec and constructor work closed it; nothing was
"fixed" for it in this round, and the fixtures are the evidence.

**Phase 7 was red because the app worker could not link.** The smoke suite's
five errors and three failures were all one cause, and the browser console
named it:

    [app-worker] fatal: LinkError: import object field '__multi3' is not a Function
    [signer-worker] boot: LinkError: import object field '__multi3' is not a Function

LLVM legalises `mul i128` (math/bits.Mul64) to compiler-rt's `__multi3`. The
PAGE host (`jsruntime/host.mjs`) has provided it since the low-word/garbage-high
-word bug; the WORKER env object in `jsruntime/bridge-common.mjs` had not, so
every worker bundle whose closure uses 128-bit arithmetic failed to instantiate.
The app then sat in `boot` forever - the page's `data-wasm-ready` flag is only
set by the worker's `ready` message, and a fatal error message never sets it -
which is why the failures looked like Selenium timeouts rather than a build
problem.

`__multi3` is now in the worker env too. The app becomes ready in about a second,
and phase 7 is green: `ui:build` PASS (nine bundles + runtime staging + relay
from source) and `ui:smoke` **11 passed** in 47s, where it was 3 passed / 3
failed / 5 errors before.

One build-product trap worth recording: `web/static/bridge-common.mjs` in the
app repo is gitignored, and `moxie build -target wasm` keeps an app-supplied copy
("the app does not ship it" otherwise). A stale copy there kept the old env in
the staged tree even after the runtime was fixed, so the fix only took effect
once the file was deleted and the build staged the runtime's own.

That is the first fully green sweep in this campaign. The two gates that were
