### Round 343: the five open items, worked

**1. Subslice passed to a writing parameter - documented, not diagnosed.** The
compilers refuse the two shapes decidable from one expression (`copy(x[a:b], …)`
and `x[a:b][i] = v`) and cannot refuse the third cheaply: `f(x[a:b])` is a lost
write only if `f` writes through that parameter, which needs a parameter-write
set per function and a call-graph walk at every call site - multi-level
inference, not a local rule. Recorded in CLAUDE.md next to the subslice rule,
with the corollary that a static analysis tool can do it offline, and with the
authoring rule it implies: never pass a parameter as a return value.

**2. legacy builds morly again (the wood-law violation).** The crash was not a
compiler bug this time - it was `<spawn>` answering a `chan struct{}` result with
no LLVM value because legacy REJECTS a buffered channel across a spawn boundary
and morly passed two of them:

    ready := chan struct{}{:64}   // server.mx:68, the store-ready channel
    ready = chan struct{}{:64}    // server.mx:284, the ingest worker nudge

Both are unbuffered now. The rule is right: `PipeChanSend` writes the SPSC ring
and never consults the channel's declared capacity, so `:64` is a promise the
wire cannot keep and the ring is the buffer either way. `legacy/moxie build`
produces a 17.7MB relay, and morly's suite is unchanged at 370/370 under stage4.

The crash path itself is fixed as a class (item 3): any `createExpr` that
answers (nil, nil) for a value that has one is now a positioned diagnostic with
an undef substitute, so the rest of the package still compiles and reports.

**4. reading stdin on wasm panics.** A browser has no stdin and no filesystem:
the descriptor does not exist, and returning 0 reported that as end-of-input,
which reads as "the stream is empty" and hides that there is no stream at all.
`MoxieRead` and `buffered()` now turn a failed `fd_read` into
"wasm: read failed: no such descriptor (a browser has no stdin and no
filesystem)", and both hosts answer EBADF for fd 0 instead of a successful
zero-byte read. EOF on a descriptor that DOES exist is still just EOF.

**5. CLAUDE.md drift.** It claimed the compiler skips any file importing
`iter`/`weak`/`crypto/internal/fips140cache` (discoverPkg, "~line 1722"). There
is no such skip-list, and there has not been one since the `any` refactor; the
paragraph now says so.

**6. the bridge-common footgun now says so.** An app-supplied
`web/static/bridge-common.mjs` is kept by the build, and a stale copy there kept
an old worker env in a staged tree for a round. The build now compares the app's
copy against `jsruntime/bridge-common.mjs` and warns when they differ, because
silence is what cost that round.

### Round 344: a spawn channel is a sized mailbox, and its frames have a declared bound

**The channel is a FIFO with a size stated in its declaration.** `chan T{}` is
ONE slot, `chan T{:N}` is N; there is no unbuffered channel, because a domain
has one thread and nothing could receive while a rendezvous sender waits. The
literal rewrite emits the default explicitly (`__slicealloc(chan T, 1)`), both
compilers reject a constant capacity below one, and `chanMake` rejects a
capacity computed at run time. Inside a thread and across a spawn boundary the
rule is the same: a mailbox, never a rendezvous.

**The declared capacity is a message count, not a byte threshold.** The ring
header gained `sentFrames` and `recvFrames`, each written by exactly one side,
so `sentFrames - recvFrames` is the outstanding count and a send parks once N
are waiting. Legacy's old rejection of buffered channels across spawn
boundaries is gone (wood law: stage4 accepted them, so legacy does now too).

**The ring is created at the spawn, sized from the element type.** A spawn
channel is an atomic FIFO: its size is fixed before the fork, so the compiler
computes an upper bound on one encoded message and the runtime sizes the pair
`pow2((N+1) * align8(4 + budget))` (at least a page, at most `ringMaxMsg`).
Every variable-length dimension takes its count from a `cap:"..."` struct tag -
one number per dimension, outermost first, in ELEMENTS of that dimension, bytes
at a `string`/`[]byte` leaf - and an unstated dimension is one page, 4096
bytes. A channel, interface, function value or type parameter in the path is a
compile error: no count bounds it. `NoteSpawnChan` carries each channel handle
to `spawnDomain`, so the depth and the budget are read from the handle itself
instead of being guessed from an argument list.

**Overrunning the budget panics with the declaration to fix.** The check runs
before the ring-size check, so the message is the one that names the problem:

    panic: runtime error at 0x...: spawn channel: encoded frame of 6011 bytes
    exceeds the 4118-byte frame budget. Variable-length fields and their cap
    tags: main.Untagged.Body unstated (4096)

    panic: ... encoded frame of 20020 bytes exceeds the 16765-byte frame budget.
    Variable-length fields and their cap tags: main.Req.Tags cap:"8,32";
    main.Req.Body cap:"8192"

Both notes are compiler-generated text carried on the channel, so a panic names
the field path and the tag a programmer has to change.

Evidence: bootstrap fixpoint `b3dfd429` (s2 == s3); a 4096-byte frame crosses a
default-budget ring and a 6000-byte one crosses an 8192-tagged body
(`tests/regressions/should_compile/spawn_frame_budget.mx`); `:0` is rejected
(`tests/restrictions/reject_chan_zero_capacity.mx`); the two panic messages
above were captured from real binaries.

**Open, found on the way (not fixed):** stage4 misprints a value that was just
received into a local and then passed to `println`/`fmt.Println` - the receive
is correct (a comparison against the expected value passes) and the printed
word is stack residue, so it is a display bug in the boxing at that call site.
Legacy builds the same probe correctly, so this is a stage4-only divergence.
The reproducer is the `workerR` shape: a spawned worker that loops
`v := <-in; fmt.Println(v)` on a `chan int64{:4}` whose frames were all sent
before the worker wakes. It is intermittent across programs, which points at
stack-slot reuse for the boxed interface rather than at the channel.

**Open, unchanged:** there is no harness that asserts a panic message, so the
two overflow messages are captured by hand; and no compiler diagnostic exists
for "subslice passed to a parameter that writes", which stays a documented
static-analysis target.

**Axiom fit.** The rule is Metal before anything else: the declaration is a key
that states exactly what may cross (`cap:"..."` per dimension, a page when
unstated), and the frame budget is that key's shape. Chain->Evade -
boundary-coherence-or-nothing - is why an unbounded dimension is refused rather
than given a heap-sized default: a spawn boundary whose message size is unknown
is not a boundary. Charm->Alert is the failure mode: the overrun dies at the
send with the actual size, the budget and the offending field paths, upstream of
the corruption, instead of wrapping a ring or growing a buffer. Fire: the ring
is a number computed before the fork, `pow2((N+1) * align8(4 + budget))`, not a
hope adjusted at run time. Earth: the memory is the channel's own, allocated
from its declaration, never resized across the boundary. Wood: legacy and
stage4 walk the same type graph and produce the same budget and the same note,
and the bootstrap fixpoint is the proof they agree.

### Round 345: the channel declaration states its per-element budget, and the two compilers agree on the number

**`chan T{:count:bytes}`** is the notation now: the first field is the number
of elements (messages) outstanding, the second is the byte budget PER ELEMENT,
and it may be any integer expression - `limit := cfg.MaxEventBytes; in :=
chan wire.Event{:16:limit}` sizes the pair from relay policy read at run time.
`chan T{::bytes}` states the budget with the one-slot default. The rewriter
splits at the first TOP-LEVEL colon (a colon inside brackets is a slice
expression), and both compilers carry the value as an SSA operand into
`chanMake`, so a constant is checked against the 16 MiB ceiling at compile time
and a computed one is checked when the ring pair is created.

**The bilateral bug this exposed: legacy's operand was silently dropped.**
`ssa.MakeChan` gained a `Budget` field, but `Operands()` did not list it, so the
load that produced the budget had no referrers; a late pass removed it and
`createMakeChan` then panicked with "SSA value not previously found". Add the
operand to `Operands()` (and to `String()`) and the load survives. The lesson is
general: a new operand on a vendored SSA node is not live until `Operands()`
says so.

**Budget parity.** The same probe built with both compilers disagreed by one
byte: stage4 added a tag byte for every basic field, but `codecEncodeValue`
writes basics RAW (`isBasicKind` -> `codecWriteRaw`). Legacy was right and
stage4 now matches, so `struct{N int32; Body []byte}` is 4117 bytes on both. The
note also lost its type name in legacy (`struct{N int32; ...}` instead of
`main.Untagged`) because it unwrapped the named type before recording the path;
the name is taken before the unwrap now.

Evidence: with legacy, `chan Body{:2:limit}` where `limit := int64(65536)`
crosses a 60000-byte body and prints `worker got 60000`; a constant budget and
a call-valued budget both work; `chan T{:0}` still rejects; `spawn_frame_budget`
skips the wasm phase because the SAB boundary owns its rings.

**The numbers.** Bootstrap fixpoint `803e0d3f` (s2 == s3, runtime baked). With
the installed stage4 compiler, `limit := int64(65536); in := chan Body{:2:limit}`
carries a 60000-byte body and prints `worker got 60000`; `chan Body{:1:1024}`
panics with

    spawn channel: encoded frame of 2007 bytes exceeds the 1024-byte frame
    budget. Variable-length fields and their cap tags: main.Body.Data unstated (4096)

so the message states what actually crossed, what the declaration allowed, and
which fields the walk would size; `0a/spawn_frame_budget` passes; and morly's
whole suite (370 tests) passes with the migrated wire types. nostr and smesh
have no `spawn` calls, so they needed no migration.

The one-line lesson worth keeping: `ssa.MakeChan.Budget` had to be added to
`Operands()`, because an operand the SSA does not list is an operand the
compiler is free to delete.

**Every field takes a variable.** `chan Body{:buffers:limit}` with both from
variables is a three-slot ring of `limit` bytes per element; `[]byte{:ln:cp}`
and `map[K]V{:mc}` take variables for len/cap and capacity. Three of the four
already worked (the literals are ordinary expressions); the map capacity did
not: `emitMakeMap` passed the reserve operand straight to `hashmapMake`, so a
variable emitted `i32` where the runtime takes a word and the IR verifier
rejected the module. It is widened with `sextToIpt` now, like a slice's len/cap.

Evidence, installed compiler: `chan cap 3`, `worker got 3000`, `slice len 4 cap
8`, `map len 1`, `ok`. Bootstrap fixpoint `34cd6dc9` (s2 == s3).

### Round 346: the spawn ABI is a signature, and the kernel is the reaper

**A spawned function is a signature the compiler can read.** A target declares
no return value (the termination breaker is the channel `spawn` returns), a
target's parameters are values (copied, frozen at the call) or channels
(shared), and a target may not reach a channel through a package global: its
parameters are the only capabilities it holds. The check reports
`must not return values` and `reads channel global`, in legacy and stage4,
native and wasm. Note the version of this rule from the same session that the
next round replaces: the target will declare `(closed chan struct{})` and return
the breaker, so the no-results half is scheduled to become an exact-signature
check, not a ban.

**The supervision gap has a kernel answer.** Every spawn is supervised: the
parent holds a breaker and reaps. But a parent killed outright - SIGKILL, a
crash - never closes anything, and a child that is not in a channel wait (a
sleep, a blocking read) never notices. `spawnDomain`'s child now calls
`prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG, SIGTERM)` and rechecks `getppid()` afterwards (the
parent may already be gone when prctl runs); the child dies by SIGTERM with no
cooperation from the parent. Measured: a parent SIGKILLed while its child loops
on `time.Sleep` leaves no child after one second.

Evidence: fixpoint `3b7c6f1c`, `reject_spawn_returns_value` passes; the reaper
probe prints `reaper ok: child gone after the parent was killed`. The
channel-global check is in place for same-package targets; a cross-package
target's body may not be loaded into the caller's SSA, so that case is recorded
rather than claimed.

**Value parameters are sized, not yet bounded.** The tag walk already computes a
budget for a value parameter's type, but the pack that carries value arguments
is a pointer array over COW pages, not a bounded encode, so nothing enforces the
budget at the spawn call yet. That is the next step: encode value parameters
into a bounded buffer with the same panic as a channel frame.

**The breaker is one object, created before the fork.** `spawnDomain` now makes
the breaker channel before `fork`, so the parent's handle (what
`SpawnLifecycleChannel` returns, and later what `spawn` returns) and the child's
`DomainClosed` are the same channel: a close by either side is visible to both,
and the child's exit still closes it through `domainReapChildren`. The runtime
side compiles (s1) with no behaviour change yet, because no compiler binds the
target's `closed` result to it - that is the next step, recorded here so it is
not re-derived:

- legacy: in `createFunction`, after the `*ssa.Alloc` whose comment is "closed"
  is created, store `runtime.ClosedBreakerChan()` into it; the target's select
  then reads the result variable.
- stage4: the same store into `NamedResults[0]` in the function prologue.
- both: the spawn rule becomes "the target's signature is exactly
  `(closed chan struct{})`", replacing the no-results check, plus the select
  requirements - `main` selects on `sigint`, a target selects on `closed`.
- SIGINT delivery: the handler in `signal.c` currently `_exit`s. It must set a
  flag and wake a futex word the domain parks on (the single-threaded wake
  word), and `sigint` must be a special word lowering to that wait; then the
  main select can observe it.
- migration: every spawn target gains `(closed chan struct{})` and its select
  case, and every `main` gains the `sigint` select (about 120 fixtures in this
  tree, morly's six targets and its main).

**The breaker is bound, asserted and closed (round 346, second half).**
`spawnBreaker` is now a control-ring-bound channel: created before the fork,
wired to `spawnCtlRing`, and `spawnBreakerMake` gives it `spawnBound` with
`ringSend`/`ringRecv` on that ring. The compiler binds it to the target's
`closed` result in the prologue and asserts it there
(`AssertBreaker`), so a direct call to a spawn target panics with
"spawn target called directly: closed breaker is nil; spawn it instead of
calling it" instead of running a select whose closed arm is nil. `spawn` records
the breaker with `SpawnTrack`; every `return` of the creating function closes
it, and `runtimePanic` closes them all (and the domain's own breaker) before it
prints. The spawn signature rule is now exact: a target must be declared
`(closed chan struct{})`, in legacy and stage4, native and wasm.

**A nil select buffer was a real segfault, found by the breaker.** A select case
that binds nothing (`case <-closed:`) passes a nil recvbuf, and the spawn-bound
`tryPipeRecv` wrote `elementSize` bytes through it. It now skips the store when
`value` is nil; that path is reachable from any spawn-bound `chan struct{}` case,
so this was a latent crash independent of the breaker.

**Verified.** Bootstrap fixpoint `496b0c21`. Probes: direct call panics with the
message above; a parent function that spawns and returns makes the child's
`case <-closed:` fire (`worker: closed`, then `ok`); a parent `panic` closes the
breakers before printing (the child is usually reaped by PDEATHSIG in the same
instant, so the cascade is enforced by the close order rather than observable
as a print). Targets migrated: moxie's seven (chanpath, futexpark x2,
tls_handshake, spawn_frame_budget, spawncost, spawnbytes) and morly's five
(Broadcast/Proxy/Ingest/Blossom workers, dbengine.Run).

**Still open, unchanged:** `sigint` (main's select) needs the signal handler to
stop `_exit`ing and wake a domain park word; then every main gains the select
and both compilers enforce it. The value-parameter budget encode is also still
unwired (the tag walk exists, the pack is a pointer array).

**The spawn signature contract is the TYPE, not the name.** Imported signatures
do not reliably carry the result name, so `isSpawnTargetSig` accepts exactly one
result of type `chan struct{}` (send-recv, empty struct element) in both
compilers; the migration still spells it `(closed chan struct{})`, and the
language documents that spelling. Without this, every cross-package spawn in
morly was rejected ("BroadcastWorker must be declared with exactly one
result") while the same-package fixtures compiled.

**Round 346 close-out: what is green and what is not.** Green: the spawn ABI
rule and the breaker lifecycle compile in both compilers, bootstrap to fixpoint
`5ef57322`, and the probes print what they should (direct call panics; a
parent's return closes the child's `closed`; a panic closes before it prints).
Morly builds (10.6MB relay). NOT green: `0a/http_header_api` now **segfaults**
after compiling, so the breaker path breaks `net/http`'s chan workers - it is
the top item for the next round, with `src/net/http/chanpool.mx`'s
`chanWorkerLoop` as the suspect (it spawns, selects, and now returns the
breaker). Morly's suite times out at 2400s with no failure reported, which is
the same class of hang and may share the cause. The full sweep has not been run
on this compiler.

**Still unimplemented, in order:** the reason-on-close (panic message sent over
the breaker before the close), the `sigint` half (handler must stop `_exit`ing
and wake the domain; every `main` gains the select; both compilers enforce it),
the select checks for spawn targets, and the value-parameter budget encode.

**The http segfault was two compiler bugs, not a runtime one.** `gdb` on
`moxie build` showed an infinite `frameBudget` recursion: the walk followed a
cyclic type graph (a struct pointing at itself) with no bound, and the recursion
only stopped when the stack died. Both compilers now carry a depth bound (48);
past it the walk counts one page, which can only over-estimate. The second crash
was the walk's own diagnostics: it called `reportCompileError` for any
chan/interface/func element type - but the walk runs for EVERY `make(chan)`,
not just spawn ones, and the message built `t.String()` for a recursive type
inside the error path. Those cases now return the page default; the spawn
validator is the gate that refuses such types, by name, where it belongs. The
third was an LLVM "instruction does not dominate all uses": the compiled
close-at-return named a spawn register from a branch in another branch's return.
The return-close is emitted only for a spawn in the entry block, which is where
the rule's real cases live (a spawn at the top of its function).

Evidence: fixpoint `1a1aeb1c`; `http_header_api` builds and prints `header ok`;
`spawn_frame_budget` builds and runs under the new import root.

**The import root is the vanity domain: `moxielang.dev`.** The permanent address
for the toolchain is the domain, not the GitHub org path: the repository stays
at github.com/moxie-language/toolchain, and the domain serves the redirect.
Every Moxie import, the loader's hardcoded toolchain path, the docs and the
scripts now say `moxielang.dev`; the legacy Go module (`moxie/...`) is internal
and unchanged. Bootstrap fixpoint `30c0c24b` (s2 == s3), and an app builds and
runs against it. morly, smesh and nostr keep their own module paths; their
toolchain imports follow the vanity root.

A note for the domain: a Go vanity import normally answers `?go-get=1` with
`<meta name="go-import">`; the Pages meta-refresh redirect described for
moxielang.dev is a browser bounce, not that, and Moxie's own loader never does
an HTTP lookup (it resolves the toolchain through MOXIEROOT and pinned repos
through MANIFEST), so nothing in this tree depends on the meta tag. The redirect
only matters to a Go tool asking `go get` for the legacy module.

### Round 347: the breaker carries a reason, and the reason is a code-first line

The breaker's element is `[]byte`, so a domain can say WHY it stopped before the
breaker closes: `runtimePanic` encodes the message as a structural `[]byte`
frame (`breakerSendReason`), sends it on the domain's breaker, then closes and
prints. The reap path sends the exit status as the same kind of frame, and
`PipeChanRecv` drains once more after the peer is found dead, because the reap
that noticed the death is what puts that final frame on the ring. On a panic
the message is the diagnostic text, whose FIRST SPACE-SEPARATED TOKEN is the
process exit code by convention (`134` for the abort a panic produces, `0` for
a clean stop, `128+signal` for a killed domain); the same text is printed to the
shared stderr, so every component's failure is readable in one stream.

Three wiring bugs were fixed on the way: the breaker had no peer pid, so the
parent's receive never noticed the child die and parked forever; the reap closed
it with the local `chanClose` instead of the ring close, so the parent never saw
it; and its frame budget was the slice-header size (24 bytes), smaller than the
encoded reason, so the panic path itself panicked.

**Still open:** the parent's receive decodes to an empty slice
(`reason len: 0 ok: false`) - the frame is sent, but `PipeChanRecvStructural`'s
decode of the runtime-encoded `[]byte` does not produce a value. Next probe:
print the first bytes of the frame at `PipeChanRecvStructural` and the `td`
kind it decodes with; the likely mismatch is the hand-built
`RawType{meta: KindBytes}` descriptor versus the compiler's descriptor for
`[]byte` (which carries `Elem`). Value-parameter budgets, `sigint`, and the full
sweep remain after it.

**The reason arrives, and the exit code leads it.** The last piece was the
spawn result's TYPE: both compilers typed `spawn(...)` as `chan struct{}`
regardless of the target, so the caller's receive used the raw path and the
reason (a structural `[]byte` frame) never reached user code even though the
child sent it. Both compilers now type the spawn result exactly as the target
declared it - the target's single result, `chan []byte` - and the parent's
receive decodes the reason: `reason len: 20 ok: true` for a child that panics,
`0 ` for one that stops cleanly. The text is the exit code first
(`134` for the abort a panic produces, `0` clean, `128+signal` killed) followed
by the diagnostic, which the failing component also prints to the shared stderr.
The reason frame is encoded cross-domain, so the parent gets its own copy rather
than a header into the dying child's arena. Fixpoint `654c8f01`.

**A compiler bug found by the probe:** `string(x)` where `x` is a `[]byte`
local produced `invalid cast opcode for cast from '{}' to '{ ptr, i64, i64 }'`
in the generated IR (the conversion emitted an empty-struct operand). The probe
prints `len(reason)` instead. That conversion is used all over the tree on
parameters and fields, so the failing shape is narrower than the operation -
recorded for a dedicated look.

### Round 348: the sigint attempt, withdrawn

What was built: a graceful SIGINT in `signal.c` (a handler that only sets a
`sig_atomic_t`, never `_exit`s), a static termination channel in the runtime
(`sigintChanStorage`, so no allocation and no global chan store), a
`SigintChan()` accessor the loader's rewrite could name, and the predeclared
word `sigint` -> `runtime.SigintChan()` in both rewriters (identifier-only,
skipping strings, backtick raw strings and comments), with the receive path
special-cased to poll the flag.

What failed: the bootstrap's stage4 self-compile died with "arena: region table
full" before any sigint code could run - and it kept dying after the
`initDomain` hook was removed and after the global chan store was replaced by
the static-struct accessor. That means the crash is in the *interaction* the
rewrite introduces (the stage4 compiler's own source contains the word `sigint`
in comments and in the new rewrite helper), not in the signal plumbing, and it
was not diagnosed before the context budget ran out. The whole attempt was
withdrawn rather than committed: `git checkout` of the six touched files, a
legacy rebuild and a fresh bootstrap put the tree back at fixpoint `88429764`
with nothing uncommitted.

Next attempt should reproduce it small: compile a one-file program containing
only `<-sigint` with a legacy-built stage4, and gdb the crash - the region-table
panic names the allocation site's return address, which resolves through the
compiler's own symbol table. The mechanism (flag + poll + static channel + the
rewrite) is otherwise straightforward and worth keeping in this shape.

### Round 349: the breaker contract is text, not slice-of-byte

`isSpawnTargetSig` required the breaker's element to be a `*types.Slice` of
uint8. That held inside one package and failed the moment the target was
imported: stage4 compiles each package in its own process and reads the other
package's declarations back from serialized type descriptors
(`compile_exports.mx`'s `parseTypeDesc`), which folds `[]uint8` into the basic
`string` - one type, two spellings - so `chan []byte` arrived as `chan string`
and every cross-package spawn in morly was refused while the same-package
fixtures compiled. The probe made it exact: a two-package program with
`func Worker(in chan int32) (closed chan []byte)` printed the imported result
type as `chan string` and was rejected; the same function declared in the
caller's package was accepted.

Both compilers now test Moxie text (`moxieTextType` in legacy,
`types.TextType` in stage4), not slice-of-byte. `Identical` already unified the
two spellings, so arguments and results type-check either way; only the
spawn-signature marker was structural. morly migrated the holders too: every
`done`/`workerDone`/`proxyDone`/`blossomDone` field, pool element, parameter
and helper result that receives a spawn result is `chan []byte` (ready
channels stay `chan struct{}`, they are not breakers). morly then builds clean
(10.6MB) against the fixed compiler, and a cross-package probe compiles and
exits 0.

Bootstrap: fixpoint `b9b336a4` (s2 == s3). The frame-budget walk already
handled the basic-string spelling on both sides, so a cross-package frame type
is budgeted the same as a local one.

Two fixture faults surfaced with the fix: `tls_handshake.mx`'s `serverDomain`
declares the breaker result but its body ended in `ln.Close()` with no
`return closed` ("missing return"), now fixed. The tree-cleanliness check in
`quickcheck` fails while a change is uncommitted, which is why it reported on
this round's run before the commit.

Still open, unchanged: `sigint` (main's select) and the value-parameter budget
encode, both as described in round 348.

### Round 350: sigint lands (the word, the flag, the poll)

Round 348's attempt is not what landed. The failure there was the *rewrite*
shape, not the signal plumbing, so this round changed the shape:

- `sigint` is lowered to a predeclared **builtin call**, `__sigint()`, and the
  call is typed `chan []byte` by the same mechanism `__slicealloc` uses. In
  legacy that is a patched GOROOT (`_Sigint` id in `universe.go`, a case in
  `builtins.go`'s `check.builtin`); in stage4 it is `BuiltinSigint` in the
  universe plus a `buildBuiltinCall` case. The compiler emits
  `runtime.SigintChan()`, so the word names the domain's channel and nothing
  else.
- The rewrite runs **first**, on the source as written: legacy's
  `mxtext.RewriteSigint` and stage4's `rewriteSigintWord` scan tokens/bytes,
  skip comments, quoted strings, raw strings and rune literals, match the
  identifier as a whole word, and leave `x.sigint` and a declaration of the
  name alone. Both later passes (channel literals, slice literals) parse the
  rewritten source as their input, so no offset compensation is needed - which
  is where round 348 went wrong.
- The runtime creates the channel lazily in the **root arena**
  (`SigintChan`), so it outlives every frame that selects on it. The C handler
  does one thing: raise `sig_atomic_t`. `sigintPoll()` closes the channel once,
  from normal context, and it is called in every point where the domain waits:
  the send loop, the receive loop, and both branches of `chanSelect`'s wait.
  The handler itself never allocates, closes or locks.
- The old immediate `_exit` path survives as the app's explicit choice
  (`moxie_install_interrupt_handler`, used by the compiler to clean its scratch
  dirs); installing it replaces the graceful disposition. The runtime installs
  the flag handler at startup.
- wasm defines `sigintPending() = false`: a browser domain is stopped by the
  host tearing down the Worker, so the channel simply never closes there.

Evidence: a one-file program that parks in `select { case <-sigint: }` prints
`waiting`, then `sigint`, then `done` when sent SIGINT - compiled by the
legacy-built stage4 AND by the bootstrapped `./moxie`. The self-compile that
died in round 348 ("arena: region table full") now completes, and the bootstrap
reaches fixpoint `dd4a0c92` (s2 == s3). `tests/restrictions` is 63/63.

Not yet done: the compilers do not yet *enforce* the select (every `main`
selecting on `sigint`, every spawn target on `closed`), and the tree's mains are
not migrated to it, so the word is available but unused. Enforcing before the
migration would break every fixture, so enforcement and migration are one
change. The value-parameter budget encode is still unwired.

### Round 354: value parameters are copied, and their budget is enforced

The spawn call packed each value parameter's own bytes and the child read them
out of the parent's frame. The bytes were copied, but their contents were not:
a slice or pointer field still pointed into the parent's frames, which pop the
moment the spawning function returns. `SpawnArgCopy` closes that: the runtime
encodes the value against the budget the compiler's cap-tag walk computes (the
same walk that sizes a spawn channel's ring), panics if the encoding does not
fit, and decodes it into the ROOT ARENA, so the graph the child reads lives as
long as the domain. Both compilers emit one call per value parameter
(`b.spawnArgCopy` in legacy, `e.spawnArgCopy` in stage4) and pack the loaded
copy; channels still cross as the shared handle they are.

Evidence, on a legacy-built stage4 and on the bootstrapped binary:
`spawn(worker, Cfg{N: 7, Name: []byte("hello")}, d)` prints `cfg n= 7 len= 5
name= hello`; and a `Cfg.Name []byte \`cap:"16"\`` holding 6000 bytes dies with

    panic: spawn argument: encoded value of 6011 bytes exceeds the 37-byte
    budget. Variable-length fields and their cap tags: main.Cfg.Name cap:"16"

(a 134 exit). morly builds and runs with its `dbengine.Config` crossing the
boundary, and that struct now states its sizes (`DataDir`/`MuteBlacklist`
1024, `Admins` 64×72) because the startup config is part of the spawn's
footprint.

### Round 355: the 90 GB package cache, and why the wasm phases melted the box

The package cache is keyed by the compiler's source hash and build id, so every
compiler build starts a new generation. Nothing ever removed the old ones,
because `removeAll` - the helper behind `cache clean`, scratch cleanup and the
generation prune - listed ONE level and `os.Remove`d each entry. A generation
directory contains `pkg/<name>/…`, so every nested directory survived, the
final remove failed, and the error was ignored. Measured: **368 generations,
90 GB**, and `cache clean` reporting success while deleting nothing.

`removeAll` now calls `os.RemoveAll`. `pruneCacheGenerations` runs at the start
of every build and drops generations nothing has touched for two hours
(keeping the current one), and `cache clean` prunes too. After one clean:
368 → 3 generations, 90 GB → 101 MB.

The wasm phases were the other half of it: the runtime package could not
compile (round 351), so every wasm unit recompiled the whole stdlib closure and
then failed - 117 times in a sweep, each with seven parallel clang/llc workers.
With the runtime fixed the cache fills, and one fixture now validates end to end
in **4.1 s** warm (native build + wasm build + browser run); the cold cost is
paid once per compiler generation.

### Round 356: moxielang.dev answers, and the README states three axioms

The vanity import root is live on the host the A records point at (smesh.lol,
Caddy). One address, three answers, each for a client that needs a different
one:

- `?go-get=1` -> 200 with the `go-import` meta tag (Go tooling; a redirect here
  is a resolution failure)
- anything else from a browser -> 301 to the repository page
- `/info/refs`, `/git-upload-pack`, `/git-receive-pack` -> 301 to
  `.../toolchain.git{uri}` with the query preserved, which is what makes
  `git ls-remote https://moxielang.dev` work (git only follows a redirect whose
  target is still a git endpoint)

`www.moxielang.dev` redirects to the bare name. The certificate was issued on
the first reload. Configs, page and verification commands live in
`site/vanity/`; the deployed copy is `/var/www/moxielang/index.html` plus the
two site blocks in `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile` (backed up first, style
`Caddyfile.bak-before-moxielang-git3-*`).

Two honest limits, both recorded in `site/vanity/README.md`: the repository is
Moxie source, so `go get` of a *package* resolves the module root and stops at
"no Go files" (no `go.mod`, no Go packages - not a gap the tag can close), and
Moxie's own fetcher does not read the `go-import` tag (`moxie get` takes a git
URL and derives the module path from it). Teaching the fetcher discovery is
open work, listed here rather than claimed.

README: it said "two axioms" while `docs/axioms.md` states three. A3 (closure -
every capability and input is declared, anything undeclared is unreachable, the
default is deny) is now in the README with the reason the three are
load-bearing together, and `docs/architecture.md` and
`docs/MOXIE_ARCHITECTURE_PATTERNS.md` no longer say "two". The README also
gains an "Address" section stating the canonical import root and what the
domain answers.

### Round 357: the fetcher resolves import paths through their own address

`moxie get` took a git URL and derived the module path from it, so an import
path like `moxielang.dev/pkg/mxutil` was resolved as host-plus-one-segment
(`moxielang.dev/pkg`) - the wrong module root for a vanity address, and no
checkout could be found for it.

It now reads the address's discovery document, the way Go's module resolution
does: `https://<path>?go-get=1` is fetched, the `go-import` meta tag is parsed
(`<prefix> <vcs> <repo-url>`, longest prefix that contains the requested path
wins), and the prefix becomes the module root while the URL becomes the clone
source. Discovery is skipped for a spec that already names a URL (scheme
present), when `-offline` is given, and when the module is already checked out,
so an existing workflow never pays for the lookup.

Evidence:

    $ moxie get moxielang.dev/pkg/mxutil
      clone https://github.com/moxie-language/toolchain.git -> /tmp/moxie-get/moxielang.dev
      Cloning into '/tmp/moxie-get/moxielang.dev'...
      /tmp/moxie-get/moxielang.dev/pkg/mxutil

The document is fetched with `curl` through the same shell path the compiler
already uses for `git`: linking an HTTP client, a TLS stack and an X.509 root
loader into the compiler to read one small page would be paid on every
bootstrap, and this compiler is measured in bootstrap minutes. A missing `curl`
surfaces as a failed discovery, and the plain-URL form still works.

The legacy bootstrap compiler has no `get`/`fetch` command at all, so there is
nothing to mirror there; this is a CLI feature of the compiler that ships, not a
codegen rule.

### Round 358: the termination select is enforced, and the tree is migrated

Both compilers now refuse a program that cannot be stopped:

- **the program entry** (the `main` function of the package named `main`, not
  the runtime's `runtime.main`) must select on `sigint`;
- **every spawn target** must select on its own `closed` breaker.

Legacy checks both in `createFunction`/`createSpawn`. Stage4 checks them in a
post-pass over the built package (`checkTerminationSelects`), because the
package's error list is read exactly once, before the emitter runs: an error
recorded during emission is printed after the package was already judged
compilable. That was measured - the check "worked" in the emitter and no build
ever failed.

The tree is migrated in the same change: 155 `main`s (the should_compile, data,
netsmoke and should_run fixtures) gained a prologue select, and every spawn
target now serves its inbox and watches its breaker in one select - the pool
worker in `net/http`, the futexpark and spawnbytes/spawncost workers, the TLS
fixture's server domain, and morly's Proxy/Blossom/Broadcast/Ingest workers,
`dbengine.Run`, its test helpers and its main. `dbengine.Run` also keeps its
`eng.Flush()`/`eng.Close()` on BOTH exit paths, because a closed inbox and a
closed breaker mean the same thing to that domain.

Two limits, both deliberate and recorded:

- a target imported from another package is not checked: its body belongs to
  that package's compilation, so the check sees what the current package
  compiled (morly's library workers were migrated anyway, because the rule is
  the rule, not because the compiler could see them);
- the rejection fixtures (`tests/restrictions`, `legacy/tests/restrict`) are
  not migrated: they are expected to fail, and the gate pins the message each
  one must fail with. The sweep checks that the pinned messages still win.

Evidence: `mxc-sel3` refuses a plain `main` ("main must select on sigint") and a
target whose loop only receives ("spawn: worker never selects on its closed
breaker"), accepts the migrated pair (which runs and prints `handled 5`), and
builds both the compiler itself and morly.

### Round 359: what the first enforcement pass got wrong

Three things the sweep caught, all fixed:

**The check ran where errors are never read.** Stage4 reads
`cctx.compileErrors` exactly once, right after the SSA build and before the
emitter; a `reportCompileError` during emission is printed after the package was
already judged compilable. The first version of the check lived in
`emitFunction`, and a program with no select compiled happily. It now runs as
`checkTerminationSelects` between the SSA build and that gate, and the probes
prove both directions: a plain `main` and a target whose loop only receives are
refused, the migrated pair compiles and runs.

**A single-arm select is not a Select.** `select { case <-closed: …; default: }`
is lowered by the legacy SSA builder into a plain receive (dumped: `select
nonblocking [<-nil:chan []byte]` once, and nothing for the target), so a check
that demanded an `*ssa.Select` refused correct code. Both compilers now accept
either shape: a select arm, or a receive of the terminator
(`terminationConsumed`). The rule is that the signal is consumed, not that one
instruction form spells it.

**A legacy binding gap, recorded not hidden.** In the legacy compiler
`addResultVar` materializes the result alloca, but for these targets the dump
shows `closed` reading as the zero value - so a legacy-built child's
`<-closed` arm is dead, while stage4's `bindSpawnClosed` binds the named result
properly. The legacy check does not judge a result it could not materialize (it
cannot see the operand at all); the shipping compiler binds and checks it. This
is a legacy-side defect, listed here rather than papered over.

Also fixed: the compiler's own generators must satisfy the rules they enforce -
`generateTestMain` now emits the entry select (a test binary is a batch
program), and `cmd/mxcover`, `cmd/mxlex` and `cmd/gen-unicode-tables` gained it.
Phase 6 caught all three.

- phases 1 and 1b GENERATE a main for their sweep package, so those scripts now

### Round 362: a select receive on a codec-framed spawn channel does not decode

Moving morly's workers from a plain receive to a select over {closed, in} broke
the relay: the feed test hung after four passing tests, blocked on the WebSocket
`recv()` that waits for the relay's OK, because the ingest worker never decoded
the event. The cause is a rule this tree already records in
`server.mx` ("a select receive on a codec-framed spawn channel does not
decode"), and it is a compiler limitation, not a morly one.

The correct shape for a domain whose inbox carries codec-framed messages is:

    for {
        select {
        case <-closed:
            return closed
        default:
        }
        msg, ok := <-in        // a plain receive decodes
        if !ok {
            return closed
        }
        ...
    }

The select only *checks* termination (non-blocking, so it reads no frame); the
message itself is taken by the receive that does decode it. morly's five workers
and `dbengine.Run` are back to that shape with the breaker check, and the two
fixtures whose elements are codec-framed (`spawncost`'s `chan []byte`,
`spawnbytes`' `chan Body`) follow it too. `chan int32`/`chan int64` frames are
raw scalars and select works there (`chanpool`, futexpark), which is why phase 6
and phase 8 stayed green through the wrong shape.

The scheduler-side gap is recorded here rather than fixed: the select path's
`tryPipeRecv` should decode exactly as `PipeChanRecvRaw` does, and until it does
the rule above is the one to write to.

### Round 363: the legacy breaker binding, from the dump

The legacy SSA for a spawn target that reads its breaker:

    func main.worker:
    0: entry:
        t0 = select nonblocking [<-nil:chan []byte]
        ...
        return nil:chan []byte

The `closed` operand is the **nil constant**, and there is no result alloca for
the `closed` result at all - so `createFunction`'s binding (which looks for an
`*ssa.Alloc` whose Comment is "closed" and stores the breaker into it) finds
nothing, and a legacy-built child's `<-closed` arm is dead. stage4's
`bindSpawnClosed` binds the named-result alloca and is correct; the shipping
compiler is stage4, and the bootstrap only uses legacy to build it (whose own
entry point reads `sigint`, not `closed`), so the impact is a legacy-built
application, not the toolchain.

The legacy check does not judge what it cannot see (a result the builder never
materialized), and the defect is recorded here as the next legacy task: either
materialize the result alloca for a named result the body reads, or bind the
breaker by a builtin like `__sigint()` instead of by an alloca comment.

### Round 364: the narrow `string([]byte)` cast bug does not reproduce

Round 349 recorded a shape where `string(x)` over a `[]byte` local emitted

### Round 368: the legacy breaker is bound at the channel operand

Round 363's diagnosis is confirmed behaviourally, and fixed. The probe: a child
parks on its breaker, the parent spawns it and returns.

    from legacy (before):   child: started / panic: deadlock  <- nil channel
    from stage4:            child: started / parent: returning / child: closed
    from legacy (after):    child: started / parent: returning / child: closed

`chanOperandValue` (legacy/compiler/channel.go) resolves the channel a receive
or select arm names, and when the current function is a spawn target and the
operand is a nil `chan` of text, it substitutes `AssertBreaker(ClosedBreakerChan())`.
The compiler's inability to materialize the result means the operand is the nil
constant, and a receive on nil blocks forever - the arm would be dead. `[]byte`
is the breaker's element and a spawn target's only result, so the substitution
is exactly the domain's breaker, and it is a lowering rule with a comment rather
than a silent default.

The check is strict again: the nil operand inside a spawn target *is* consumption
(`closedConsumedAsNil`), which is what the lowering acts on. Verified both ways -
the probe and futexpark build and run, and a target whose loop only receives is
refused with the termination message.

### Round 369: the build host is provisioned, not accumulated

A fresh Ubuntu 24.04 host could not build this tree, and every failure was state
a machine accumulates and the repository never described. Each one is now a line
of `scripts/provision-build-host.sh`, which is the only supported bootstrap:

- **The unversioned LLVM tools do not exist on Debian/Ubuntu.** The compiler
  invokes `clang`, `opt`, `llvm-link`, `llc`, `ld.lld` and `llvm-config` by bare
  name on purpose (a `-22` suffix on a binary that is really 23 is the lie that
  let this stack drift), and the distro installs `opt-22` only. The first
  bootstrap on the box died at `mxc: opt failed`, halfway through, with the
  binary it had already built sitting there looking finished.
- **`lib/compiler-rt-builtins` was a tracked ABSOLUTE symlink** into one
  developer's llvm checkout, so a fresh clone's first builtin failed to build
  with no clue why. Untracked, ignored, and the script sparse-clones
  llvm-project at `release/22.x` for it.
- **`llvm-glue/libmoxie-llvm-glue.so` is a build product** and a stale one is a
  hard failure at start-up (`missing symbol MoxieCreateCompileUnit`). The stale
  `legacy/llvm-glue` duplicate carried two of the three shims, nothing
  referenced it, and building it was how a wrong `.so` reached `lib/`.
- **Go is 1.25.3 exactly, not "1.25+".** `patch-gotypes.go` patches `go/types`
  by exact source text; 1.27.3 refuses to apply.

The script also does what `build.sh` does not: `s1`, `s2`, `s3`, the `s2 == s3`
fixpoint, install, and the runtime bake with the installed compiler. `build.sh`
produces one generation and then runs `update --all` and phase 0a, which is a
developer's loop, not the bootstrap. `--check` reports what a host is missing
and changes nothing, which is how the missing-tool class got a name instead of a
stack trace.

### Round 370: `update --all` rebuilt packages in filesystem order

The rebuild loop walked the cache directory and recompiled each package on its
own, in readdir order. A package is type-checked against its imports' exports
and its SSA resolves imported symbols through them, so a package whose imports
had not been rebuilt first came back with every imported name undefined - 200
errors and `compile error for runtime` on the box.

That is not an edge case. A runtime bake is the only thing that writes a new
generation to the cache, so a fresh host's generation holds `runtime` alone, and
`build.sh` runs `update --all` on every bootstrap: it failed there, every time.
The cache now names WHAT to rebuild and the set is each cached package's closure
from `resolveAll`, concatenated with duplicates dropped. The proof that this
keeps dependencies first is one sentence: any list holding a package also holds
its imports earlier in that same list, so a package's first occurrence never
precedes an unbuilt import.

`legacy/` has no `update` verb - the package cache is stage4's - so there is no
mirror for this one.

### Round 371: a cold cache lost the dispatch table

The box's phase 0a failed three units, then passed one of them on a rerun, and
the same sources built correctly on the local machine. Reducing it:

| cache | binary | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| empty | `moxie` (legacy-built) | fmt prints `?` |
| warm | the same binary | correct |
| empty | local fixpoint compiler | fmt prints `?` |
| warm | the same binary | correct |

So the input was not the compiler, the toolchain or the optimizer - `opt` was
blamed first and cleared, as was LLVM 22 versus 23 - it was the *cache*, and the
pass/fail was deterministic per cache state. `strace` named it in one run: the
dependency pre-pass writes `_tmp_t/4f14e1d0.mxh` and three worker pids then look
for `_tmp_t/91f10802.mxh`. Two names for one package's export data, inside one
build.

The cause is `pkgHash`, the OBJECT key: it folds in `bst.pkgDispFingerprint` when
that has been measured and falls back to the link-set key when it has not. The
export blob was named from it, so the pre-pass (before
`measureDispFingerprints`) and the compile phase (after) disagreed about the
name. On a generation that had never been written the read missed, the worker's
sub-registry stayed empty, and the dispatch table it emitted was short: fmt
carried **78 impls instead of 86**, the 8 missing ones being the root package's
synthesized `String` methods. Disassembling both `fmt` bitcodes showed the
difference as exactly that: the count in the panic string, plus the
`reflect/types.type.pkgpath:main` descriptor the cold build never referenced.

Why it survived every gate: a cache generation is per compiler build, so the
first build after any compiler upgrade is cold, and everything after it is warm.
The suite is a sequence of warm builds, and the local machine's cache had been
warm for days. The first program a new user builds is the broken one.

The fix is the right key rather than a bigger one. `pkgExportHash` covers what
export data IS a function of - the sources for this target plus the imports'
export keys - and `cachedMxhPath` derives its own name from the package, so no
call site can pass an object key to an export path again. The fingerprint stays
on the object key, where it belongs, because dispatch arms are baked into the
object.

`tests/phase0c_coldcache.sh` makes the class a gate: it points `MOXIEPATH` at a
fresh cache (twice, plus a forced warm rebuild) and builds with `-j 4`, because
the loss was in the workers' registry and a serial build has the whole link set
in one process. Verified red then green on the same box: the unpatched compiler
fails cold and passes warm, the patched one passes all three cases.

### Round 372: running the bootstrap script for real

`scripts/provision-build-host.sh --bootstrap` from a clean tree found three
more defects, each of which had been a manual step that "worked" because a human
was watching:

- **s1 must come from the reference compiler.** `build.sh` picks its bootstrap
  binary in the order `./moxie-new`, `./moxie`, `./legacy/moxie`, then `$PATH` -
  a developer's order, right for iterating on a tree whose compiler works and
  wrong for a bootstrap, where `./moxie` is the binary being replaced. Measured:
  a stale `./moxie` built s1, s1 inherited its short interface-dispatch table,
  and s1 then panicked compiling `compress_roundtrip` with `interface dispatch:
  no impl for Read (16 impl(s), none matches)`. A bootstrap that reproduces the
  bug it exists to replace. The script now passes `MOXIE=legacy/moxie`.
- **Convergence took the extra generation.** s2 != s3, s3 == s4, which is the
  documented arrival (CLAUDE.md, Convergence: the legacy pipeline differs and
  the first bootstrap inherits that). The script demanded s2 == s3 and reported
  a convergence failure at the exact point where the compiler had converged. It
  now accepts s2 == s3 or s3 == s4, refuses only "no generation reproduces
  itself", and installs the generation whose successor reproduced it.
- **`build.sh`'s regression gate examined nothing.** `unitrun.sh` skips a unit
  that already has a verdict, so on a host that has run the suite before, the
  bootstrap's `--phases 0a --fail-fast` ran zero units, printed no verdicts, and
  returned success. The gate now passes `--force`.

One same-family fix went in with it: a worker process assembled `pkgByPath` from
canonical paths only, while `resolver.walk` keys it by the import spelling *and*
the package path. Any import whose spelling differs from its package's path made
the worker's key disagree with the parent's, which is the export/object split of
round 371 in a different place: the worker asks for a file the parent never
wrote. The worker now adds each package's import spellings too.

End-to-end on the box, from a wiped tree and an empty cache: `s1` (legacy-built)
→ phase 0a **33/33 PASS** on a cold cache → `s2` → `s3` → `s4`, `s3 == s4`
(`c546da31`), installed as `./moxie` → runtime bake written. The 33 units are
the ones without verdicts; the honest full-count run is `--force`.

### Round 373: a language rule that depended on the job count

`0b`'s `reject_plus_text` and `reject_plusassign_text` - the fixtures that pin
`'+' is not allowed for text concatenation` - passed on the local machine and
failed on the box with "compiler did not reject (exit 0)". Same sources, same
compiler binary (`c546da31`, checked by hash), same fixture file (checked by
hash). The determining variable was neither the host nor the toolchain: it was
the number of compiler worker processes.

`plusIsBanned` asks `targetIsMainModule()` and then `isTargetPkg(pkgPath)`, which
is `pkgPath == bst.targetPkgPath`, falling back to the module prefix - which is
`""` for a program that lives in no module, as a fixture does. The worker
metadata carried `rootModPrefix` but never `targetPkgPath`, so in a worker
`bst.targetPkgPath` was `""`, the comparison failed, the module prefix said "no
module", and the rule did not apply. Serial builds applied it; worker builds did
not. The local machine's TLS probe had been forcing the serial path, which is
why the gate was green there.

That is a language rule whose answer depended on `-j`, and it required neither a
new feature nor a guard to fix: `targetPkgPath` is now part of the module context
the workers receive, like `rootModPrefix`. Verified on the box with the
rebuilt compiler: `-j 1` and `-j 4` both report the restriction, and `0b` is
**64/64** at the default job count. `legacy/` has no worker processes and always
applied the rule, so there is no legacy mirror.

### Round 374: the wasm target had not been verified, and it did not work

With the box finally able to run a browser, `phase 5` reported 117 units and
**116 SKIPPED** ("chromium not available to playwright"). A suite that skips is
not a suite that passed - and underneath the skips was a target that could not
run a single program:

    [domain] RuntimeError: unreachable
        at app.wasm.runtime.codecReadVarint
        at app.wasm.runtime.codecDecodeValue
        at app.wasm.errors.New
        at app.wasm.errors.main

`errors.init` calls `New`, `New` returns an `error` interface, and the return
protocol's decode ran off the end of its buffer. Instrumenting
`codecDecodeValue` showed the shape in two lines: decode at `pos=0 len=6
kind=20` (interface), then decode at `pos=6 len=6 kind=21` - the encoder had
written the interface's tag and type descriptor and **nothing for the value**.

The encoder writes an interface's value only when the descriptor pointer passes a
plausibility guard, and that guard was `tc > 0x1000`: a native null-page
constant. `wasm-ld` places the first data segment at 1024, so a real descriptor
lives below `0x1000` - measured at `0xAC8`. The decoder has no such guard; it
follows whatever descriptor it is given, so it walked into the empty tail and
trapped. The same class was hiding one line up the file: a string whose base was
below 65536 was encoded as an EMPTY string, so on wasm every string below 64 KiB
would have been silently dropped.

Both floors are now target functions (`codecDataFloor`, `codecVoidPtr`): 1024
where a word is 4 bytes, the existing `0x1000`/64 KiB values on 64-bit targets.
`codec.mx` is one file shared by both compilers, so the fix is bilateral by
construction. Verified: a trivial program that trapped at `errors.init` prints
`hello wasm` in the browser (rc=0), and `phase 5` went from 3 pass / 9 fail to
the run recorded in round 376.

The lesson is not "wasm was broken"; it is that **the skip was invisible**. A
phase that cannot run its subject reports the same green as one that ran it, and
a browser-less host had been reporting green for a target that trapped before
`main`.

### Round 375: what a test host needs that a compiler host does not

Three gates reach outside the toolchain, and each one was found by a failure that
read like a compiler defect:

- **A browser.** Phases 1c and 5 run wasm modules in Playwright's chromium. The
  provisioning script now installs `playwright` plus its chromium and refuses to
  finish unless chromium launches, because the alternative is 116 silent skips.
- **The sample app and its relay.** Phase 7 builds `../smesh` and `../morly`,
  then runs the app's own Selenium suite: Python with `selenium`, `pytest`,
  `websocket-client`, and a Firefox + geckodriver. Ubuntu ships firefox only as
  a snap, so the box got Mozilla's tarball and geckodriver's release binary;
  `docs/building.md` states the requirement and the variable that overrides the
  app path (`MOXIE_UI_APP`).
- **Patience about parallelism.** `-j 4` on a 30 GB host put four compiler
  builds and a 250-package fixture in flight at once; `phase 6`'s legacy build
  died mid-run with a Go trace under that pressure and passed when re-run alone.
  The box runs the full sweep at `-j 2` for the record.

### Round 376: a domain is a thread

`spawn` forked. Every domain carried a PID it never needed, and the whole
termination story existed to manage that: `pdeathsig`, `waitpid`, a pid table, a
reaper, a lockdown pipe, and a class of bugs where a wedged or abandoned domain
outlived its owner as a stray process - one relay accumulated 2,600+ live
domains, all children of a single process.

A domain is now a pthread: same address space, its own TLS (domain root,
arenas, package globals) and its own stack. `src/runtime/thread_unix.c` is the
primitive (64 MB stack, trampoline into `moxie_runtime_thread_entry`), the same
shape the compiler's own worker pool had been using in `_mxc_stage4/host.c` all
along. `spawnDomain` builds the breaker, the ring pairs and a `spawnHandoff` in
the root arena and starts the thread; the child entry runs `InitCShared` (its
own root, heap and package initialisers) and copies the handoff into its TLS,
because fork handed all of that over by inheritance and a thread does not
inherit TLS.

Three defects showed up the moment the model changed, and each one is worth
keeping:

1. **One channel object cannot hold two directions.** A forked child used to get
   its own copy of the channel struct with `ringSend`/`ringRecv` swapped; two
   threads share the object, so the parent's binding and the child's
   overwrote each other and both ends parked on the wrong ring - a send and a
   receive that never met. The struct now stores the PAIR once and the direction
   is chosen by role (`chSendRing`/`chRecvRing`).
2. **`exit(0)` on peer death killed the process.** `PipeChanRecv` exited the
   child PROCESS when its parent was gone. That is right for a process and fatal
   for a thread: it terminated every other domain in the program - the symptom
   was a program that stopped mid-sleep with status 0 and no output. It now
   returns `ok=false`, which is the target's termination arm.
3. **Legacy had no per-thread globals.** stage4 emits
   `thread_local(initialexec)` for package variables; legacy emitted plain
   globals, so a legacy-built program shared one copy of every global across its
   domains and a spawned thread corrupted the parent's state (an immediate nil
   dereference in a probe that only spawns a worker). `getGlobal` now sets
   thread-local storage, which is the bilateral half, and
   `legacy/compileopts` lists the new C file so the legacy link finds
   `moxie_thread_spawn`.

Termination moved with the model. A closed breaker used to reach the target
through a signal only because the target was a process; now the runtime makes
the close reach the WAITS: a spawn target's channel operations recheck its own
`DomainClosed`, so a receive parked in a work loop returns instead of sleeping,
and a spawn channel records the breaker of the domain it was handed to
(`ownerBreaker`), so a parent parked on a channel whose domain ended wakes and
reports the close. A domain that never returns to a check is reclaimed by the
process: when main returns every domain goes with it. No signal, no reaper, no
pid table, no stray process.

Deleted with the model: `moxie_fork` as the spawn path, `pdeathsig`, `getppid`
liveness, `waitpid`/`kill`, the domain pid table and its reaper, the secalloc
lockdown pipe, and `moxie_kill`. `Fork()`/`Waitpid()` remain as explicit
cross-process utilities for tests that genuinely want a second process.

Verified narrowly (no suite runs, per the instruction): one domain (1 process, 2
threads), 50 domains (1 process, 51 threads, correct sums), value parameters
with a cap-tagged slice, on both compilers; breaker close ends a parked receive;
`futexpark`'s two assertions (wake ok, dead ok); a domain parked in a 30 s sleep
is reclaimed at process exit with no stray process; wasm still builds.

`spawn_frame_budget` was recorded here as decoding its frames as zeros. It is
fixed on this tree: the built binary prints `req 1 tags 3 body 5`,
`req 2 tags 1 body 6000`, `untagged body 4096`. The codec/frame work in Round 377
closed it. The regression runner only checks the exit status, so a passing
fixture is not evidence the values are right - this was read off the binary.

### Round 377: the extent is the message

A thread domain made the codec optional in a way the fork domain never could.
The codec exists to turn a value into bytes another machine with a different
layout can read; both ends of a spawn channel are now threads in ONE address
space running ONE binary, so for an element type that holds no references the
bytes in the sender are already the bytes the receiver wants. A memcpy into the
ring is the whole protocol.

The compiler now asks the element type first, and the extent check runs BEFORE
the codec question:

- no references -> `runtime.chanSend`/`chanRecv` -> `PipeChanSendRaw`/
  `PipeChanRecvRaw`, a memcpy of the element's extent;
- references and a custom codec -> `ChanSendDual`/`ChanRecvDual` (the codec IS
  the relocation);
- references and no codec -> `ChanSendStructural`/`ChanRecvStructural`.

The predicate is `typeNeedsReloc` (legacy) / `elemNeedsReloc` (stage4). It treats
a channel and a function value as handles, not payloads - their bytes ARE the
message - which is what the old `elemNeedsStructural`/`typeNeedsStructural`
already did, except that it did not count a STRING as a reference. A `chan
string` across a spawn boundary was therefore raw-copied: a {ptr,len} pair
pointing into the sender's arena. Under fork that read allocator metadata; under
threads it read live memory until the sender's frame popped, so it appeared to
work right up until it did not. Fixed by the same predicate that routes the
extent path.

Measured on a 12-byte struct with a deliberately wrong codec (EncodeTo writes
zeros, DecodeFrom sets -1), 2000 one-slot round trips, same probe source, old
compiler vs new:

    before  codec path   191 ms   95 us/round trip   value arrived as -1
    after   extent path   34 ms   16 us/round trip   value arrived intact
    legacy  extent path   57 ms   28 us/round trip   value arrived intact

The case that must NOT be skipped still is not: a struct carrying a `[]byte` AND
a codec still arrives through `DecodeFrom` (proven by its marker), and a
pointer-carrying struct with no codec still arrives through the structural codec.

Found on the way, both pre-existing and both fixed here because they blocked the
bilateral check:

1. **`legacy/moxie build-runtime` had been broken.** `src/runtime/
   spawnhandshake.mx` (the fork-era cross-binary hash exchange, referenced by
   nothing since the fork path was deleted) used `+` for text concatenation,
   which both compilers reject, so the legacy bake died there; behind it,
   `pipe_channel.mx` used `itoa`, which is not a runtime function at all (the
   runtime's own decimal renderer is `codecItoa`, and the pipe path is
   linux-only while `codecItoa` is shared). The dead file is deleted and the four
   call sites use `codecItoa`. A stage4 bake now compiles the same file the
   legacy bake does, which is the point of the bake being bilateral at all.
2. **`PipeChanRecvRaw` reported a size mismatch as `ok=false`.** Both ends are
   generated from one declaration, so a frame whose length is not the element
   size is a compiler bug - and returning false presented it as an ordinary
   close, which a receiver would treat as its termination arm. It panics with
   both sizes now.

### Round 377 (continued): the select arm was the other half

The round's own probe found a worse defect on the way out, and it is worth the
space because it was LIVE in morly: a `select` arm on a spawn-bound channel moved
the element as raw bytes (`tryPipeSend`/`tryPipeRecv` used `ch.elementSize`),
while a direct send on the same channel encodes it. The two paths therefore
disagreed about the frame, and the failure was not subtle:

    case 1  direct send -> select recv     arrived as zeros (frame consumed, dropped)
    case 2  select send -> direct recv     "codec expected struct tag" + core dump

`pkg/relay/server/server_workers.mx` does `case resp = <-s.proxyOut[i]` on a
channel of `wire.ProxyResponse`, which carries a `[]byte`, so every proxy
response was arriving zeroed.

A select arm now carries the frame format with it. `chanSelectState` is
`{ch, value, codec, td}`, filled by the compiler per arm: the element's own codec
when its type has one, the structural codec's type descriptor when it has not,
and both null for a self-contained element (extent) or a local channel. The
runtime encodes at the moment the arm FIRES (`tryPipeSend`/`tryPipeRecv`), not
before: a frame premised on an arm that may never win would pay a caller-written
`EncodeTo` for nothing. Encode and decode are now ONE pair of functions
(`codecFrameEncode`/`codecFrameDecode` in chan.mx, shared by both targets) that
every channel entry point routes through - the extent, codec and structural
paths, and the select path, on native and wasm - so there is one place where "how
an element becomes a frame" is decided.

Verified with the same probe source on both compilers: select recv of a struct
carrying `[]byte` and a string, select send of the same, direct send/recv
unchanged, 12-byte extent round trip still 17us, wasm module still builds
(917 KB). Bootstrap: s1 de8dd490, s2 == s3 414d77a9.
### Round 377 (continued): a returning frame is not an owner

The relay was run against the new compiler and its workers died instantly, once
per respawn, forever (61 respawns in 4 s). The cause was not the runtime and not
the worker's inputs:

- The worker's first statement selects on `closed`; `closed` was already closed
  microseconds after the thread started.
- Both compilers emitted `runtime.SpawnClose(breaker)` at **every return** of the
  function that spawned it ("a child never outlives the frame that spawned it",
  `533add8a`). morly spawns inside `newProxyWorker` and RETURNS the breaker to
  its caller, so the callee closed the very handle it was handing over.
- `pollProxyWorkers` then saw `workerAlive(done) == false` and called
  `respawnProxyWorker`, which is morly code - the runtime has no restart, retry
  or reaper at all (grep `respawn|restart|reap` in `src/runtime`: one comment
  saying there is nothing to reap).

The rule is gone from both compilers. A frame returning is not the owner deciding
a domain is finished - a pool constructor hands the breaker out precisely so the
caller owns it. The owner ends a domain with `close(breaker)`; `main` returning
ends every domain with the process; a panicking domain aborts the process
(`abort()`, status 134), which is what makes a panic terminal rather than a
respawn loop. `SpawnTrack`/`SpawnCloseAll` stay for the panic path.

Verified narrowly, both compilers (s1 c800ef9c, s2 == s3 6b199c0b):

- a worker spawned by a helper that RETURNS its breaker keeps beating after the
  helper's frame is gone (3 beats, then `close(breaker)` stops it cleanly);
- a worker that panics aborts the whole application: `panic: worker exploded on
  purpose`, status 134, core dumped, and main never reached its next line;
- morly (`make build`, new compiler) starts 13 worker domains and keeps them:
  no `respawned` lines, `/health` 200, threads grow with the spawn tree.

Note for the panic path: `runtimePanic` still closes the breakers and sends a
reason frame BEFORE it prints, let alone before `abort()`. Nothing can read that
reason - every domain is in the same process and the process is dying - so the
reason-carrying breaker protocol is fork-era machinery. Recorded as STANDING
ISSUES 1 (print to stderr first) and 2 (roll the breaker back to
`chan struct{}`) at the head of this file.

Also confirmed by accident, and worth writing down because it looks like a bug
and is not: a plain function whose signature is `func f(...) (chan []byte)` is a
spawn target by signature, so calling it directly panics with "spawn target called
directly: closed breaker is nil". Spawn it, or give the helper a second result.
(That was the shape-only rule; Round 378 makes the result NAME part of the
contract, so this function is ordinary and calls directly.)

### Round 378: the name is the target

A spawn target was identified by its SHAPE: exactly one result of type
`chan []byte`. That made every ordinary function returning a `chan []byte` a
spawn target, so calling one directly died in its prologue with "spawn target
called directly". A helper of morly's that returned a channel was the case that
found it.

The contract is now the NAME with the type: the sole result must be named
`closed`. `closed` is the predeclared word a target selects on, and the runtime
binds the domain's breaker into it; the shape alone was a proxy that held only
until a helper returned a channel.

`closed` has to reach a caller in another package, so the name must cross the
export boundary. Result names are not carried in export data, and the spawn call
site can be in a different package - morly spawns `wire.ProxyWorker`,
`wire.IngestWorker`, `wire.BroadcastWorker`, `wire.BlossomWorker` and
`dbengine.Run` from other packages - so it is encoded on the func line as

    func closed <name> <sig>

and not in the signature descriptor, because descriptors are compared as TEXT
when an interface impl is matched to its method and a name in there splits every
match. `generateMxh` writes it for a sole result named `closed` and of channel
type; `loadMxhDataIn` consumes that word as a marker and parses the function name
and signature exactly as before.

- `TargetDeclared bool` on `Signature` (`pkg/types/tc_types.mx`), set by the
  loader from the marker and consulted by `isSpawnTargetSig` (`ir_call.mx`).
- Legacy has no marker and needs none: it parses every imported package from
  source with go/parser, so `r.Name()` is already `closed` across a boundary.
  Both predicates now require the name - legacy `spawn.go`, stage4 `ir_call.mx` -
  so the two compilers agree on what a target is even though they learn it by
  different routes.

Verified:

- stage4 built and triple-bootstrapped (16:03-16:05; s2 == s3, 5bc1dd10).
- morly, cold `make build` with mxc-stage4 and again warm: 15 threads (13 worker
  domains among them), stable across 8 s, **0 `respawn` lines**, `/health` 200.
  The 377 ownership fix and the name marker hold together.
- new fixture `tests/regressions/should_compile/spawn_closed_crosspkg`:
  `lib.Worker` (result named `closed`) is spawned from `main`, `lib.Plain`
  (result named `out`) is called directly, and both run. Green on stage4 through
  `tests/regressions/run.sh`, and on legacy.
- the marker is load-bearing, measured: the fixture's lib mxh carries
  `func closed Worker chan:[]byte,chan:[]byte->chan:[]byte` and
  `func Plain chan:[]byte->chan:[]byte`. Stripping `closed ` from `Worker`'s
  line and forcing ONLY `main` to recompile (lib stays cached) fails the build
  with "spawn: Worker must be declared with exactly one result, (closed chan
  []byte)...". Regenerating lib's mxh restores the run, so the importer reads the
  marker rather than source it happens to have.

No migration: every spawn target in the tree already names its result `closed`
(17 in morly; the moxie stdlib and fixtures likewise) and no function returns a
`chan []byte` under another name, so the marker describes existing code rather
than imposing a new rule.

Round 377 audit (who owns a spawned pool): the apps own what they spawn. morly
keeps every breaker in the server or broadcaster it hands to the caller and
closes a slot's breaker before replacing it; musiquay has no `spawn`. The one
dropped breaker in the stdlib is `net/http.ChanServeTimeout`, which spawns its
worker pool and discards the breakers - if it returns on a listen or serve
error, the pool now outlives its frame (every current caller is about to exit,
so the process ends it). The frame is the owner and should close what it
spawned on the way out - STANDING ISSUES 5. The same function's workers also read
`chanGlobalMux`/`chanSlotBuf`, package globals the parent writes after the
spawn; under the thread model each domain has its own copy, so the
`DispatchSpawned` path is broken now, not merely suspect: one request panics
with `chanpool: slot window out of range` because the worker's TLS copy of
`chanSlotBuf` is empty. The dispatch break is STANDING ISSUES 4 at the head of
this file.

Found while running the wasm phase, and NOT caused by 377 or 378: the wasm target
did not build with stage4 at HEAD. `17cceab8` added the `c == nil && td == nil`
branch to `spawn_wasm.mx`'s `tryPipeRecv`, and its nested `n :=` shadows the
function-body `n` declared later. The no-shadowing rule is position-insensitive
by design ("a name is taken for the whole block it appears in"), so this is a
real violation rather than a checker bug: legacy's `checkScopeShadowing` should
reject it too. Every wasm fixture failed with
`tryPipeRecv: 'n' shadows declaration in enclosing scope`, including
`close_breaker.mx`, which predates both rounds, and `src/runtime` was unmodified
by those rounds - the commit's "wasm module still builds" was a warm runtime,
not a compile of this source. Fixed by renaming the nested declaration to `got`:
the wasm target builds again and `close_breaker.mx` passes the browser
comparison (1 passed, 0 failed). It is its own commit, because it is
`17cceab8`'s regression rather than this round's.

The fixture above is native-only (`//:wasmtest skip`). `validate.sh` now honours
that header for directory fixtures as well as `.mx` files: its discovery loop
only checked the `.mx` shape, and an explicit target - the driver runs one
fixture per job - never passed through it, so a directory fixture could not opt
out at all.
